News.title: Russell Brand's downfall in full – swirling allegations to sexual predator's conviction for rape — updates
News.content:
Russell Brand, at his height of fame was a hugely popular TV personality, will be sentenced on Monday after being found guilty of one count of rape and three charges of sexual assault

Russell Brand had always vehemently denied rape and sexual assault — telling his social media as early as September 2023 following his relationships had always been consensual.

The TV personality had said in a video he "was very, very promiscuous" but refuted what at the time were described as "very serious criminal allegations".

But today Brand, 51, was convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others on allegations dating back years. The disgraced entertainer has now been warned he faces a significant period behind bars. His downfall came after what police described as "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward".

Speaking outside court, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said: "Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible. Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women."

Brand, who hosted his own radio show and was nominated for a BAFTA, told his wife Laura Gallacher were “Laura, I love you” before he was found guilty. At which point, the former actor showed no reaction, other than closing his eyes. Now, the Mirror has outlined Brand's downfall in full across posts in our live blog on the case.

For updates on Russell Brand, follow our live blog below

News.title: 'I fill the kitchen sink up to wash myself so my kids have presents on Christmas day'
News.content:
'I fill the kitchen sink up to wash myself so my kids have presents on Christmas day'

Around four in 10 parents expect to go into debt to afford Christmas, while half of parents are worried that a magical Christmas will be harder to afford this year, Barnardo's research found

View 3 Images Struggling parents are making sacrifices to ensure their children enjoy the magic of the festive season (Image: Getty Images)

Nearly half (45%) of parents in the UK have skipped meals or reduced how much they eat to afford Christmas for their children, grim polling shows.

‌



‌



Around four in 10 (43%) expect to go into debt to afford Christmas for their children, while half (52%) of parents are worried that a magical Christmas will be harder to afford this year compared to last year, Barnardo's research showed.

‌



Struggling parents told the charity they were choosing between heating or eating this Christmas to ensure their children enjoy the magic of the festive season. One dad said he sits with the lights off, or washes over the kitchen sink instead of having baths or showers, to save money for Christmas.

‌



Asked what financial sacrifices they make, more than a quarter (27%) of parents said saving for emergencies, one in six (16%) said heating their home and a similar proportion (17%) said paying household bills on time.

In a powerful stunt, Barnardo's earlier this week set up a pop-up shop disguised as a gift shop in central London to lay bare the tragic struggles of parents this festive season. The charity replaced the price tags on children's gifts and clothing with labels telling heartbreaking stories of what struggling parents have sacrificed to afford Christmas for their child.

To find out more about Barnardo’s and how you could help support children, young people and families, visit barnardos.org.uk.

‌



View 3 Images Dame Helen Mirren, actress and Barnardo’s ambassador said: 'Some struggling parents are making significant sacrifices to be able to afford a magical Christmas for their children' (Image: Marion Curtis/StarPix for Bleecker Street/Shutterstock)

One dad-of-two, aged 58, from Edinburgh, who was featured in the collection, said: “I’ve saved enough money to get the kids some dinner and gone without myself. I’d eat whatever they didn’t eat off their plates. I’ve tried cutting back on things, like keeping the electric off when the kids aren’t there.

‌



"I’ve sat without the lights on before to save on electric, with just the TV on so the glow from the TV lights up the room. I’ve also gone without heating when the kids aren’t there and sat in the cold with a blanket over me so I had enough on the meters to warm the house up for when they were coming.

"There have been times when I’ve filled up the sink and had a wash down rather than having a bath or shower to save on the electric and hot water. Sometimes you have to sacrifice things so your kids can eat, and be warm, and have presents to open on Christmas morning.”

‌



One mum-of-two, 38, from Edinburgh, also told the charity: "I slept on the couch because there wasn’t enough space in my two-bedroom house with three kids. Everything was spent on the kids, and I wasn’t taking care of myself. I don’t tell my kids when I’m struggling and I didn’t let them know I couldn’t afford things at Christmas.”

And a 19-year-old said his mum has “been in tears the past few Christmases because of the stress of getting everything sorted”. The teenager, from County Armagh, Northern Ireland, said: “I don’t like Christmas. I’ve struggled a lot with it in the past. It affects my mum quite a bit. She’s been in tears the past few Christmases because of the stress of getting everything sorted.

‌



"I try to get any part-time work I can find around Christmas time. It’s very stressful, and to be honest, it can feel quite depressing. My mum still works her magic and is able to get things for us. She hides how much she struggles from my siblings."

View 3 Images Eastenders star Michelle Collins said: 'I was brought up by a single mum who worked incredibly hard, juggling jobs and doing everything she could' (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Dame Helen Mirren, actress and Barnardo’s ambassador, said: “I grew up in post-war Britain when money was very tight. My dad worked extremely hard to support the family, to make sure we had everything we needed. Parents always want the best for their children – but for some families living in poverty that just isn’t possible.

"Some struggling parents are making significant sacrifices to be able to afford a magical Christmas for their children. That’s why Barnardo’s is helping families in poverty and together we can make sure more children enjoy the warmth, joy and wonder that Christmas should bring.”

‌



Eastenders star Michelle Collins said: “Supporting Barnardo’s child poverty campaign is something very close to my heart. I was brought up by a single mum who worked incredibly hard, juggling jobs and doing everything she could to make sure my sister and I never felt we were missing out. But I know it wasn’t easy. Far from it. The sacrifices she made, the pressure she was under, and the constant struggle to make ends meet are things I appreciate even more now. "

Barnardo's chief executive Lynn Perry, whose charity is urging the public to donate, said: "These findings paint a deeply worrying picture of the pressure many families are facing as Christmas approaches. Behind every statistic is a parent doing everything they can to protect their children from hardship, often by going without themselves.

Article continues below

"For many of us, Christmas is a time of excitement, joy and family traditions. But for far too many children growing up in poverty, it can also be a time of anxiety and uncertainty.

::: Censuswide surveyed 2,763 UK parents of children aged under 18 between October 6 and 16.

News.title: Hospice UK slams 'worrying trend' as one million people in last year of life end up in A&Es
News.content:
Hospice UK slams 'worrying trend' as one million people in last year of life end up in A&Es

People in their last year of life are increasingly going to A&E — in part due to a lack of home support — and experts have called this "a worrying trend"

View 4 Images People nearing the end of their lives are having to go to A&E (Image: Getty Images)

A&Es are full of people in the last year of their lives who don’t need to be there, experts have warned.

‌



‌



A study by King’s College London found lack of social care support at home and proper palliative care means the frail and terminally ill are ending up in emergency departments. In the latest 12 months, analysed people in the last year of life accounted for almost 770,000 ambulance trips to emergency departments, more than one million A&E visits and almost 890,000 emergency admissions.

‌



A joint report on the research conducted with Marie Curie found A&E visits involving people in the last year of life increased by 21% between 2014 and 2023, from 900,295 to 1,089,365.

‌



Charlie King, director at charity Hospice UK, said: "This report confirms a worrying trend — it is getting harder and harder for people to access the end-of-life care they need. No one should die in a hospital corridor.”

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror just click on the link here to find them at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images Lack of out-of-hours support in the home means people end up in A&E (Image: Getty Images/Westend61)

‌



Devastating catalogue of NHS scandals coming directly after Tory's disastrous austerity READ MORE :

Marie Curie said that while some patients will need hospital care, gaps in 24/7 end-of-life care in the community mean a growing number are turning to urgent and emergency care when they "don't have to be there" Its report concludes that people in the last year of their life took up 11.5 million "unplanned hospital bed days" in the latest year analysed.

Some 7% of emergency department attendances were made by someone in the last year of their life between 2014 and 2023. This group also accounted for 19% of ambulance transfers to hospital, 18% of unplanned hospital admissions and 29% of "unplanned bed days".

‌



View 4 Images Experts say A&Es are often not the best place for the terminally ill (Image: PA)

Dr Sam Royston, executive director of research and policy at Marie Curie, said: "We know that too many people die in pain and without the support they need for their symptoms, and gaps in 24/7 community care prevent people from dying in comfort at home.

‌



"Behind some of these statistics will be patients and families who have called an ambulance or gone to hospital because, in their time of need, there was nowhere else for them to turn.”

The report says "too many" people are being identified as being in the last part of their lives too late and cannot access care and support outside working hours.

‌



View 4 Images Corridor care became widespread in A&Es in the last decade

Shan Newhouse cared for her husband Grant, a former teacher, before his death from pancreatic cancer in 2024 when he was 69. Shan, a retired GP from Essex, said: "Four or five weeks before Grant died, there were two consecutive nights when we had to visit the emergency department.

‌



"Grant was admitted, but there wasn't a bed available, so we had to sit on chairs in a corridor. The doctors knew Grant had pancreatic cancer, but they still couldn't find a bed. He was feeling ill and vomiting, so in the end he had to lie across a few of the chairs. The general impression I had was of a system that was completely overwhelmed, working desperately to try and cope."

Dr Ian Higginson, president of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, said: "People approaching the end of their life deserve comfort, dignity and access to specialist care. As this important report highlights, many patients attend emergency departments (ED), often on multiple occasions, in the last year of their life due to complications with their conditions.

‌



"Sometimes, these attendances are unavoidable, and an ED is the right place for the patient. But that isn't always the case. Too many people with palliative care needs are ending up with us, some in the last days or hours of their life - and not by their own choice.

“These last patients typically need a quiet and comfortable environment, where they can be surrounded by loved ones and have access to specialist clinicians. Instead, they may end up in a loud, bright and overcrowded ED because of a lack of community care provision."

‌



Treating more people out of hospital in community clinics or their own home is one of three “shifts” Labour announced for the NHS after coming to power in 2024. The new study only covers a period up to 2023.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said: “We recognise the financial pressures many hospices are currently facing and we are working with the sector and NHS partners to create a more sustainable funding approach, building on the £125 million we have already invested to improve hospice facilities.

Article continues below

"The Prime Minister and Health Secretary have made clear their commitment to improving palliative and end-of-life care. Our forthcoming Modern Service Framework will help address some of the most significant challenges facing the sector, including regional variations in access and quality, gaps in support, and workforce shortages."

News.title: Donald Trump casually floats agreement with Putin which will affect 'all of Europe'
News.content:
Donald Trump casually floats agreement with Putin which will affect 'all of Europe'

Trump also said he'd met with an envoy from Russia, and had hatched a "big beautiful agreement" that will involve "all of Europe"

View 2 Images Trump invited media to the Oval Office to talk about interior design (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump casually floated an agreement with Russia during an event about interior design.

‌



‌



The US President, still licking his wounds after the generational thumping handed to his Republican Party in Tuesday's midterm elections, called what is left of the White House press corps to the Oval Office to see him sign an executive order - designating the room a national monument.

‌



But after the signing, he was asked about reports he intended to return to bombing raids on Iran.

‌



"We control everything that we want to control," he said. "And now we make a decision. Do we want to go further, by certifying it? And by certifying I mean, making sure that it'll never happen again."

He added: "I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible. But maybe I'll have to. You'll know soon enough."

View 2 Images A hat with the word "veto" on it was seen on the Resolute Desk (Image: AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

‌



He was also asked about a meeting with a Russian envoy at the Oval Office today.

The envoy was attending a pseudo-peace summit hosted by Melania Trump, who has been engaging in back-channel communications with Vladimir Putin that diplomats around the world find truly baffling.

‌



"I think we're going to be close to settling Russia and Ukraine," Trump said.

But asked if he'd met with the envoy, Trump said he had.

‌



He added: "I can't tell you what we discussed. But I'm just telling you there's going to be an agreement, it's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine. I could even say it's going to involve all of Europe. It's going to be a big beautiful agreement and everyone's going to be thrilled."

He did not meet with the representative from Ukraine.

‌



In keeping with this week's theme, the order was about the design of the Oval Office itself - designating it a national monument, meaning any physical changes to it would require congressional approval.

President Trump has spent time during his second term glamming up the Oval, installing countless gold-coloured mouldings on the wall and hanging giant mirrors and placing gaudy trinkets wherever space allows.

‌



He reportedly used Krazy glue to stick gold medallions to the fireplace. And just yesterday he gave reporters a tour of the building site for his opulent new vanity ballroom, to make way for which he demolished more than a third of the White House complex.

Outside the Oval, he has had "The Oval Office" painted on the wall in gold cursive script. And he installed a "Presidential Walk Of Fame" on the Colonnade, the outdoor walkway to the Oval, featuring photographs of every president bar one, with descriptions of each in his own unmistakable style. Where Joe Biden's portrait is supposed to be is a photograph of an autopen.

‌



For more of our coverage of Trump's America: Subscribe to The Trump Desk on YouTube

Subscribe to the US Dispatch - our weekly newsletter exclusively for Mirror+ readers - following all the gossip and intrigue from Trump's DC swamp

- following all the gossip and intrigue from Trump's DC swamp Follow Mikey Smith on Twitter, TikTok, Bluesky or Facebook.

It's unclear if Trump's modifications would be covered by the order, but he said no major changes could be made going forward "without the approval of Congress."

‌



"So if they want to ⁠say 'let's not have Oval anymore, let's make it square', what happens is they have ⁠to go back to Congress, and hopefully the Congress... will ⁠be smart enough not to let that happen."

Democrats took control of both houses of Congress in Tuesday's election. It is unlikely they would block any move to reverse Trump's changes, when he leaves office.

‌



"I'm going to be signing a document which will make them into a landmark for the ages," he said. "It won't be able to be taken down, destroyed, touched, or anything else. It's a federal landmark. And when completed, and when we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it'll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space."

A reporter noted that Hillary Clinton had criticised his use of gold in decorating.

Article continues below

"She did?" He replied. "I don't like her house either. I know her house very well.

"The Oval Office is a place of victory. See the white wall? There's no gold on that. The exterior of the White House, there's no gold."

News.title: Marco Rubio among five of Trump's team 'planning to resign' after humiliating midterm result
News.content:
Marco Rubio among five of Trump's team 'planning to resign' after humiliating midterm result

Marco Rubio's race for the Republican candidacy in 2028 would likely see him go head-to-head with Donald Trump's right-hand man, US Vice President JD Vance.

View 3 Images US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is considering resignation from the Trump administration, according to reports (Image: Andrew Harnik, Getty Images)

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is considering resigning from the Trump administration to run for president in 2028, according to reports. It comes as US President Donald Trump's inner circle faces a major shake-up following a crushing midterm defeat to the Republican Party.

‌



‌



Mr Rubio is reportedly one of five members of President Trump's current cabinet who are thought to be preparing to jump ship. His race for the Republican candidacy in 2028 would likely see him go head-to-head with Mr Trump's right-hand man, US Vice President JD Vance.

‌



The report from The Independent cited anonymous sources who are said to be close to Mr Rubio. A Republican source reportedly told the news outlet, "Rubio will be gone after the midterms.

‌



View 3 Images US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"There will be about four or five them running for the hills. The country has completely turned against Trump. People cannot even say where Iran is on a map and do not get this war."

Mr Rubio's office has been quick to shut down the reports. Dylan Johnson, assistant secretary of state, told NewsNation, "This is complete and total fake news based on the word of anonymous sources, befitting a tabloid.

‌



"The Secretary has not discussed leaving his role and he will continue to proudly serve in President Trump’s administration long after this fake news is revealed as yet another baseless hoax," he added.

View 3 Images Democrats defeated Republicans in the midterm elections this week (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The US leader said Tuesday night that he does not plan to make changes to his cabinet.

News of a potential White House shake-up follows bloodshed at the polls for the Grand Old Party (GOP) on Tuesday, with the Democrats winning both the House and Senate.

Article continues below

Multiple members of President Trump's cabinet could become the renewed targets of impeachment investigations when Democrats are sworn in early next year. Among the list of those who could face renewed scrutiny are Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon.

They were all subjects of impeachment investigations or inquiries prior to the midterm elections.

News.title: Bosses will be ordered to declare salaries on job adverts under new law
News.content:
Bosses will be ordered to declare salaries on job adverts under new law

Less than half (41%) of employers always publish their salary ranges and only 1 in 5 (18%) always publish specific salaries, according to figures from the CIPD

View 2 Images The Government will bring in a 'say what you pay' law (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Bosses will be ordered to declare salaries on job adverts under a new “say what you pay” law.

‌



‌



Less than half (41%) of employers always publish salary ranges and only 1 in 5 (18%) always publish specific salaries, according to figures from the CIPD. It means jobseekers are forced to waste time applying for roles without knowing the potential pay packet.

‌



The move is designed to help address entrenched pay inequalities that disadvantage women and to help young people applying for their first job, as part of the Government's efforts to fix the crisis of young people out of work, employment or study.

‌



Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: “Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it. That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.”

John Healey says young workers might not get minimum wage boost before next election READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham said jobseekers should know what a role pays before applying for it (Image: Getty Images)

Writing in the Mirror, Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson said women were much less likely to receive fair pay if they walk into negotiations without knowing the salary.

‌



She said: "The evidence shows that women are less likely than men to negotiate pay and more likely to face backlash when doing so, cliches around being "too demanding" putting their chances of getting the job at risk.

"The result: women are given a lowball offer, held back by lower starting pay that drags down their earnings for the rest of their careers. Unequal pay takes root, helping the gender pay gap to stubbornly persist."

‌



Penny East, Chief Executive of the Fawcett Society, said it would mean women no longer have to make decisions based on vague promises or unclear terms.

She said: “For too long, salary secrecy has put women at a disadvantage, leaving them negotiating in the dark and making it much harder to challenge unfair and unequal pay. Requiring employers to publish salaries in job adverts is a significant step towards making work fairer for women and tackling the gender pay gap."

‌



Top union leader Paul Nowak welcomed an end to the "disrespectful practice" of leaving candidates in the dark on pay. The TUC General Secretary said: "Why should a candidate be expected to go through a lengthy application and interview process without knowing whether the job will actually pay them enough to get by?

"It's absolutely right that the government clamp down on this disrespectful practice. Employers should be upfront with potential recruits and clearly state how much a role will be paid.

Article continues below

"All too often, it's women, Black, minority ethnic or disabled workers who end up paying the price - being offered lower salaries than their colleagues, or finding the role lacks the flexibility they need. That's why the government should also require employers to list flexible working options in every posting."

The Government will bring forward legislation as soon as possible to enforce the demand - but the Prime Minister has urged all businesses to act now, rather than wait for the law to change.

News.title: Man in hospital with serious injuries after stabbing near Manchester shopping centre
News.content:
Man in hospital with serious injuries after stabbing near Manchester shopping centre

Greater Manchester Police are investigating a stabbing near Middleton Shopping Centre that left a man in his 30s seriously injured.

View 2 Images A large police cordon was put in place following the stabbing in Middleton, Greater Manchester. (Image: MEN)

A man has been rushed to hospital with serious injuries after a stabbing near a shopping centre in Greater Manchester.

‌



‌



Emergency services rushed to the incident in Middleton, Greater Manchester, at around 2.20pm where a man in his 30s had sustained serious injuries and was rushed to hospital.

‌



Witnesses reported a large police cordon behind Middleton Shopping Centre, with Limetrees Road closed to traffic and a heavy police presence in the area.

‌



View 2 Images A police cordon near Middleton Shopping Centre following reports of a stabbing. (Image: MEN)

Six killed and nine injured as massive fire rips through New York home READ MORE :

Images from the scene showed three police vehicles close to the cordon and what appeared to be discarded clothing on a pavement, reported the Manchester Evening News.

‌



Officers from Greater Manchester Police could be seen making door-to-door inquiries in the aftermath of the incident while witnesses were also spoken to at the scene.

The closure of Limetrees Road has led to significant traffic congestion in Middleton town centre.

Article continues below

Greater Manchester Police confirmed that no arrests have yet been made in relation to the incident and enquiries are ongoing.

A GMP spokesperson said: "We were called to reports of a stabbing shortly after 2.20pm at Middleton Gardens, Middleton. A man in his 30s has been taken to hospital with serious injuries. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing."

News.title: Part of Learjet engine recovered from Florida plane crash site where nine people died
News.content:
Part of Learjet engine recovered from Florida plane crash site where nine people died

Nine people were killed on a Learjet 60 when it crashed in a ball of flames in Greenacres, Florida, en route from Austin to the Bahamas, with an investigation underway into the cause

View 4 Images The plane crashed in Greenacres (Image: @X)

Investigators have recovered part of a private jet's engine from the scene of a horror plane crash in Florida that killed nine people.

‌



‌



The plane burst into flames when it crashed in Greenacres, about seven miles southwest of West Palm Beach, with thick black smoke engulfing the crash site.

‌



A huge hole was left in the ground after the plane plummeted to the ground and now the National Transportation Safety Board said that a "portion of one engine" was found while officials excavated the area.

‌



View 4 Images Investigators at the scene of the crash (Image: AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)

Victims included the 20-year-old co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, who made the final radio transmissions, as well as technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two young children.

A statement from the NTSB on X read: "NTSB investigators and local officials continue recovery efforts for the wreckage of the Learjet 60 that crashed on Nov. 1 near Greenacres, Florida.

‌



"Excavation work at the crash site began late yesterday and continues today, which included finding a portion of one engine.

View 4 Images Nathalia Gadelha, 20, was the co-pilot (Image: itsnatfilg/Threads)

‌



"Debris has been found away from the impact location and also on the roofs of homes and buildings near the crash site. All recovered wreckage will be sent to a secure location for further examination."

The plane, a Learjet 60, had departed Austin, Texas and was en route to the Bahamas when it crashed on Sunday having encountered an unusual convective storm system.

‌



People who may find pieces of wreckage from the plane are also being urged to pass it to investigators.

The statement from the NTSB continues: "If you have found or collected any debris from the Learjet 60 crash, please do not keep it or attempt to move, alter or dispose of it. Even small pieces of the wreckage may contain important evidence that could help investigators determine what happened.

‌



View 4 Images Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children, Emma and Charlie (Image: Family Handout)

"We ask that you contact the NTSB at witness@ntsb.gov to arrange its recovery. Please include a photo of the debris, if possible, in your email. Recovering all available wreckage is critical to the investigation and helping to determine the cause of the crash."

‌



The plane appears to have attempted to climb above the storm, having requested and received clearance at 35,000ft to ascend to 37,000ft after reporting freezing temperatures and ice forming on the jet’s hull. Ice can be dangerous as it affects the air flows around the wings and makes it harder for the plane to remain aloft.

When there is ice on wings it is harder to achieve lift - and the angle where a plane can stall is lower than would normally be the case. And so it is possible that an attempt to climb with ice on the wings led to the plane stalling.

Article continues below

The aircraft likely started breaking apart before it slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball, a federal investigator has said. The jet did a steep nosedive, leaving behind a crater and a wide debris field as rain pounded the area.

News.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
News.content:
Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault, and is now expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

A jury found the entertainer guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault. The jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.

Brand was taken into custody after the verdicts were delivered, and was refused bail. He is due to be sentenced on Monday.

It can now be reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and the 51-year-old has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

Brand, who told his wife Laura Brand "I love you" after entering the dock, displayed no emotion as the jury delivered its verdicts.

Afterwards he mouthed "I'm good, I'm good" to his defence counsel as he left the dock. His walk was steadily paced, and he continued to show little emotion.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

News.content:

News.title: Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
News.content:
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.

Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".

The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union., external

Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna, external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.

Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".

He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".

News.title: Thatcher's Right to Buy split my estate. Now its days could be numbered
News.content:
Growing up in a council flat in the 1980s and 1990s, my mum would often point out homes that tenants had bought from the council. You could usually tell just from looking. A plain wooden door had been replaced with something fancier. New windows had appeared. Sometimes there was a porch or pillars outside the front door.

Those houses were bought under the Right to Buy scheme - arguably the most consequential housing policy of my lifetime. It was introduced in 1980, three years before I was born, when Margaret Thatcher's government gave council tenants in England the legal right to purchase their homes at a discounted price.

Supporters welcomed the chance for working-class families to own their own home and build wealth. Critics argue it hollowed out the country's stock of social housing and contributed to today's housing crisis.

Some of my neighbours "made a killing" from the policy, in the words of my mum. One bought an almost identical flat to ours in 1989 for Â£21,200, after receiving a discount of Â£18,800. Eight years later it sold for Â£54,500. Five years after that it changed hands again for Â£143,000. (Notably, the person who made the most money from that flat wasn't the original council tenant - it was the people who bought it afterwards.)

News.title: King relishes 'politically charged' deployments, Palace aide says
News.content:
The King relishes the "tough parts" of his role and will continue to be used in "politically charged situations", a senior palace aide said at the end of the King's tour of the Caribbean.

Over the past nine days, the King visited the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda and has been used as "a great secret weapon", the aide said.

Questions over whether the UK should apologise and pay reparations for its role in the transatlantic slave trade were a theme of the visit.

"I think what we're seeing is a very clear pattern emerging of the government asking the King to head into quite politically charged situations, quite challenging situations," the aide said.

"We have to tread quite a careful line sometimes between government policy and the King's role."

The leadership of all three countries visited on the Caribbean tour wanted reparatory justice.

"I would say, in the round, this has been a complex visit. It's been challenging. It's been exhausting," the aide said. "But the takeaway is that it's been very successful and I think the King has demonstrated his statecraft both by word and deed."

Most of the King's visits outside the UK have seen him draw on some delicate diplomatic skills on behalf of his government.

In the US, he used his speech to Congress to remind President Donald Trump of the UK's value as an ally.

A year earlier he made a flying visit to Canada to welcome new Prime Minister Mark Carney as the latter faced an onslaught of threats and insults from Trump.

Visits to Germany and France in the early part of the King's reign were designed to establish new UK alliances post-Brexit.

"The King is not just King for the easy parts of the job, but the tough parts of the job, too," said the aide.

"In fact, that's probably the part of the job that he relishes most, whether that's leading on the environment, whether it's renewing and refreshing and reinvigorating relationships with nations where there have been some complex political issues at play, that is what he lives and breathes for."

News.title: Andrew received up to £2,000 per month from sub-letting, watchdog reports
News.content:
But it emerged that as a tenant he had been intermittently sub-letting three cottages that were part of the property, which was thought to be for staff and at a below market rate, with Mountbatten-Windsor keeping the income.

The Crown Estate had told MPs that it did not have any oversight over how much Mountbatten-Windsor charged - and sub-letting was allowed as part of his lease.

But the MPs have recommended that in future the default position for such Crown Estate properties should be that such sub-letting should be banned, unless there was a specific exemption.

The Public Accounts Committee report also confirms what has happened since Mountbatten-Windsor's departure from Royal Lodge.

There was a payment of about Â£300,000 due to him for his early surrender of his lease, but because of "dilapidations" in the state of the building, there was a repair bill of Â£1.8m.

That meant the Crown Estate was owed Â£1.5m, which King Charles paid on his brother's behalf.

The watchdog's report also highlighted concerns about the level of rent being charged to non-working royals who had been given accommodation in three royal properties.

That was believed to be Mountbatten-Windsor's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, and Prince and Princess Michael of Kent.

A National Audit Office report had revealed earlier this year that Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie do not pay anything themselves for their accommodation in St James's Palace and Kensington Palace respectively.

The King pays their rent to the Royal Household from his own private income.

But the group of MPs were concerned about whether the level of rent on such properties for non-working royals was based on up-to-date valuations and recommended a more consistent approach to ensure value for money.

There was criticism too for the Crown Estate concentrating too much of its urban property portfolio in London and the south east of England, with MPs calling for more of a regional spread.

There were also warnings about how the Crown Estate's administration costs had increased significantly, at a time when MPs noted government budgets were under pressure.

The report said administration costs had risen by 129% since 2020-21 and that the chief executive, Dan Labbad's salary had risen by 106% over that time. In 2025-26 his pay package was worth Â£2.3m.

In response, a Crown Estate spokeswoman said: "The Public Accounts Committee report is an important part of our accountability to Parliament. We are considering its findings and recommendations and will respond to the Committee in due course."

News.title: Messages reveal how hoax threat was passed on by air traffic control
News.content:
More than 20 aircraft across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats. It's the second time this week, which the UK has called a "malicious hoax".

BBC Verify has been analysing the messages sent by an aircraft to find out what happens when a flight receives a bomb hoax - as Thomas Copeland explains.

Additional reporting by Emma Pengelly. Produced by Aisha Sembhi. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Sally Nicholls.

News.title: UK doctor infected with Ebola being treated at London hospital
News.content:
A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been flown back to the UK.

The man, who has not been identified, landed at RAF Northolt before being transported to a specialist infectious diseases unit at the Royal Free Hospital in north London.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.

Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of the All Hazards Public Health Response team at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said there are "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and the risk to the public remains low.

News.title: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
News.content:
Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US-Iran war is resolved.

Rates rose to 4% from 3.75% in a bid to curb inflation mainly driven by the conflict's impact on global oil prices.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank's governor, said the decision "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes", but warned "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase".

The higher level will increase the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, but will also lead to higher returns on savings.

The Bank's rate-setting committee all backed increasing interest rates, with eight out of nine voting in favour of the rise to 4%. One member wanted an even bigger increase to 4.25%.

Bailey said the hike was warranted due to higher energy prices and pointed to what happens in the Middle East as the main factor in future decisions.

"Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East," the governor said.

Bailey said he could "see the argument" for a further rate hike, before taking a "more conditional approach" dependent on the path of energy prices and inflation in the coming months.

However, the views of members on the rate-setting committee differed on the path forward.

Clare Lombardelli agreed there was "likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term", while Megan Greene went further, suggesting "additional hikes" might be likely depending on how inflation impacted wages, prices and the jobs market.

However, Alan Taylor said the rate rise was a "a risk-management 'one-for-now' insurance hike".

News.title: Henry Nowak’s killer has minimum term increased to 25 years by Court of Appeal
News.content:
A man jailed for life for murdering Henry Nowak has had his minimum prison term increased to 25 years by the Court of Appeal.

Vickrum Digwa was serving a minimum of 21 years for stabbing 18-year-old student Nowak with a large dagger in Belmont Road, Southampton, on 3 December 2025.

The Attorney General referred the case to the Court of Appeal on the grounds it was "unduly lenient", while Digwa also challenged his jail term as "manifestly excessive".

The Lady Chief Justice quashed the sentence, ruling the original term "did not adequately reflect the overall seriousness of the murder".

Digwa, who was also refused permission to appeal, told police Henry had attacked and racially abused him, which led to Henry, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, being handcuffed as he lay dying.

The trial judge later found Digwa's accusations of racism to be a lie. Then 22, he was jailed for life at Southampton Crown Court in June.

News.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after BBC revealed rape allegations
News.content:
Married at First Sight UK will not return, Channel 4 has said, following a BBC investigation into the hit reality TV show.

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis earlier this year, after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

A review was commissioned by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster, with details of the allegations we had heard.

On Thursday, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

The broadcaster's chief executive Priya Dogra said she was "very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt", adding that the show's budget would be reinvested in "distinctive new programming".

The Panorama investigation in May, in which three women made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny, made the following allegations:

One woman said her onscreen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her onscreen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - accused her onscreen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading, and that it acted appropriately in all these cases.

Channel 4 had initially told Panorama that all the allegations were "wholly uncorroborated".

Dame Caroline Dinenage MP, chair of the House of Commons culture and media committee, said the decision to axe the show "makes sense" given the review's findings and the "seriousness of the allegations".

"Reality TV contestants have often been treated as a commodity, with duty of care a slogan rather than a genuine principle. Everyone involved in producing and regulating reality TV must now learn and act," she added.

A spokesman for Ofcom said the broadcast regulator would "carefully consider the reports published today as we move to strengthen our guidance for broadcasters".

"We are clear that broadcasters have a duty of care towards members of the public who participate in their programmes."

News.title: Farage says he is worried Trump will step up Iran war after midterm 'disaster'
News.content:
Nigel Farage has said he fears Donald Trump will "aggressively" continue his war with Iran after his "disaster" in the US midterm elections.

The Reform UK leader said the US president was still a friend, but accused him of having "broke a promise" to the American electorate by launching the war.

The war in Iran, which the US began in February 2026, weighed heavily in the midterm election results earlier this week in which the Democrats swept Trump's Republicans out of power in Congress.

Farage, who had initially urged people to support the war, said that following the election results he worried Trump would respond with more strikes on Iran.

Asked how he thinks President Trump will respond, Farage told broadcasters on Thursday: "I suppose I worry that the president will continue aggressively attacking Iran.

"That worries me because that would have even more serious implications for the price of oil, for inflation, for the whole western world".

He acknowledged he had initially supported the war but stressed he "never supported endless war".

Asked if the war was a mistake, he said: "There's no question about it."

The US president had "always kept his promises," added Farage, but "in this case, he said no more foreign wars and here we are in month eight of a war with no sign of ending."

"That and the resulting fuel prices are what in the end has done the damage."

Trump said on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in oil prices.

But he insisted he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran.

News.title: More Mandelson papers set to be published before Christmas
News.content:
The government is preparing to publish more documents about the appointment of Lord Mandelson as US ambassador.

Batches of papers were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a Metropolitan Police investigation.

The Cabinet Office has now said a number of extra documents will be published, likely before Christmas. Some will still be withheld at the request of the Met.

Cat Little, permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office, said that some of the documents could "now be published without prejudicing their investigation".

The Met Police had launched an investigation over allegations that, while he was serving as a government minister, Lord Mandelson had passed on market-sensitive government information to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Writing to the chair of Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee, Little said: "The Cabinet Office is now beginning the process to prepare these documents so that they may be laid before the House in response to the humble address motion as soon as possible."

She said the documents would be reviewed and in some instances may need to be redacted "for the purposes of avoiding prejudice to national security or international relations".

The process is expected to be completed before Parliament rises for the Christmas recess on 17 December.

Lord Mandelson was arrested on 23 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

He has repeatedly let it be known that he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

"Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing," the Met Police said in a statement.

The lifelong Labour politician became the British ambassador to the US in February 2025, but was sacked in September after Downing Street said new information about the extent of his relationship with Epstein had emerged.

After his sacking, the government - then led by Sir Keir Starmer - was heavily criticised for giving Lord Mandelson the job and in February MPs voted to force the government to publish papers relating to his appointment.

Mike Wood, shadow Cabinet Office minister, said: "We still haven't got to the bottom of the Mandelson scandal.

"Labour did their utmost to hold this information back and it was only released because of the Conservatives humble address."

News.title: Met 'reset' means fewer police at major events
News.content:
A "resetting" of policing priorities in London will mean that some incidents at major events and protests will now "take longer to squash", the Metropolitan Police has said.

Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley told a session of the London Assembly that officers were being moved away from policing major events and into community policing instead.

The decision, he said, freed up 6,000 shifts in October.

The commissioner asked the Assembly for "support" in making the changes, which he said were due to "financial pressures".

Sir Mark said to Assembly members: "London's politicians, including yourselves, regularly say to me, 'My local neighbourhood officers are great, but you abstract them too much.'

"So this is about reducing that, but it does come with a challenge.

"It will mean that sometimes events in the centre of London will happen in a way that wasn't anticipated, and will take longer to squash and deal with.

"So I would ask for your support when that happens because the prize for taking that more measured approach is that we have more resources in local communities."

News.title: Pound rises to its highest level since the Brexit referendum
News.content:
The pound has risen to its highest overall level since the Brexit referendum over a decade ago.

Sterling has risen notably in recent weeks against the euro and the dollar, ahead of an expected rise in interest rates.

The most-watched measure of the value of the British currency against a basket of 18 of the world's main currencies this week reached its joint highest level since the June 2016 referendum, according to Bank of England figures.

The value reached 86.4 on an index where 100 equals the value in 2005. The Bank will officially confirm the calculation on Thursday.

News.title: New £200m fleet of publicly funded trains in Wales barely used after three years
News.content:
A new fleet of publicly funded trains that cost more than Â£200m still remain mostly unused more than three years after the first one was delivered.

They were initially promised to be fully up and running by 2022 but Transport for Wales' (TfW) boss has said he expects all of the tram-trains will be in full service by the end of 2027.

Data obtained by the BBC reveals that less than half of the 36 fleet - what TfW call the "final piece" in their Â£2bn South Wales Metro project - have passed rigorous statutory testing.

TfW chief executive James Price said he wants trains that work "100% well, 100% of the time" before putting them into full service.

News.title: Abdul El-Sayed has already found something he wants to work with Trump on
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has already found something he wants to work with President Donald Trump on — cutting aid to Israel.

The Michigan Democrat — who has been an outspoken critic of Israeli leadership during the war in Gaza, which he calls a genocide — backed Trump’s idea to cut $4 billion in aid to Israel by the end of the year, saying that he would “love to work with him on doing that.”

“I don’t think we should be continuing to subsidize a foreign military that has done the worst things with our money,” El-Sayed told the hosts of MS NOW’s Morning Joe Thursday. “In fact, I don’t know that we should be continuing to sell weapons to a country that is, again, using our weapons to do awful things.”

Israel has vehemently denied it is committing a genocide in Gaza.

Trump announced the U.S. was cutting aid to Israel on Fox & Friends Tuesday as Americans were heading to the polls for the midterm elections, saying that Israel no longer needed the money.

open image in gallery The Michigan Democrat — who has been an outspoken critic of Israeli leadership during the war in Gaza, which he calls a genocide — backed Trump’s idea to cut $4 billion in aid to Israel by the end of the year, saying that he would ‘love to work with him on doing that’ ( Getty Images )

“Why? Because they don’t need it, Brian. I mean, I asked them, because they don’t need it. And because why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it,” Trump told co-host Brian Kilmeade.

“It is a bad talking point. Because when you say, ‘Why don’t we give everybody $4 billion?’ Israel is our number one. We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it.”

Trump said the decision to cut aid was made with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “He brought it up, he said, ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid,’” the president said.

During Thursday’s interview, El-Sayed made clear that he is not against Jewish people, but rather the wartime actions of Israel.

“We have to separate between Judaism and the Jewish people and Israel and its actions. We have to,” El-Sayed said.

open image in gallery Trump announced the U.S. was cutting aid to Israel on Tuesday as Americans were heading to the polls for the midterm elections, saying that Israel no longer needed the money ( AFP via Getty Images )

“We have broken our own principles when it comes to Israel time and again. And I want to have a conversation; I’ll stop here, where a Palestinian child and a Jewish-Israeli child growing up in the Holy Land can look forward at their life and say, ‘my life is not going to be curtailed by somebody’s violence,’” he said, asking, “How do we get there?”

El-Sayed will become the first Muslim senator when he is sworn in next year.

While campaigning for his Republican opponent Mike Rogers ahead of the midterms, Trump attacked El-Sayed, baselessly calling him a “jihadist” and demanding he go through metal detectors at the U.S. Capitol building if elected.

“I’m here to keep a Jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump said. El-Sayed has vehemently denied any ties to the Islamist organization.

El-Sayed, in turn, taunted Trump during his victory speech, saying, “I know you struggle with my name, so after [Vice President] JD [Vance] swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator.”

News.title: Inbetweeners star Emily Atack says Rivals role 'completely changed my life'
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Emily Atack has described her role in the hit series Rivals as a major turning point in her nearly two-decade career, revealing that the part has "completely changed my life".

The 36-year-old actor previously established a successful television career spanning comedy, sketch shows, reality programmes and presenting roles, such as hosting I’m A Celebrity… Extra Camp, after first rising to prominence on screen.

In the award-winning Disney+ drama, set against the backdrop of the 1980s Cotswolds and the competitive world of British television, Atack stars as the multi-layered Sarah Stratton, showcasing her talent in a complex dramatic role.

Reflecting on her career path in an interview with the Press Association, Atack said: "It’s completely changed my life. I don’t even know how to describe it.

"I’ve worked in television for a long time, but what I’ve always wanted to do was come back to acting. That’s where I started, and that’s where my heart has always been."

open image in gallery Atack previously starred in The Inbetweeners ( Channel 4 )

Atack began acting at the age of 16 in the ITV crime drama Blue Murder, before achieving widespread fame in 2008 as Charlotte "Big Jugs" Hinchcliffe in the E4 teenage sitcom The Inbetweeners. Following the typecasting and stereotyping that arose from that breakthrough role, she chose to pursue opportunities in reality TV, alongside comedy and presenting work.

"Different paths took me into different jobs and gave me some amazing opportunities in television, for which I’m incredibly grateful," she said.

"But making that transition back from television into acting isn’t always straightforward. It can be quite difficult, and sometimes that move isn’t necessarily welcomed.

"So to feel so embraced and welcomed back into acting has meant an enormous amount to me."

She added: "I know it probably sounds indulgent talking about it like this, but it really is a dream. An absolute dream.

"It reminds me that this is where my heart is. I’m so lucky to have had all those other experiences and opportunities, but this is truly where I belong. This is what I love."

Based on the celebrated novels by the late Dame Jilly Cooper, Rivals launched in 2024 with a high-profile cast that includes Atack, David Tennant, Danny Dyer, Katherine Parkinson and Aidan Turner.

The popular television series will return on November 11 with its second installment of series two episodes, beginning with a three-episode premiere on Disney+ in the UK and internationally, and on Hulu in the US.

News.title: Beavers make historic return to Loch Ness after 500 years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For the first time in five centuries, beavers have returned to the catchment around Loch Ness following the successful reintroduction of a family of six.

The animals were relocated from another part of Scotland under licence from NatureScot and released on Wednesday at a lochan on Dundreggan, a 10,000-acre rewilding estate in Glenmoriston managed by the charity Trees for Life.

Speaking shortly after the event to the Press Association, Steve Micklewright, chief executive of Trees for Life, described watching the animals return to their native habitat as a "very beautiful thing to see".

"I can see them swimming and very calm, which is a really good sign," he said, noting that the family appeared "very settled" right away.

The group comprises a mother, two two-year-old juveniles, and three kits born earlier this year.

They were originally captured in Tayside, where they had been creating difficulties for local farmers, before being taken to a specialist zoo facility for health screening and subsequently released near Loch Ness.

open image in gallery The beavers were relocated from another part of Scotland ( PA )

"Now they’re out in the wild, and to see them just being really relaxed is amazing," Mr Micklewright said.

"The little ones have been swimming around, and those are the ones I’ve been watching on the side of the loch grooming each other, which is a real sign that they are settling in."

He added: "Everyone has found this quite emotional. I’m looking at a beaver in a little shrub and it’s having a chew on some bark and things.

"Just to see beavers behaving naturally in the wild in a place where they are welcome, and where they will thrive, has been a very emotional experience."

All six animals entered the water immediately to explore, putting "on a good show" for those present, Mr Micklewright noted.

“I think they’ll be very happy here," he said.

The release marks the beginning of the Ness Beaver Project, a joint initiative between Trees for Life and the Beaver Trust that aims to introduce at least 15 beaver families to the Loch Ness catchment over the next three years.

The charities hailed the initial release as a "major milestone for nature recovery in Britain".

open image in gallery The beavers are back in the Scottish Highlands ( PA )

Dr Roisin Campbell-Palmer, head of restoration at Beaver Trust, said: "It has been profoundly rewarding to release the first beavers at Dundreggan, marking the start of their return to the Loch Ness catchment.

"The extensive woodland and suitable habitat here offer real opportunities for the animals to thrive and bring lasting biodiversity benefits."

Alan McDonnell, Trees for Life’s head of nature restoration, highlighted the species' wider return as one of the country's "biggest rewilding success stories".

He said: "Hunted to extinction centuries ago, beavers are reclaiming their place in our rivers and wetlands – breathing new life into precious landscapes, boosting biodiversity, and bringing eco-tourism opportunities.

"Five hundred years since Loch Ness became the last recorded site of Scotland’s beavers before they were eradicated, they are back with the space and habitat to flourish – bringing with them the potential for new wetlands, more wildlife, and healthier rivers."

Future releases will be announced only after the animals are safely in place, ensuring they can adapt to their surroundings without disturbance.

Prior to reintroduction, all animals are assessed at a dedicated holding unit at Five Sisters Zoo near West Calder.

Gary Curran, collection manager at the zoo, said: "Since Scotland’s first official reintroduction trial in 2009, growing wild populations of beavers have shown what is possible when people work together to restore a lost species.

open image in gallery The return of beavers to Loch Ness has been hailed by charities ( PA )

"The return of beavers to Loch Ness, one of Scotland’s most iconic landscapes, marks a major turning point in this extraordinary national recovery, and we are delighted to be playing a role in this."

Conservationists believe establishing a self-sustaining population around Loch Ness will secure the mammal's future across the Highlands while yielding ecological and community benefits.

Through dam and canal construction, beavers revitalise river and wetland networks, supporting biodiversity while mitigating environmental challenges such as flooding, drought and wildfires.

The project is also expected to enhance local eco-tourism in an economy heavily reliant on natural landscape appeal. Once the family has settled, Trees for Life intends to run guided tours to offer visitors a firsthand look at the animals and their landscape restoration work.

News.title: Prince William opens up about private life in special edition of Country Life
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prince William will share rare insights into his public role and personal life as he guest-edits Country Life magazine.

The Prince of Wales has spent the past six months working with the publication, which celebrates rural life, to create his 300-page commemorative issue, which will be published next week on Wednesday, November 11.

William met with Mark Hedges, Country Life’s editor-in-chief, and managing editor Paula Minchin last month at Windsor to preview the draft and examine the proofs and layout.

The prince will also be the cover star for the special edition, in which he will share more personal aspects of his life, including his fondness for an occasional pub visit for a pint of cider with ice.

Mr Hedges previously described the heir to the throne as a “passionate countryman” when his role as guest editor was announced in June.

open image in gallery The Prince of Wales has spent the past six months working with Country Life magazine ( Getty )

William inherited the Duchy of Cornwall landed estate, which spans 128,000 acres over 19 counties, when his father became King.

He also has a countryside retreat, Anmer Hall, in Norfolk.

A Kensington Palace spokesperson said: “The Prince of Wales has a long-standing passion for the countryside and the vital role it plays in the nation’s life, culture and wellbeing.

“His guest editorship of Country Life reflects a desire to celebrate the people, places and innovative stewardship helping to secure its future for generations to come.”

open image in gallery The photograph of the Queen Camilla taken by her daughter-in-law the Princess of Wales ( Country Life )

William follows in the footsteps of his father, the King, stepmother, the Queen, and his aunt, the Princess Royal, who have all been guest editors.

Camilla's guest edition in 2022 to mark her 75th birthday was the biggest-selling issue of all time, with the front cover picture of the then-duchess of Cornwall, now Queen Camilla, taken by the now-Princess of Wales.

The King, then the Prince of Wales, twice guest-edited Country Life, firstly for his 65th birthday in November 2013, and then for his 70th in 2018.

In 2020, the Princess Royal guest-edited an edition for her 70th birthday.

Last month, William opened up about his childhood dream to become a policeman or DJ during a surprise appearance on The Graham Norton Show.

“I did want to be a policeman when I was younger, I did think I would be a good policeman,” he said.

“And then I went through a phase where I wanted to be a DJ, which didn’t go very well, and I came up with a name, I was called DJ Xara with an X, it wasn’t good.”

News.title: Parents issue urgent plea for stem cell donor to save baby boy with rare blood condition
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The parents of a baby boy suffering from a rare, life-threatening blood condition have issued an urgent plea for a stem cell donor to afford their son "a chance to grow up".

Ellis Feldon, who lives in North Devon, has spent much of his young life unwell, with his parents Matt and Caitlin initially believing he was suffering from allergies.

Now aged 10 and a half months, the infant requires a vital stem cell transplant, but no suitable matches currently exist on the international register.

Shortly after birth, Ellis was admitted to hospital with jaundice, and by last Christmas he was struggling to keep down his normal milk formula. As further symptoms developed, including severe eczema and blood spots across his skin, doctors carried out blood tests.

Following months of medical appointments, he was diagnosed with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS), an extremely rare genetic condition that almost exclusively affects boys.

The disorder impairs the body's capacity to fight off infection, causing symptoms such as severe eczema, easy bruising, bloody diarrhoea, and prolonged bleeding from minor scrapes. It is caused by genetic flaws on the X chromosome and affects roughly three in every million boys worldwide.

open image in gallery Ellis has been diagnosed with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome ( Family handout )

Mr Feldon explained: "In normal circumstances, you’d be able to really enjoy those first few months as first-time parents with your little baby, but Ellis has been ill since he was so small. He was back in hospital days after he was born, and things have only snowballed from there."

He added: "Initially, we were told that the team was confident they would find a match for Ellis. We thought there would be plenty of options, given how many people are registered around the world. But the news isn’t as good as we had hoped."

The family were informed of only two potential matches worldwide, but one cannot donate for over a year and the other is just an 85% match.

Doctors have urged them not to delay the procedure, yet proceeding with an imperfect match leaves Ellis at risk of rejection and further health complications.

Having relocated from Guildford, Surrey, to Caitlin’s hometown of Chulmleigh to be near relatives, the family are now partnering with blood cancer charity DKMS to encourage people to join the register.

Anyone aged 16 to 55 can sign up by completing a health questionnaire and submitting a simple cheek swab using a free kit ordered online.

Mr Feldon said: "It’s frustrating to think that there could be someone walking around who is a perfect match for Ellis, but because it’s an opt-in system, they can’t be checked.

"We want to do everything we can to give him the best possible chance, but we also want to help make sure other families don’t find themselves in this position.

"People don’t always realise how straightforward it is to sign up, or how easy the donation process is. You could be the person who gives a child like Ellis the chance to grow up."

open image in gallery Ellis’ parents say he ‘loves watching Ms Rachel’ ( Getty )

Although the family are trying to celebrate his childhood developments, Mr Feldon acknowledged the underlying anxiety.

"He’s doing so many lovely things. He loves watching Ms Rachel, he has six teeth, he’s crawling at speed and he’s taken his first few wobbly steps.

"We want to enjoy all of that, but there is always that sadness in the background. You want to be able to enjoy those milestones without worrying about what might happen next."

A DKMS spokesperson added: "For Ellis and so many other patients, the right person signing up to the stem cell donor register could make all the difference.

"It takes just a few minutes to register, but if you are matched with someone in need, your donation could give them a future they might otherwise not have.

"We urgently need more people to come forward and join the register, helping to give Ellis and other patients diagnosed with blood cancers and disorders the best possible chance of finding a suitable donor."

News.title: Mapped: UK's most affordable towns where homes can be snapped up for less than £300k
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Zoopla has identified more than 30 towns across the UK where homes can potentially be bought for less than two years' worth of household earnings.

Its analysis, covering 929 towns across Britain, revealed that a typical home is valued at £299,100. This figure works out at 4.3 times annual household earnings.

Shildon in County Durham was named the most affordable town of all, with homes there costing 1.15 times two full-time annual wages on average.

Scotland accounted for 23 of the 36 towns Zoopla identified where homes typically cost less than twice the annual wages of two full-time workers.

Meanwhile, the North East of England made up eight locations, and the North West accounted for four.

Dover was identified as the South East's most affordable town, although a home there would typically cost nearly three times annual household earnings typically, Zoopla said.

In London, the most affordable borough was Tower Hamlets, with homes there typically costing 4.91 times a household income with two full-time workers.

Richard Donnell, executive director at Zoopla, said: "House prices have been rising more slowly than incomes, helping to improve housing affordability, but higher mortgage rates continue to offset some of these gains by increasing the monthly cost of buying a home.

"Affordability varies widely across the country, with many towns in northern England and Scotland offering much better value relative to local household earnings.

"However, lower house prices don't always mean it's easier to buy, as access to employment, deposits and mortgage costs remain important considerations.

"Buyers have more homes to choose from than a year ago, and there is greater scope to negotiate on price, particularly in southern England.

"Anyone considering a move should take a fresh look at what they can afford and what's available locally.

“Expanding a search to neighbouring towns could make a meaningful difference to their buying options.”

Only postal towns with 5,000 homes or more were taken into consideration by Zoopla for the research.
