World.title: ZACOSO backs fish inclusion in school meals
World.content:
The Zambian Aquaculture Cooperative Society Limited (ZACOSO) has expressed optimism over the planned integration of fish into the school feeding programme, citing opportunities to create new markets for local producers while promoting entrepreneurship among learners.

The statement follows the Government’s call for the integration of nutrient-dense aquatic foods to improve learner nutrition and strengthen local food systems.

ZACOSO General Manager, Evans Chilandani said the initiative, if implemented, would increase demand for locally produced fish by encouraging schools and other production units to venture into fish farming.

Mr Chilandani emphasised that introducing fish ponds in schools would also provide learners with practical skills in fish production, including how to rear and manage fish, equipping them with entrepreneurial knowledge they could use after completing their education.

Meanwhile, Zambia Aquaculture Alliance Cooperative Society Secretary General Ferdinand Simfukwe has called on the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock to involve small aquaculture associations and cooperatives in the proposed school fish feeding programme, stating that their participation will be key to creating reliable markets for local producers.

Mr Simfukwe said the initiative will help many small-scale fish farmers who struggle with markets.

He further urged the Ministry to bring together relevant stakeholders and establish clear mechanisms for small-scale aquaculture associations to participate and benefit from the programme, saying their inclusion would strengthen its implementation and ensure that local fish farmers are not left out.

World.title: Shiwang’andu farmers urged to expand cultivation
World.content:
Farmers in Shiwang’andu District have been challenged to increase agricultural production by taking advantage of the district’s 59,200 hectares of arable land, of which only 21,000 hectares are currently under cultivation.

District Agricultural Coordinator (DACO) Chewe Mutale said the district has vast agricultural potential which, if fully utilised, could contribute to the country’s national maize production targets by 2031.

Ms Mutale told the media in an interview that about 38,200 hectares of arable land remained available for agricultural expansion.

She disclosed that the district recorded a maize output of 27,900 metric tonnes against a target of 66,000 metric tonnes during the 2025/2026 farming season.

The DACO attributed the low adoption of good agricultural practices among farmers as one of the major challenges affecting increased agricultural production.

“Low levels of mechanisation, inadequate storage facilities and poor road infrastructure were also contributing to low productivity” she said.

Meanwhile, Shiwang’andu District Commissioner Maureen Bwembya has urged farmers to embrace modern farming practices and fully utilise the available arable land to unlock the district’s agricultural potential.

Ms Bwembya has challenged farmers and agriculture officers to work towards achieving the district’s maize production target of 82,000 metric tonnes by 2031, thereby contributing to the national target of producing 10 million metric tonnes of maize within the same period.

World.title: President Hichilema calls on Leaders to prioritise service delivery
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has urged newly elected and other Members of Parliament, councillors and party officials to work for the people, saying they owe their positions to the electorate and must prioritise service delivery over political disputes.

Speaking during a community engagement in Mandevu, Lusaka, President Hichilema said the United Party for National Development (UPND) Government is in office to serve the people and deliver on its development promises.

“We are in government to serve the people and to deliver on our development promises,” President Hichilema said.

“I want you the people of Mandevu to hold your elected leaders accountable,” he added.

He said access to clean water remains a fundamental need for Mandevu constituency, hence the need for the Member of Parliament to use the component of Constituency Development Fund (CDF) for clean water provision.

“Water is a fundamental need. We must ensure that our people have access to clean water,” he said.

President Hichilema also identified security as another key priority for his administration, highlighting the need to curb junkies in the communities and take them for skills training for them to contribute to the country’s economy positively.

“Security is important. Government is committed to creating an environment in which citizens can live safely and contribute to national development,” he said.

The Head of State also stressed that every child of school-going age must be in school, adding that every citizen who is not in a position to pay school fees must utilise free education policy which is coupled with the feeding programme

“Every child of school-going age must be in school. Education is what will transform our young people into productive citizens,” he said.

He further said his administration wants to transform citizens into productive members of society through opportunities for education, skills acquisition and economic participation.

“We want to transform our citizens into productive members of society through education, skills acquisition and economic participation,” he said.

President Hichilema pointed to the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) as an important instrument for community development.

“The CDF is an important instrument for community development. We have allocated K40 million for constituency development and K40 million for skills training,” he said.

He also highlighted the importance of inclusive representation in Parliament, pointing to the participation of women, young people and persons with disabilities.

“We have provided opportunities for broader representation in Parliament, including women, young people and persons with disabilities,” he said.

The President thanked Zambians for supporting the UPND and acknowledged party structures across the country, including provincial, district and constituency officials, as well as grassroots representatives for their role in mobilising support.

President Hichilema said the government would continue working for Zambians, reiterating that service delivery remains its primary agenda.

“We will continue working for Zambians. Service delivery remains our primary agenda,” he said.

He thanked the people of Mandevu and reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to national development.

And Mandevu Member of Parliament, Adrian Banda has assured electorates of Mandevu of the much-needed development in the area with the use of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

“We will use the CDF to provide the much-needed development for the people of Mandevu. The people voted for development, and that is what we are going to deliver,” Mr Banda said.

He said the fund will be directed to priority areas that will improve the lives of residents, adding that his office will work closely with the community to ensure the projects reflect the needs of the people.

World.title: Nalumango calls for stronger market linkages
World.content:
Vice-President Mutale Nalumango says Zambia must go beyond increasing production to effectively connecting its products to local, regional and international markets if the country is to achieve meaningful economic transformation.

The Vice-President said Government’s ambitious production targets under the Grow Zambia Agenda will only translate into economic value if supported by strategic marketing, quality standards and competitiveness.

Mrs Nalumango said this in a speech read on her behalf by Copperbelt Province Minister Emmanuel Kasambo during the official opening of the 2026 Prestigious Copperbelt Regional Marketing Conference at Garden Court Hotel in Kitwe.

She commended the Zambia Institute of Marketing (ZIM) and its partners for convening the conference to explore how marketing can contribute to Zambia’s trade, investment and economic growth.

The Vice-President noted that increased production alone does not guarantee economic transformation.

The Vice-President said marketing Zambia and its economic opportunities is a shared responsibility.

She said the Government will continue to create an enabling environment for trade, investment and enterprise, while the private sector must invest, innovate and produce competitively.

She also urged stakeholders to embrace digital technologies, market research and intelligence to identify emerging opportunities.

Mrs Nalumango said the Copperbelt is an appropriate setting for the conference, noting that while the province has long been central to Zambia’s mining industry, its future prosperity must extend beyond mineral extraction.

World.title: Government, Partners commit to sustain school meals
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to working with partners to sustain the school meals programme.

In a speech read on her behalf by Minister of Education, Harry Kamboni at the close of the Global Child Nutrition Forum, Mrs Nalumango called for stronger partnerships and commended participating countries and stakeholders for their contributions.

Global Child Nutrition Foundation Executive Director Arlene Mitchell said participants’ actions were important in making a positive impact on children’s lives.

Ms Mitchell also thanked the Zambian Government for its commitment to co-hosting a successful forum.

Earlier, Permanent Secretary in the Office of the Vice President, Lillian Kapusana led delegates on visits to about 11 schools in Lusaka, where they observed the School Feeding Programme.

The four-day forum, held under the theme “From Vision to Action: Achieving Ambitious School Meal Programme Objectives,” brought together more than 400 participants from over 65 countries.

They collaborated to turn global knowledge and research into practical strategies.

World.title: Africa: Deadly Viruses Know No Borders, Nor Should Our Resolve to Stop Them
World.content:
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland.

guest column

In this guest column for AllAfrica, the Dutch Trade and Development Minister and the head of the World Health Organization stress that addressing viral health crises anywhere protects everyone everywhere. The government of the Netherlands is committing funding both for the current Ebola crisis and flexible funding to quickly respond to new or emerging global threats.

COVID-19 may feel like a distant memory to many. But the virus claimed millions of lives around the world, including approximately 50,000 in the Netherlands. The lesson is clear: preparedness is not optional.

Preventing health crises abroad is in the interest of all countries, including the Netherlands.

Governments everywhere face competing priorities and constrained budgets. But infectious diseases do not respect national borders. In an interconnected world, health threats that emerge in one place can quickly become risks for all of us. No country can safeguard its health security alone.

That lesson is evident today in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where a major Ebola outbreak is unfolding in a region already affected by insecurity, displacement and limited access to health services.

Already the outbreak has crossed national boundaries, underlining how quickly a health threat in one country can become a shared international concern.

Responding effectively requires rapid action, strong local leadership and international solidarity. Under the DRC Government's leadership, the World Health Organization (WHO) is working closely with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, local authorities, communities and partners to contain the outbreak in the DRC and save lives.

Mystic Stock Photography / Shutterstock.com The MV Hondius, a cruise ship owned by the Dutch company Oceanwide Expeditions experienced a Hantavirus outbreak last year. The Netherlands and the World Health Organized collaborated to safely evacuate passengers and crew.

To support these efforts, the Netherlands is providing €7 million to WHO for the Ebola response. But responding to outbreaks requires more than emergency funding alone. It requires flexible, predictable financing that can be directed rapidly to where needs are greatest. That is why the Netherlands is also providing a new €10 million flexible contribution to WHO for future emergencies, enabling the WHO to rapidly respond to health threats while helping countries strengthen preparedness and prevent future outbreaks whenever possible. This is additional to the existing €9.6 million yearly core funding to the WHO.

No country can safeguard its health security alone.

Some may ask why the Netherlands, or any country, should invest in health emergencies far from its own borders when domestic health systems also face challenges. The answer is simple: diseases do not stop at borders. Supporting countries to detect and contain outbreaks early is not only the right thing to do. It protects local populations while reducing the risk of wider international spread. Investing in health security abroad is also an investment in health security at home.

Outbreaks are most effectively controlled at their source. Local leadership is essential. National authorities understand their communities, their health systems and the challenges they face. WHO's role is to support those efforts, coordinate international expertise and ensure that countries have access to the tools, funding and technical assistance they need.

International cooperation remains the foundation of effective health security. This year, for example, a hantavirus outbreak on a Dutch-flagged cruise ship was swiftly contained through rapid collaboration among countries and partners coordinated through WHO. During an earlier outbreak caused by the "Sudan virus" species of Ebola in Uganda, investments that helped advance an Ebola vaccine developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) and Batavia Biosciences contributed to global preparedness efforts. These examples demonstrate that cooperation works.

Dany Bitita/WHO Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances.

Yet this progress cannot be taken for granted. The international health system is under growing strain, even as health threats continue to increase. Climate change is altering the distribution of infectious diseases. Europe has already seen growing concern from vector-borne diseases, including West Nile virus, while other diseases such as dengue and malaria are expanding into new regions. At the same time, funding for global health, including for WHO, is declining.

Diseases spreading to new areas amid decreased global health funding is dangerous.

This is a dangerous combination. The need for cooperation, preparedness and rapid response is growing, just as the resources required to sustain them are coming under pressure.

We therefore call on European governments to strengthen their support for global health security by increasing flexible and unearmarked contributions to WHO. Such investments enable outbreaks to be detected earlier, contained more rapidly and addressed where they begin, before they become larger regional or global crises.

No one can rule out the possibility of another pandemic. . But we can ensure that we are better prepared for the next one. Strong health systems in the DRC, and in countries everywhere, are not only vital for the local communities. They are an investment in a safer, healthier and more secure future for us all.

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma is the Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization.

World.title: South Africa: Parties Keep Close Watch As Election Results Trickle in
World.content:
The 2026 Local Government Elections results process continues to advance, with 24% of votes counted nationally. These are the results at 10am SAST on November 5, 2026.

The Electoral Commission of South Africa's (IEC) national Results Operations Centre (ROC) in Midrand is abuzz with activity, as political parties closely monitor the first results from the 2026 Local Government Elections.

Party representatives have gathered at the centre as preliminary results started trickling in this morning, following Wednesday's voting, with parties hoping for a strong showing in the contest for control of municipalities across the country.

The Commission will be briefing the media at 10am.

World.title: Africa: Africa Made It Unveils Blueprint To Capture Usd 34B In Gdp And Accelerate African Industrial Sovereignty
World.content:
press release

Africa Made It, the continental movement driving Africa's industrial sovereignty, today officially launched its campaign, "Power, Protect and Purchase," at the CANEX weekend in Lagos, Nigeria. Aimed at unlocking USD 34 billion in annual GDP contribution through a structural transition from unprocessed raw cotton exports to end-to-end local garment processing, the initiative seeks to turn Africa's vast natural wealth into sovereign, self-sustaining economic power.

Africa Made It is driven by a consortium of leading pan-African organisations, advocacy groups, and media organisations who are positioning Africa as a global investment hub. Its flagship campaign, spotlighting the fibre-to-fashion value chain, presents a clear roadmap for continental industrialisation: securing competitive energy power for local industrial mills, enacting policy measures to protect emerging domestic manufacturers from unfair foreign imports, and rallying African consumers to purchase locally manufactured apparel. Together, these three pillars ensure that value created from African resources remains on African soil.

Africa Practice research shows that Africa exports up to 98% of its raw cotton overseas and captures only 2% of its total value while incurring a USD 35 billion annual trade deficit. Building the continent's domestic processing capacity in spinning, weaving, and sewing locally produced cotton will sustain nearly two million permanent industrial jobs and inject approximately USD 33 billion directly into domestic household incomes every year, in addition to a recurring contribution of USD 34 billion to the continent's GDP.

While these figures reveal the immense macro-economic potential of the value chain, the true heart of this transformation lies in its human impact. Industrial wages and local lint purchases leading to increased capital circulation in rural communities can drive community micro-economic vitality and contribute to rural poverty reduction. Additionally, formal employment opportunities can expand drastically for women, as they currently make up between 70-90% of garment factory workers on the continent.

Realising this vision and changing the lives of millions of people requires a deliberate combination of targeted investments, supportive trade policies, and consumer mobilisation. A USD 1.8 billion capital allocation toward critical structural enablers for garment transformation is the foundation for bridging Africa's missing middle in the fibre-to-fashion value chain.

Marie Wilke, editor-in-chief of the Africa Made It magazine, said, "African culture, design, and storytelling influence global fashion, music, and media like never before. Yet, without domestic manufacturing infrastructure, Africa's creative authority yields very little economic return. Linking raw cotton harvest directly to local processing ensures that the intellectual property, commercial margins, and industrial jobs remain on the continent. It is time to wear our power."

To learn more about the potential of Africa's fibre to fashion value chain, watch the campaign video or read the Africa Made it magazine . Access the campaign website and resources in English and French .

About Africa Made It

Africa Made It was established as a continental advocacy platform to accelerate Africa's transition from a primary exporter of raw materials to a global powerhouse that controls, processes and monetises its own resources. The fashion industry is only the first example. It is coordinated by a network of partners including AllAfrica Media, Africa24, Africa No Filter, Africa Practice, Afreximbank, AKAS Consulting, Bird Story Agency, IC Publications, and Research Alpha.

For regular updates on the campaign and its progress, follow Africa Made It on Instagram ( @africa_madeit ) and LinkedIn ( Africa Made It )

The judgement, if upheld by the higher courts, means the ADC, a major challenger to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), is barred from fielding candidates in the upcoming general elections.

The Federal High Court in Abuja on Thursday sacked the leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) under former Senate President David Mark and voided the party's presidential ticket held by former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.

Judge Peter Lifu said the "Mark-led Caretaker Committee, which conducted the party's presidential primary that produced Atiku Abubakar as its flag bearer," is illegal.

The judge sacked the entire national officers of the party, including Rauf Aregbesola as the National Secretary, alongside all the candidates the party presented to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) for the 2027 elections.

World.title: Tanzania/Uganda: Billions Pour Into Stadia - How EAC Nations are Investing for AFCON
World.content:
DAR ES SALAAM — TANZANIA, Kenya and Uganda are investing heavily in modern sports infrastructure ahead of the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), combining new stadium construction with the modernisation of existing facilities to meet international football standards.

The investments, which involve hundreds of millions of dollars, are expected to strengthen East Africa's capacity to host major sporting events while creating lasting infrastructure for football development, sports tourism and commercial activities.

The projects include new stadiums in Arusha, Zanzibar, Nairobi, Hoima and Lira, alongside major upgrades to established national facilities in Dar es Salaam, Nairobi and Kampala.

Beyond providing venues for the continental tournament, the investments reflect the three East African region's ambition to develop modern, multifunctional sports facilities capable of hosting international competitions, entertainment events and other major gatherings.



Tanzania's AFCON 2027 infrastructure programme is anchored by three principal match venues: Samia Suluhu Hassan Stadium in Arusha, Benjamin Mkapa National Stadium in Dar es Salaam and Fumba Stadium in Zanzibar.

The projects combine the construction of new stadiums with the modernisation of existing facilities, expanding the country's capacity to host international football competitions.

The new Samia Suluhu Hassan Stadium in Olmoti, Arusha, represents one of the country's largest investments in sports infrastructure, with a cost of 338.54bn/, equivalent to approximately 128.2 million US dollars.

The project includes a planned seating capacity of approximately 32,500 spectators and is being developed as a modern sports complex with facilities designed to meet international competition requirements.

According to the Tanzanian government, the contract value increased from an original estimate of 187bn/- to 338.54bn, representing an 81 per cent increase.

Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Information, Culture, Arts and Sports, and Chief Government Spokesperson Gerson Msigwa, attributed the increase in the construction cost of the stadium to changes in the project's scope and technical requirements following Tanzania's selection to co-host AFCON 2027.

Msigwa explained that the initial budget was prepared in 2021, before Tanzania secured the rights to co-host the continental tournament alongside Kenya and Uganda.

He said the original design was based on general stadium requirements, but the country's selection as an AFCON host necessitated substantial improvements to meet CAF Category Four standards, which are required for hosting toplevel international matches.

The stadium's engineering design incorporates a reinforced-concrete structural frame, complemented by a sophisticated steel roof and facade system featuring trusses and a singlelayer spatial grid.

The roof structure uses approximately 7,762 tonnes of steel to provide extensive coverage over spectator areas.

The facility also incorporates modern spectator seating, VIP and hospitality facilities, players' and officials' facilities and technical installations.

Its development is intended to meet the enhanced requirements for CAF Category Four stadiums, including improved playing surfaces, floodlighting, safety systems, media facilities and emergency power.

In Dar es Salaam, the 60,000-capacity Benjamin Mkapa National Stadium is undergoing extensive rehabilitation to meet the technical and operational requirements of AFCON 2027.

The government initially disclosed a rehabilitation programme valued at approximately 39bn/-, equivalent to US$14.7 million. A major component involved replacing all 60,000 spectator seats, which is estimated at 39bn/-.

Other improvements have covered the playing surface, drainage, floodlighting, VVIP facilities, players' dressing rooms, media areas, sound systems and supporting technical infrastructure.

The latest rehabilitation phase has placed particular emphasis on reconstructing the playing surface to improve drainage and meet international football standards, alongside improvements to hospitality, spectator movement, security and backup power.

In Zanzibar, Fumba Stadium is emerging as another major addition to Tanzania's sporting infrastructure.

The new facility, being constructed by Turkish contractor Orkun Group, is designed to accommodate approximately 36,500 spectators, at a cost of about 400bn/-. The stadium is part of the wider Zanzibar AFCON Sports Complex.

The development includes modern spectator facilities, covered seating areas and supporting infrastructure.

It also incorporates two additional outdoor football grounds, each with a seating capacity of 5,000 spectators, to support training and other sporting activities.

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed's pattern of hostile exchanges with reporters draws scrutiny after viral moment
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., went viral this week for his latest altercation with a reporter, putting a spotlight on a history of tense exchanges with the press.

El-Sayed had a combative exchange with Sky News reporter James Matthews just hours before his victory during Tuesday's midterm elections. The exchange began when the British journalist attempted to question El-Sayed, but it was hardly the first time that El-Sayed appeared to either lose his temper, interrupt a journalist or respond sharply to a reporter.

Heritage Foundation media fellow Tim Young is well aware that President Donald Trump also has a long history of criticizing reporters, but he believes the situations are "completely different."

"El-Sayed gets angry at the media for asking actual questions about him and his relationship to organizations like the Muslim Brotherhood. He legitimately doesn’t want to answer those questions, so he snaps," Young told Fox News Digital.

ABDUL EL-SAYED PUTS HANDS ON SKY NEWS REPORTER IN HOSTILE CONFRONTATION HOURS BEFORE ELECTION VICTORY

"Trump gets asked the same narrative-shaping questions all the time, then watches networks create false narratives about him on air, which makes him angry," Young continued. "The two are not the same."

El-Sayed recently scolded a reporter for asking him about Democratic Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens, sarcastically declaring, "You’re really asking the questions that the people want to hear."

"Ask me a serious question," he added.

El-Sayed also got testy with NBC News anchor Tom Llamas in October after Llamas questioned him about allegations involving his family's ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.

"It’s funny to me. I was born in 1984, down the street in Rochester Hills. I was raised here in Michigan, went to the University of Michigan, rebuilt the health department in this city, led the health department in this county, and you want to ask me about Egypt in 1970? Are you serious?" he retorted.

El-Sayed then accused Llamas of using "hearsay evidence from a tweet" and suggested the "NBC Nightly News" anchor was "not serious" before asking, "Are you insinuating that somehow, I was lying?"

EL-SAYED MOCKS TRUMP, VANCE AND ROGERS IN GLOATING VICTORY SPEECH SIGNALING COMBATIVE TONE IN SENATE

That same month, El-Sayed shut down Free Press reporter Audrey Fahlberg for asking about private comments he made on leaked audio regarding some Michigan residents mourning the death of Ayatollah Khamenei.

El-Sayed insisted he would answer questions about gas prices and groceries but declined to "talk about leaked audio" and accused Fahlberg of seeking clickbait.

"I’m just not interested in this dog and pony show," El-Sayed said. "Ask smart questions."

Fahlberg responded that his thoughts on Khamenei were relevant, considering that he frequently discusses foreign policy, but El-Sayed refused to engage.

Fahlberg later said that El-Sayed appeared to become furious whenever asked about the Iranian regime.

Weeks later, El-Sayed clashed with Fox News "Special Report" anchor Bret Baier, repeatedly interrupting Baier during an exchange over the Muslim Brotherhood.

El-Sayed has also spoken about confronting media personalities.

"You know how many terrible things Bill Maher has said about people like me? Terrible, awful things," El-Sayed said during a September interview with Chuck Todd.

"I would go on that show," El-Sayed continued. "I wanna give people the image of watching him get his a-- whooped on his own show by a guy who prays like I do."

UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN STUDENTS RALLY BEHIND ABDUL EL-SAYED AFTER HIS SENATE WIN OVER MIKE ROGERS

As for El-Sayed’s latest encounter, the viral Election Day moment occurred when he walked up to Matthews and asked, "Are you registered to vote in the state of Michigan?"

"I'm not," the British U.S.-based correspondent responded.

"Why would I care to have a conversation with you?" the Democrat fired back.

After Matthews answered that he was a journalist, El-Sayed scoffed while responding, "in the U.K."

"You know how many votes I want to get in the U.K.? Zero," El-Sayed told Mathews as he put both his hands on the reporter's shoulders. "I'm never running for office in the U.K."

Matthews stressed that the 2026 U.S. midterm election "matters to the world" and told El-Sayed he was "bidding to be a senator."

"A senator in where? What country? What country?" El-Sayed retorted while placing his hands on Matthews' shoulders again.

"The United States," Matthews answered.

"What country are you with?" El-Sayed then asked.

"I'm based in the United States," Matthews said.

"But you report for where? Where are your viewers?" El-Sayed interrupted.

El-Sayed dismissed Matthews after the reporter explained that Sky News serves an international audience, insisting "Sky News is not viewed in the United States of America," then sneering that "like five people" watch the network in the US.

"I've answered all the questions, I've answered all the questions for the viewers of the United Kingdom. So I'm going to ask you to stop chasing me around. Please," El-Sayed said before walking away. Matthews denied to El-Sayed he was "chasing" him around.

"If you keep being in my way, I'm not going to be very happy," El-Sayed told the reporter.

EL-SAYED MOCKS TRUMP, VANCE AND ROGERS IN GLOATING VICTORY SPEECH SIGNALING COMBATIVE TONE IN SENATE

Footage of the incident quickly went viral and many observers criticized El-Sayed for physically touching the reporter. Piers Morgan called it "pathetic" and "very patronizing," Reason’s Reem Ibrahim said El-Sayed "looks like an absolute prick" and former Israeli spokesperson Eylon Levy called him a "bully."

Students for Trump founder Ryan Fournier called the behavior "unhinged," while Spencer Pratt asked, "Why is this angry little Elf Sayed so comfortable putting hands on another man like that?"

Communications trainer Jocelin Martinez, who provides media training and message development to clients, doesn’t feel El-Sayed needs to change his approach after he crushed Republican rival Mike Rogers in the critical Senate race for a seat Republicans were hoping to flip this election cycle.

"El-Sayed's communication style got him elected in Michigan because the moment requires leadership with gumption," Martinez told Fox News Digital.

The El-Sayed campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Big Ten conference commissioner gives tone deaf statement about 24-team College Football Playoff
World.content:
If it feels like it's a ridiculous time to be a college football fan, that's because it is.

While the AP Top 25 poll has become a running joke, at least fans can comfort themselves with the knowledge that it has little importance when it matters. Then the College Football Playoff selection committee released their poll this week and, well, to say it was indefensibly bad is a charitable overstatement.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

It's atrocious. It's humiliating. It's disgraceful. And it requires an entire overhaul of the selection committee process.

WE NEED TO ABOLISH THE CFP SELECTION COMMITTEE AFTER YET ANOTHER EMBARRASSMENT

Don't worry though, because starting in 2027, the powers that be have voted to make more money and further remove what made college football special with a participation trophy 24-team playoff. This proposal had widespread support among many coaches who will now have greater job security, as well as some conference commissioners who have never actually watched or followed college football.

Case in point? Big Ten conference commissioner Tony Petitti.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL MOVES CLOSER TO 24-GAME PLAYOFF AND THE DESTRUCTION OF THE BEST REGULAR SEASON IN SPORTS

Just this week, he defended the enlarged format with "logic" that is so disconnected from actual objective reality and history that it beggars belief.

In an interview with College Sports Radio on Sirius XM, Petitti explained his "thinking" on the 24-team playoff coming next season and how it will impact the importance of games across the sport, week in and week out.

"More games are going to matter," he said, inexplicably. "The way this format works is it’s got all different kinds of incentives, right? You’re going to fight like crazy to be inside the top 24, and then you want to get a home game, so you’re going to fight like crazy to be inside 16, and then you want to be inside eight, so you get a home game and a bye.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"So you’re always playing for something. There’s a lot at stake across all of this, and I think this year has just proven that trying to separate 12 teams from everybody else is just going to be incredibly difficult in the way college football is structured right now, and how tough it is to win the road. How the talent has kind of been more dispersed over many more programs, and then last thing is we just need to have give fans games that matter … I don’t think there’s any controversy in that at all."

It's worth raising the question, do the people who run college football actually follow the sport? Has Petitti ever watched college football? Part of what makes it special and unique, as opposed to the NFL's regular season slog, is that the games actually matter. There are stakes, because the margin for error is so small. Expanding the playoff removes those stakes, particularly for the superconference teams and especially the SEC.

This season, thanks to the selection committee's incompetence, we're already heading towards a three-loss SEC team, if not multiple three-loss teams, reaching the tournament. In a 24-team format, we'll have four-loss teams, if not five-loss SEC teams, reaching the top-24. Results are going to matter less than ever.

In a roundabout way, this might actually help lead to more games between marquee opponents, specifically because the outcome doesn't matter. But claiming that fans will feel the same level of intensity, stakes, excitement and energy over fighting to be in the top-8 so they can get a bye? That's insanity.

To be fair to Petitti, he did identify that home playoff games would be a big draw for fans.



"So I think look, and then when you get to the playoff, you know fans are going to show up," Petitti said. "These on-campus games are one of the best parts about it. Going the 16 on-campus games is going to be absolutely great. You know, when fan bases get a home game, especially if that’s unexpected when the season started, you’re going to see incredible reactions across college football."

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

The issue? They'll be a big draw because the regular season is now so meaningless. We've already seen big programs struggle with attendance this year, outside marquee opponents. Just imagine how little interest there'll be in USC-Maryland or Miami-Stanford when the results don't mean anything.

What makes all this even more frustrating is that everyone knows the actual motivation behind the playoff expansion: money. More playoff games means more high-value television properties to sell. The 24-team format ensures that programs from the Big Ten and SEC with large, passionate fanbases will have reasons to watch games, even when they're 6–4.

It's rewarding mediocrity in search of more financial rewards. Which is what college football has become in recent years.

World.title: Tourist hot spot faces housing revolt as locals demand cuts to vacation lodging
World.content:

One of Spain's most popular vacation islands is facing calls for a limit on tourist accommodations to curb crowding.

Jordi Mora, president of Pimem, a federation representing small and medium-sized businesses in Mallorca, said the island needs to take stronger steps to control tourism, according to the Majorca Daily Bulletin.

"We need to curb tourism, which includes reducing the total number of tourist beds," Mora told the outlet.

POPULAR DESTINATION CRACKS DOWN HARD ON TOURISTS AS NEW LIMITS THREATEN SUMMER GETAWAYS

Mallorca, one of the Balearic Islands, received some 13.5 million visitors in 2025, a significant number for an island measuring roughly 1,400 square miles, Fox News Digital previously reported.

Mora's proposal would include reducing the number of accommodations available in registered vacation rentals and taking stronger action against illegal rentals, the Majorca Daily Bulletin reported. Fox News Digital reached out to Pimem for comment.

Mora said some smaller hotel operators would support reducing accommodations if the changes were made through agreements and incentives.

"If this is approached through consensus and incentives, it is possible to move toward a more sustainable model," Mora said.

CLICK HERE TO 

A travel expert previously discussed the issues faced by the Balearic Island with Fox News Digital.

"Once a place goes viral, it can get flooded with visitors really quickly. It’s great that people want to explore new places, but those places aren’t always set up to handle that kind of attention," travel expert Jordi Lippe-McGraw said.

Mallorca's large visitor numbers have also brought other tourism concerns into focus.

"That’s when you start to see overcrowding, higher costs for locals and more pressure on the area overall."

Mallorca has also been exploring a shift toward attracting fewer visitors who spend more money.

Pedro Homar, managing director of Palma's tourism board, said Mallorca would prefer to attract wealthy American tourists, Fox News Digital reported.

"Tourism is our way of life," Homar told The Wall Street Journal. "The change of model is quality over quantity. We need to have fewer tourists who spend more."

American tourists in Spain spent about $410 per day this past July, compared with $240 for German visitors and $260 for British travelers, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Mora also said the island does not need more tourists to grow its economy.

"We must increase value and ensure that this growth benefits society as a whole," he told the Majorca Daily Bulletin.

The clash with residents is especially noticeable in Mallorca, where thousands took to the streets in June 2025 to protest the growth of tourism on the island, Fox News Digital reported at the time.

World.title: Head of DOJ Civil Rights Division resigns after GOP midterms loss
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Harmeet Dhillon, the Republican attorney who oversaw a massive overhaul of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, submitted her resignation Thursday.

Attorney General Todd Blanche posted on X that he has accepted Dhillon’s resignation. He wrote that she “defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor” and that the DOJ “is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors.”

Dhillon posted Thursday on X that the job had been the “honor of a lifetime.”

“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” she wrote.

The departure of Dhillon, who had a long history of working as an election lawyer for the GOP, comes just two days after Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections.

Under Dhillon’s leadership, the Civil Rights Division led some of the Trump administration’s most controversial legal maneuvers, including lawsuits that cited claims of discrimination at elite universities. The division declined to open a use-of-force investigation into the ICE officer who shot and killed Renee Nicole Good in Minnesota earlier this year.

Her office also filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., in an effort to obtain voter registration lists from the states in the months before the election, with federal judges dismissing 27 of those cases. Dhillon was a regular presence on conservative media in the run-up to Tuesday’s elections, promoting the work of the Civil Rights Division.

Dhillon is set to speak at the Donald Trump Ballroom at the Mar-a-Lago Club during the Conservative Political Action Committee’s Circle Retreat and Gala on Thursday.

Bloomberg Law first reported her resignation plans.

Dhillon’s office recently attempted to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former Trump administration official who testified before the House Jan. 6 committee about Trump’s actions during the Capitol siege.

Her office also brought a criminal case against former CNN journalist Don Lemon and protesters over a demonstration at a church in Minnesota under a statute historically used to protect reproductive rights facilities.

Stacey Young, the executive director of the group Justice Connection, called Dhillon “the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history,” and said in a statement that she “wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court.”

Dhillon “decimated” the Civil Rights Division, Young said, and called on the incoming Senate “to exercise its full advice and consent powers to ensure the next Assistant Attorney General fulfills the division’s congressional mandate to enforce all Americans’ civil rights diligently and fairly.”

Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel and the former chief of the Civil Rights Division during the Biden administration, said Dhillon “abdicated her responsibility to enforce our nation’s federal civil rights laws and destroyed the crown jewel of the Justice Department.”

Clarke said in a statement that Dhillon “abandoned cases, purged the work force and weaponized the Division to target institutions to achieve illegitimate, partisan goals” and that the NAACP would demand that her replacement “respect the agency’s sacred mission, enforce the law fairly, and protect our civil rights.”

World.title: Wisconsin reports its first measles death in decades, the third in the U.S. this week
World.content:
An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the state health department said Thursday — the third measles-related death reported in the U.S. this week.

It’s Wisconsin’s first measles-related death since 1990, the Health Service Department said, adding that a coroner had listed measles as the infant’s immediate cause of death.

The news came just one day after Pennsylvania’s Health Department reported another measles-associated death there — the state’s sixth this year. It said Wednesday that an unvaccinated resident in Jefferson County who tested positive for measles had died.

On Monday, New York health officials announced that a child in Lewis County had died of measles. Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency over measles in early October.

In total, the U.S. has recorded eight measles-associated deaths this year, according to state health department data. It’s the highest measles death toll in the country since 1991.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed four of those deaths. It says it will update its count “as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed.”

None of the eight people who have died were vaccinated, according to state health departments; some were ineligible because of their age or health status. Typically, the first dose of the vaccine is administered around a child’s first birthday.

Before the outbreaks in Wisconsin, New York and Pennsylvania, none of the states had recorded a measles death in more than 30 years.

Dr. Stephanie Schauer, the immunization program director at the Wisconsin health department, said some chains of transmission started with residents traveling out of state to events like funerals and weddings.

The department is recommending an early dose of the measles vaccine for infants as young as 6 months who are at increased risk of exposure. Around 500 such early doses have been administered since August, Schauer said.

Around 85% of kindergartners in Wisconsin have been vaccinated against measles — below the national average of 92%. Experts say 95% is the threshold needed to keep the population protected.

“We can actually eliminate transmission of measles in the community by getting enough people vaccinated,” said Dr. Ryan Westergaard, the state epidemiologist for communicable diseases. “We have the opportunity to take a disease that could affect everybody and essentially make it go away.”

The health department said it has sent out 2,000 additional measles vaccine doses to local health departments over the last few months.

World.title: Nithya Raman ousts incumbent Karen Bass in LA mayor's race, CBS News projects
World.content:
Councilmember Nithya Raman will be Los Angeles' next mayor after defeating incumbent Karen Bass in the November general election, CBS News projects.

Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day.

The last time a challenger ousted a sitting LA mayor happened in 2005, when Antonio Villaraigosa defeated incumbent James Hahn.

Nithya Raman defeats incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral election, CBS News projects. CBS News

Raman released a video statement on Thursday afternoon saying she is deeply honored to be the next mayor of LA.

"Thank you to the thousands of people who knocked on doors, sent texts, made phone calls, convinced their neighbors to believe in the promise of this big, beautiful, joyful city that we get to call home," the video said.

Raman spoke directly to people who voted for Bass or didn't vote at all, saying she is "going to City Hall to work every single day to earn your trust, and to earn your trust in this city again."

In the video, Raman also paid tribute to Bass, thanking her for her decades of service and highlighting her as the first woman mayor of LA.

"She has served Los Angeles for so many decades and I know so many people, not just across this city but across this country, are grateful for her dedication to the promise of Los Angeles," Raman said.

Bass released a statement on Thursday morning conceding to Raman, saying she called her to congratulate her on the victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken. I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition," Bass wrote.

Bass thanked her supporters and other leaders who helped during her campaign. She added that she will continue to "ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

Raman, a Democratic socialist, has been riding her momentum after pushing past Spencer Pratt in the June primary, but suffered a setback with voters a week before the election, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times.

A survey released by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the LA Times shortly before the election showed Bass and Raman tied, with 40% support among likely voters.

Bass and Raman became frontrunners after the primary election when they rallied ahead of third-place candidate Spencer Pratt.

Councilmember Nithya Raman

Raman announced her surprise bid for mayor in February after previously endorsing Bass' reelection bid.

During the primary, Raman called her campaign a "long shot" before ultimately overtaking Pratt to face Bass in the general election.

Before being elected to Los Angeles City Council in 2020, Raman served as the co-chair of the Silver Lake Neighborhood Council Homelessness Committee and co-founded a homeless advocacy nonprofit.

One of her most notable acts in office came in 2025, when she introduced a motion capping maximum annual rent increases for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments built before 1978. It eventually passed 13-2. She said she hoped to undertake similar work to help small businesses.

"I congratulate Nithya Raman on her victory. The voters have spoken, and now it's time to govern," LA County Supervisor Kathryn Barger wrote in a statement. "Whether it's homelessness, public safety, housing affordability, or preparing for the Olympics, we need to work together. I'm remaining focused on finding common ground and delivering real results for the people we serve."

Mayor Karen Bass

After serving more than two decades in public office as a congresswoman and as LA's 43rd Mayor, Bass said this race will be her last campaign for office.

Bass was raised in LA with her three brothers. She began her professional career as a nurse and physician assistant, where she later founded the Community Coalition to help underserved residents of South LA battle substance abuse, poverty and crime.

She kickstarted her career in politics in 2004 as a member of the California Assembly, where she became the first Black woman to serve as Speaker of a state legislative body. She left the Assembly in 2010 to run for Congress, where she served in the House for 12 years.

Leading up to the primary election, Bass received endorsements from notable politicians including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Nearly a week before the November election, billionaire Rick Caruso threw his support behind his former rival in the 2022 mayoral race and vowed to vote for her in November.

"For the love of LA, I must put the past behind me because this election must be about our future," Caruso said in a post to X. "I will be casting my ballot for Mayor Karen Bass."

He also said in the video that he had concerns about Raman that were not "much about ideology, but about competence."

World.title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
World.content:
Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.

But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.

Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:

Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.

Republicans won 24 seats and Democrats won 14 seats in the midterms, making Texas a dummymander.

Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Eight Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night. Republicans only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.

North Carolina

Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of Thursday, nine Democrats had won — including Davis — and CBS News estimated five districts with Republican incumbents were toss-ups, making the state a dummymander.

Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives.

As of Thursday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 6th District is a toss-up and the 5th District race will go to a runoff. If Democrats win either of those districts, Louisiana will be a dummymander.

Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled, making Alabama a dummymander.

Tennessee

Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. As of Thursday, Republicans had won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, and one seat is estimated as a toss-up. If Democrats win the remaining toss-up race, the state's House delegation will remain the same.

Florida

Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. As of Thursday, Republicans had won 17 seats, Democrats had won seven and there were four districts that CBS News estimated were toss-ups. If Democrats win any of the toss-up races, Florida will be a dummymander.

Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.

Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.

Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held onto their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.

South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Two other races are considered toss-ups.

California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. As of Thursday, Democrats won in 44 districts, while CBS News estimates another four are likely Democratic. Republicans have won two districts and another two are likely Republican.

Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.

Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.

Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.

Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.

Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won eight seats and Republicans won three.

Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

World.title: Feds warn of potential cyberattacks on industrial refrigerators
World.content:
The U.S. government encouraged grocery stores, healthcare facilities and other businesses that use commercial refrigeration to tighten their security measures on Thursday following a series of cyberattacks that remotely changed the temperatures of commercial freezers and fridges across Europe.

Five federal agencies issued a joint notice, warning of "ongoing cyber threat activity" that could target refrigeration systems used across healthcare, agriculture, transportation and other U.S. industries.

Bad actors globally are exploiting vulnerabilities and weaknesses in refrigeration systems that are "unpatched" or connected to the internet, the agencies said.

"If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system," the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said in a statement, which was issued in conjunction with the FBI, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Agriculture and Department of Transportation.

In a fact sheet, CISA said businesses that rely on industrial refrigeration should take precautions to protect their systems, including changing passwords, disconnecting system devices from the internet and making software updates to address vulnerabilities.

"Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target," Chris Butera, acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity at CISA, said in a statement.

The agencies did not specify if any refrigeration systems have been targeted in the U.S.

Wave of refrigeration attacks

The warning follows reports of refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases in August. The Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, a U.S. federal law enforcement unit, has launched an investigation into the incidents, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News on Thursday.

Similar incidents have occurred around Europe in recent weeks, with hackers targeting fridges and freezers across numerous grocery chains. Food retailers reported unexpected temperature spikes in their refrigeration systems, causing food to spoil in stores in Luxembourg, Belgium and Sweden.

Officials in France, which has also been hit by grocery store cyberattacks, said on Wednesday that its national emergency blood supply network was targeted by hackers who tried to raise refrigeration temperatures at several blood banks.

Joshua Corman, executive-in-residence for public safety and resilience at the Institute for Security and Technology, a security think tank, said he expects more such attacks, warning that refrigeration systems used by medical labs, grocery stores and bulk warehouses in the U.S. could be compromised.

"There's only so many players that do industrial-level refrigeration, and they're likely also just as vulnerable," he told CBS News.

World.title: Democrats have flipped over 40 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
World.content:
Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Tuesday by flipping more than three dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.

Winners in dozens of races have yet to be projected by CBS News.

So far, 42 districts have shifted to Democrats and two have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:

Upsets

In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz of Indiana speaks at the Capitol on April 26, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Rematches

A few Democrats won against Republicans who they'd faced before — in one case, multiple times.

Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria of Virginia speaks at a hearing on the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, on Dec. 19, 2022. J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Northeastern Battlegrounds

Both parties invested in districts in the Northeast, including seats with a history of swinging from one party to another, and a competitive Pennsylvania seat that was held by an overperforming Republican for a decade.

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania, speaks during a news conference at the Capitol on March 6, 2024. Tierney L. Cross / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Tight Midwestern Districts

A few Midwestern states will have dramatically different congressional delegations starting next year.

Michigan Democrat William Lawrence greets supporters at an election night event in Lansing on Nov. 3, 2026. AP Photo/Kristen Norman

Western States

Some Western cities and states elected their first Democrats to the House in years.

Montana's 1st District : Former smokejumper and union leader

: Former Utah's 1st District : Democrat Ben McAdams won the newly drawn district, which encompasses Salt Lake City and its suburbs. After a lengthy legal battle, court-ordered redistricting produced one Democratic-leaning district in the state, giving the party its best opportunity in nearly a decade to flip one of the state's four House seats.

: Democrat Ben McAdams won the newly drawn district, which encompasses Salt Lake City and its suburbs. After a lengthy legal battle, court-ordered redistricting produced one Democratic-leaning district in the state, giving the party its best opportunity in nearly a decade to flip one of the state's four House seats. Colorado's 5th District : GOP Rep. Jeff Crank lost reelection to Jessica Killin, who will be the first Democrat to ever represent the Colorado Springs-area district. Crank won by nearly 14 points in 2024, but the area has shifted left over the years.

: GOP Rep. Jeff Crank lost reelection to Jessica Killin, who will be the first Democrat to ever represent the Colorado Springs-area district. Crank won by nearly 14 points in 2024, but the area has shifted left over the years. Colorado's 8th District : Democrat Manny Rutinel defeated

: Democrat Manny Rutinel Arizona's 1st District : Democrat Amish Shah beat Republican former NFL kicker Jay Feely in a seat left open by GOP Rep. David Schweikert's run for governor. Two years ago, Schweikert narrowly defeated Shah.

: Democrat Amish Shah beat Republican former NFL kicker Jay Feely in a seat left open by GOP Rep. David Schweikert's run for governor. Two years ago, Schweikert narrowly defeated Shah. Arizona's 6th District: Democrat JoAnna Mendoza defeated two-term GOP Rep. Juan Ciscomani in this competitive district, which stretches from the Tucson-area suburbs down to the southeastern corner of the state along the U.S. Mexico border.

Sam Forstag Courtesy of Sam for Montana campaign

Texas

Republicans in the Lone Star State redrew their House maps last year with the goal of picking up as many as five seats that were held by Democrats. Ultimately, one seat flipped to the GOP, and two red districts were captured by Democrats. The shifts coincided with a slate of statewide Democratic wins in Texas, which elected its first Democratic senator and governor in decades.

Bobby Pulido, a Latin Grammy winner and Democratic candidate for Texas' 15th Congressional District, at a campaign event in Weslaco, Texas, on Oct. 25, 2026. Gabriel V. Cardenas /AFP via Getty Images

California

Voters in California approved their own redistricting plan after Texas redrew its maps, aiming at moving several California seats to the left. Democrats have picked up all five of the seats they had hoped to flip.

Republican Rep. David Valadao of California on May 12, 2022. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

North Carolina

A handful of House seats in North Carolina changed hands, including some upsets in places that were tilted to the GOP in redistricting a few years ago, part of a wave in the Tar Heel State as Roy Cooper decisively won the state's Senate race.

North Carolina Democratic congressional candidate Jamie Ager greets a supporter in Asheville on Oct. 31, 2026. Allison Joyce / Getty Images

Other Districts

World.title: Lawler defeated in New York battleground district
World.content:
Washington — Democrat Cait Conley defeated two-term Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, winning a highly competitive seat in New York's Hudson Valley region, CBS News projected.

Lawler's loss is another setback for Republicans. CBS News has projected that Democrats will take control of the House in January with a wide majority.

Lawler called Conley to concede Tuesday, though vote-counting continued for longer than expected due to issues at polling precincts in Westchester County.

"I have never been afforded in any of my elections a concession on election night and I fundamentally believe it's the right thing to do," he said. "And so I congratulate Cait on her win and wish her well as our next member of Congress."

Before redistricting shuffled the boundaries in several states for the 2026 election, Lawler was one of just three Republicans who won districts carried by Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024.

A West Point graduate, Conley served six tours overseas before joining the National Security Council and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency during the Biden administration. Though she grew up in a neighboring area, she moved to the 17th District months before announcing her campaign.

In their Sept. 30 debate, Conley said she supports continued military aid to Israel and did not believe that Israel's actions in Gaza constitute a genocide — positions at odds with many in her party, but which could be crucial given the district's demographics.

Lawler has held the lower Hudson Valley seat since 2023 after narrowly ousting Democratic incumbent Sean Patrick Maloney, who served as House Democrats' campaign chief. In 2025, Lawler considered running for New York governor, but opted to run for a third term as Republicans sought to hang on to the crucial battleground seat.

Lawler has cast himself as a moderate who has been willing to buck his party, including on immigration protections for Haitians and on extending the now-expired enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits. Lawler also played a central role in securing a temporary increase to the cap on state and local tax deductions — a bipartisan issue on the East and West coasts — as part of President Trump's sweeping tax and spending package, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

In the recent debate, Lawler tried to appeal to voters on both sides, claiming that he ranks "among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress."

But Lawler has also embraced Mr. Trump, campaigning with him in May even as he risked alienating swing voters who are pessimistic about the president's handling of the economy and Iran war.

World.title: These are the races in the House and Senate that haven't been called yet
World.content:
These are the races in the House and Senate that haven't been called yet

Loading...

Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined and several races are still outstanding.

A few in California are being contested by two candidates in the same party. So it's clear which party will hold the seat, even if it's not clear who will win. Others are too close to call or there aren't enough ballots counted to know which candidate will prevail. In many places in the country, it takes a while to count votes. That's normal and expected.

Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called in the House by The Associated Press:

Sponsor Message

Loading...

In the Senate, there are two races outstanding, Alaska and Mississippi. Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting and no candidate in the four-person race has achieved a 50% majority in the count, it may proceed to another round of counting later this month. Mississippi uses a more traditional electoral system but a large number of provisional ballots — called affidavit ballots in the state — are taking time to count. Less than 2,000 votes separate the top two candidates in that race.

World.title: Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine
World.content:
Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine

toggle caption i Samuel Corum/Getty Images

First lady Melania Trump hosted a rare meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize a temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine.

The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the divisions of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace."

Trump has accomplished something that has so far eluded her husband - helping broker a temporary ceasefire and bringing together representatives of the two sides in acknowledgement of the human costs of the war.

Sponsor Message

The White House sees it as a diplomatic breakthrough, but some European analysts worry the efforts can backfire.

The temporary reprieve, which expired on Sunday, enabled humanitarian aid to reach the city while allowing hundreds of residents to be evacuated.

Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special envoy, thanked the first lady. He said Putin personally gave the instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the ceasefire.

"On behalf of President Putin, on behalf of the people of the Russian Federation, we would like to thank first lady Melania Trump for her distinguished humanitarian role in resolving a key situation and resolving this humanitarian issue," he said.

Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets presented Melania Trump with an award for her humanitarian work. The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, is Ukraine's highest award for women.

"I have only one request from all Ukrainian nation," Lubinets said, "please continue doing your wonderful work and support people."

The event comes just days before the U.S. leads a new round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.

President Trump also met with Dmitriev at the White House.

Trump told reporters that the sides were close to reaching a deal.

Sponsor Message

"It's going to be an agreement. It's going to be a big agreement, ‌and ⁠it's going to involve more than Ukraine," he said. "I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's ⁠going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."

Heather Conley, who worked on European issues in President George W. Bush's State Department, supports all efforts to help suffering Ukrainians, but she also said the U.S. must be careful not to normalize Russia's bad behavior.

"In this White House ceremony, we were honoring the Russians that were the cause of both the occupation of Oleshky, the starvation of Oleshky, and now we're honoring them for allowing aid to come into Oleshky," said Conley, who is now a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. "The more we create this equivalency where the Russians and the Ukrainians are equal in this crisis, it is putting this thing upside down."

World.title: How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts
World.content:
How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts

toggle caption i A.M STEWART/AFP via Getty Images

The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates.

Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.

As of Thursday, the AP had called nine of the state's 14 House seats for Democrats and none for Republicans. It's a startling result for a delegation that went into Tuesday with 10 Republicans and four Democrats.

Races called Thursday that flipped from Republican to Democratic control included:



High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson over first-term incumbent Rep. Addison McDowell in the Triad's 6th Congressional District.

Former West Virginia State Senator Richard Ojeda over National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Rep. Richard Hudson in the 9th Congressional District.

Paul Barringer over first-term incumbent Rep. Brad Knott in the 13th Congressional District, which wraps around the Raleigh exurbs.

LaKesha Womack over first-term incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, who previously served as speaker of the N.C. House of Representatives, in the 14th Congressional District.

Sponsor Message

North Carolina's Congressional map was redrawn in 2023 to significantly favor Republican candidates, and these four districts performed that way in 2024. The 14th District was the closest in that election, with Moore winning by about 16%, while the 6th District was the least competitive, with McDowell winning by more than 38%.

One of the candidates vying to replace Hudson as NRCC chair is U.S. Rep. Brian Jack, a Georgia Republican.

He wrote in a letter to fellow House Republicans that fellow GOP lawmakers may have contributed to the challenging environment. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, won the race for North Carolina's open U.S. Senate seat by nearly 20%.

Statewide Races What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina North Carolina Blue Wave Listen · 4:17 4:17

"When Senate Republicans withdrew support from North Carolina weeks ago, they created a cascade that likely swept away many of our colleagues from that state," Jack wrote.

The AP also called northeastern North Carolina's 1st Congressional District for incumbent Democrat Rep. Don Davis on Thursday.

Loading...

That's a district legislative Republicans redrew last year in an effort to make it easier for GOP candidates to win there, pulling Republican-leaning counties from the state's 3rd Congressional District to do so.

Yet as of Thursday, Davis was leading Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout by more than 10,000 votes. That's a larger margin than he won by in 2024.

North Carolina's 3rd Congressional District is one of five in the state that remain uncalled, with incumbent Republican Greg Murphy leading Democrat Raymond Smith by just 233 votes in a district where Democrats didn't even run a candidate in 2024. That race is likely headed for a recount.

In the 5th Congressional District, Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard is leading 11-term Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx by 99 votes — that's another race that may go to a recount.

If all of the remaining results hold, the state's congressional delegation would flip from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to 10 Democrats and four Republicans.

World.title: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
World.content:
