Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse

toggle caption i Jorge Saenz/AP

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.

The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.

Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation later Thursday, clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial.

Sponsor Message

Opposition senators were still demanding a trial, arguing that allowing Peña to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution.

toggle caption i Ted Shaffrey/AP

As lawmakers debated his impeachment, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations that the Trump administration lifted last year.

Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.

"I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."

The turmoil has hit Paraguay's currency. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the U.S. dollar Thursday, bringing its losses this week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data.

Sponsor Message

From star lender to seized bank

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.

"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.

Sponsor Message

As recently as last month, Peña defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

Long lines outside branches but customers are locked out

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank announced the lender's seizure Tuesday, beginning a process to transfer deposits and recoverable assets to other banks before liquidating what remained.

Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.

Officials have appealed for calm. Under a law rushed through Congress on Wednesday, a state guarantee fund must repay stranded depositors within five business days, starting Thursday with small accounts of up to about $1,600 held by customers with no debts to Ueno. The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97% of clients.

On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, jailed pending trial and two others placed under house arrest. Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud, alleging that Ueno made large loans to related companies without adequate guarantees and diverted some of the money to other group businesses.

Gustale's lawyer pushed back on the charges, arguing that senior executives had relied on staff for lending decisions. "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan," José Fernández Zacur told local media.

Sponsor Message

Protesters in the streets

Still in their Ueno uniforms, young employees burned their credit cards and cursed Peña outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages. Peña's resignation did little to calm them. Many vowed to keep protesting until lawmakers finished impeaching him, saying his departure alone would neither bring accountability nor return their money.

"Let the impeachment process take place and let him lose his immunity," said Adolfo Villalba, one of the protesters on Thursday.

The Labor Ministry estimates the collapse has affected about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and its related businesses.

Many saw Ueno's collapse not just as reckless banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on Transparency International's latest index of perceived corruption.

"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said Belarmino Balbuena, one of thousands who marched on Congress in the capital, Asunción, on Wednesday.

The crowds shouted, "We want your head, Peña!" Their signs branded him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded, "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets to push them back.

At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. Across the capital, fresh graffiti called politicians thieves.

World.title: Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns
World.content:
Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge, during which she radically reshaped the unit's mission, oversaw the mass exodus of career staff, and aggressively pursued President Trump's agenda.

Dhillon is the first senior department official to depart the Trump administration since Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in midterm elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, announced Dhillon's resignation and thanked her for her service.

"She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he wrote. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

Sponsor Message

In her own statement, Dhillon said the job had been "the honor of a lifetime."

"We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women in girls' sports, and so much more," she added.

During her tenure, Dhillon implemented dramatic changes in the Civil Rights Division, pushing out roughly 300 career attorneys, hiring inexperienced ideological allies to replace them, and using the division's enforcement powers to advance Trump's MAGA policies.

The changes marked a dramatic shift for the division, which was created some 70 years ago during the civil rights movement to end racial segregation in the U.S. For decades, it fought to protect the constitutional rights of all Americans across all aspects of life, from housing and employment to education and policing.

Dhillon, a conservative attorney and Trump loyalist, came into office with a different view. In her eyes, the division had narrowed its mission in recent decades to only protecting the rights of people of color, and she promptly shifted to aggressively pursuing conservative priorities.

"We don't just slow down the woke," she said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."

Under her leadership, the division redirected its energies to enforce Trump's executive orders, including ending the alleged radical indoctrination in schools, defending women from "gender ideology extremism," and combatting antisemitism and purported anti-Christian bias.

In the run-up to the midterm elections, the Civil Rights Division sued dozens of states demanding they turn over voter information — in furtherance of Trump's allegations of voter fraud.

Election officials pushed back, and courts tossed the department's lawsuits.

The division also accused numerous universities and law schools of discriminating against white and Asian students, and sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.

Sponsor Message

In an email to division staff, Dhillon said she informed Trump in early October that she planned to return to private practice after the midterms, and now is the time to do so.

"I'm proud of all we've accomplished during this time to ensure our nation's civil rights laws protect every American," she wrote in the email, a copy of which was obtained by NPR. "I'm also grateful for the hard work of the dedicated employees within the Division and the rest of the Department of Justice."

For many division veterans who were highly critical of Dhillon's treatment of career staff and her enforcement goals, her departure was a welcome development.

"Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history," said Stacey Young, a former division attorney. "Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court."

"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it," said Young, who now heads who Justice Connection, a group of department alumni that provides support to DOJ employees.

World.title: Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?
World.content:
Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?

toggle caption i Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images for BET

After spending three hours counting the pores on Elizabeth Holmes' and Nathan Fielder's faces, I couldn't help but think how perfect Yung Miami's "Spend Dat" would've played over the closing credits. Whatever you feel about the veracity of the protagonist in the blockbuster doc You Can See Everything, there is no doubt about her innate ability to cop and blow money fast. She's probably about as familiar with Diddy's favorite City Girl as she is with Abbott & Costello. But a scammer of such ill repute deserves an apropos theme song. Hell, maybe we all do.

Sponsor Message

When people complain about hip-hop no longer being political, what they're really talking about is commercial rap's long-fizzled countercultural agenda. The politics of consumption and corruption however have never enjoyed a louder ringing endorsement. Like a billionaire hogging the bully pulpit. To that end, no song in 2026 comes closer to mimicking the feeling of being the violated and the violator. On its face, "Spend Dat" is a get-money flex dedicated to all the "scammers" and "booster b*****s." But behind that seductive veneer is the sadomasochistic loop of late-stage capitalism's long, punishing con. An inflation indicator like no other, it's easily our most American anthem of the year. And we're all transfixed, nodding along in unblinking commitment to the charade.

The video for "Spend Dat" feels like a throwback to the early 2000s, when making it rain in strip clubs was still obligatory signposting for selling the dream. It almost feels trite now that prediction markets allow us to place digital bets on democracy and buy-now, pay-later loans keep expanding on our freedom to fall deeper in debt. At least a good lap dance came with a tangible return on investment. Now we're all just being teased to death.

YouTube

When India.Arie echoed the public denouncement of "Spend Dat" — which included a call for Black folk to boycott the Billboard-charting song of the summer — another film, I Love Boosters, had just hit streaming. Unlike the aforementioned documentary on the blonde-haired, blue-eyed, white-collar scammer Holmes, rapper-turned-director Boots Riley's fictional narrative centered on the supposed scourge of the hood. In it, Keke Palmer plays an illegit booster, selling high-end fenced clothing out of the abandoned fast-food chicken joint she's squatting in while harboring her own fashionable aspirations. It takes an international worker-led intervention — and a sci-fi bopgun full of Marxist intentions — for her to realize the minor disruption she and her shoplifting girlfriends are causing is but a necessary cog in the ever-churning, exploitative wheel of global capitalism.

Sponsor Message

What Riley wants us all to understand, as an avowed communist who switched his weapon of choice from fronting Bay Area rap group The Coup to writing screenplays, is that we the people are hardly the problem. Even when sufferers turn into self-styled hustlers out of desperation instead of pooling their collective power. Like WEB DuBois before him, Riley calls his art propaganda. And he's equally adamant about calling art on the other end of the spectrum of propaganda, too. "When The Coup first came out they would call us a political rap group. And we'd be like, 'No,' " he said on a recent episode of Novara Media's podcast Downstream. "Don't call us that unless you're calling everybody that. Because what it then made it seem like was as if everything else was just what it is." Rather, art magnifying the status quo is not some benign representation of a fixed reality but an uncritical regurgitation of everything indoctrinated by the moneyed elite.

When the controversy surrounding "Spend Dat" reached a fever pitch earlier this summer, it came with the usual diatribe. The song was criticized for being culturally degrading. Even India.Arie caught a bunch of flak for stating the obvious when she said, "Everything you listen to see or eat is going to influence you." I don't blame anybody Black for getting in their feelings over the seemingly negative portrayals or stereotypical depiction centered in rap. But the buck doesn't stop there. It never has. "We are bound by all sorts of customs that have come down as second-hand soul clothes of white patrons," as DuBois so eloquently stated 100 years ago this month in his essay Criteria of Negro Art. "We are ashamed of sex and we lower our eyes when people will talk of it," he says, concluding with this thought: "Our worst side has been so shamelessly emphasized that we are denying we have or ever had a worst side."

Sponsor Message

YouTube

The same week "Spend Dat" went platinum, Yung Miami appeared on "The Breakfast Club" to promote the release of her solo debut, Watch Dis. When asked about the criticism the song received, she defended it as inspirational music "that builds you up to want to be somebody." Rap may have started at the bottom. But at some point the script flipped. The systems hip-hop was oriented to rebel against became the metric for its success. The victors, in this case, were found striving for the same spoils. Having finally achieved the market share and visibility we'd been denied for decades, we became centrists: a marginalized culture subsumed by the mainstream. Commercial rap made itself a useful tool of the establishment, and the perfect racially coded scapegoat.

If the American Dream really is a pyramid scheme, as commonly critiqued, all hail the original scammers who bricked up the foundation. Even with their fuzzy slave-owner math (discounting Blacks as three-fifths human) and gender restrictions on equal rights (ratified while rocking powdered wigs), the nation's so-called founders created a system even the lowest caste could be constrained and cajoled into aspiring to.

It reminds me of the funniest meme I encountered online last week: a comic strip calling cap on the promise of Black capitalism. It pictures two brothers chopping it up, with one plainly stating, "You can't buy your way out of a system that was built on selling you." Totally undeterred, the other replies back, "Well, I'm gonna try!" before invoking the Black power era's "by any means necessary" rhetoric. In the next panel, Malcolm X expresses frustration over his words being misused to validate participation in the futile American experiment.

We've been hoodwinked, indeed. Bamboozled. Led astray. Run amok and flat-out deceived like a mug.

The grift is so complete that it's almost impossible to distinguish the mark from the actual con artist. Whether it's a convicted felon hiding fraudulence behind white tears, or a ride-or-die who bossed up with the boosters and got it off the muscle. In a year when prediction markets and predatory installment loans sucked us all dry, inflation skyrocketed and tech billionaires quickened the apocalypse, an ode to America's undying hustle and flow might be the closing credits theme we all deserve.

World.title: Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term
World.content:
Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term

toggle caption i Alberto Pezzali/AP

London — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges involving four women on allegations dating back more than 20 years.

Judge Joel Bennathan said the British actor-comedian faces a "significant" prison term when he is sentenced Monday. Brand had been free, but the judge rejected a bail request because of the possibility he might flee and he was taken into custody.

"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."

Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said at trial.

Sponsor Message

Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.

He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."

The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.

Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

Sponsor Message

In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, but cleared of orally raping her in a restroom.

He was also found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 and of anally raping a fan he met backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009.

The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an  in 2009.

Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party's annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men's bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.

The Associated Press doesn't name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

Brand said in the witness box that the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.

"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.

Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.

Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.

His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defense, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

World.title: First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
World.content:
First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

The share of first-time homebuyers remains at a near-record low of 22% as a housing shortage and high prices sideline many, according to a new report by the National Association of Realtors. But those who are managing to buy are older and wealthier than in the past, and 1 in 10 paid all cash, a record high since such data was collected starting in 2003.

"Inheritances are really driving this," said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist at the NAR.

First-time buyers who paid all-cash were more likely than those who financed a house to use an inheritance (28%) or proceeds from the sale of an inherited property (21%). They were also older.

Sponsor Message

NAR finds the median age of all first-time buyers remains at 40, a record high. For first-time buyers who financed a purchase it was 38, while for those who paid all-cash it was 54. "They waited a significant period of time for that generational transfer of wealth to come through," Lautz said.

For first-time buyers overall, personal savings was the biggest source of funding for a down payment. But in another shift, more people used assets – like a 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency – than financial help from family or friends. Older buyers have had more time to save up, Lautz said, but she thinks there's another factor: "I think it's uncomfortable to ask mom and dad for a gift or loan when you're hitting 40 versus your young 30s."

The share of first time buyers using an inheritance is likely to grow in coming years as boomers reach their 80's and beyond. As the report noted, "there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth."

Real estate agents around the country are seeing the change.

"I would say in the first 15 years of my career, I saw virtually zero first-time home buyers paying all cash," said Jason Miller, a broker with Trust Real Estate Company in St. Cloud, Minn.

But he's had a number of them since the COVID-19 pandemic, when homebuying surged. "They knew they had to absolutely have the most sterling offer possible to compete in the competitive marketplace," he said.

High mortgage rates are also driving all-cash bids, Miller said, since they make it far more expensive to finance a home for 30 years. And not all families wait until death to pass on wealth. Miller sees more clients getting help from family members who may have paid off their own home, or have equity in a second property they can sell and "are gifting some or all of that money." They're viewing it as a kind of "future inheritance," he said.

Sponsor Message

For some younger first-time buyers, relatives may only be "lending them the cash" to make a bid more attractive, said Nate Johnson, a broker associate with RedKey Realty Leaders in St. Louis. Even with much of the national housing market in a major slump, he said his local market is still intensely competitive for buyers.

"They just know that if we're looking at five or six offers on the table, let's call it 10 offers on the table, which is not uncommon…maybe three of those offers will be all cash," he said.

After closing on a property, Johnson has seen some buyers refinance into a mortgage and pay back their family member.

The rise of all-cash offers makes the market even tougher for those who struggle to save up for a down payment with today's sky-high home prices.

"For a long time I thought I wanted to buy a house," said Seth Daphne Esmeson, who lives in Seattle and will soon turn 33. They and their spouse have good jobs, but also debt, including a car payment and student loans. Not only does Esmeson think they may never be in a position to buy, they've also decided it does not make sense at today's prices.

toggle caption i Jane Corbit

"Being that debt burdened, and also having to fix things on your home, like, it sounds really terrible," they said.

Esmeson is also not convinced that home equity would outpace other investments. They like their current rental and landlord so are sticking with it for now.

Still, it's frustrating that the housing market worked better for previous generations. "We have the short end of the deal," they said, and "the gap is expanding."

There's probably only one way they might ever be able to buy. "If I received an inheritance," they said. But "I love my mom dearly and I don't want to look forward to that, or really want to strategize around that."

World.title: Liberal government's 2026 budget doubles down on plan to build economy at home
World.content:
Poilievre says budget should have been focused on 'real people' and affordability

Budget 2026: Opposition leaders express disappointment in Liberal government's plan for Canada's economy

Cheers — and jeers — in the House as Champagne talks trust after budget release | Duration closed caption 2:00

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne drew applause and heckling from opposition members as he spoke on Thursday, promising a federal budget that will unlock Canada's 'full growth' potential.

World.title: From groceries to tax credits, how much is in the federal budget for your wallet?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

From a grocery benefit expansion to rental assistance and payments for more low-wage workers, Thursday's federal budget includes a number of measures aimed at making life more affordable.

But they were still eclipsed by a focus on investment.

One of the main direct pocketbook measures is a top-up to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit — a pre-existing program that gives quarterly payments to Canadians with low and modest incomes.

The top-up will increase those payments by 50 per cent for the 2026-27 program year. Combined with previous increases, a single person could get up to $1,290. A couple with two children could get up to $2,570.

The government says the program will give Canadians collectively $4.1 billion more in support to help pay for essentials.

The plan also expands the Canada caregiver credit. Budget 2026 makes the tax credit refundable, helping caregivers who have incomes so low that they don't pay tax. The move would help extend the credit — which could give caregivers up to $1,260 back annually — to about 180,000 people who don't currently get it.

For those saving for retirement, the government also plans to merge Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) and Registered Retirement Income Funds (RRIFs). Right now, when Canadians turn 71 and can no longer contribute to their RRSPs, they have to convert that account into an RRIF and begin withdrawing from it.

The "RRSP-for-life" plan would eliminate the need to switch — and would also allow a surviving partner of the RRSP holder to transfer those savings tax free.

Other measures aimed at bringing down costs were already announced. The government suspended the excise tax on fuel — which saves Canadians about 10 cents a litre on the cost of gasoline — in April, and later extended that to the end of January 2027. The tax will come back at a 50 per cent rate until the end of March 2027 and then return to its regular level.

In all, the budget shows the government earmarked $5.3 billion on that relief at the pumps.

WATCH | Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel: Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel | Duration closed caption 6:06 Crude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are slowly recovering, so why is the price of diesel skyrocketing? The National's Eli Glasner breaks down what’s causing the increase, and why diesel prices likely won't drop anytime soon.

Overall, the federal government's fiscal plan pledges $22 billion for new spending on affordability measures.

But aside from some relief on things like groceries and gas — measures that will support Canadians in the short term — economist Armine Yalnizyan says there's little in the budget for everyday people.

"It's not like they're doing nothing," Yalnizyan said. "But the short answer is Canadians are going to need a lot of patience because this budget is not there to support them."

Some Canadians are hopeful the measures could help them in their daily lives.

Sushama Chakraverty said that any potential savings on food are welcome, especially since the grocery aisle and fuel pump are the main places squeezing her budget lately.

"We'll take any of the rebates we can get, right?" Chakraverty told CBC News in downtown Toronto after the budget details were announced.

Many might not be surprised at the level of affordability measures announced, though. In a survey of 1,809 Canadian adults conducted by Abacus Data ahead of the budget, only 10 per cent expected it to make things better for their household — and another 30 per cent said they thought it would make affordability worse.

Almost two-thirds of respondents said affordability was one of the most important issues facing the country.

WATCH | Cost of living measures 'missing in action' from federal budget, NDP leader says: Cost of living measures 'missing in action' from federal budget, NDP leader says | Duration closed caption 1:18 While he applauded its measures to combat homelessness, NDP Leader Avi Lewis said Prime Minister Mark Carney's second federal budget is lacking 'the things that lower Canadians' actual cost of living.'

The biggest-ticket spending on affordability is related to housing, with $11.2 billion dedicated to ending homelessness within 10 years. That money would help build supportive and transitional housing and provide support to facilities that care for people in a mental health or substance abuse crisis.

What questions do you have about the federal budget? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.

To help low-income renters, the government is also renewing the Canada Housing Benefit for 10 years to support Canadians with direct monthly rental assistance, to the tune of $1.7 billion starting in the 2028-29 fiscal year.

Yalnizyan said the pledge to end homelessness is a welcome one — as is the commitment to extend the ban on foreign purchases of rental properties to January 2029. But the housing benefit doesn't go far enough, she says, and the money to fund new housing projects won't benefit Canadians for years to come.

New homes under construction in the community of Upper Caledon East. The federal budget pledged $11.2 billion to end homelessness, as well as more money to build non-market housing and regular homes. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

"There is money there for it but it's not coming through fast enough," Yalnizyan said. "There's too much wait and see, come and talk to us later," Yalnizyan said.

Those affordability measures are also eclipsed by tax cuts and investments in infrastructure and other major projects. The previously announced productivity mega-deduction alone accounts for $36 billion worth of spending, compared to $22 billion overall for affordability.

Rather than boosting everyday Canadians, Yalnizyan says the budget is focused on catalyzing investment and attracting new spending within Canada.

"It's not a bad budget for all of that, but they've left out the people," Yalnizyan said.

While there are relatively few new details aimed at leaving Canadians with a little more money in their pockets, a handful of other affordability odds and ends made it in.

More low-income workers will get benefit payments to help them make ends meet. Those who make a minimum of $3,000 annually get a refundable tax credit under the Canada Workers Benefit, but that threshold is being lowered to $500 for all workers. The budget also increases those credits slightly, to $1,859 for single individuals who don't have kids and $3,143 for families.

It also proposes permanent, free entry to museums for kids and young adults under 25 years old.

The Canada Strong Pass will also be extended for another summer. That program gave free admission to national parks, and free or discounted access to galleries, Via Rail rides and more for two past summers. It will now be expanded to include discounted access to Indigenous-led museums and cultural centres.

World.title: Canada's new budget proposes $5B for culture. Here's where it would go
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Carney government's new budget proposes roughly $5 billion over the next five years toward several initiatives to promote Canadian culture, including building new recreational facilities and ice rinks, supporting national museums and permanently making their admissions free for people 25 and younger.

That figure includes more funding for CBC/Radio-Canada and the Local Journalism Initiative.

"Being sovereign means building a country where Canadian culture in all its diversity and creativity thrives," the 2026 budget reads, adding Ottawa is "investing in the stores, places and experiences that connect Canadians to their country and to one another."

The budget proposes providing $1.5 billion over nine years through the Build Communities Strong Fund to support the construction, expansion, retrofit and rehabilitation of community recreational facilities and ice rinks across the country.

WATCH | Carney says budget focused on affordability, opportunity and sovereignty: Budget focused on affordability, opportunity and sovereignty, Carney says | Duration closed caption 0:44 Speaking to reporters ahead of Thursday's federal budget release, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the economic plan will bring 'good news' for Canadians.

It also intends to provide $783.1 million over five years, starting this year, to support Canada's national museums, the National Battlefields Commission, the National Arts Centre and Library and Archives Canada.

"This investment will help repair and renew aging facilities, protect national collections and sustain the exhibitions, performances and services that connect Canadians to our history and culture," the budget says.

The national museum funding includes $46.3 million over five years for permanent, year-round free admission for children and youth under 25, plus $11.5 million ongoing.

Other notable items include $76 million in 2027-28 to renew the Canada Strong Pass for another summer.

WATCH | Ottawa launches 'Canada Strong Pass' in June 2025: Ottawa launches 'Canada Strong Pass' to promote domestic tourism | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 2:45 Minister Steven Guilbeault announced on Monday that the federal government will launch the Canada Strong Pass — a move to promote domestic tourism that makes Canada's historic sites and parks free to visit and rail travel less expensive for young people. The pass launches on Friday and ends Sept. 2, with Canadians and foreign tourists eligible.

The pass gives people free entry to all sites operated by Parks Canada, and free or discounted Via Rail trips depending on age.

Ottawa is proposing a $300-million Canada 160 Fund, an initiative to mark the country's 160th anniversary. The fund will support Canada's Heritage Minutes, the Trans Canada Trail and other community spaces.

It also intends to provide $15.9 million over four years, starting next year, and $2.1 million ongoing to Veterans Affairs Canada to "acquire, remediate and operate" the National Field of Honour military cemetery.

There is a proposal to provide $11.4 million over three years, starting this year, to Veterans Affairs Canada to support the commemoration of defining moments in Canada's military history.

Funding for journalism, media, artists

The budget pitches an additional $300 million over two years, starting this year, to CBC/Radio-Canada to "strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country."

It proposes $134 million over four years, starting next year, and $41 million ongoing to Canadian Heritage for the Local Journalism Initiative , which is meant to help organizations hire or pay journalists in underserved communities.

The federal government also wants to extend the enhanced 35 per cent Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit — set to expire next month — to 2028.

TV crew pass a CBC logo at their headquarters in Toronto, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Print journalism currently has access to the credit, and Ottawa wants to expand the credit to "qualifying private audio and audiovisual news organizations, in line with support provided to news organizations that produce written news."

The budget says the extended and expanded credit would cost an estimated $501 million over five years, starting this year, and $85 million ongoing.

The budget also proposes to establish a free national digital book collection. The federal government aims to provide $32.2 million over four years, starting next year, to get the collection started.

According to the budget, the digital collection would launch with at least 200 titles in 2027, then grow to more than 2,000 titles with capacity for up to two million loans annually by 2031.

A man walks past a part of the Emily Carr collection titled, "Fresh Seeing a French Modernism and West Coast," on exhibit at the Royal BC Museum in Victoria, B.C., on Oct. 28, 2020. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

The federal government says it will consult with Canadians and the cultural sector on a new Canada Creative Credit — which is expected to take the form of a non-refundable personal income tax credit.

The budget says when combined with the basic personal amount every filer has exempted from income tax, artists could have up to $45,000 of annual net business income derived from original and creative works exempted.

Details on the Canada Creative Credit will be announced in the 2027 spring economic update, the budget said.

Money for ocean preservation

The federal government classifies its proposed investments in Canada's oceans under its cultural plan.

To that end, the 2026 budget pitches establishing and operating two additional National Marine Conservation Areas. Ottawa is proposing $282.7 million over 11 years, starting next year, and $18 million ongoing to Parks Canada toward the initiative.

Plus, the budget proposes $9.2 million to Parks Canada and $10.5 million to Fisheries and Oceans Canada to support feasibility assessments for up to three additional National Marine Conservation Areas in the North.

Both those sums would come over four years, starting next year.

World.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after review, sexual assault allegations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Britain's Channel 4 says it will not bring back Married at First Sight UK, following the results of an external review into contributor welfare.

It was commissioned after three female cast members came forward with allegations of sexual assault on set.

The show follows strangers matched by relationship experts who meet for the first time at the altar, take part in a mock wedding ceremony and move in together as newlyweds.

The U.K. version of the program was considered to be a massive ratings juggernaut for Channel 4, and ran for 10 seasons.

In May, BBC's current affairs program Panorama spoke to two women who said they were raped by their on-screen husbands, and a third who alleged her on-screen husband subjected her to a non-consensual sexual act.

The men denied the allegations. I n June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.

Channel 4 commissioned a review tasked with examining whether the show's welfare protocols met its duty of care obligations — and whether those protocols needed to be changed.

The results of that review, released Thursday, found the show's welfare protocols were extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard — though in some isolated incidents, not fully implemented.

Measures to improve welfare

The final report also included recommendations to improve the welfare of Married at First Sight UK cast members — including putting couples in separate bedrooms on wedding night and honeymoon, reviewing the frequency with which couples are asked about the physical side of their relationship, and removing Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week.

It also suggested installing CCTV and sound recording equipment in all areas of the apartments to be monitored 24/7 by a welfare-trained team, and providing two lockable ensuite bedrooms for cast members.

Channel 4 headquarters in London, U.K. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

" MAFS UK has been enjoyed by millions of viewers, made possible by the willingness of its contributors to embrace the social experiment at the heart of the show and the many talented people involved in its production," said Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra in a statement.

She thanked the team for its efforts to protect the welfare of contributors, but said " the series will not return to Channel 4, with the show’s budget reinvested in distinctive new programming."

Dogra also repeated her apology to the female cast members who came forward with their allegations.

"This review did not have the authority to adjudicate on the very serious allegations made by three women in the Panorama program, but I would like to repeat that I am very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt."

She said she hopes Channel 4's swift action demonstrates "our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards."

The show is part of an international reality-TV franchise with editions in countries including the U.S. and Australia.

CBC News has not had any response to questions about whether those shows will continue.

World.title: Man accused of killing 11-year-old Burnaby boy makes 1st court appearance
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of two people charged in relation to the death of an 11-year-old Burnaby, B.C., boy appeared in a Vancouver courtroom for the first time on Thursday.

Branko Bijelic, 51, is charged with second-degree murder and indignity to human remains in the death of Kai Pavlovic.

He and 46-year-old Sarah Bijelic, who was also charged with manslaughter in the case, were both family members of the boy, according to police.

A publication ban prevents CBC News from reporting on any details about Sarah Bijelic's court proceedings.

Police allege Kai Pavlovic was killed prior to being reported missing on Sept. 26, 2025. (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)

Branko, who has yet to enter a plea, appeared by video link dressed in a red sweatshirt and glasses.

He sat quietly during proceedings, which were put over until later this month.

A family member from New Zealand, who identified herself as Kai's grandmother, was present in court gallery, but declined to speak with journalists.

In a statement to CBC News, Kai's aunt Helen Kok said the family remains "absolutely devastated" by his death, and will "forever have a Kai shaped hole in our hearts."

Kai's aunt Helen Kok said the family remains 'absolutely devastated' by his death, and will 'forever have a Kai shaped hole in our hearts.' (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)

"Kai was the light of our lives and we will miss the joy, creativity, and sense of adventure he brought with him wherever he went — and that is how we will remember him," the statement adds.

"We are grateful for closure after a long time of not knowing."

The family also asked the public to refrain from judgement, conjecture and speculation.

The Lower Mainland's Integrated Homicide Investigation Team (IHIT) announced charges in the case on Nov. 2, more than a year after the boy was reported missing.

Police allege Kai was killed prior to being reported missing on Sept. 26, 2025.

The boy's remains were discovered at an undisclosed location earlier this year, according to IHIT. (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)

According to police, Burnaby RCMP had received a request to check on the boy's well-being that day, and escalated the case to the Serious Crimes Unit when they were unable to locate him.

The case was later escalated again to IHIT.

The boy's remains were discovered at an undisclosed location earlier this year, according to IHIT.

Family members have launched a fundraiser with the goal of transporting Kai's remains to Montenegro so he can be buried with his father, and for the creation of a memorial garden in New Zealand.

World.title: U.S. midterms are a 'vindication' of Alberta's approach to tariffs, says Premier Smith
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says sweeping Democrat wins in the U.S. midterm elections prove her province was on the right path in the cross-border trade war.

"It is a vindication of our approach when it comes to tariffs," Smith told the house during question period Wednesday.

"We always have objected to tariffs. We know it hurts us. It hurts the Americans."

The Democrats on Tuesday took control of both houses of Congress and flipped long-held Republican Senate seats and state-level positions.

The results are seen as a widespread rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump and his policies, including his treatment of trading partners like Canada.

Smith said she hopes the midterm results are an opportunity to improve the relationship between Canada and the U.S.

She pointed to her government's efforts to build relationships across the aisle, including with Adam Schiff, a Democrat senator from California.

Resisting retaliation

Smith's government has stood apart from other provinces in the trade dispute. Alberta has for the most part resisted retaliatory tariffs or trade action while encouraging continued diplomacy.

Alberta only briefly halted sales of U.S. liquor in 2025, and Smith has steadfastly opposed the idea of leveraging oil and gas exports as an economic weapon in the fight.

But earlier Wednesday, as a result of the ongoing trade dispute, her government announced a new policy to prioritize Albertan and Canadian companies for small government contracts.

"We're putting local businesses first, supporting Canadian suppliers and making sure more of our government spending helps create opportunities and jobs here at home," Smith said in a news release.

The new measures apply to future contracts but existing deals are also to be reviewed when they come up for renewal.

WATCH | Trump weighs in on midterm blowout, ballrooms and ballots: Trump shrugs off midterm blowout as blame game kicks off | Duration closed caption 2:54 U.S. President Donald Trump shrugged off massive Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm election. Trump, who seemed more interested in his new ballroom, blamed the blowout on his name not being literally on the ballot, but conceded the war in Iran was likely a factor.

Service Alberta Minister Dale Nally said it gives qualified local companies a better shot at bidding on about $350 million in government spending, or five per cent of procurement contracts.

He said 95 per cent of government contracts already land with Canadian companies.

"This is just a practical, common-sense way that we can help businesses that we know could be struggling or impacted because of the current tariffs," Nally said in an interview.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters that the United Conservative Party government is two years too late.

"We've been asking for this exact thing for over two years, from the day Trump was re-elected," Nenshi said.

"Imagine the wealth you could have created and the jobs you could have created in Alberta, if you had just done it two years ago when everyone else did."

Nenshi said that beyond tariffs, he feels the U.S. midterm results were a sign that voters everywhere are tired of "culture war" politics — which he accused Smith of championing.

In question period, he pointed to a government bill tabled this week that would require post-secondary schools to develop neutrality policies.

"Who exactly asked the premier for this, and what difference is it going to make to a single student?" he asked.

Smith, in response, said her government was only trying to counteract NDP policies and influence. "They create a hostile environment for free speech," the premier said.

"We're undoing their culture war."

World.title: Google offers schools AI-boosted search or none at all
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Google weaves artificial intelligence more deeply throughout its applications, the tech giant says school board leaders can choose to flip AI tools on — or off — for elementary and secondary students using their classroom apps.

But to keep using Google's ubiquitous search engine within that school-tech ecosystem, an AI-boosted version will soon be the only option.

For kids today, the company name itself is synonymous for researching online, so coupled with how deeply its products are embedded in education systems, this week's announcement quickly set off alarm bells — especially among those questioning putting AI tools at students' fingertips.

Yet others see the move as an impetus for schools to prioritize AI literacy and teaching responsible usage now, from the earliest grades onward.

WATCH | Google offers schools AI-boosted search engine, or none at all: Google tells schools to accept using its AI tools or lose full web search access | Duration closed caption 1:54 Concerned Canadian educators are speaking out after Google announced that students will not be allowed to access its main search engine unless their school systems also opt in to its AI features.

Entrenched in education systems

Google and Microsoft are the dominant tech players in Canadian schools, says education technology researcher Beyhan Farhadi, with their apps entrenched into the student experience.

In the case of the former, for example, teachers might post and mark schoolwork in Google Classroom. That, in turn, connects with their students' Gmail accounts, apps like Google Docs or Slides where kids create assignments and a version of Google's web browser for searching information, said Farhadi, an assistant professor of educational policy and equity at the University of Toronto.

Many students also work within this ecosystem on school-issued Chromebooks, the pared-down laptops running Google's operating system and apps .

Given that integration, Farhadi is concerned about Google making "pedagogical decisions that often school boards are beholden to, because they have already invested so much money into the technology."

Considering how central online research is for student learning today and Google having the most popular search engine, "I don't think you can understate how big of a thing it would be to suddenly have Google search just not be available," said Adam Dubé, an associate professor of learning sciences at McGill University in Montreal.

Google revealed updates to its offering to schools on Tuesday, including a new chatbot feature that coaches students to learn through back-and-forth exchanges that was made available immediately inside Google Classroom

That "guided learning" capability will also be blended into Google Search for students "in the coming months," Chris Phillips, Google's vice-president and general manager for education, wrote in a blog post, following a pilot in some U.S. schools this month.

The company offered more details in a social media post later Tuesday in response to ripples of negative reaction, saying the changes stem from educator feedback in recent months.

"If a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have search on at all," Phillips told education outlet Chalkbeat.

A Google statement on X this week offered more details about the changes, saying they were informed by recent feedback from educators. (News from Google/X)

Alternatives and workarounds

Non-profit group Common Sense Media deemed Google Search's AI Overview and AI Mode as an "unacceptable risk" for kids and teens this summer, and some may be considering AI-blocking browser extensions or rival search engines to keep a more traditional web search for students, says education policy consultant Tom D'Amico.

But going that route doesn't solve ongoing issues such as youngsters accepting AI-fuelled search summaries without checking sources or using chatbots for schoolwork instead of doing it themselves, he added.

"As soon as that student leaves school and they go home ... they have access" to AI, perhaps through a Google or ChatGPT search on a non-school device, said D'Amico, a former director of education at the Ottawa Catholic School Board who now consults school leaders on AI policy.

LISTEN | Google search revamp leans into AI: Cost of Living 11:17 So long, Google search bar Google is changing how we Google. It's revamping its iconic search function and handing the reins over to AI. So, is this the end of the search engine as we know it? Paul Haavardsrud searches for answers with Siva Vaidhyanathan, the authour of The Googlization of Everything [https://www.ucpress.edu/books/the-googlization-of-everything-2/paper].

Instead, D'Amico believes now is the time for schools to prioritize teaching students AI literacy and responsible use of the technology across subjects and from the earliest grades.

"Students are going to go for the easy route," he said from Ottawa. "We need our teachers to teach them why that's not the right path."

Pushback on inevitability

That Google is positioning its search engine "as synonymous with artificial intelligence ... saying if you use Google, you're using AI" comes at a time of major debate about and emerging evidence suggesting AI usage leaves students worse off, said Dubé.

Art teacher Joyce Hatzidakis uses the AI tool Google Gemini in her high school classroom on Jan. 22 in Riverside, Calif. (Damian Dovarganes/Associated Press)

Polls have also indicated Canadians have "a negative or cautious stance towards AI and yet we're seeing it pushed ... and we're being told that it's inevitable," he added.

Farhadi feels schools are right to consider gradually exposing kids to AI tools, but she also thinks students don't have to be using them to learn about them.

"Just because students are using something outside of the classroom all the time doesn't mean that the classroom [can't] be a space of exception," where young people can practise thinking and communicating without being constantly shaped or influenced by technology, she said.

World.title: 15 patients released, 5 still hospitalized following bus crash near Mackenzie, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Northern Health says 15 people have been released from hospital and five are still receiving care following a major bus crash near Mackenzie, north of Prince George, B.C., Wednesday.

WorkSafeBC and RCMP are still investigating what police described as a "chaotic scene" when the northbound shuttle bus went off Highway 39, causing hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie to declare a code orange. No other vehicles were involved.

Six air ambulances and six ground ambulances treated and transported 20 patients with injuries ranging from minor to serious, according to B.C. Emergency Health Services.

Northern Health says all 20 patients were taken to hospital in either Prince George or Mackenzie, with fifteen being treated and released. Four others remain in care locally, while one was airlifted to another facility elsewhere in the province.

WATCH | Major bus crash in northern B.C.: About 20 people hospitalized after bus crash near Mackenzie | Duration closed caption 2:20

Updates on their conditions are not being shared by BCEHS, Northern Health or RCMP, who all cited patient privacy.

Operations at both hospitals have since returned to normal, with Northern Health thanking "the physicians, nurses, first responders and other health professionals in Mackenzie and Prince George whose rapid and highly-professional response saved lives and prevented this tragic incident from taking an even greater toll on the victims."

'Nothing has been ruled out': Police

B.C. Highway Patrol has taken control of the investigation, with RCMP saying that while no arrests have been made, "the cause of the crash is still uncertain" and "nothing has been ruled out."

WorkSafeBC is also investigating with a spokesperson saying they are " working with law enforcement partners to establish an understanding of the factors related to this incident. "

The shuttle bus was carrying workers subcontracted by Iren, a multinational data centre company with facilities in Mackenzie and Prince George.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Paraguay’s Santiago Peña tenders his resignation, but Congress presses ahead with impeachment
World.content:
Paraguay’s Santiago Peña tenders his resignation, but Congress presses ahead with impeachment

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:12 UTC Full article

“I have decided to submit my resignation from the Presidency of the Republic. I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” Peña said

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña tendered his resignation on Thursday, cornered by the collapse of Ueno Bank, but minutes later the Chamber of Deputies unanimously voted to impeach him, in an attempt to prevent him from taking up a lifetime Senate seat with immunity from prosecution once he leaves office. The final decision rests with the Senate.

“I have decided to submit my resignation from the Presidency of the Republic. I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” Peña said in a video posted on social media as deputies debated the charges. “My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added, referring to the frozen savings of nearly three million of the bank’s customers. Interior Minister Enrique Riera formally submitted the resignation to Congress at around 1.30 p.m.

Less than an hour later, all 78 deputies present approved the impeachment charges, which now go to the Senate, where a two-thirds majority is needed to remove the president. The chamber rejected impeachment proceedings against Vice President Pedro Alliana, who would take over the presidency until the end of the term on August 15, 2028.
