But other experts believe Iran was deliberately holding out to pressure Trump before the midterms. Now the election is over, the Iranians may be more willing to negotiate a peace deal.

Unwilling participants

All this leaves the Gulf states, who have been the main targets of Iranian attacks since the conflict began, in a difficult position.

"We find ourselves drawn within a crisis that we worked diplomatically very hard to try to avert," Anwar Gargash, a foreign policy adviser to United Arab Emirates leadership, said at a security conference in Bahrain last weekend, the Manama Dialogue hosted by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS. "We are clearly seeking a political off-ramp."

Qatar has been trying to negotiate between the US and Iran but has also been conducting emergency drills at its airport. The Emiratis have been doing similar drills. And Saudi Arabia is looking at a war on two fronts: The oil-rich state is already under attack from the Houthi militia in neighboring Yemen. Even Egypt has reacted, reportedly strengthening air defenses around the Suez Canal.

Still, no matter what happens next, the US-Israel-Iran war has already made Gulf states evaluate defense partnerships with the US. Rather than making them safe, US bases have made them a target.

"There is widespread disappointment across the region with the US over the folly of the war, the erratic nature of Washington's military and diplomatic conduct, and its decision to prioritize Israel's defense over that of its Gulf partners," Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow at the IISS, told news agency Bloomberg this week. "If the US liberation of Kuwait in 1991 was the moment that established America's role in the region, the 2026 war may be remembered as the moment that undid it."

Replacing America?

Gulf states are widening their outreach with, for example, the UAE getting closer to Israel and the Saudis entering the Mecca defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey.

"The Gulf states have already moved toward strategic autonomy and self-reliance," Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London, wrote for online outlet Middle East Eye this week. "A lame-duck Trump will speed that process."

That's even though a Democrat-led Congress might make the US a slightly more reliable partner again.

Krieg argues that Gulf states should come together to pressure the US not to attack Iran and then negotiate a non-aggression pact with Iran — without US involvement.

Whether that kind of unity is possible in the Gulf is dubious, Ryan Crocker, a former US ambassador to the region and distinguished fellow with MEI, replied to a question from DW during the MEI's online briefing.

Reevaluating the relationship? Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan (left) and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at a recent G20 meeting in the US Image: Megan Varner/AFP

"I'm afraid that meaningful Gulf unity is not coming to a theater near us anytime soon," Crocker said. The Qataris remain untrusting because of how other Gulf states acted against them in 2017. And, he added, "there are well known differences between Saudi Arabia and the UAE we see in Sudan [and] in Yemen, and, of course, the profound differences … on relations with Israel. So I would not expect any meaningful moves toward [Gulf] security cooperation."

What's more likely in the long term is Gulf states eventually coming to some kind of understanding with Iran.

"The Gulf states understand that they probably can't buy their security only from Washington, and that they're going to have to buy it, to some degree, by some kind of a relationship with Tehran," the MEI's Harrison added. "It's inevitable. Geography reigns."

What that sort of non-aggression pact looks like remains to be seen, he added. That's why one of the big concerns for Gulf leaders now, is the conflict escalating again to a point where the path back to some sort of diplomacy is lost, Harrison concluded.

World.title: Pete Hegseth under fire as Republicans trade blame for midterm debacle
World.content:
Iran war hawk Pete Hegseth is facing the fallout from Republicans' midterms losses as high energy prices turned voters toward Democrats. US President Trump continues to support his embattled defense chief — for now.

Republicans in Washington continued to assess the damage on Thursday, after a resounding electoral defeat in the midterm elections two days prior saw Democrats take over Congress by large margins.

Republican Party insiders told US outlets CNN and The Washington Post that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is feeling the heat over criticism that the war in Iran, which he supports, cost his party the elections.

Trump on Wednesday acknowledged that the Iran war affected the midterms, saying that voters were frustrated how the 8-month-long conflict has cause gas and diesel prices to skyrocket.

"The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it," Trump told reporters, but he ultimately defended the war effort and denied any plans to fire his defense secretary over it, saying Hegseth was "doing a very good job."

On Wednesday, Trump said it was 'likely true' the Iran war led to the Republicans' midterm rout Image: CNP/AdMedia/picture alliance

But US Vice President JD Vance has sought to distance himself from the war, questioning whether it was worth the cost.

"The ⁠reason ⁠we lost is the war," Vance said on X. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so."

'Knives out' at the Pentagon

Hegseth has been a loud voice in Washington for the US attacking Iran, and has publicly chastised lawmakers and journalists for raising questions about the conflict's strategic objectives, cost and lack of congressional authorization.

The defense secretary has also been accused of not being forthright about the damage to US bases in the Middle East and the severity of troop casualties. He has also purged dozens of high ranking military officers, while denying promotions to others on dubious grounds.

Hegseth was in hot water even before the Iran war. In October 2025, a Signal group chat between himself and Vice President JD Vance discussing a military strike on Yemen in October 2025 accidentally included a journalist, and led to calls for Hegseth's dismissal.

According to CNN's reporting, multiple Republicans told the network on condition of anonymity that many in their party are now turning against the defense secretary.

Sources also told the Washington Post that the political situation at the Defense Department appears "very dynamic at the moment," with "knives out."

With Trump backing Hegseth for now, The Post reported that those close to the Trump administration have floated the notion that the president might dismiss General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Admiral Brad Cooper, who has overseen the war, instead of the embattled Hegseth.

House plans Hegseth impeachment vote

Pressure is mounting in Capitol Hill, as Hegseth's critics from both sides of the aisle turn their focus on him.

CNN reported that House Republicans are expected to hold an impeachment vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days.

Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who has been a critic of Trump, told CNN he plans to trigger the impeachment, which multiple GOP sources say is expect to pass.

In September, Massie had said he would force a vote in the House on impeaching Hegseth, which led to House Speaker Mike Johnson sending Congress into recess until after the midterms.

On Thursday, Massie posted on X that his impeachment resolution is a "much gentler" version of what's coming when the Democrats take over Congress in January.

"They'll have hearings & trials," he wrote.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth "will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists."

"We will continue to drive President Trump's agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office," Parnell added, using the administration's name for the Department of Defense.

Incoming Democrats plan probes

Fresh off their sweeping wins, Democrats will have the power to launch investigations on Hegseth and even slash funding for the Defense Department and the Iran war.

"I'm going after Pete Hegseth. Not only is he incompetent and corrupt, he's undermining our national security and the safety of our troops," said Representative Jason Crow, a Democratic member of the House Armed Services Committee.

Representative Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the committee, said a top priority would be "to conduct vigorous oversight of the Department of Defense and the Trump Administration," including on "the illegal war against Iran."

World.title: Does the Oleshky ceasefire signal progress to come in Ukraine?
World.content:
Hundreds of civilians were evacuated from the city of Oleshky after Russia and Ukraine agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire. Some observers have expressed optimism that more such humanitarian missions might follow.

Nearly 800 residents have been evacuated from the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. This was announced by US first lady Melania Trump, who was credited with helping to mediate the ceasefire. The mission was coordinated by Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.

Most evacuees chose to be sent to Ukrainian-controlled territory, although some opted for transfer to Russia. Currently, more than 1,000 people remain in Oleshky, according to Kherson's regional administration. They were supplied with food, water and medicine.

Melania Trump hailed the mission as a success, taking to social media to thank Kyiv and Moscow for their "leadership and cooperation." She said the Oleshky ceasefire could go on to inspire a "lasting peace between the two peoples."

Dmytro Lubinez similarly wrote on the Telegram messaging platform that it is "important to maintain this cooperation mechanism," adding that "we are currently exploring options with Yana Lantratova to continue similar humanitarian efforts."

Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets (center) poses for a photo with residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky Image: Genya Savilov/AFP

The Kremlin, however, was quick to dampen any such expectations, making clear that no further plans for humanitarian missions exist at this stage.

Did Russia exploit the ceasefire to strengthen military hold?

One day after the ceasefire ended, Ukraine's general staff stated that Russia had "used the humanitarian pause to fortify its positions." It also said Russia had carried out troop rotations, expanded its anti-drone defenses, and brought in ammunition.

British broadcaster Sky News aired drone footage, produced with the support of the Ukrainian army, showing the Russian army transporting heavy equipment, weapons, personnel and food to Oleshky and neighboring villages.

"It was clear to the Ukrainian government and international mediators that Russia could exploit the pause in this way. But it was the right thing to do to allow people to leave the country," Volodymyr Vyatrovych of the Ukrainian European Solidarity opposition party wrote on Facebook.

Oleshky evacuees recount survival under occupation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He believes Russia would do the exact same thing if Kyiv were to withdraw its troops from the Donetsk region, as Russian President Vladimir Putin is demanding.

"Russia would use this to prepare for its next offensive, to further destroy Ukraine," Vyatrovych wrote. That said, humanitarian missions have their place, says Ihor Chalenko of the Ukrainian Center for Analysis and Strategies. "We shouldn't speak ill of the Oleshky mission, even though it's clear that the Russians have used the ceasefire in the occupied territories to their advantage," Chalenko told DW. That's why he says Kyiv should insist on banning such behavior in future ceasefires.

What did Washington and Moscow gain from the pause in fighting?

The Oleshky mission took place just shortly before US voters headed to the polls in the midterm elections. Dmytro Levus of the United Ukraine research center believes the timing was no coincidence. "The Russian side played right into the hands of US President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party was expected to face a crushing electoral defeat," Levus said.

Involving Melania in the mediation was a "subtle public relations move" for Trump, through which he hoped to score points ahead of the election, Levus explained. First Lady Melania Trump has long been an advocate for humanitarian causes.

First Lady Melania Trump played a leading role in the ceasfire deal Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Chalenko says the Oleshky ceasefire was in Washington's interest because it allowed Donald Trump to cast himself as a "peacemaker."

Moscow also hoped it could improve its image through the humanitarian mission, especially as it caused Oleshky's humanitarian catastrophe in the first place, Chalenko said. Rescuing civilians is intended to serve as proof that "not everything is bad in Russia."

What can the Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners accomplish?

Cooperation between the two human rights ombudspersons had reached "a new level," Chalenko said, adding that the Oleshky case was just one of several noteworthy examples that also included prisoner swaps and foreign representatives gaining access to Ukrainian political prisoners held in Russia.

He does not, however, believe that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova makes her own decisions. "We are seeing a certain top-down realignment of Russian policy," Chalenko told DW. He also said it was important to further develop this communication channel. The lessons learned from the evacuation of Oleshky could be applied to other towns along the front, Chalenko believes.

Dmytro Levus says the Oleshky mission has proven that, if Moscow were so inclined, a ceasefire could be established along the entire front line. Yet Russia has so far shown no willingness in doing so, partly because Ukraine has not agreed to Putin's terms, Levus explains.

Will the ceasefire inject momentum into the upcoming talks?

Preparations are underway for a new round of negotiations between Ukraine, the US and Russia on November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi. Dmytro Levus believes the Oleshky ceasefire could provide substance to talks on humanitarian issues. He does not, however, think there will be much progress on a political level, even though he does see scope for a ceasefire at sea, for example.

Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpark Dmytro Lubinets speak to the press ahead of the evacuation Image: Office of the Ombudsman of Ukraine/AP Photo/picture alliance

Levus says that the US will be particularly keen to present further humanitarian successes. Ukraine may use the talks to negotiate a new prisoner exchange, though Levus says Russia will likely only budge under pressure.

Ihor Chalenko says one should not expect too much of the upcoming talks. He believes that Russia is looking for a pretext to withdraw from the negotiations, preferring instead to expand its cooperation with the US, without wanting to make any concessions to end the Ukraine war.

Samuel Greene of King's College London is similarly skeptical. "I assume that at some point, the Kremlin will come to realize that there is nothing left to gain on the battlefield and that they will have to reach an agreement."

"That moment hasn't yet come though," Greene told DW, adding that Russia was still trying to buy time by feigning a willingness to engage in dialogue with the US.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: France: More than 600,000 protest as anger grows over cost of living
World.content:
Demonstrators took to the streets in several French cities to call for government action on the high cost of living. Protests were largely peaceful, but there were some reports of escalation, including in Paris.

Hundreds of thousands of people descended on the streets of French cities on Thursday for a new round of protests over rising cost of living.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the total number of protesters ballooned over the course of the afternoon, from 270,000 to 600,000 by the evening.

The five unions that organized the protests represent public and private sectors, and are calling on the government to address deteriorating public services and high prices of goods.

Public and private sector workers were joined by students, who have organized their numerous protests of their own over the course of the past month.

Protesters gather in Place de la Republique in Paris Image: Geoffroy Van Der Hasselt/AFP

One of the biggest student protests in October turned violent, with rioters having vandalized stores. Flames went up from the roof of the town hall of Limoges in central France.

French President Emmanuel Macron blamed ultra-left groups for the violence and vowed more security personnel at protests.

Cost of living protests in major French cities

Like what was seen in October, major rallies took place in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and elsewhere, with about 70,000 police officers and security forces deployed throughout the country.

Protests were largely peaceful, though there were reports about riot police having clashed with protesters in Lyon.

There were reports about incidents of escalation in Paris, where the Eiffel Tower remained closed for the day. Police at one point used tear gas against protesters in the French capital.

A protester throws a tear gas canister back at police in the city of Lyon Image: Denis Balibouse/REUTERS

Some reports of violence earlier in the day in Brittany, Rennes, Toulouse

Demonstrations kicked off in the southern cities of Marseille and Lyon, and Nantes in the west, on Thursday morning.

Authorities in the western region of Brittany said "masked individuals" had tried to block roads in the city of Rennes.

Broadcaster BFM TV reported that a high school near the southwestern city of Toulouse was set on fire.

The main protest in Paris began at 2 p.m. local time (1300 GMT). Daily newspaper Le Monde reported that the demonstrators in Paris began to clear by the evening.

Reuters reported that high school students and other protesters had already faced off against riot police in the French capital on Thursday morning after they blocked a street with rubbish bins.

France has seen frequent nationwide protests over the cost of living in recent weeks Image: Christophe Archambault/AFP

Public services go on strike

Public and private education unions called for staff to walk off the job, as well as unions representing rail workers, public hospitals and postal services.

They are demanding an increase in the minimum wage, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people.

The Education Ministry said just over 15% of French teaching staff went on strike. French power unions also joined the action, state-owned utility EDF said.

About a third of France's high schools were closed, either because of student blockades or striking teachers.

Media reports said state railway operator SNCF expected only minor disruptions to long-distance services.

World.title: Arrests and investigations as Serbia begins post-election clean-up
World.content:
The landslide victory of the Students' List in Serbia's general election seems to have removed a blockage in the justice system: Cases that were long stalled are now suddenly moving forward.

Air Serbia flight JU134 from Belgrade to Moscow on November 3 was already deep in Lithuanian airspace when the crew received instructions to return to the Serbian capital.

Among the passengers were three senior figures from the regime of former President Aleksandar Vucic: Aleksandar Vulin, former defense and interior minister and former head of Serbia's Security Intelligence Agency (BIA), Dusan Bajatovic, long-serving director of state-owned gas company Srbijagas, and Nenad Popovic, a minister without portfolio.

All three are well known in Serbia for their close ties to Moscow and for controversies, including allegations of corruption and abuse of public office.

According to unofficial reports published by several media outlets, the plane was ordered back because of a security breach: Vulin had allegedly boarded without undergoing the mandatory security screening.

Since 2023, Vulin has been under US sanctions over what Washington described as "engaging in corrupt and destabilizing activities that undermine the rule of law in the Western Balkans."

Unusual episode

Vulin told the media that he was travelling to Moscow to discuss extending a gas agreement with Russia.

Former Serbian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandar Vulin (left, pictured here in 2024 with Russian President Vladimir Putin) has been under US sanctions since 2023 Image: Kristina Kormilitsyna/Sputnik/AP/picture alliance

Bajatovic, however, said he did not know why Vulin and Popovic were travelling to Moscow and denied that the two would attend the scheduled meetings on gas supplies.

The incident might have remained nothing more than an unusual news item had it not occurred at a time when Serbia is undergoing a major political transformation.

Judicial developments unfold at remarkable speed

Just nine days earlier, on October 25, the student-backed list won a landslide victory over the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the parliamentary election, ending 14 years of political dominance by Aleksandar Vucic and the SNS, who maintained close relations with Moscow.

Although the new majority has yet to take control of any levers of power, the days after the election brought a series of developments that would have seemed unimaginable just a few weeks ago.

Arrests, new criminal proceedings and the reopening of previously unresolved cases began to unfold at remarkable speed. Some of these cases strike at the very foundations of the system built during the SNS years in power.

"This paints a sad picture of the Serbian prosecution service," prosecutor Bojana Savovic told DW.

Public prosecutor Bojana Savovic told DW that the burst of activity from prosecutors shows 'what they could have done but were unwilling to do until just ten days ago' Image: Maxim Konankov/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Savovic sees the sudden action on the part of prosecutors as an attempt to ingratiate themselves with the new authorities.

"With these actions, they are showing what they could have done but were unwilling to do until just ten days ago," she told DW. "I hope this speed of action will not come at the expense of the quality of indictments and that these are not personal vendettas within the old regime."

Allegations of vote-buying and high-level corruption

Prosecutors have also launched a series of investigations into suspected electoral manipulation, corruption and abuse of public office.

Four people were arrested on suspicion of vote-buying in Novi Sad. Six others were detained in Mali Zvornik on suspicion of helping citizens from Bosnia and Herzegovina register their residence in Serbia so they could vote.

One of the most high-profile cases is the arrest of Davor Macura, the owner of Alta Bank, who is suspected of illegally accessing the bank's vault and removing the equivalent of about €383 million ($430 million).

His arrest came just days after the National Bank of Serbia revoked Alta Bank's license and initiated bankruptcy proceedings. Macura has been publicly associated with the SNS, while his bank had significant business dealings with the state and a large number of Russian clients.

Senior police officials, the head of the Republic Hydrometeorological Institute and several managers of public companies have also been arrested over suspected abuses of office and rigged public procurement procedures.

Alleged destruction of documents

Students and representatives of the new political majority are demanding investigations into corruption cases that have remained unresolved for years.

Their message is that no one should be above the law and that prosecutors and courts must do their jobs — or be held accountable for failing to act.

'It would be tragic if the biggest players […] were prosecuted without sufficient evidence. Or if they were charged with something far less serious than what they actually did,' lawyer Tanja Arsic told DW Image: Maxim Konankov/NurPhoto/picture alliance

"When you want the rule of law and when you want something to be done, it is possible. Our regulations allow for it. But it was obvious that there were people obstructing the entire system, putting cases in drawers and leaving them unresolved," Tanja Arsic, an incoming MP from the Students' List, told DW.

In the days after the election, however, reports and video footage emerged that suggested official documents may have been removed or destroyed in state institutions and public companies.

On October 29, Prosecutor General Zagorka Dolovac responded by issuing a binding instruction to all chief public prosecutors to prevent the destruction of official and other records.

The Students' List also called on employees in state institutions and the media to report any destruction of documents to prevent what they called abuse by the outgoing authorities during the transition of power.

Savovic points out that even an attempt to destroy official records is punishable by law.

How high up will investigations reach?

But will the institutions really investigate those who were once at the very top of Serbia's political power structures?

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said he is not afraid of being arrested and that no evidence of financial wrongdoing will be found against him.

"I don't sign or do anything when it comes to money, and nothing can be found in that regard," he said.

But accountability is not just about who signed a document. It is also about establishing who made the decisions, who gave the orders and who wielded the real power to influence the deals now under investigation.

After years of stalled and unresolved cases, police and prosecutors in Serbia have begun making arrests and launching investigations Image: Sanja Kljajic/DW

"It would be tragic if the biggest players, whose arrests are expected, were prosecuted without sufficient evidence. Or if they were charged with something far less serious than what they actually did," said Tanja Arsic.

The real test is yet to come

Bojana Savovic makes a point of saying that ultimately, the success of the prosecution service won't be measured by the number of politically popular or populist arrests that are made, but by final convictions and the permanent confiscation of assets acquired through crime.

Arsic agrees and warns that conducting high-quality investigations and gathering robust evidence must take precedence over speed.

"The prosecution must not bring indictments if there is not enough evidence. That would be disastrous," she said. "If things are rushed just to achieve a result, only for the cases to end in acquittals because the prosecution failed to prove the charges against people who were at the top of the government — that would be even more disastrous."

But will that be possible within the existing structures? Savovic is not convinced that it will.

"For decades, people whose only qualification was blind obedience, reading the political climate and self-censorship were promoted in the prosecution service and the courts. Without fundamental changes in the judiciary, the police and the security structures, I see no possibility of a substantial and lasting transformation of society," she said.

The real test will come in the courtroom. The verdicts in these cases will show whether Serbia is finally breaking with its old system of power or merely replacing one set of power brokers with another.

World.title: Una nueva oleada de falsas amenazas de bomba afecta al menos a 27 aviones en Europa
World.content:
Tres aeronaves han tenido origen o destino en Madrid. Bruselas pide colaboración a los Estados para aclarar la incidencia, similar a la registrada el martes en otros siete vuelos

El tráfico aéreo en toda Europa se ha visto afectado este jueves por una nueva oleada de falsas amenazas de bomba contra más de una veintena de aviones. El episodio parece un acto coordinado en un momento especialmente turbulento en Europa, según observadores y expertos consultados. Al menos 27 vuelos con destino a ciudades europeas — y al menos tres de ellos con origen o destino en Madrid— han sufrido este jueves falsos avisos de bomba que les han obligado a realizar aterrizajes de emergencia, sin contratiempos en todos los casos. Además, tres aviones han sido desviados y varios han sido escoltados por cazas de Italia, Francia, Bulgaria y Austria.

Las incidencias, que investigan las autoridades nacionales, han afectado a aeropuertos de España, Francia, Italia, Bélgica, Bulgaria, Chequia, Rumania, Polonia, Irlanda, Dinamarca y Austria. Se producen, además, solo dos días después de que otros siete vuelos registraran falsas amenazas de bomba. Todos sobre el espacio aéreo europeo. En total, al menos 35 vuelos se han visto afectados desde el lunes.

Las amenazas se han recibido por correo electrónico en varios aeropuertos europeos. En el caso de los correos dirigidos al aeródromo de Roma llegó un mensaje firmado por Fighters of the Male State (Luchadores del Estado masculino), un grupo radical ruso de machistas y supremacistas blancos que se hizo conocido por sus campañas de odio contra las mujeres y que ha abrazado la guerra de Rusia contra Ucrania. “Vuestro régimen feminista lo recordará para siempre. La explosión se producirá en 60 minutos. Hoy vuestro cielo será rojo”, decía el correo electrónico, según relata la prensa italiana. Las autoridades del aeropuerto de Roma han confirmado que el correo, que alertaba de los vuelos procedentes de Helsinki y Dublín, estaba escrito en italiano. Rusia declaró extremista a ese movimiento en 2021, y en 2022 su nombre ya apareció en falsas amenazas de bomba contra escuelas de Montenegro, cuya autoría negó su fundador.

Fuentes de inteligencia europeas creen que el nombre de esa organización se puede estar usando como una maniobra de distracción. En cualquier caso no dudan de que la oleada de amenazas de bomba es una acción coordinada que busca no solo generar caos y angustia en los pasajeros sino también analizar la respuesta europea y el tiempo de actuación. Las autoridades nacionales no han apuntado todavía a una pista de la supuesta autoría.

La oleada de amenazas falsas coincide con otros episodios alarmantes en Europa, como los ataques cibernéticos a decenas de supermercados para alterar las temperaturas de sus sistemas de refrigeración, lo que ha llevado a la pérdida de millones de euros en alimentos. También llega después de un grave y sofisticado ataque cibernético contra el Establecimiento Francés de Sangre (EFS), que saboteó los sistemas de congelación de tres de sus principales plantas de almacenamiento biológico.

Colaboración europea

El comisario de Transportes de la UE, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, ha remarcado este jueves que es aún “demasiado pronto para sacar conclusiones sobre si los incidentes notificados están relacionados entre sí”, pero ha subrayado que Bruselas sigue la situación muy de cerca junto a la Agencia Europea de Seguridad Aérea y a los Estados miembros, que tienen las competencias de investigar lo sucedido. “Cualquier amenaza contra la población civil es inaceptable”, ha aseverado Tzitzikostas en un comunicado.

Se trata de incidentes que han afectado a varios países, y por ello la Comisión Europea ha pedido a las autoridades nacionales —responsables de evaluar las amenazas a la seguridad, investigar los incidentes e implementar las medidas de seguridad aérea pertinentes— que colaboren estrechamente con los operadores aeroportuarios, las aerolíneas y las fuerzas y cuerpos de seguridad, ha explicado el comisario griego.

Al menos tres vuelos implicados en la alerta de este jueves han sido notificados en el aeropuerto de Madrid-Barajas. Fuentes de la Guardia Civil, que han procesado las alertas, aseguran, sin embargo, a este periódico que los vuelos eran seis, no tres, informa Óscar López-Fonseca. Iberia ha confirmado que dos de sus aviones, procedentes de Milán y Roma, han recibido amenazas falsas: las alertas han llegado al aeropuerto de Barajas, se han comunicado a los comandantes y ambos aparatos han aterrizado sin incidentes hacia las diez de la mañana. Air Europa ha explicado que su vuelo a París aún no había despegado cuando llegó el aviso y que el avión ha sido evacuado e inspeccionado y, tras comprobarse que se trataba de una falsa alarma, ha despegado y ha aterrizado en París sin problemas. Aena, la empresa pública que gestiona los aeropuertos, ha explicado que, tras constituirse un comité de seguridad con las fuerzas de seguridad del Estado y realizarse las comprobaciones pertinentes, la amenaza de bomba ha sido descartada en todos los casos, informa Javier F. Magariño.

Un avión de Ryanair, este jueves en el aeropuerto de Sofía (Bulgaria). Stoyan Nenov (REUTERS)

Estas incidencias se suman a las que se vivieron el pasado martes en otros siete vuelos con destino a ciudades europeas: Varsovia, Sofía, Roma y Murcia. Todos recibieron amenazas de bomba, uno de los aparatos tuvo que ser desviado y se produjeron perturbaciones en varios aeropuertos, donde fueron movilizados los artificieros, aunque finalmente no fueron hallados explosivos en ninguno de los aviones. La víspera, el lunes, otro avión que volaba de Londres a Sofía había sido desviado a Budapest, escoltado por un caza húngaro, por idéntico motivo.

Por ahora, nadie ha reivindicado esas amenazas falsas y ninguno de los países afectados ha señalado a algún otro Gobierno o grupo terrorista, aunque expertos consultados por EL PAÍS sostienen que esa concentración de amenazas de bomba en cuestión de horas y un mismo espacio aéreo no puede ser casual.

Robert Jordan, del centro británico de estudios de defensa RUSI y antiguo responsable en el Ministerio de Defensa británico de las políticas para prevenir amenazas terroristas contra la aviación civil, explica por correo electrónico que la tolerancia al riesgo es muy baja: si una aerolínea no puede descartar rápidamente que un aviso es falso, actúa cuanto antes. La consultora británica de riesgos Dragonfly sostiene en un intercambio de mensajes que lo que distingue esta campaña de las numerosas falsas amenazas registradas en los últimos años en aeropuertos europeos es que parece coordinada y probablemente obra de un único grupo o de una red reducida de personas afines. Dragonfly no se aventura a señalar quién puede estar detrás de estas acciones, que hacen que las miradas de expertos se dirijan a Rusia, y señala que se trataría, en ese caso, de tácticas nuevas empleadas por Moscú. Jordan recuerda que grupos rusos e iraníes han reclutado por internet a personas para acciones similares, pero no descarta que se trate de alguien que disfruta provocando el caos.

El ministro de Defensa danés, Jeppe Bruus, ha evitado vincular estos incidentes con Rusia, pero ha afirmado a la radiotelevisión pública DR que Europa vive “una escalada de los ataques híbridos” rusos y que los europeos deben prepararse para más episodios como los de este jueves.

World.title: Jueves negro para la Bolsa: el Nasdaq sufre un batacazo por el miedo al frenazo de la IA
World.content:
La contundente victoria de los demócratas en las elecciones de mitad de mandato de Estados Unidos sigue resonando en los mercados, pero en un tono muy distinto al del miércoles postelectoral. Wall Street ha sufrido hoy un jueves negro en el sector tecnológico, donde se intensifican las incertidumbres ligadas a la inteligencia artificial. El índice Nasdaq, referencia de la industria, cerró la jornada con un batacazo del 5,5% en su peor jornada desde abril de 2025 y entra en el terreno de la corrección al caer más del 12% desde sus máximos. La caída ha supuesto una destrucción de valor de 2,5 billones de dólares (casi 2,3 billones de euros), la mayor en una sola jornada en toda su historia. La tecnología ha arrastrado a la baja al S&P 500, que se ha dejado un 4,35%. El índice selectivo Nasdaq 100 sufrió la peor sesión desde marzo de 2020 tras dejarse un 6,36%. Las Bolsas europeas han borrado sus ganancias de la mañana, y solo ha logrado resistir el Ibex, que ha cerrado con un alza del 0,4%.

En el fondo de la oleada vendedora están las perspectivas de frenazo en la instalación de centros de datos y, por tanto, de inversiones en tecnología. Estas dudas han desatado una estampida de inversores del sector tecnológico, que acumula varias semanas de castigo en Bolsa, dudas sobre su modelo de financiación y unos resultados peores de lo esperado tras varios trimestres con beneficios récord. Llueve sobre mojado en un sector que ve poco a poco cómo la confianza de los inversores se va diluyendo y se acelera la rotación de sus carteras. Los desplomes son particularmente severos en las empresas que están en la cadena de valor de los centros de datos: fabricantes de chips, procesadores y memorias son el eslabón más débil si se concreta la temida ralentización de las inversiones en IA, principal catalizador de las subidas de la renta variable durante los últimos años.

Entre las grandes castigadas figura SanDisk, con un desplome superior al 22%, por un 18% de Western Digital y un 9,5% de Qualcomm se hunden hasta un 20%. AMD y Micron, piezas clave en la industria de semiconductores, han corregido más del 17%. No se libra de las caídas Nvidia, uno de los iconos empresariales de la fiebre de la IA, que ha encajado un recorte superior al 9,2%. El castigo se ve limitado entre los grandes hiperescaladores, empresas con negocios diversificados pero que operan infraestructuras de computación en la nube a gran escala. Microsoft ha recortado un 3,58%, por un 2,2% de Amazon, y un 1,94% de Alphabet. Un panorama que ha llevado al índice de semiconductores de Filadelfia a encajar un castigo de más del 12,2% en la jornada. “Las acciones tecnológicas necesitan que continúe el auge económico, como un tiburón que tiene que seguir nadando para sobrevivir”, advierte Trevor Greetham, director de multiactivos en Royal London Asset Management, en declaraciones recogidas por Financial Times.

Las dudas ya arrancaron en los mercados asiáticos, donde el Kospi de Corea del Sur —el más beneficiado de la apuesta por la IA en todo el mundo— cerró con una caída del 5,2%, con valores como SK Hynix hundiéndose un 9,5% y Samsung Electronics, un 7,6%. En Europa, ASML, que diseña las máquinas utilizadas para la fabricación de chips, ha encajado una caída del 6,5%. JP Morgan defiende que “el bum de la IA mantendrá el rumbo, aunque puede volverse más caro, más lento y más concentrado en los próximos años”.

El resultado electoral llega con el terreno ya abonado para que afloren las dudas. Desde hace un mes la euforia de la IA ha dado paso al escepticismo, ante las mareantes inversiones necesarias para desarrollar los centros de datos: en apenas una semana siete empresas han colocado deuda y acciones por 388.000 millones. Y, por más que el uso de la IA sea cada vez más generalizado y especializado, los ingresos de momento están muy lejos de poder pagar esas hipotecas. Además, la última ronda de resultados del sector ha sido decepcionante, con Alphabet marcando la mayor caída de su historia en Bolsa.

Las alarmas no han saltado esta semana: en un mes el índice de semiconductores de Philadelphia se ha desplomado el 29%. “Estamos viendo una clara continuación de salida de dinero de los fabricantes de chips”, afirmó Tim Waterer, analista jefe de mercados de KCM Trade. Coco Zhang, estratega de ING, añade que se espera un aumento del escrutinio de las empresas tecnológicas por parte de los demócratas en los dos próximos años, al tiempo que intentan desarrollar una regulación de la IA. “Sin embargo, es improbable que una regulación más estricta de la IA y los centros de datos altere la trayectoria de crecimiento del sector”, afirma.

La fuga de inversores de la tecnología ha tenido eco en todos los mercados, aunque a otra escala. En Wall Street empresas tradicionales como Goldman Sachs, Caterpillar o Boeing bajan con fuerza. Se ven, por un lado, arrastradas por las ventas automáticas que generan los fondos indexados al S&P 500, producto que ha crecido vinculado a la tecnología. Pero, a la vez, la IA ha sido en los últimos trimestres un soporte clave para la economía de EE UU. El dinero, mientras, ha buscado puertos donde refugiarso, como la deuda estadounidense, en particular la de corto plazo: el rendimiento del bono a dos años ha bajado 10 puntos básicos, que han sido tres para el de una década. En Europa la deuda se ha mantenido relativamente estable, pero han aumentado las primas de riesgo periféricas. El yen japonés ha salido reforzado (0,5%), pues es un habitual puerto seguro, pero el euro se ha mantenido estable.

Petróleo por debajo de los 100 dólares

En el mercado energético, el petróleo brent rebota hoy más del 3% y corrige así parte de las fuertes pérdidas que sufrió ayer (bajó un 8%), situándose en los 98 dólares el barril. En lo que va de semana, el brent ha bajado 20 dólares, cerca de un 18%, un comportamiento sin precedentes desde los tiempos de la pandemia. Las expectativas de paz en Oriente Medio se han visto reforzadas una vez que el vicepresidente JD Vance ha asegurado que el malestar de los votantes por la guerra y por la relación entre Estados Unidos e Israel condenó a los republicanos en las elecciones. El líder demócrata en minoría en el Senado, Chuck Schumer, prometió poner fin al conflicto, que ya ha entrado en su noveno mes.

“Un Trump obligado a negociar es, en principio, una buena noticia para los mercados financieros, aunque el efecto será desigual, porque será más difícil aprobar un nuevo estímulo fiscal. El primer efecto visible es la moderación de las rentabilidades de la deuda y esto favorece a la renta variable, en particular a las compañías más endeudadas y a las ligadas a la IA, sobre las que pesa el temor a un deterioro de su estructura financiera”, explican los expertos de MacroYield.

World.title: Así se prepara la banca para los próximos años
World.content:
El avance de la inteligencia artificial en bancos como CaixaBank convive con iniciativas de inclusión como SVisual, el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos.

Más educación financiera, planes acordes con la mayor longevidad de la población y digitalización inclusiva. En el horizonte, las entidades bancarias quieren pasar de un papel reactivo a otro más proactivo que acompañe, oriente y anticipe las necesidades de los clientes

La banca del futuro se imagina a menudo dominada por los algoritmos. Sin embargo, cuando se escucha a los expertos y a quienes la construyen, brota un cariz más humano: todos coinciden en que será híbrida. La tecnología es eficaz en lo cotidiano, está disponible a cualquier hora, concede una autonomía impensable hace unos años, cuando la relación con el banco tenía el rostro del trabajador y no una interfaz. Sin embargo, hay circunstancias —las decisiones más vitales— en las que se prioriza el trato personal. Son momentos en los que la conversación con alguien que orienta adquiere un valor irremplazable. Por eso, entidades como CaixaBank entienden el mañana como una suma compleja: más tecnología y más innovación sin desdeñar la posibilidad de acceder a especialistas y gestores cuando sean necesarios.

La inteligencia artificial (IA) permitirá que la relación sea más sencilla y personalizada, pronostican desde CaixaBank. Su cambio estructural consistirá en pasar de una banca principalmente reactiva, en la que el cliente busca una solución cuando surge una necesidad, a una banca con mayor capacidad para acompañar, orientar y anticiparse. Imaginan una relación en la que el banco tenga más capacidad de acompañar de forma proactiva.

Las funciones de esos modelos inteligentes ayudarán a traducir información compleja, a facilitar la comparación entre alternativas y a generar recomendaciones más adaptadas a cada perfil, como anuncian desde este banco. Como concreta Alejandro San Nicolás, docente del máster en Formación Permanente en IA para el Sector Financiero de la Universidad Internacional de Valencia (VIU), la banca conocerá mejor al usuario a través de sus hábitos, comportamientos, emociones y tendencias de consumo. Este docente añade que los entornos bancarios evolucionarán hacia una suerte de marketplace, donde el cliente podrá contratar productos, realizar compras o acceder a financiación directamente desde la plataforma digital bancaria pertinente: “El propio banco va a empezar a lanzarte ofertas basadas en tus necesidades y en lo que te gusta”, explica San Nicolás.

Las entidades financieras aspiran a esa hiperpersonalización que, como señalan desde CaixaBank, “da la oportunidad de reducir ruido y proporcionar al cliente sólo la información apropiada para su situación personal”. Por eso, insisten en que la formación en competencias digitales, la educación financiera y la prevención del fraude son también una parte crucial de ese nuevo acompañamiento.

Habla

Cómo construir una banca integradora, según CaixaBank La evolución de la interfaz Habrá una generalización del móvil como canal financiero. Las plataformas digitales seguirán en constante cambio. Evolucionará con los agentes de IA, que podrán interpretar necesidades, mantener conversaciones complejas y simplificar procesos completos. Su actuación reducirá la complejidad de gestiones que hoy requieren múltiples pasos. Una longevidad diversa Llegados a la jubilación, se generan necesidades que van más allá del dinero. Por eso, desde la entidad se trata de fomentar el ahorro desde edades tempranas, complementar ingresos en la jubilación, ayudar a optimizar el patrimonio financiero e inmobiliario o acompañar a las personas durante toda esa etapa posterior a la laboral. Un error común es considerar que todas las personas mayores son iguales, señalan desde CaixaBank. Algunos se sienten cómodos con los entornos digitales, otros prefieren la atención telefónica y algunos exigen presencialidad. El colectivo senior es especialmente diverso en cuanto a autonomía financiera y uso de canales. Atención a las necesidades específicas CaixaBank hace hincapié en la inclusión: el 94% de sus oficinas, el 99% de sus cajeros y su aplicación móvil CaixaBankNow son accesibles. Además, dispone de la Tarjeta Braille para personas con discapacidad visual, el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos SVisual para clientes con discapacidad auditiva, TPV accesibles, comunicaciones en lectura fácil, una guía adaptada para ayudar en la toma de decisiones financieras y el programa Día a Día Apoyo Capacidad Jurídica. La transformación de las sucursales Las oficinas físicas evolucionarán, aunque seguirán desempeñando un papel importante. CaixaBank tiene más de 4.200, repartidas por España. Además, la entidad tiene presencia en cerca de 3.700 municipios: en 2.234 localidades con el modelo tradicional y en más de 1.420 poblaciones a través de 32 oficinas móviles. Estas permiten a clientes (y no clientes) realizar las operaciones bancarias más habituales en localidades sin oficina bancaria o con restricciones que limitan el acceso a los servicios financieros en poblaciones en las que residen más de 632.000 personas. El 70% de los usuarios tienen más de 65 años.

Mantener la confianza... ‘online’

Dar cierta credibilidad a la IA es fundamental para que su implantación sea efectiva. Pero trabajar en entornos tecnológicos plantea riesgos relacionados con la privacidad, la seguridad de los datos y la posible sensación de vigilancia excesiva, como enumera Juan Carlos López-Robles, profesor de ESIC University que imparte en ámbitos como la Informática Aplicada, las Tecnologías de la Educación y las Tecnologías Móviles e Internet de las Cosas (IoT).

Los ingredientes para que la IA tenga una buena integración, según López-Robles, son tres: que sus respuestas sean útiles, que se comprendan sin necesidad de tener un alto nivel de conocimientos específicos y que sean transparentes. “Los usuarios aceptamos mejor una recomendación cuando entendemos el porqué, el para qué y tenemos la sensación de control sobre la decisión final”. Y añade: “La confianza se construye con explicaciones claras y resultados consistentes “. Hay una necesidad de entender los criterios, de conocer las reglas del juego de algoritmos.

Los usuarios están dispuestos a compartir información cuando perciben un beneficio claro y confían en la entidad. Por eso, para CaixaBank, “la personalización solo tendrá recorrido si va acompañada de seguridad, privacidad, transparencia y capacidad de control por parte del cliente”. Un ejemplo de su compromiso es su nueva Dirección de IA y Datos, que coordina de forma transversal esta área y facilita el desarrollo de soluciones escalables, seguras y responsables. Gestiona todo el ciclo de vida de las iniciativas, desde la identificación de oportunidades hasta su diseño, implantación y supervisión. Además, integra el cumplimiento normativo y la gestión de riesgos desde las fases iniciales; se asegura de que los desarrollos sean responsables.

La IA se emplea con criterio, pero también permite al banco ser más seguro. La han incorporado a sus sistemas de defensa para reforzar las tareas de detección, análisis, actuación y para proteger los nuevos entornos. También vigila los agentes, una función que, más allá de responder a preguntas como un chat tradicional, razona, planifica y ejecuta acciones de forma autónoma para cumplir un propósito. Estos sistemas incorporan herramientas como la identificación y corrección automatizadas de vulnerabilidades, la evolución de su centro de operaciones de seguridad y el empleo de sistemas capaces de detectar indicios de actividad sospechosa, correlacionar señales, evaluar amenazas y activar medidas de protección de manera autónoma.

Sobre todo, inciden en que combinan la capacidad analítica de la IA con la supervisión y responsabilidad humanas. En esa mezcla está la virtud, secunda López-Robles: “Nadie quiere pedir cita para hacer una transferencia o revisar los movimientos de la cuenta, pero casi todo el mundo quiere hablar con una persona antes de firmar una hipoteca o una cartera de inversión”.

La atención presencial no puede desaparecer, reconocen los expertos, pero su transformación es inevitable. “Dará paso a una red mucho más reducida, orientada a un trato más personal, en un espacio con sofás y en los que le ofrecen un café”, describe San Nicolás. De ahí que sean fundamentales las citas previas; serán más puntuales, planificadas y especializadas.

Las entidades financieras se adaptan a los nuevos hábitos y refuerzan sus servicios digitales. CaixaBank aumentó en un 30% las altas digitales en el ejercicio 2025, en gran parte gracias a imagin, el banco digital del grupo dirigido especialmente a clientes jóvenes, que cuenta con alrededor de 4,3 millones de clientes. La penetración en el Grupo CaixaBank de clientes financieros de edad de entre 16 y 34 años alcanza el 42%. La tendencia online también se aprecia en los hábitos de pago. En junio, CaixaBank superó el récord histórico de pago con el móvil en España, con 139,7 millones de operaciones en un mes.

La generación de transición

¿Quiénes son los que se pueden sentir más abrumados por los cambios? San Nicolás, como experto en IA para el sector financiero, señala que los que están “en tierra de nadie”. Por ejemplo: “Los mayores de 50 años, una generación que ha visto llegar toda esta transformación cuando ya tenía gran parte de su vida financiera construida”.

La tecnología puede convertirse en una nueva forma de exclusión, advierte López-Robles, profesor de ESIC. “A medida que aumente el número de personas mayores, la clave no será ofrecer más tecnología, sino hacerla accesible, dinámica, sencilla y fluida”, sostiene. Es uno de los motivos que lleva a CaixaBank a ir más allá de la jubilación, que les mueve a planificar una etapa de la vida cada vez más larga y diversa y apostar por un acompañamiento integral. Para López-Robles, el objetivo que se deben proponer las entidades es construir una banca “no solo más digital, sino más inteligente, más sencilla y, sobre todo, más relevante para cada cliente”.

World.title: En el contrato anual con el inquilino hay una cláusula para que mis hijos recuperen la casa. ¿Aplica la prórroga de dos años?
World.content:
Pregunta. Tengo un piso alquilado que cumple el contrato anual el 31 de diciembre. Cuando renovamos el año pasado, incluimos una cláusula por la que se rescindiría dicho contrato si uno de nuestros dos hijos lo necesitaba. El inquilino aceptó las condiciones. Queremos saber si obligatoriamente tiene que estar dos años más, aunque nuestros hijos lo necesiten, avisando con los plazos legales. C. Sisamon

Respuesta. Entiendo que se está refiriendo a la prórroga extraordinaria de dos años prevista en la disposición final quinta del Real Decreto-ley 29/2026, de 6 de octubre, por el que se adoptan medidas urgentes para la protección de la función social de la vivienda y la ampliación de la oferta de vivienda asequible. Este Real Decreto entró en vigor el 7 de octubre de 2026.

Si el contrato de arrendamiento al que se refiere en la consulta tiene una duración de un año (actualmente denominado contrato temporal o de temporada) y no es de vivienda habitual, no se encontraría dentro de los supuestos en los que puede solicitarse la citada prórroga extraordinaria de dos años. Por tanto, el compromiso de desalojo pactado en favor de los hijos del arrendador debería ser respetado por la parte arrendataria. Además, dicha prórroga extraordinaria no resulta aplicable a los contratos temporales.

No obstante, conviene realizar una precisión importante. Si, tal y como parece desprenderse de la consulta, se vienen formalizando contratos de un año de duración, no prorrogables, sobre la misma vivienda y con los mismos arrendatarios, debe tenerse en cuenta que, si el Real Decreto es finalmente convalidado por la Diputación Permanente, el próximo contrato de temporada que se suscriba (en principio en diciembre de 2026) deberá recoger de forma expresa y obligatoria la causa concreta que motiva el desplazamiento temporal del arrendatario y que justifica la temporalidad del arrendamiento. Asimismo, corresponderá al arrendador acreditar la existencia de dicha causa.

En caso de no poder demostrarse la necesidad temporal que justifica este tipo de contrato, el artículo 7.2 de la Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos, en su redacción dada por el Real Decreto, establece que esta circunstancia “lo privará de su naturaleza temporal y comportará su sumisión al presente título en las mismas condiciones que los contratos de arrendamiento de vivienda habitual, con efectos retroactivos a la formalización del contrato”.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Unfair rent clauses: why thousands of tenants may get money back
World.content:
Did you know that, as a renter, you may be entitled to money back? Read on to see if you qualify.

It all centres on unfair clauses regarding rent increases and recent legal rulings – to the benefit of renters.

Dutch courts, including the Supreme Court, have ruled that a clause in private-sector leases allowing an annual rent increase in line with the Consumer Price Index (consumentenprijsindex, CPI) plus a surcharge of up to 3% is, as a rule, not unfair.

A higher surcharge, though, may be deemed unfair: in December 2025, the Amsterdam Court of Appeal held a surcharge of up to 5% unfair.

“If you believe you paid too much based on an unfair rental clause, you can claim money back,” says Robert Berendsen, founder of Mr. Berendsen Advocaten in Amsterdam. “Many tenants don’t realise they have strong protections in this tight housing market.”

The high court rules

When the Supreme Court made that ruling in November 2024, it set a legal precedent: the CPI and the additional surcharge can be split, meaning that even if the CPI is legal, the surcharge can be seen as unfairly burdensome.

“Until then, that was deemed legally impossible,” says Berendsen of the fair-unfair division. “There was huge interest in the outcome of this case. Hundreds of thousands of tenants may be owed money. Which means potentially hundreds of millions of euros paid out. It has a huge economic impact.”

Most affected would be landlords, housing associations and investors, who would have to return the money.

DIY

Berendsen advises tenants to check their leases and see what surcharge on top of inflation the rent increase clause allows. If it’s more than 3%, enter your data into your AI program of choice and let modern technology do the rest.

“Enter the start date of your lease, the initial rent excluding service charges and every annual increase,” says Berendsen. “Then ask: ‘suppose the rent had only been increased with inflation each year, without the surcharge. What would the rent be today, and how much did I overpay?’”

Only the surcharge can be reclaimed; the inflation increases stand.

“If you believe you are owed money for the unfair surcharges only, write a letter to your landlord. If they don’t react or decline, says Berendsen, you (the tenant) can take the claim to the subdistrict court (kantonrechter). In all cases concerning a lease, even those brought by a landlord, the court must check whether the surcharge clause is unfair, even if the tenant does not raise the issue.”

The future

In July 2026, the Amsterdam District Court referred questions regarding “the splitting of the rent change clause and whether the clause is unfair or not” to the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg in the cases of 19 tenants seeking a refund.

While any decision is likely years away, Berendsen advises tenants not to worry. “The Supreme Court’s ruling is the starting point for tenants; I do not expect the EU court to make their position worse,” he says.

“The idea behind the rules is that tenants operate in a tight market, and it’s not reasonable to expect them to vacate their rental homes if they don’t agree with rent increases,” says Berendsen. “Tenants must be protected from unfair practices.”

If you want legal help from an actual person, contact Mr. Berendsen Advocaten.

World.title: KLM to cut 5,000 jobs amid high fuel prices and global unrest

National airline KLM is slashing around 5,000 jobs, almost 15% of its workforce, in a move the company says is necessary to survive.

CEO Marjan Rintel announced in a press release on Thursday that without serious action the airline, which was founded in 1919 and is one of the oldest in the aviation industry, could fold.

High fuel prices and global unrest are major factors in pressure the company is facing.

KLM was effectively taken over by Air France in 2004, though the Dutch brand kept its own name and management. Of the jobs being cut, 2,000 will be moved to the Air-France KLM group.

Labour unions have expressed concern about the move, with FNV and CNV saying workers are footing the bill for a major corporation.

KLM says compulsory layoffs likely won’t be needed, and that voluntary departure schemes and not replacing staff who leave will help make the needed cuts.

World.title: Human rights orgs cut ties with ICC under US sanctions pressure
World.content:
At least 20 human rights organizations have ended or considerably reduced cooperation with the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague over US-imposed sanctions against the court and its employees, and that may just be the tip of the iceberg.

So found investigative journalism platform Investico and German daily Süddeutsche Zeitung after surveying 100 non-profit organizations, including big names like Human Rights Watch and the Center for Constitutional Rights.

The Trump administration has declared war on what it calls a “rogue court”, sanctioning judges, prosecutors, human rights organisations and, in October, the court as a whole.

“They want more power, and they want it at the expense of our sovereignty as a nation,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X at the time.

“And President Trump will never allow the ICC to prosecute Americans… We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources, and crippling their ability to operate against us. The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”

ICC employees have faced visa restrictions, a loss of access to their American property and financial assets and seen their accounts with American financial service institutions cut as a result of the sanctions, with one judge saying she lost access to all her American credit cards earlier this year.

Human rights organizations

While human rights organizations don’t work directly for the court, they provide valuable information in criminal cases, including eyewitness testimony and local law knowhow.

“They are a very important part of our work,” former Chief Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda told Investico. “They do not conduct investigations on our behalf, but they do provide us with leads, which help us find ways to substantiate evidence.”

Bensouda worked at the ICC until 2021 and was herself sanctioned by the US in 2020, which froze her American assets.

Chilling effect

Some organizations not directly covered by the sanctions have also stopped cooperating with the ICC.

“We cannot accept the risk of being sanctioned ourselves and that all our other work is at risk,” a German NGO told the researchers.

Save the Children Netherlands also says it is struggling to find new ways of working with the court.

As the host country of the ICC, the Netherlands is obliged to protect the court’s work from “interference”. But a spokesperson for the foreign affairs ministry told Investico that the country bears “no special responsibility as a host country” to protect NGOs from the consequences of sanctions.

Midterm elections

While Democrats won control of the US House and Senate in this week’s midterm elections, that won’t change the current sanctions.

“That foreign policy is firmly in the hands of the White House,” legal historian Iva Vukušić from Utrecht University told Dutch News. “But the election results may distract the White House with domestic issues and investigations against them and whatnot. It also changes the mood of invincibility of the White House and that may hold them back a bit.”

World.title: Half of rental agents willing to exclude foreign tenants: study
World.content:
Almost half of rental agents contacted for a government-commissioned study were willing to discriminate against potential tenants with foreign roots, researchers have found.

The study, conducted by the Verwey-Jonker Institute, used actors posing as landlords to phone rental agents and ask them if they could avoid renting to “foreigners; Moroccans, Turks or Poles”.

They found that 97 out of 200 agreed outright with the request. Another 30% didn’t refuse, mostly saying it was up to the landlord, and only 20% said no.

“Expat” privileges

In 36 of the cases, agents distinguished “expats” as good foreign tenants, describing them as highly educated and well paid, with reliable employers. Some also said they tend to leave after a while, which they presented as a way around the 2024 ban on most temporary leases.

“Let me put your mind at rest, neither do we,” one agent told an actor who said they did not have a good feeling about foreigners. “The foreigners we usually talk about are the expats, who just come here to work for the big companies.”

Another said: “Officially we’re not allowed to discriminate, of course, but if you say you don’t want people from certain types of countries, I don’t need to put them forward to you.”

Moroccan-sounding names

In separate tests on 1,662 listings on the rental site Pararius between December and May, applicants with Moroccan-sounding names were invited to viewings less often than otherwise identical applicants with Dutch-sounding names.

For men, there were 14% of cases where only the Dutch-named applicant got an invitation, and 16% for women. Last year’s monitor found no significant discrimination against any group for the first time. The researchers found none this year against Polish-sounding names or same-sex couples.

Findings of the investigations were sent to MPs on Wednesday.

A majority of MPs are seeking to have soon-to-be-redundant civil servants at the education, culture and science ministry (OCW) retrained as teachers.

The VVD will bring the proposal, which also has the backing of political parties D66, CDA, JA21 and 50Plus, the to the cabinet Thursday.

VVD MP Arend Kisteman believes the plan will “kill two birds with one stone”.

“The announced cuts are a great opportunity to have these enthusiastic people voluntarily retrained for a job in education at the expense of the government,” Kisteman told broadcaster NOS.

The cabinet plans to eliminate 25,000 civil servants over the next nine years, a cut of some 16% by 2035. The OCW will not be spared.

Supporters say retraining already enthusiastic education workers as teachers will help alleviate chronic teacher shortages nationwide, especially in the country’s big cities.

But similar past initiatives have gotten low marks over schools’ reluctance to hire people with little to no classroom experience and civil servants’ reluctance to take salary cuts.

World.title: Disgruntled estate agents plan rival to property site Funda
World.content:
A group of disgruntled real estate brokers is starting a rival online real estate marketplace to the dominant Funda, saying it is “building a platform in which the broker is no longer a cash cow but is at the helm.”

The new platform, called Homek, is expected to launch in March 2027. For now, it’s appealing to brokers to join the platform, with RTL Z reporting that it won’t launch until at least 1,000 agents have bought in or the foundation has raised €1 million.

The increasing price of placing a property on Funda is one of the irritants that led the brokers to start the rival site.

“Homek is the fair, transparent alternative to Funda, without expensive packages or paid priority,” says Homek’s website, which currently doesn’t list any properties for sale or rent.

Only certified brokers affiliated with industry associations can use Homek, unlike Funda, where unaffiliated real estate agents who meet the site’s conditions can place properties.

Brokers on Homek will also share in the profits.

“The high placement costs and priority paid at Funda require an alternative: a housing platform where real estate agents themselves are in charge,” says Homek’s website. It promises “fair rates, equal opportunities and control for the affiliated brokers and offices.”

Supply problems

Funda was established in 2001 by the brokers’ association NVM.

“As brokers, we came up with Funda ourselves,” says Toine Naber, former chairman of the NVM branch in West-Brabant and a past member of Funda’s advisory board. “With Homek, we get the chance to do it again, but this time without giving away control of our own future.”

Sven Heinen, who is slated to be chairman of the Homek Foundation, told RTL Z he recognises that to become successful, Homek must have the goods to offer home buyers or renters.

“In the past, there have been plenty of competitors of Funda who wanted to take a piece of this market, but they all stalled because the supply was too limited,” Heinen says. “Only when many real estate agents join us and share their housing supply…can we become a serious competitor of Funda.”

Heinen says that within 48 hours, they’ve already raised €200,000.

Funda says it’s not worried about the competition for now. “In a healthy market, there is competition, and sometimes new players join,” spokesperson Claire Verhagen told RTL Z. “We look forward to that with confidence.”

World.title: Coalition parties ready to vote against each other on tax plans
World.content:
The ruling coalition parties have signalled they could vote against one another on amendments to the 2027 tax plan before parliament votes on it next week, after a debate that went ran late into Wednesday night.

Prime minister Rob Jetten’s centrist social-liberal D66 and the centrist Christian Democrat CDA said they could back opposition amendments even if their coalition partner, the right-wing liberal VVD, voted against them, broadcaster NOS reported.

“It is not an unthinkable situation,” D66 finance spokesman Henk-Jan Oosterhuis said after repeated questions from MPs. “The coalition is not a merger party.” CDA MP Inge van Dijk said split voting was “certainly not the intention” but did not rule it out.

Senate hurdle

The tax plan sets income tax rates and other levies for next year, and must be passed in time for the tax office to bring in the changes. If it fails, the cabinet will almost certainly fall, NRC reported.

Earlier this week the cabinet offered about €350 million in concessions to opposition parties on the left and right, which have formed rival blocs and demanded that the coalition choose between them.

The coalition holds 66 of the 150 seats in parliament. It now looks likely to win next week’s vote with the help of the ChristenUnie, 50PLUS and the group led by former PVV MP Gidi Markuszower. But that is not enough in the senate, where it needs the support of either Pro and Volt or the BBB.

Left-wing parties attacked the coalition for relying on Markuszower, after MPs, including the coalition parties, voted earlier this year against deals with politicians who call for violence against refugees. Markuszower had said Palestinian refugees should be stopped “with maximum violence”, the Volkskrant reported. Pro, Denk and the PvdD said extra police funding credited to him amounted to buying his support.

Oosterhuis said there was “no agreement” with Markuszower, but added: “If Mr Markuszower wants to support the tax plan, I am not going to ask him to vote against it.”

Wealth tax offer

The Pro and Volt alliance used the debate to table an amendment that would shift €1.5 billion of tax from workers to the wealthiest. Income tax would be lowered, paid for by a higher tax rate on the largest fortunes, higher tax on business owners’ income from their companies and an end to tax breaks on passing on family businesses.

The VVD’s Wendy van Eijk said it was “unthinkable” that any coalition party would back the proposal “in this form”, and that her party would not support higher taxes on wealth.

Parliament votes on each amendment before voting on the plan as a whole. That means the VVD could vote against a wealth tax rise but still back the final plan, if D66 and the CDA help the amendment through.

MPs vote on the tax plan on November 12, and the senate in the week before Christmas.

World.title: Sunny end to week, but near-freezing nights ahead
World.content:
Thursday and Friday will be sunny and dry across the Netherlands, but temperatures won’t rise past 10° and could drop close to freezing overnight, according to the KNMI forecast issued at 6am on Thursday.

The national weather institute KNMI said Thursday afternoon would bring plenty of sunshine, with a high of around 10°. Wind from the east will make it feel colder.

Thursday night will stay dry. Temperatures will fall to near freezing in the east, and stay at about 6° on the Wadden islands. Fog is possible in the far southwest.

Friday will be sunny and dry again. Highs will range from 8° in the far north to 12° in the southeast. Clouds will build in the southwest late in the afternoon.

Saturday may start with fog, mainly in the south and southwest, and some frost is possible inland, the KNMI said.

Chinese fast fashion platform Shein has announced a €500 million (2.2 billion zloty) investment to expand its logistics centre in Poland, a move it says will create around 2,000 new jobs by the end of this year. The announcement comes amid growing controversy over the impact of Chinese e-commerce platforms on European businesses and follows a recent decision by the European Union to introduce a special fee on low-value parcels sent from outside the EU and European Free Trade Area. SHEIN investește 500 mil. euro în Polonia. Extinde hub-ul logistic europeanhttps://t.co/WNbib4dFta pic.twitter.com/KiI1AB4wFM — Cristi Dorombach (@piticu21) November 4, 2026 The investment will expand Shein’s existing logistics facility in Magnice, near the city of Wrocław in southwestern Poland, which has been operating since 2022. The expansion will bring total employment at the site to around 10,000 by creating 2,000 jobs in logistics, supply chain management, technology and warehouse operations, according to local news service Wroclaw.pl. The facility will also host 6,500 autonomous robots for sorting items. Shein says that the move will help it cut delivery times in Europe, allowing some orders to arrive within 48 hours. “This investment in Poland clearly demonstrates our commitment and belief in the potential of the European market,” said Leonard Lin, the firm’s global head of public affairs. “Poland has become one of the pillars of our operations in Europe,” he added. “This latest investment is a testament to our confidence in the country’s potential, the competencies of its workforce, and its business environment.” The expansion comes as Shein faces a tougher trading environment in Europe. Its sales in the region fell by 13.9% year-on-year to $3.77 billion in the second quarter, while net profit dropped by 67%. The decline comes as the EU steps up efforts to curb the influx of low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which European retailers say pose unfair competition. In July, the bloc introduced a €3 fee on parcels worth less than €150. From 1 November, a further €2 handling fee was added to all imported parcels, regardless of their value, to cover customs processing costs. China overtook Germany to become Poland’s biggest source of imports for the first time in July, ending a period of around 35 years in which Germany had consistently held top spot https://t.co/U6rQwfEJ7I — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026 Shein has also faced accusations of labour-law violations at its facilities in China, including concerns that it may use cotton produced through forced labour. The company disputes many of the allegations, saying that it prohibits forced and child labour and regularly inspects working conditions at its suppliers. China is an increasingly important trading partner in Poland. In July, it overtook Germany to become Poland’s largest source of imports for the first time, driven by rising purchases of cars, computer hardware and consumer goods. Poland has detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components. Investigators say that over 2 million zloty (€450,000) worth of equipment was smuggled into the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The arrests, which took place on 21 October and 2 November, were announced on Thursday morning by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and National Prosecutor’s Office. 🚨 ROSYJSKI WYWIAD. PRZEMYT CZĘŚCI DO PRODUKCJI UZBROJENIA. 6 ZATRZYMANYCH.@ABW_GOV_PL rozbiła grupę podejrzaną o działalność na rzecz rosyjskich służb specjalnych. 🔴6⃣ osób zatrzymanych, 🔴2⃣1⃣przeszukanych lokalizacji, 🔴 4⃣osoby z zarzutami szpiegostwa – wszystkie trafiły… pic.twitter.com/L90n3rf5rY — ABW (@ABW_GOV_PL) November 5, 2026 Prosecutors report that all six suspects have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group that sought to export weapon components from Poland to Russia in violation of a ban on such trade. Four of the suspects have also been charged under Poland’s espionage law, accused of acting on behalf of Russian intelligence in return for financial benefits. Those four individuals have been placed in pretrial detention. The other two were released with preventative measures put in place. The ABW says that the criminal group “illegally supplied Russia with significant quantities of military components, including those used in the production of ammunition and weapons systems”. “This type of activity may lead to the strengthening of the Russian arms industry and the military capabilities of the Russian Federation, and thus pose a serious threat to Poland’s security and interests,” wrote the agency. Prosecutors say that the group operated at least between June 2023 and December 2025 in Poland, Lithuania and Russia. Members were responsible for procuring goods and transporting them to Kaliningrad, which borders Poland and Lithuania. “Vehicles equipped with hidden compartments were used to transport the goods,” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The suspects repeatedly crossed the Polish-Russian border, and some of the transports were intercepted by Polish border guards.” Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, revealed that the six suspects include five Polish citizens, aged 25 to 52, and one Russian woman, aged 37. Onet, a leading news website, reports, based on unnamed sources, that the Russian citizen acted as a liaison between the group and the foreign intelligence agency behind the operation. Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 6 osób podejrzanych o udział w zorganizowanej grupie przestępczej działającej przeciwko Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej. Wśród zatrzymanych jest pięciu Polaków w wieku od 25 do 52 lat i 37-letnia Rosjanka. 🛑 Sąd – pod zarzutem szpiegostwa -… — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 5, 2026 Poland has seen a huge rise in espionage cases in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage.
