World.title: Rando Kuustik: The perpetual saving of Estonian education
World.content:
Estonian education is a remarkably resilient phenomenon. No matter how many times it is reformed, it always manages to find itself in such poor shape ahead of the next election that it needs rescuing once again. And then along come the politicians with their solutions.

Some suggest reorganizing the school network, others promise to give teachers the recognition they deserve, while still others argue that money is being spent in the wrong places. Meetings with school principals are also essential because how else could politicians later claim to have listened to them? It all sounds promising. About as promising as it did during the last election.

I have worked in education for nearly 30 years, more than a dozen of them as a school principal. I have seen wise decisions and dedicated people, but also reforms that simply gave old problems new names. The trouble is that the power to make decisions and the obligation to take responsibility do not reside at the same address.

A politician can make a decision, an official can approve it and the next government can reverse it. But come Monday morning, the school principal still has to make sure there is a teacher in front of every class, every child has a place to learn and the school is running. You cannot hang a sign on the school door saying, "Classes are suspended until political accountability has been established."

Historic schools had courageous leaders

The history of Estonian education is also a story of people who dared to think beyond the immediate future. Jakob Westholm and Hugo Treffner, for example, had a vision of the kind of person a young student could grow into and the kind of school they would need.

We tend to label historic schools as elite schools and expect them to deliver excellent results, uphold traditions and offer innovative teaching. Preferably without spending too much money.

Jakob Westholm High School waited nearly 30 years for an extension. Governments and promises came and went, children grew up, but the need for more space remained. The school, operating across multiple locations, was expected to deliver ever-better results. In December 2025, construction finally got underway. That deserves recognition, but it does not erase the preceding decades.

Now we are once again hearing representatives of several political parties argue that too much education funding is being spent on concrete. Of course, every investment must be justified and an impressive building is no substitute for a good teacher. But nobody expects a surgeon to perform a world-class operation while insisting that what matters is the doctor, not the operating room.

"Some discussions have been substantive, while others have been half-hour meetings with everyone's eyes fixed on their phones and calendars."

Yet in education, we somehow manage to have an entirely serious debate about whether the environment needed for teaching is part of educational quality or merely an unnecessary luxury. The cost of construction is clearly visible in the budget, but the cost of failing to build, particularly over 30 years, is far harder to calculate.

Half an hour of listening followed by four years of silence

Through school leadership organizations, I have met with representatives of political parties. We have discussed teachers, the responsibilities of school principals and unnecessary restrictions. Some discussions have been substantive, while others have been half-hour meetings with everyone's eyes fixed on their phones and calendars. Then come the thanks, assurances that it was all very interesting and everyone goes their separate ways. The meeting took place and the box has been checked.

But what changed? Which proposal made it into a party platform or legislation? Which unnecessary obligation was eliminated? When were school principals told, "Your reasoning was better than ours, so we're changing our plan"? I have received fewer answers than invitations to further meetings.

Politicians do not always have to agree with us because school principals make mistakes too. But listening that has no potential to change anything is more of a courtesy ritual than genuine engagement. It is easy to prove that a meeting took place, but harder to show what was learned from it.

A school principal must be a strategist, a human resources manager, a crisis manager, sometimes a lawyer and a psychologist and solve by morning a problem that has been under review elsewhere for years. Responsibility is at the heart of leadership, but it only makes sense when you have the power to influence the outcome.

The public sector needs rules and oversight, but oversight must not become an end in itself. Sometimes it seems that the more we document something, the more convinced we become that it actually exists. Meanwhile, the problem at school may quietly persist.

We call teachers professionals and expect them to be creative, then ask them to demonstrate in ever-greater detail exactly how they exercise that creativity. No reporting form has ever sparked a child's curiosity. That takes a teacher who has the time and freedom to put their knowledge to use.

Who should manage education?

The school network needs to be reorganized because student numbers are declining in some areas, while others face a shortage of school places. Politicians should set the goals and provide the funding, while professionals must be allowed to develop the solutions. A wise politician must know how to consult those who understand the work and then do something with their answers.

"No reporting form has ever sparked a child's curiosity. That takes a teacher who has the time and freedom to put their knowledge to use."

The state, local governments and education professionals should agree on goals for the school network, teachers and learning environments that span an entire student's school years. Publicly established deadlines and clearly assigned responsibilities would prevent each new administration from starting from scratch.

School principals must be able to make decisions about staffing, work organization and budgets within agreed limits. In return, they should be evaluated on results, not the number of approvals they obtain. Every reform needs an impact assessment establishing who will do the work, with what funding and within what timeframe and which existing task will be eliminated. Finally, the results of stakeholder consultations should be made public, showing which proposals were accepted and why others were rejected.

Ahead of the 2027 Riigikogu elections, I would like political parties to answer a rather uncomfortable question, in addition to making their usual promises: What decision-making powers are you prepared to give up so that teachers can teach and school principals can lead?

Jakob Westholm and Hugo Treffner are not remembered for how obediently they followed regulations. They are remembered for the schools and opportunities they managed to create. They dared to make decisions and take responsibility for them. Why do we regard such courage as exemplary in historical school leaders, yet tend to restrict it today?

Politicians come and go. School principals remain. To shoulder the responsibility. But perhaps it is finally time to entrust them with the authority to lead as well.

World.title: Gallery: Holger Marjamaa performs with Take 6 in Tallinn
World.content:
Jazz pianist Holger Marjamaa's trio and acclaimed American vocal group Take 6 performed at Alexela Concert Hall on Wednesday, with saxophonists Aleksander Paal and Mairo Marjamaa joining as surprise guests.

Marjamaa and the 10-time Grammy-winning Take 6 have collaborated extensively in the United States in recent years, but the Tallinn concert marked their first joint performance in Europe.

The 33-year-old Marjamaa has spent years dividing his career between Europe and the United States. In 2023, he performed at Alexela Concert Hall with his trio and special guest Chad Lefkowitz-Brown.

Founded in 1980, Take 6 blends gospel, jazz, soul, R&B, and pop music. Over the years, the ensemble has released more than 10 studio albums and collaborated with artists including Whitney Houston, Stevie Wonder, and Ray Charles.

Marjamaa has performed in the United States and across Europe and Asia at venues and festivals including the Seoul Jazz Festival, Monterey Jazz Festival, Dallas Symphony, Atlanta Symphony Hall, Sony Hall, Lincoln Center's Dizzy's Club, Mezzrow Jazz Club, Smalls Jazz Club, Blue Note Tokyo, Blue Note New York (2019–2023), Blue Note Beijing, Blue Note Jazz Cruise, and Blue Note Shanghai.

He has released two solo albums and appeared as a guest musician on more than 30 recordings.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate rises against Iraqi dinar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar against the Iraqi dinar experienced a slight increase on Thursday in both Baghdad, the Iraqi capital, and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

The US dollar exchange rate rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,683 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,682 Iraqi dinars on Thursday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,687.5 Iraqi dinars and 1,677.5 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate also increased, fluctuating between 1,682.5 and 1,681.5 Iraqi dinars.

US dollar exchange rates rose noticeably in the Baghdad and Erbil markets on October 7, following the cabinet’s decision to revalue the official rate of the local currency, causing turbulence and instability in the parallel market.

Iraq officially depreciated its national currency, with the baseline dropping from about 1,300 Iraqi dinars to 1,500 dinars per US dollar.

The Iraqi cabinet approved the structural adjustment, which marks a 14.5 percent decline compared to the previous official framework that had been in place since early 2023.

Following the announcement, parallel market rates in Baghdad and Erbil soared, with exchange shops reporting market gains of more than 1,700 Iraqi dinars per US dollar.

World.title: BP, PetroChina to reduce budgets for oil projects in Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – British Petroleum (BP) and PetroChina have agreed to reduce the monthly budgets for two major oil projects at the Rumaila oilfield in southern Iraq.

The decision, made in collaboration with their Turkish contractor Tekfen, will ensure the continuation of the projects; however, it will significantly slow down the pace of activities. according to the British magazine Middle East Economic Digest (MEED).

A combination of regional geopolitical crises, operational obstacles, and Baghdad’s vigorous state-level austerity push are driving the spending reduction.

The total value of the impacted projects is less than $100 million. They entail building new facilities at the Rumaila oilfield in addition to modernizing and fixing vital upstream infrastructure that already exists.

Equipment import delays through the Strait of Hormuz, directly linked to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, have significantly disrupted supply chains.

Due to temporary facility closures brought on by these delays, PetroChina’s foreign output has already decreased by over 14 percent.

The enormous Rumaila field is located just 60 kilometers from the Iranian border, making it extremely vulnerable to regional military conflict, according to industry sources.

To reduce state spending without lowering real raw output, the Iraqi Oil Ministry ordered a $1.4 billion cost-cutting directive for 2026 oil field budgets.

The remarkable 346 percent increase in Iraq’s budget deficit, which reached $23.9 billion during the first nine months of the year as a result of declining oil revenues, is the driving force behind this austerity.

World.title: Iraqi PM, US president discuss regional security
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and US President Donald Trump discussed on Thursday the latest developments in the region, security issues, and prospects for the next phase.

During a phone conversation, the two sides discussed measures to promote regional stability, as well as cooperation between Iraq and the United States that addresses current challenges.

To manage crises, reduce tensions, and stop the conflict from getting worse, both sides stressed the need to prioritize dialogue and diplomacy, according to a statement released by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

To protect the security of the region and the stability of citizens, al-Zaidi reaffirmed Iraq’s commitment to respecting state sovereignty, avoiding the use of its territory to attack neighboring countries, and adopting peaceful solutions and constructive dialogue.

Additionally, to improve bilateral relations and advance shared interests, both parties stressed the significance of continuing communication and coordinating views on matters of shared concern.

The phone call comes in the wake of shocking losses for the Republican Party in the US midterm elections, putting Trump under more pressure to handle the complexities of the Middle East and the ongoing discussions over the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: US Special Envoy Tom Barrack meets Iraqi PM in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – US Special Envoy Tom Barrack met this week with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Baghdad to discuss regional stability, post-withdrawal plans, and bilateral ties.

Following the conclusion of the US-led international coalition’s mission in Iraq on September 30, the discussions turned to diplomacy, investment, and economic cooperation.

The high-level discussions focused on transitioning the US-Iraq relationship away from its historic, purely security-based framework toward a broader, comprehensive economic and institutional partnership.

The two sides discussed regional developments, efforts to reduce tensions, and the situation of armed groups and firearms outside the government’s control.

The discussion was constructive, according to Barrack, who added that leaders who chose the hard route are the ones who build stability.

Both parties stressed prioritizing trade, cross-sector infrastructure projects, and shared economic interests above military arrangements.

In addition to his meeting with Prime Minister al-Zaidi, Barrack spoke with Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zaidan and Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein.

World.title: KBR to design gas capture project for Iraq’s West Qurna-1 oilfield
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – AKT Oil Services Company has given KBR a comprehensive engineering design contract for the West Qurna-1 Low-Pressure Gas Capture Project in Iraq.

KBR will deliver comprehensive multidisciplinary engineering design services for the Gas Compressor Station 6 located at the West Qurna-1 oilfield.

The contract was awarded by AKT Oil Services Company, which is managing the EPC project for Basrah Gas Company (BGC).

To reduce emissions and lessen reliance on energy imports, the project aims to capture low-pressure associated gas that is currently flared during production at the West Qurna-1 oilfield.

The gas captured from the oilfield, which has over 20 billion barrels of recoverable reserves, will be routed into the domestic energy chain.

By lowering dependency on gas and power imports, the project helps Iraq achieve energy self-sufficiency. Additionally, it fortifies KBR’s four-decade foothold in the infrastructure and energy sector of Iraq.

The development took place after Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister for Energy Affairs Mohsen al-Mandalawi and a delegation from US-based KBR discussed in late October the development of the country’s oil and gas sectors.

According to a statement cited by the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), the meeting addressed prospects for joint cooperation in the oil, gas, and energy sectors, as well as leveraging the firm’s expertise to develop infrastructure and enhance the efficiency of strategic projects.

According to al-Mandalawi, the government aims to implement actionable programs for the Majnoon oilfield and the recovery of associated gas at the West Qurna-1 field, as well as initiatives for ammonia production and efforts to minimize gas flaring at oil fields.

World.title: Race for 2028 heats up after US midterms firestorm
World.content:
Washington – President Donald Trump’s stunning midterms defeat by the Democrats has upended another US election — the race to replace him in the White House in 2028.

The crushing defeat for the Republicans is particularly stinging for Vice President JD Vance, who had been the frontrunner but now risks being seen as tied to his lame-duck boss.

But the midterms are a potential launchpad for rising Democratic stars like Georgia senator Jon Ossoff, whose youthful vibe has already drawn comparisons to former president Barack Obama.

– Republicans in turmoil –

The MAGA coalition that shot Trump to power in 2016 and 2024 effectively collapsed in Tuesday’s midterms, leaving any presumptive Republican heir with a mountain to climb.

Long seen as the odds-on favorite for the Republican nomination in 2028, Vance is the most obvious victim after hitching his wagon to Trump throughout the midterms campaigns with rallies in swing states.

The ambitious 42-year-old quickly tried to distance himself from the electoral disaster, blaming it on Trump’s unpopular war on Iran in a long thesis posted on X on Wednesday.

But voters are likely to reject his attempts to disown Trump.

It’s a familiar problem for US vice presidents. Former Democratic candidate and vice president Kamala Harris suffered from a similar problem in 2024 when she said that “there’s not a thing that comes to mind” when asked how she’d differentiate herself from Joe Biden.

“The bad news for Vance is that sitting vice presidents seldom win the presidency,” James Lindsay of the Council for Foreign Relations, said.

Trump’s Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s name has also been bandied about.

Rubio, 55, has kept a far lower profile during the midterms but any top official in Trump’s administration will struggle to wash their hands of the Iran war.

The Republicans’ midterm disaster could, however, be a boost for other possible candidates.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, 48, who ran against Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, has suddenly become very vocal.

He described the Democratic sweep as “the political equivalent of a meteor strike” — and pointed out that it was only in his own state that Republicans held them off.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz, 55, has also left the door open, having run against Trump in 2016 — although his chances may have been harmed by the Democrats’ stunning senate and governor wins in the midterms in his state.

– Democrats on a high –

The Democratic field is crowded but the midterms have given some likely candidates a boost.

Ossoff’s reelection as Georgia Senator has fueled speculation about a 2028 run by a telegenic politician who has already gained attention for mocking Trump’s relationship with a young staffer.

The 39-year-old has said that he has “zero interest in running for president” but his swiftly-declared win in Georgia — and his victory speech — have bolstered his status in the party.

Before the midterms Kamala Harris, 62, had been the favorite for the nomination, but there are many in the party who would prefer to have someone without a losing track record.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, 53, who was interviewed by Harris to be her running mate in 2024, had a good night on Tuesday as he stormed back to reelection in the key battleground state.

Outgoing California Governor Gavin Newsom, 59, is another big name who has repeatedly taken on Trump. He predicted in an interview with AFP in September Trump’s presidency “as we know it would be over after the midterms.

But Newsom, like Harris, may be seen as more of an old guard figure in a party that is looking to its rising stars.

A prominent but potentially divisive choice would be left-wing New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who said in September that she was weighing a run, musing about whether a Latina could win in a country that rejected female nominees in 2016 and 2024.

Other possible contenders include former Chicago mayor Rahm Emmanuel, JB Pritzker, the billionaire Illinois governor who set out a lengthy national agenda after winning a third term on Tuesday, Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, and Arizona senator and former astronaut Mark Kelly.

World.title: Sixers roll on to down Pistons, Knicks gore Bulls
World.content:
Los Angeles – Jaylen Brown and Joel Embiid combined for 56 points as the Philadelphia 76ers defeated the Detroit Pistons 112-106 in their heavyweight top-of-the-table NBA Eastern Conference clash on Wednesday.

Brown finished with 30 points and Embiid added 26 to give the Sixers another impressive road win that moved them to 8-1 at the top of the standings, with Detroit (6-2) in second.

Brown and Embiid led another balanced offensive performance from Philadelphia, who saw all five starters reach double figures.

LeBron James added a double-double with 13 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists while Tyrese Maxey drained three three-pointers on his way to a 19-point haul.

Brown, who arrived from the Boston Celtics in the offseason, said he was “still adjusting” to his new team-mates.

“I’m still figuring it out,” Brown said, before paying tribute to the performance of 41-year-old team-mate James.

“LeBron has been great,” Brown said. “To see what he’s doing at his age makes sense for LeBron James, but for nobody else would it make sense.”

The Sixers moved into the lead towards the end of the first quarter and kept their noses in front for the remainder of the game, stretching the lead to 18 points before a late rally from Detroit.

Duncan Robinson led the Pistons with 27 points while Cade Cunningham added 26.

The reigning champion New York Knicks scored their biggest win of the season with a 135-105 blowout over the Chicago Bulls at Madison Square Garden.

The Knicks, who have made a slow start to the new campaign, improved to 4-4 after a dazzling 33-point performance from Jalen Brunson, who drained five three-pointers while making 10-of-17 from the field.

O.G. Anunoby scored 18 points while Karl-Anthony Towns added 17 for a Knicks team who led by as many as 44 points midway through the third quarter.

In Boston, the Milwaukee Bucks threatened to pull off a huge comeback before finally succumbing 109-102 to the Celtics.

Paul George (25 points) and Derrick White (24) led the scoring for Boston, who appeared to be cruising after leading by 20 early in the third quarter.

But a 38-point third quarter from Milwaukee flipped the script and the Bucks edged into a 96-95 lead with five minutes remaining.

Boston regained control down the stretch with George and White closing out the win.

World.title: Gaza turns rubble into power with homemade wind turbines
World.content:
Khan Yunis – Above a maze of tents in a crowded displacement camp in Gaza, homemade wind turbines made from scrap metal and salvaged debris spin in the sea breeze, bringing electricity to struggling Palestinians.

In the southern Khan Yunis camp, Kamal Al-Dabary, a former engineering student, has put his skills to work for families who, like most Gazans, live in displacement with no direct access to the tiny territory’s shattered power grid.

According to the World Bank, more than 90 percent of Gaza’s power generation and distribution capacity was destroyed in April 2026, much of it in Israeli strikes that devastated homes and infrastructure.

Sitting on the ground, Dabary tinkered with electrical wires, metal parts and basic tools on a plastic table.

After carefully twisting cables together and testing them with a multimeter, a small bulb flickered on, then another, signalling that the current was flowing.

“When solar panels were still relatively affordable, we bought one and kept moving it around to follow the sun,” the 60-year-old, displaced by the fighting between Israel and Hamas, told AFP.

The war was triggered by the Palestinian Islamist movement’s deadly October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

But after three years of war, prices have soared as aid and commercial supplies trickled into Gaza through crossings tightly controlled by Israel.

A single solar panel now costs at least 15,000 shekels (nearly $5,000), putting it out of reach for most Gazans, Dabary said.

– ‘Changed everything’ –

“We haven’t had work or income for three years,” he added.

“That’s when the idea of a wind turbine came to mind. Why not harness the wind? So we salvaged parts from the rubble.”

The turbines are built from scooter motors and old water tanks cut into blades.

As the wind turns the blades, they drive a motor that generates electricity. The power then passes through circuits assembled from parts recovered from destroyed homes before being stored in batteries.

This provides enough electricity to charge phones and run lights, fans and even electric razors, small comforts that have become a luxury for families still living in tents and shelters.

Nearly all of Gaza’s residents were displaced at least once during the war, and most now live in a small area still under Hamas rule, while Israel controls more than 60 percent of the territory along its perimeter.

“They help us hold on… until God delivers us from this ordeal and we can return home,” said Dabary, known locally as Abu Ayman.

The output remains modest. But in a camp where shortages are constant, every watt counts.

The system “has changed everything,” said 50-year-old Saleh ben Hasan.

With healthcare and medication hard to access in Gaza, the power can also help keep medical equipment running.

“If a child needs a nebuliser (a device used to inhale medicine) in the middle of the night, who else can we turn to?” he said.

“Electricity is needed… So we turn to our brother Abu Ayman.”

World.title: Special summary roll revision in 6 states, UTs; draft on Nov 30
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The

on Thursday announced the annual Special Summary Revision of electoral rolls in Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Mizoram, Odisha and Sikkim.

The poll roll revision exercise seeks to enrol eligible voters, particularly young and first-time electors, and facilitate advance applications from those who will become eligible on April 1, July 1 and Oct 1, 2027. Draft rolls will be out on Nov 30. The final publication of electoral rolls will take place on Jan 21.

Deletion applications must undergo field verification in cases involving repeated or multiple entries. EROs must personally cross-check deletions exceeding 2% of electors at a polling station. Furnishing Aadhaar details in Forms 6 and 8 will remain voluntary. No application for enrolment can be rejected for failure to provide Aadhaar.

World.title: Party after gun buy ends in a death
World.content:
A late-night liquor party among friends to celebrate the purchase of an illegal firearm ended in the death of a 25-year-old man during celebratory firing in Bhubaneswar early Thursday.

Eight friends of the deceased, Tapu Nayak, were arrested. All the accused were employed at a private construction company. Despite indications that the firing may have been accidental, police booked all accused for murder. While drinking together, one of the accused allegedly fired. The bullet struck Nayak. He was rushed to a hospital. As Nayak's condition deteriorated, he was shifted to a private hospital, where doctors declared him dead. Preliminary investigation suggested no apparent motive to target Nayak. His wife has sought an impartial probe.

World.title: Firecrackers stored in house explode, kill 1
World.content:
.

A 20-year-old college student was killed when firecrackers bought for Diwali celebrations exploded at his friend's house near Melur in Tamil Nadu's Madurai early Thursday. The student's friend and his mother were seriously injured in the blast that brought down a part of the building's upper floor.

World.title: Mulling panel to review UGC equity norms: Government
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Centre told Supreme Court on Thursday that it is considering appointing a committee to review provisions of the UGC (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2026, the operation of which was stayed by SC saying its provisions could fuel divisions in society.

Solicitor general Tushar Mehta told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi that govt was contemplating setting up an expert panel to revisit provisions of the regulations to ensure that "nobody has any apprehension or anyone is left dissatisfied".

The move appears to be aimed at assuaging the "hurt" among upper castes over having been excluded from among those who can complain against caste abuse ahead of polls in UP and Uttarakhand.



Upper castes, a vocal constituency and an influential part of BJP's social base, argue that the "equity guidelines" framed at SC's instance, does not take into account the changed socio-economic conditions which have seen dominance shift to the newly-empowered OBCs, and would leave them vulnerable to harassment.

CJI Surya Kant said the provisions must ensure that "concerns of every student, the next generation and the young generation are addressed" appropriately.





The SC adjourned hearing on a batch of petitions, including one filed by the mothers of Rohith Vemula and Payal Tadvi who committed suicide allegedly after failing to endure caste-based discrimination on college campuses.

Mehta said govt shared SC's concerns and intends to revisit the provisions of the 2026 regulations. The same bench of CJI Kant and Justice Bagchi had on Jan 29 kept in abeyance the controversial regulations taking exception to several provisions.

World.title: Government buys time on UGC rules without committing to withdrawal or retention
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Centre's move to consider a fresh review of the controversial UGC equity regulations are being seen as an olive branch to agitating upper caste groups, while giving BJP room to avoid a fresh caste controversy ahead of the assembly elections, particularly in Uttar Pradesh.The regulations, which extended specific protection against caste-based discrimination to OBCs alongside SCs and STs, had triggered protests among general category students who feared exclusion and possible misuse of the provisions.Centre told Supreme Court Thursday that it was contemplating setting up a committee to reconsider the regulations, ensuring that no section of students felt excluded or apprehensive. The move gives govt time to revisit the issue without committing itself to either withdrawing or retaining the rules.A complete rollback has been a key demand of upper caste organisations, whose protests also caused unease within BJP. Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh have been leading govt's outreach to agitating youth outfits. Both had met representatives of Kshatriya Karni Sena-led 'UGC Rollback Campaign' in Sept, after which a proposed mahapanchayat was postponed.The Jan notification had caused resentment among sections of general category students who felt the regulations portrayed upper castes as the principal perpetrators of caste discrimination. The absence of a specific provision against false complaints added to their concerns.At the heart of the controversy is the wording of the regulations. While one provision defines caste-based discrimination specifically as unfair treatment of SC, ST and OBC members, another prohibits discrimination against any student, including on caste grounds.General category students argue that this creates confusion over whether they would receive the same protection if they face caste-based discrimination.Supporters of the regulations argue that historically disadvantaged communities need specific safeguards against discrimination.For BJP, a complete withdrawal carries political risks. OBCs and Dalits form an important part of its social coalition, especially in Uttar Pradesh, where caste identities remain politically sensitive.

World.title: Umar, Sharjeel move SC for bail
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Referring to the contradictory orders given by Supreme Court in the matter of bail to the accused on the ground of delay in trial and long incarceration for UAPA offences, which have been referred to a larger bench for authoritative pronouncement, former student activists Umar Khalid and

have moved SC for bail in 2020 Delhi riots cases.

The accused submitted that two co-accused, including Tasleem Ahmed, were granted bail by SC on the grou-nd that determination of the issues by the larger bench would take time, and they could not be made to suffer continued incarceration.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Seeking parity with the co-accused, Sharjeel Imam, who has already spent six years and nine months in custody, said in his petition, filed through advocate Fauzia Shakil, that two co-accused in the same FIR were released on interim bail by the court on May 22 under a principle which applies to him in greater degree.



The accused moved SC after their plea for bail was rejected by the trial court and Delhi High Court on the ground that the apex court had purportedly set a deadline of Jan 5, 2027, for them to file a bail petition.

The petition asked "whether the principle recognised by this Court in Tasleem Ahmed v. State order dated 22.05.2026, that an accused cannot be made to suffer continued incarceration merely because an important question of law has arisen for authoritative settlement, can be withheld from the petitioner alone by reference to the role attributed to him, when the question referred to concerns the correctness of the very judgment which declined his bail and relief in Tasleem Ahmed case was granted without any examination of role?"

It further argued, "Whether liberty reserved by this Court in a judgment declining bail, to renew the prayer for bail at a defined point, operates as a bar upon the statutory jurisdiction of the Special Court and of the High Court to consider an application for bail founded on supervening circumstances be-fore that point, when the same paragraph of the judgment holds that pre-trial detention cannot be permitted to continue without regard to the progress of the trial and that Article 21 operates as a continuing check against continued incarceration without substantial progress of the trial?"

World.title: The silver hands of Hupari
World.content:
On an afternoon just about a month before Deepavali, Kanchan Katkar, 76, deftly picks up silver ghungroos with a pair of iron tongs that fit into her palm. She attaches them to chain loops. “I have been doing this for decades and will continue to do this as long as I am able,” she says, her voice bearing a gentle tremor. Deep inside her dimly lit house, hidden within the twisting lanes of Hupari town, where rooms line up like wagons on a track, Katkar sits in the shadows.

Back in 1970, Kanchan was one of the few girls who completed school in Hupari. Marriage then was taken for granted, but after her two sisters wed, she decided to stay single to care for her parents, who had actively participated in the Indian freedom struggle.

Her decision sent shockwaves through her family and village, breaking an unwritten social code. “Why should only a son bear the responsibility of caring for ageing parents?” she says. “Why can’t daughters?” Had she ever agreed to marry, it would have been on one non-negotiable condition: that her parents remain her primary care and priority. Eventually, her parents accepted her choice.

“I learnt sewing and soon entered the silver industry,” Kanchan remembers. “For any woman seeking autonomy and control over her own life and resources, the very first step is economic self-reliance. Hupari’s silver trade gave me and many others that foundation.”

Decades later, Kanchan is neither a factory owner nor a trader. Like thousands of women in her town, she works from home, fitting delicate craftsmanship into the quiet spaces between her daily domestic chores.

In the bustling lanes of Hupari, a town in Kolhapur district celebrated for over a century as Maharashtra’s Silver Capital, the soft clinking of delicate ornaments carries a quiet story of women’s liberation and financial independence.

Here, in an industry generating an annual turnover of ₹1,000 crore, women comprise 60-70% of the town’s 25,000-strong artisan workforce, say records of the Chandi Karkhandar Association (Silver Manufacturers Association), whose members comprise 4,000 or so silver-business owners. A publication brought out by the association says the industry began here in 1904.

Silent labour

While men traditionally handle heavy, factory-bound tasks like melting silver, rolling strips, and soldering broad frames, the heart of Hupari’s silver industry beats inside the homes of the women. Across the town’s winding alleys, populated by about 40,000 people, a domestic production model thrives on women’s quiet labour, fuelling the local economy, with a national supply chain and exports around the globe.

The town is India’s prominent producer of seamless ghungroos, the tiny tinkling beads that define traditional payals (anklets).

Artisans shape and seal these hollow silver spheres by hand. But they also produce several other pieces of jewellery, including anklets, toe rings, and waistbands.

The production cycle begins with molten metal in factory crucibles operated by men. Women use different techniques to finish the ornaments. Using jaali (filigree) techniques, they twist, bend, and mould fine silver wires into complex geometric and Nature-inspired motifs. Their fingers coil thin wire into individual rings, assemble foundational chains, thread beads, link loops, and align delicate charms. They also use meenakari (enamelling) to inject colour into grooved motifs. In this way, they turn industrial output into a living cultural legacy.

Despite hours of painstaking labour, many earn between just ₹200 and ₹250 a day, largely because there are no organised labour unions to demand higher wages or fair returns for their work. The piece rate remains meagre: for 2,000 ghungroos, an artisan gets ₹400. While a few women manage to complete 2,000 beads in a single day, many make far less, underscoring the gap between their vital craft contribution and their financial compensation.

Those at the helm of the industry acknowledge this reality. Dinkar Sase, vice-president of the Chandi Karkhandar Association, admits that, “Ha udyog mahilanchya jivavar chalala ahe (This entire industry rests on the shoulders of women).” Founded in 1944, the association kept its doors firmly closed to women for seven decades, opening membership to female manufacturers only in 2014. Even today, though women run manufacturing units, their husbands often step forward as the public faces of membership.

“Now, the picture is slowly changing and more women are becoming members,” says Dinkar. The irony is embedded in the trade’s identity: the association’s annual report likens Hupari to a saubhagyarupi nari, a woman who embodies grace, marital bliss, and auspiciousness, under the spiritual gaze of the village deity, Goddess Ambabai.

According to Dinkar, female artisans require no formal training because the craft flows naturally through generations of hands. Yet, leadership stays entrenched in male hands.

Almost 8,000 manufacturing operations are male-dominated at the commercial front, with men travelling to trade ornaments across Indian cities, while women manage the daily operations back home.

Since its inception, the association has relied on unanimous decisions led entirely by male presidents. Dinkar maintains that wages are settled collaboratively without dispute, and that the association resolves any grievances without distinction between owners and workers. He says the industry’s latest challenge is meeting Gen Z’s growing demand for fresh, trend-forward silver ornament designs.

A new direction

Sharwari Waingade, now in her 40s, is actively tackling a shift in a century-old craft. Designing contemporary silver pieces, including oxidised-silver lines, says, “The industry will have to adapt to new challenges.” She highlightes both the changing aesthetic demands and the need to mechanise parts of production with modern technical knowledge.

Her entry into the craft was unexpected. While pursuing an MSc in Microbiology in Pune, she met Rajesh. Rajesh came from a family deeply rooted in Hupari’s traditional silver manufacturing. After they married, Sharwari developed a keen interest in carrying that legacy forward.

Inside a traditional stone-structured house attached to their manufacturing unit, she brings out from the cupboard her latest oxidised creations. “This new format of jewellery was introduced by her,” says Rajesh, proudly. He also shows off the antique dies preserved by his family over generations. “We continue to design new pieces based on these traditional dies, and we have a strong B2B clientele for this collection.”

As Sharwari brings in coffee, she reflects on her transition into the family trade: “I wasn’t aware of this industry initially, but now I’m fully immersed in it and working on new marketing strategies, including expanding our presence on social media.”

The industry’s impact extends far beyond individual workshops. Rajesh’s mother, 64-year-old Ambutai, says silver unit work is woven into the social fabric of the region.

“Any woman in Hupari and the surrounding five or six villages gets work by default,” Ambutai says. “It is never the case that there is no work for women’s hands here.”

Ambutai and other local women run self-help groups to save and manage their earnings independently. Having worked shoulder-to-shoulder with her husband throughout her life, she now works alongside her children. She speaks proudly of Rajesh, who has taken on a leadership role within the industry association.

Silver sparks

Navita (name changed to protect privacy) married into a small ornament-manufacturing family in Hupari 15 years ago. Her father — a mill worker in the neighbouring town of Nippani in Karnataka — had insisted she accept the proposal from what he saw as a prosperous merchant family. She had just finished Class 10, and says she was forced into the marriage.

“But then I accepted the reality of life, and decided to navigate it. I learnt the craft, trade secrets, and also began managing a workforce of five people,” Navita says, with a broad smile. “I’m sure that we will grow our business.”

Her husband shares the ambition to expand into new markets, though opinions differ on the path forward. When Navita suggests bringing in artisans from Agra to introduce fresh designs and cross-regional techniques, her husband dismisses the idea with a laugh: “I know what needs to be done.”

When she opens up about her childhood ambition to pursue an education and how she was married off below the legal age, her husband’s eyes widen in alarm. Speaking about these matters to a journalist, he warns anxiously, could land him in jail.

As her husband steps away to negotiate with a trader sourcing small silver idols of Lakshmi for the upcoming Deepavali season, Navita speaks candidly about her broader mission: helping the next generation of women in the craft.

“I had three college girls who came to me to learn the craft,” she recalls. “I trained them, and they worked with me for three years. During that period, I insisted they save their earnings. I told them, ‘Once you save enough money, you have the power to reject unwanted marriage proposals and choose the partner you want.’”

The advice took root. All three women eventually made their own choices in marriage. Today, with Navita’s guidance, they are trying to set up their own manufacturing units in the villages where they now live.

For Navita, breaking the gender gap in Hupari’s silver industry remains the ultimate goal. “Generally, male artisans work in the field for a few years and then transition into manufacturers or traders, but women remain workers forever,” she says. “This has to change.”

Her husband, however, argues that the core of the business requires toughness, which women don’t have.

Jayshree Lohar, 51, firmly rejects the idea that women cannot navigate the realities of business. The only thing she feels that needs to be strengthened are women’s wings. Lohar and her husband, Prakash, 57, run their own manufacturing unit. Unlike many traditional business families, they chose not to force their children into the legacy trade, encouraging them to pursue higher education instead. Their son completed a postgraduate degree in computer science in the United States and works there, while their daughter earned an engineering degree and works at an IT firm in Pune.

Prakash credits Jayshree for the family’s success and their children’s independence.

“All these years, she handled almost 50-60% of the work and responsibilities in our unit,” Prakash says. “Today, our children have found their own path.”

The challenges

It is late noon in Hupari, and the town is abuzz with work as artisans scramble to meet the surging national demand for the Deepavali festival. Kanchan is working overtime to complete her orders. “Women don’t complain. We work hard, and don’t leave any battle halfway,” Kanchan says. “Not because we are born like that, but because the world around us makes us that way. A woman has to stand up for herself.”

As young men find employment in the nearby government industrial estate at Kagal town, Hupari’s young women have stepped in, with better education than even a generation ago. Yet, behind the festive rush, Hupari’s famed silver industry faces severe structural bottlenecks.

Sharp fluctuations in global silver prices routinely compress profit margins for local artisans, while a continued reliance on hand tools restricts production speed and design consistency.

Financial vulnerability runs deep: limited access to formal banking drives small workshop owners into high-risk informal credit networks just to keep their businesses afloat. Compounding these issues are low piece-rate wages and demanding physical labour, which make it difficult to retain skilled artisans or attract younger generations. Furthermore, the absence of direct export facilities and modern digital marketing leaves the entire hub dependent on middlemen, preventing artisans from capturing the true value of their craft.

The industry now pins its hopes for long-term sustainability on the proposed Silver Ornament Cluster and the Geographical Indication (GI) tag Hupari Silver Craft received in 2024.

However, for true transformation to take root, Kanchan and many like her believe the path forward is clear: women must be brought to the forefront and given opportunities to lead new aspects of the trade.

After the Deepavali orders leave Hupari’s narrow alleys to sparkle across the nation, the soft clinking of silver will continue to echo in its dim homes all year round.

World.title: Just one local terrorist active in Kashmir, but terror threat remains: IGP Sujit Kumar
World.content:
The militancy graph in Kashmir has dropped to one local recruit but the inputs on impending attack keep security forces on an alert mode, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Sujit Kumar said on Thursday (November 5, 2026).

“One terrorist who orchestrated the Anantnag attack on [July 25, 2026] remains the lone active local in Kashmir. He is supported by a few foreign terrorists, who keep on transiting from one point to another and constantly change their location. We are tracking them,” said IGP Kumar.

The police identified Lateef Ahmad, 21, a resident of south Kashmir’s Kulgam, as the terrorist behind the Anantnag attack, which left one policeman dead in Anantnag’s Lal Chowk.

IGP Kumar said the upper reaches of the Poonch-Budgam axis, connecting the Pir Panjal valley with the Kashmir valley, “was being dominated by specialised policemen”. The route is considered key for terrorists to transit from Line of Control (LoC) in the Pir Panjal valley into the Kashmir valley.

“Policemen were dominating the heights. Security forces were taking all measures to track the foreign terrorists,” said IGP Kumar.

Refusing to divulge details on the technology employed by the hiding terrorists to bypass online tracking and communicate across the border, IGP Kumar said, “Whatever technology is being employed, they are on our radar.”

Regarding the stringent security protocols on the highway in Kashmir, Mr. Kumar said these protocols were put in place after previous terror incidents. “Threats remain there. Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) are being recovered. This is a sensitive issue and all considerations are being factored in,” said Mr. Kumar.

Meanwhile, IGP Kumar identified three major challenges involving local youth, including drug abuse, involvement in cybercrime and violation of traffic rules. “I appeal to youth and elders to come forward and report cases of drug abuse. The police will stand by them and extend all support,” said the police officer.

This year, the police have arrested 1941 locals in 1651 cases under the provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. “Narco kingpins, whether here or across the border, distribute the earnings through overground workers to push terrorism,” said Mr. Kumar.

The police have attached properties worth ₹154 crore of the accused, and ₹1.71 crore was frozen in bank accounts. Mr. Kumar said the police received around 12385 complaints of cyber fraud, “with many local youths involved in it”.

World.title: Trump designates Oval Office as national monument
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an order on Thursday (November 5, 2026) designating the Oval Office as a national monument, redoubling his focus on beautifying the White House despite a brutal midterms defeat for his Republican Party.

Critics accused Mr. Trump of ignoring voter concerns over the Iran war and affordability ahead of Tuesday’s (November 4, 2026) midterm elections and obsessing instead on multiple construction and renovation projects in the capital.

The day after Democrats won the House of Representatives and Senate, Mr. Trump virtually ignored the result and showed off construction work on his new White House ballroom instead.

This time Mr. Trump’s focus was on the Oval Office, which he has bedecked with gold ornaments since returning to power last year, and the neighboring Cabinet Room.

He said the proclamation would “make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space” and prevent future presidents from carrying out any building work on the two rooms.

“It won’t be able to be taken down, destroyed, touched, or anything else. It’s called actually a national monument,” Mr. Trump told reporters.

The move, however, fueled speculation that Mr. Trump could be preparing further work on the West Wing, after several hints that he could move reporters out of the famed briefing room located near the Oval.

Mr. Trump’s signing of the order in the Oval Office was not broadcast on major U.S. networks, as he has banned CNN from the rotating “pool” of television outlets that cover White House events.

Mr. Trump did give one nod to the midterms, with a red baseball cap with the word “veto” on the Resolute Desk in front of him.

The 80-year-old Republican has threatened to use his presidential powers to block Democratic legislation, although saying he was also ready to work with the rival party.

World.title: Eisenkot tipped to seek Israel government with backing of Arab lists
World.content:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday (November 8, 2026) whom he will task with trying to form a new government, after the opposition’s Gadi Eisenkot secured a commanding number of recommendations to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Mr. Herzog held a second day of consultations with political parties on Thursday (November 5, 2026) after the October 27 election, in which neither Mr. Netanyahu — a polarising right-winger who has led Israel through three years of war — nor Mr. Eisenkot — a former military chief promising to restore national unity — secured enough votes for a majority.

Mr. Herzog will make his choice, but traditionally the mandate is given to the person recommended by more parliament members. Sixty-seven picked Mr. Eisenkot, 46 opted for Mr. Netanyahu, while seven abstained.

“The results of the consultations may appear clear, but the authority vested in me by law is to determine who has the ability to form a government, and that is not entirely clear, given the mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves,” Mr. Herzog said on Thursday (November 5, 2026).

“I will try to determine this directly and quickly, in personal talks with some of the party leaders.”

Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party said on Thursday (November 5, 2026) that “the citizens of Israel have chosen change and expressed a complete lack of confidence in outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his government”, and called for the “immediate establishment of a national emergency government that will begin working for all citizens of Israel”.

Two Arab-majority lists won an unprecedented 19 seats in the election, making them potential kingmakers if Mr. Eisenkot’s opposition chooses to work with them, which remains unclear.

Both Arab lists on Thursday (November 5, 2026) said they were backing Mr. Eisenkot.

However, another party in Mr. Eisenkot’s camp, right-wing Israel Beiteinu, has repeatedly indicated it will not sit in a government that relies on support from Arab parties.

Party leader Avigdor Liberman, a former Netanyahu ally turned critic, cited as a reason the refusal by Arab parties to explicitly define Hamas as a “terror group” — even though they have repeatedly condemned the organisation’s attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.

Ultra-Orthodox exemptions

Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, which backed Mr. Netanyahu after the previous five elections, in its meeting with Mr. Herzog declined to recommend Mr. Netanyahu again as premier, although it also did not side with Mr. Eisenkot.

The party informed Mr. Herzog “that it has decided not to recommend any member of the Knesset to form a government”, the president’s office said in a statement, referring to the 120-member parliament in which United Torah Judaism won seven seats.

Alongside Shas, another ultra-Orthodox party, they have pushed to maintain the exemption from military service for religious students.

Mr. Netanyahu has preserved the exemption but stopped short of enshrining it in law, in the face of major resentment from many other Israelis, as reservists serve multiple tours due to the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

“In whatever government is next formed, our immediate item is sorting out the status of Torah students,” United Torah Judaism lawmaker Isaac Pindrus said.

Mr. Eisenkot, who has tried to appeal to secular Israelis from left to right, has been adamant about ending exemptions for military service.

Some of his opposition allies have criticised the ultra-Orthodox — who make up about 14% of the population but have far higher birthrates than secular Israelis — as a drain on the state.

Observers say United Torah Judaism’s tactic is likely aimed mostly at punishing Mr. Netanyahu and showing that their votes cannot be taken for granted, while they would still serve in a government if he were to form one.

Arab parties play key role

Once Mr. Herzog gives his mandate to a lawmaker, the person will have 28 days to form a government, with a potential 14-day extension. If the lawmaker fails, Mr. Herzog will then task someone else.

Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc, including United Torah Judaism, has 53 seats in the new parliament, compared to 48 for Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc.

Arab-majority parties scored historic gains on the back of anger over Mr. Netanyahu’s hard-right government and longstanding complaints about racism from some ministers and discriminatory treatment of Arab Israelis.

Mr. Netanyahu has relentlessly attacked the opposition for even the prospect of an alliance with Arab lawmakers.

In a video on Wednesday (November 4, 2026), Mr. Netanyahu alleged there were “serious suspicions” that foreign powers put money into the election and questioned the loyalty of Arab citizens.

World.title: Petitioners in Delhi SIR case seek FIRs over alleged forgery of Form 7s in Mustafabad
World.content:
Petitioners in the Delhi special intensive revision (SIR) case before the Supreme Court have written to the Chief Election Commissioner of India, two Election Commissioners, and the Delhi Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) on Thursday (November 5, 2026), seeking an immediate investigation and legal action over alleged forgery and identity fraud in the filing of Form 7 deletion applications in Mustafabad.

Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri, in the letter, cited a report published in The Hindu on Thursday (November 5, 2026), which found that 16 of the 20 BJP-appointed Booth-Level Agents (BLAs), who are named objectors in deletion applications filed in Delhi’s Mustafabad, denied submitting, signing or having any knowledge of the forms.

It highlighted that, of the 1,021 deletion applications received in Mustafabad, at least 787, accounting for 94% of third-party deletion requests, were filed in the names of 20 BJP-appointed BLAs. All the applications targeted Muslim electors.

The findings, the petitioners said, raised “serious concerns about possible systematic and fraudulent attempt to disenfranchise legitimate electors through the deliberate misuse of statutory procedures”.

They have urged the ECI to direct the registration of FIRs under relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for forgery, criminal impersonation, identity fraud and submission of false declarations. They also sought a comprehensive audit of all Form 7 applications filed across Delhi during the SIR to establish whether the named objectors had authorised and signed them.

The petitioners further called for deletion proceedings arising from third-party applications to be stayed until independent verification with the affected electors and the listed objectors was completed.

They also sought action under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, against those found to have knowingly submitted false declarations, besides publication of verification reports and all Form 7 applications on the CEO Delhi website.

“Given the grave threat to voter rights, an immediate and transparent response is imperative,” the letter said.

World.title: Parts of Delhi continues to reel under ‘severe’ air pollution
World.content:
The air quality of the national capital continued to be in the “very poor” category for the fourth consecutive day on Thursday (November 5, 2026), while many parts of the city reeled under “severe” air pollution, according to official data. The overall air quality is expected to deteriorate to the “severe” category during Deepavali.

“Severe” level air pollution affects healthy people and seriously impacts those with existing diseases, as per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).

On Thursday (November 5, 2026), many parts of the city, including Alipur, Bawana, ITO, Dwarka, and Jahangirpuri, witnessed “severe” level air pollution.

“The air quality is likely to be in the severe category from 06.11.2026 to 08.11.2026. The outlook for the subsequent 6 Days: The air quality is likely to be in the severe to very poor category,” as per the Central government’s ‘Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi’.

The contribution of stubble burning in neighbouring states to PM2.5 (a chief pollutant) in Delhi on Thursday is expected to be 15.6%, slightly down from 16.28% on Wednesday, according to the Union Ministry of Earth Sciences data. This is predicted to rise to 19.2% on Friday (November 6, 2026).

The political blame game between the BJP and the AAP over the air pollution continued on Thursday (November 5, 2026).

Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said that Delhi’s AQI (Air Quality Index) stood at 117 on October 31 but climbed to 377 by November 4. “During the same period, Punjab witnessed a significant surge in farm-fire incidents, with 584 fires recorded on November 3 alone. He said the growing contribution of stubble burning to Delhi’s pollution made Punjab’s failure to control farm fires a matter of serious concern,” Mr. Sirsa said.

The Minister said that while the Delhi government is undertaking continuous monitoring, enforcement and on-ground interventions, the Punjab government must also take responsibility for controlling pollution at its source.

Continuing to attack the BJP government over alleged manipulation of AQI data by spraying water at AQI monitoring stations, AAP Delhi president Saurabh Bharadwaj said, “The AQI data is completely fabricated. Water is being sprayed on monitoring sensors to fake the readings. The real air is thick with invisible, toxic PM2.5 particles.”

He alleged that “fudging” AQI data is not just corruption, but is life-threatening. “When you lie about pollution, you trick parents into a false sense of security and kill our children,” Mr. Bharadwaj added.

BJP-AAP spar

The 24-hour average overall Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 369 (very poor) on Thursday at 4 p.m. on Thursday, slightly down from 377 (very poor) a day earlier, as per the Central Pollution Control Board’s daily bulletin, which is treated as the day’s AQI. A higher AQI means worsening of air quality.

Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and the bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

World.title: Christian community hits the road over recent mob attacks on churches
World.content:
Hundreds of people from the Christian community marched to Kolkata’s Esplanade on Thursday (November 5, 2026) in protest against the rising cases of mob attacks on churches across West Bengal.

A mega-prayer rally was called by the Bangiya Chirstiya Parishad at Rani Rashmoni Road in Esplanade on Sunday (November 1, 2026). A sea of people from Kolkata and surrounding districts walked from Sealdah, Birla Planetarium, and Howrah to gather there and express their dissent over the rapid attacks.

“An unprecedented crisis has brought us together today at this prayer gathering in Kolkata. Over the past five months, coordinated attacks, vandalism, and atrocities targeting prayer meetings, worship centres, and churches have been taking place relentlessly across various districts,” said Herod Mullick, state secretary of BCP.

At least 48 such incidents have been reported since May across the state. However, the first information reports could be lodged in only 15 cases. Out of the 48 targeted churches, 7 belong to mainline denominations—6 Catholic and 1 Church of North India (CNI).

Mr. Mullick said that the central allegation levelled against the community is ‘forced conversion’. He said it is a ‘false narrative’ deliberately used only to frame peaceful Christian prayer gatherings as illegal conversion events.

“Our repeated appeals to the Chief Minister to uncover the truth remain unheeded, while miscreants who take the law into their own hands operate with complete impunity. While the victims have chosen forgiveness and you have continued to pray in silent endurance, the reality on the ground remains grim,” he added.

He also addressed the deep anxiety among the Christian community in Bengal over the upcoming Christmas festival in December. He said that the people are scared to celebrate any event or even to step out due to these recent incidents. However, Mr. Mullick assured them that the organisation is speaking to the administration and the dialogue seems positive.

Seeking a constructive way forward, a five-member delegation of the BCP also met the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) State Head, Dr. Jishnu Basu, on Wednesday. “Dr. Basu firmly assured us that attacks or vandalism on places of worship are entirely unacceptable and cannot be justified under any circumstances. He committed to personally taking up this matter with the CM,” he said.

The development comes only four days after a newly erected church at Basanti in South 24 Parganas was vandalised by a violent mob belonging to some Hindu outfits. Several priests and also the Bishop of the church have been injured during the incident.

A similar incident also took place at a prayer meeting in Malda’s Harishchandrapur on the same day. However, nobody was injured in this incident. Another under-construction church was also vandalised by a mob on July 5 at Subhashgram in South 24 Parganas.

Archbishop Joseph D’Souza, the President of the All India Christian Council and National Federation of Churches, Bishop Shyamal Bose, Bishop Nirmal Gomes, Bishop Subodh Mondal, Rev. Samaresh Naik from the National Council of Baptist Churches, Odisha, and representatives of Churches and Organisations from Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Nagaland were also present at Thursday’s (November 4, 2026) mega prayer rally.

“Attacks on the Christians are not new. We have been victims of such religious oppression historically. We must stand together against such barbarism unleashed on the Christian community. We are all the children of God, and he shall protect us. Our fight will continue,” said Mr. D’Souza, addressing the rally.

Meanwhile, a separate rally was also held at Basanti, where a newly constructed protestant church was attacked by a group of people on its inaugural day. The local Christian people marched to the local BDO office and submitted a memorandum demanding swift action against the culprits.

World.title: West Bengal govt’s new investment policy promotes job-linked growth, incentives for plant and machinery
World.content:
Offering incentives to industries that employ more women and assistance for investments in plant and machinery, as well as a fixed timeline for approval of projects, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government in West Bengal on Thursday (November 5, 2026) announced a new investment promotion policy.

The West Bengal Investment Promotion Policy, 2026 that comes into effect from May 9, 2026 the day when the first BJP government in the State took office, offers up to 120 % assistance to a thrust sector unit in a priority area on the share of fixed capital investment (FCI) made in plant and machinery.

The announcement of incentives marks a policy shift for West Bengal, the fourth most populous State in the country, as the previous Trinamool Congress government had passed the Revocation of West Bengal Incentive Schemes and Obligations 2025, retroactively scrapping three decades of industrial incentive schemes and subsidies.

“The previous government had cheated the industrialists,” Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said while unveiling the much-awaited policy document for the revival of industries in the State. The Chief Minister said that West Bengal will try to emerge from the “bad experiences” as far as industry was concerned of the previous two regimes.

“We will neither have a forcible land acquisition policy like the Left Front nor will we have a flawed land policy like the Trinamool Congress, asking industries to buy their own land without support from the government,” Mr. Adhikari said.

Under the policy of ‘jobs come first’, the State government has announced extending substantial employer EPF contribution reimbursements, leading with 100% reimbursement for women and transgender employees in MSMEs for 10 years, 75% for women in eligible service units and robust support for large and strategic industrial projects.

The ceiling for the amount of assistance given on the share of (FCI) made in plant and machinery is 100 % for regular units, 110 % for units in thrust sectors or priority areas, and 120 % for thrust-sector units located in priority areas. The assistance will cease when the applicable ceiling is reached or 10 years after commercial production begins, whichever is earlier.

The State government has identified several sectors as thrust areas, such as semiconductors and electronics, green hydrogen and waste-to-energy, emerging digital technologies, EVs and batteries, defence and food and marine processing, among others.

On the fixed timeline for approval of projects, the State government has also announced a 30-day delivery of certificates of intent, a 45-day timeline for certificates of eligibility and a dedicated relationship officers for large projects.

The policy promises a waiver of surcharges on renewable energy open access until March 2030, and sick and closed industrial units that can be revived will receive special assistance. Non-profits, such as hospitals and universities who invest more than ₹100 crore can keep at least a quarter of their capacity fee, for groups the State notifies for 10 years along with extra benefits.

The Chief Minister, who interacted with captains of industry during the launch of the policy, sought their opinion on whether they had witnessed any change in the past five months since the BJP government came to power. “If industrialists cooperate with the government, the government will always stand by them and protect their interests,” he said.

One of the promises made by the BJP during the West Bengal Assembly polls 2026 have been to revive industrial fortunes of the State, a commitment that has turned out to be its biggest challenge.

Mr. Adhikari said that he has ended “ended extortion” and added that his government has been “positive about industrialisation and an industry-friendly atmosphere in Bengal”. The State’s Industries and Commerce Minister Tapas Roy and Finance Minister Swapan Dasgupta were also present at the launch of the investment promotion policy.

While the Chief Minister assured that the concerns about land acquisition for industry will be addressed, senior officials of the State government said that a GIS-mapped land inventory for industries is being prepared. The State government is likely to have a fresh policy as far as making land for industries was concerned.

Mr. Adhikari said the government had already handed over land to 33 business groups and was in a position to meet the current demand for industrial plots of around ₹1 lakh crore over the next few months.

World.title: Petrol price slashed by Rs9.41 per litre, high-speed diesel by Rs5.56
World.content:
The government on Thursday dropped the price of petrol by Rs9.41 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs5.56, in the fourth consecutive reduction in fuel prices.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs352.59 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs382.25 on Nov 6 (Friday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Monday for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said efforts were being made to introduce a similar system for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

Meanwhile, the Jamaat-i-Islami and the government are set to follow up on their recent discussions on possible relief in petroleum prices and hold another round of talks on Thursday, the party said.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: Collision between passenger bus, truck near Pakpattan claims 11 lives
World.content:
LAHORE: A collision between a passenger bus and truck on Thursday claimed the lives of 11 people and left 33 others injured near Pakpattan.

Rescue 1122 said that 11 people had died in the collision. It added that eight people had sustained minor injuries, while 25 others were shifted to the District Headquarter Hospital (DHQ) in Pakpattan.

According to a press release by the district administration, the collision occurred on Depalpur Road between a passenger bus travelling from Multan to Kasur and a truck coming in the opposite direction.

Upon receiving news of the accident, Deputy Commissioner (DC) Asif Raza and District Police Officer (DPO) Javed Iqbal Chadhar immediately arrived at the scene to oversee rescue operations, working alongside teams from Rescue 1122 and the district administration, the statement said.

The three-hour rescue operation used cranes and other heavy machinery to extract passengers trapped in the wreckage.

“Given the gravity of the incident, DC Raza declared an emergency at the DHQ Hospital, Pakpattan and summoned additional doctors and medical staff,” the press release added.

Later, the DC and DPO visited the hospital to enquire after the injured and review the arrangements for their medical care. DC Raza directed the hospital administration to ensure the provision of “prompt, high-quality medical care” to all the injured.

The statement said DC Raza expressed grief at the lives lost and also extended his condolences to the bereaved families.

“Extending his best wishes for the speedy recovery of the injured, he directed the relevant authorities to continue providing all possible support for medical treatment and relief operations,” it added.

President Asif Ali Zardari expressed “profound grief and sorrow” over the “tragic loss”.

A statement on social media said that the president extended his condolences to the bereaved families and prayed for the early recovery of the injured in the accident.

Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz also expressed “deep sorrow” over the loss of lives in the accident, according to a handout issued by the province’s Directorate General of Public Relations (DGPR).

She directed authorities to ensure the best possible medical treatment for the injured passengers.

CM Maryam “prayed for the speedy recovery of the injured passengers and extended her heartfelt sympathies and condolences to the bereaved families”, the statement said, adding that she sought a report on the accident.

Separately, National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq also extended “heartfelt sympathy and condolences to the bereaved families”. He also prayed for the early recovery of those injured in the accident.

World.title: Gadi Eisenkot tipped to seek Israel government with backing of Arab lists
World.content:
Israel’s largest Arab list on Thursday said it would back Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government, bolstering his chances of being picked over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who lost the support of an allied religious party.

President Isaac Herzog was holding a second day of consultations with political parties after the October 27 election, in which neither Netanyahu — a polarising right-winger who has led Israel through three years of war — nor Eisenkot — a former military chief promising to restore national unity — secured enough votes for a majority.

Herzog will himself choose whom to ask to form a new government, but traditionally the mandate is given to the person recommended by more parties, which would be Eisenkot.

Arab-majority lists won an unprecedented 19 seats in the election, making them potential kingmakers if Eisenkot’s opposition chooses to work with them — something which remains unclear.

Both Arab lists on Thursday said they were backing Eisenkot.

The Joint List, which bagged 11 seats, said in a statement that “it will inform Herzog this evening of its decision to recommend that Gadi Eisenkot be tasked with forming the government”.

Raam, which won eight seats, also endorsed Eisenkot.

Ultra-Orthodox exemptions

Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, which backed Netanyahu after the previous five elections, in its meeting with Herzog declined to recommend Netanyahu again as prime minister, although it also did not side with Eisenkot.

The party informed Herzog “that it has decided not to recommend any member of Knesset to form a government”, the president’s office said in a statement, referring to the 120-member parliament in which United Torah Judaism has won seven seats.

Alongside Shas, another ultra-Orthodox party, they have pushed to maintain the exemption from military service for religious students.

Netanyahu has preserved the exemption but stopped short of enshrining it in law, in the face of major resentment from many other Israelis, as reservists serve multiple tours due to the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

“In whatever government is next formed, our immediate item is sorting out the status of Torah students,” United Torah Judaism lawmaker Isaac Pindrus said.

Eisenkot, who has tried to appeal to secular Israelis from left to right, has been adamant about ending exemptions from military service.
