World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.title: Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.content:
For nearly 27 years, Starbucks coffeehouses in China have been a haven for non-paying patrons attracted by its comfortable seating, ample power outlets, air conditioning, and free restrooms.

This stemmed from the American company’s foundational brand concept of making its outlets “third places” — safe, accessible spaces between home and work to relax and connect with friends, whether you intend to spend or not.

Now, it seems, spending is mandatory.

In late October, Starbucks China introduced a nationwide purchase-required seating policy, pledging to be “clear in its rules but warm in its execution,” with staff encouraged to politely stop non-paying customers from hogging tables and chairs. At the same time, it unveiled plans to invest more than 300 million yuan ($45 million) in reshaping the in-store atmosphere.

As the company undergoes major corporate restructuring while continuing to expand, does it risk losing its “third place” image in China?

Stirred up

The first Starbucks on the Chinese mainland opened in Beijing’s World Trade Building in 1999. Today there are about 8,000 outlets across 1,100 counties in the mainland.

Li Kele regularly visits her local store in the southwestern Sichuan province. After walking in and sitting down on Oct. 21, taking a moment to browse various online platforms for discounts, Li was soon approached by a barista brandishing a menu and asking if she needed any help. “The store never used to push customers to place an order,” she says.

Starbucks outlets have been attracting non-paying patrons since the 1980s, and the company officially adopted a worldwide open-door policy in 2018.

However, concerns over disruptive behaviors, alongside the company’s desire to prioritize paying customers and staff’s experience, prompted the global headquarters to reverse the policy in January last year.

The change began at its North American stores, where a new code of conduct stated that Starbucks coffee shops, patios, restrooms, and other facilities were for employees and customers only.

Anecdotal evidence suggests baristas in China began nudging seated patrons to make purchases in early 2026.

One customer shares that in January they observed employees at a Starbucks branch in Beijing’s central Xidan shopping district walking around the store offering table service to people without drinks, which is not typically available, and promoting discount coupons. Sometimes they’d subtly point out that the store was crowded and seating was scarce.

On Oct. 19, social media users in several cities began posting about signs spotted at Starbucks stores that stated customers should “make a purchase before taking a seat.”

When a domestic media outlet contacted Starbucks China for a response that same day, a spokesperson denied any plan to introduce a purchase-required seating policy. But within 48 hours, the company made a complete U-turn, announcing that such a policy would take effect on Oct. 22.

The move has sparked much debate online. Yet in real terms, implementation has so far been limited to advisory measures, such as signage.

“The latest wording is that they (head office) encourage us to ask people to leave,” says Zhang Yi, a part-time Starbucks barista. “They want us front-line staff to persuade non-paying customers to give up their seats in whatever way we consider peaceful.”

However, because the practice isn’t tied to their performance review, employees might be reluctant to enforce the new rules, Zhang adds. “If I’m on shift, I won’t do it. I’ll just work the way I always have.”

In the grind

Starbucks built its “third place” branding concept based on the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg’s 1989 book, “The Great Good Place,” in which he describes the human need for communal, welcoming social environments separate from home (the “first place”) and work (the “second place”).

This positioning requires providing space for relaxed socializing. But when revenues don’t keep pace with increases in rent and operating costs, it becomes a potential pain point.

When Brian Niccol was appointed CEO of Starbucks in September 2024, same-store sales — a metric that measures revenue growth from established locations — were on the slide in the U.S. market.

To reverse the trend, he launched “Back to Starbucks,” a plan aimed at “rediscovering the power of third places” by improving the in-store experience, such as reintroducing old-school ceramic mugs and handwritten names on cups, as well as more comfortable seating. He then scrapped the 2018 open-door policy.

Investor data suggests the changes have already had an effect in North America, where same-store sales were up by 8.1% year on year in the third quarter of fiscal 2026 (Sept. 29, 2025, to Sept. 27, 2026) and same-store transactions grew by 4.5% over the same period.

In China, recent growth in same-store sales has been powered more by product innovation, deliveries, and price adjustments, according to Cathy R. Smith, Starbucks’ chief financial officer.

As online take-out orders increase and in-store spending declines, running a brick-and-mortar “third place” becomes more expensive. In this case, seat-hogging shifts from being a tolerable service issue to an operational problem.

Pressing issue

In April this year, Starbucks completed a $4 billion joint-venture transaction with Boyu Capital, a China-focused alternative asset management and private equity firm based in Hong Kong. The deal gives Boyu a 60% share in Starbucks’ China retail business and transitions all 8,000 coffeehouses into licensed operations.

The U.S. coffee giant says it expects the transaction proceeds, along with the value of its retained 40% stake and licensing agreement, to account for more than $13 billion over the next decade. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, Starbucks’ international segment operating margin increased to 19.1%, up from 13.6% a year earlier.

However, while the deal benefits global headquarters, Starbucks China still faces pressure to expand. At a partner forum in April, CEO Molly Liu confirmed the company is already two-thirds of the way to its goal of opening stores in more than 1,500 counties over the next three years.

With this in mind, the purchase-required seating policy looks more like an efficiency drive, as the company attempts to cut costs.

This also comes amid a major restructuring of Starbucks China’s workforce. As all staff are now part of the joint venture, they can no longer hold Starbucks shares, which trade on New York’s Nasdaq exchange. This means the end of the Bean Stock program in China, which since 1991 has awarded full- and part-time employees shares after a certain tenure.

Liu said at April’s partner forum that benefits would continue through fiscal 2026, with a new long-term incentive plan to be introduced in the fourth quarter. As of Nov. 4, there had been no further announcements.

As social insurance contributions are mandatory only for permanent staff in China, barista Zhang believes the company prefers to hire part-time workers. Jiemian News reported in January that Starbucks China’s official recruitment channels were promoting vacancies in 269 areas, with full-time positions making up just over 20%.

Behind its new seating policy is a contradiction Starbucks China cannot easily escape: the “third place” concept justifies the brand’s premium, yet recent growth has come from deliveries and discounts, bringing sales without a customer ever sitting down.

The joint venture and its target to grow to “as many as 20,000 locations over time” sharpen that contradiction. Smaller markets and leaner per-store costs make it hard to build to the original standard.

Therefore, tightening seating rules, restructuring its workforce, and expansion look less like separate decisions than part of one cost logic.

(Due to privacy concerns, Li Kele and Zhang Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Zhan Fangge.

A version of this article originally appeared in Baobian News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A sign asks customers to make a purchase before taking a seat at a Starbucks. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.content:
A Chinese app designed to report hotels that allegedly have bedbugs and other pests has been updated and re-released following controversy over the validity of the claims. The app attracted more than 300,000 users at its peak, flagging over 600 hotels nationwide, according to its creator.

In a Sunday post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, the creator of the app, a WeChat mini-program called “Bedbug Map,” announced that he alone would now review bedbug reports — previously, evidence was approved if a majority of users verified it. He also clarified that users are required to upload photographic evidence of bedbugs. The next day, he also posted a review of nearly 300 rejected bedbug reports, explaining why each had been declined.

Released Sept. 16, the mini-program lets users report hotels with bedbugs, cockroaches, or other pests, resulting in a bug or question mark icon over the hotel’s location. Tapping it reveals the number of user reports.

Controversy arose after reports that multiple hotels were asked by customers for refunds after they reported having found bedbugs via the app after their stay. One hotel was allegedly asked to refund 3,000 yuan ($450) in room charges after a report citing “two bumps” on a guest’s body was posted on the map and approved by users. According to the report, the hotel later asked a third party to inspect the premises, but found no traces of bedbugs.

The creator, a 26-year-old manufacturing industry worker who asked to remain anonymous, told Sixth Tone that in the past few days he had personally reviewed more than 700 pieces of photo evidence submitted over the previous two months.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone revealed that 232 hotels are now marked on the mini-program’s map, down from the more than 600 reported before Monday. The mini-program currently lists 36 hotels as having successfully appealed reports after submitting third-party evidence.

The app has also been taken down twice, most recently in late October, by WeChat parent company Tencent, citing its restrictions on applications run by and registered to individuals.

The creator told Sixth Tone that Bedbug Map was created with the help of AI in under two weeks. He said he got the idea after searching online for bedbug information after he and his girlfriend developed bites following a move, discovering most bedbug posts involved hotels.

On the day of its release, the mini-program attracted over 100,000 users, according to the creator. Under his release announcement on Xiaohongshu, many commented asking him to expand the function to public transportation, which he then added to the app. However, the function was removed in subsequent updates.

“I guess the reason the app was well-received is that it addresses a key pain point for the average traveler: the lack of cleanliness and the resurgence of bedbugs.”

The mini-program previously allowed users to submit reports without photo evidence. However, after users raised concerns about the potential for people to maliciously target hotels without evidence, the program was updated in late September to allow users to upload photographic evidence. Photos can be either uploaded or taken directly via the mini-program — in the latter case, the app automatically adds a watermark showing the time and location.

“I’m simply the initiator,” he said. “The goal is to get everyone involved in managing the mini-program’s data and reviews.”

Hotels can also appeal bedbug reports — indicated on the map by blue semicircular icons above such locations — as well as upload disinfection records, business licenses, and photos of pest-control operations.

The creator said he even recruited volunteers at one point to inspect the hygiene of hotels that filed appeals. However, the function was soon taken down because of concerns about volunteers’ safety, among other issues.

He said that managing the mini-program alone has “brought pressure and criticism,” adding that he hopes the government will “provide professional guidance to improve (the app’s) credibility.”

In an interview with domestic media, Lin Feiran, a lawyer at Beijing King & Capital Law Firm, suggested the company bring in professionals to identify insects reported at different locations.

State media outlet CNR News wrote in a Monday commentary that “a map pieced together by internet users being used to fill the gap in hygiene information shows that formal (reporting) channels are lacking,” encouraging hotel booking platforms to display bedbug records publicly.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Weibo and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.title: Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.content:
A few weeks ago, I served as a judge on a food program in China, where I met many chefs and got a close look at how they develop new dishes. I was particularly impressed by one dish: a steamed egg custard topped with a rich crab paste made from crab roe and fat. It was a combination I had never considered before. The crab paste had a delicate aroma and a rich, oily texture, while the steamed egg custard was soft and silky, perfectly balancing its richness.

I was struck by the dish’s ingenuity, but it also raised a question: Would people be willing to pay for the recipe and instructions on how to make it?

I put this question to one of the chefs on the program. He smiled at me as though I were a child and asked why anyone would pay for a recipe. He then let me in on an industry secret: When a restaurant discovers that a competitor has introduced a new dish, it will order it and have its own chefs taste it, analyze its ingredients, cooking techniques, and seasonings, and work out how it was made. In most cases, they can reproduce it. The chef told me he had recreated other people’s dishes and had his own copied by others.

It all sounded rather cutthroat. The person who bears the cost of innovation often reaps little of the reward.

In Chinese cuisine, creating a new dish is not nearly as simple as diners might imagine. Chefs must find the right ingredients, adjust proportions, experiment with different cooking temperatures, refine textures, and continually adjust based on customer feedback. Developing a successful dish can involve dozens or even hundreds of failed attempts before it is ready to serve.

The time, ingredients, and labor costs of this trial-and-error process are all borne by the original creator. Yet as soon as the dish reaches the table, anyone can observe, taste, analyze, and even reproduce it. For a competitor, learning most of the techniques needed to make a dish may cost little more than the price of a meal.

Even more frustrating, many of these innovators lack the resources to promote their creations. A small restaurant might be the first to develop a dish but lack the advertising budget, media exposure, or network of locations to popularize it. Meanwhile, a larger restaurant can simply copy the dish and quickly introduce it to a wider audience. Since more people encounter it there first, they may assume the larger restaurant came up with it.

This suggests that the first-mover advantage does not necessarily apply in the restaurant business. Being first matters only if consumers know who created the dish and the original creator has the resources and business acumen to turn that innovation into a brand and a source of revenue. Otherwise, the creator is essentially providing free research and development while introducing consumers to a dish that benefits the entire market.

The challenge of protecting intellectual property is not unique to Chinese cuisine. It affects chefs around the world. Business schools often hold up KFC’s fried chicken recipe as a classic example of a trade secret, but the company’s real competitive advantage lies in its supply chains, restaurant network, and brand value. The law does not prohibit you from reverse-engineering KFC’s fried chicken and making it yourself, or even selling it to your neighbors, provided you don’t market it as “KFC Original Recipe Chicken.” For smaller restaurants, therefore, protecting a recipe may matter less than building the brand and reputation that give it lasting commercial value.

The celebrated 18th-century Chinese food writer Yuan Mei associated dishes with particular names as a way of preserving their origins. For example, in his influential cookbook “Suiyuan Shidan” (“Recipes from the Garden of Contentment”), he included dishes called “Prefect Wang’s eight-treasure tofu” and “Governor Yang’s tofu.” In this way, no matter how often later generations copied these dishes, their names remained tied to their origins.

However, this naming convention has its limitations. Prefect Wang, Governor Yang, and the better-known Kung Pao (of Kung Pao chicken fame) all refer to the chefs’ employers rather than the people who actually did the cooking. Only in his “Biography of Chef Wang Xiaoyu” did Yuan Mei praise a chef, elevating an obscure kitchen worker to a culinary figure remembered by later generations.

Similarly, General Tso’s chicken is familiar to almost everyone in the United States, yet few know the name Peng Chang-kuei, the chef credited with creating the dish and introducing it to America. Diners know the name of General Tso, but not the person behind the dish.

One way to recognize innovative chefs would be to give them explicit credit for their creations. For example, instead of simply labeling a dish “Chef’s Recommendation,” menus could identify the chef or team of chefs who developed it, along with the restaurant and year it first appeared. This would acknowledge the contributions of both the creators and the restaurants that invested in their work.

Chefs could also license their original recipes to restaurants and large chains. Another possibility would be to establish an industry-wide registry of original dishes, where chefs and restaurants could record development dates, launch locations, photographs, and successive versions of their recipes. That way, even if other restaurants later copied a dish and achieved greater commercial success, its creator’s contribution would not simply be forgotten.

Of course, implementing such measures would not be easy. The greatest resistance might not even come from imitators, but from within the restaurants where new dishes are developed.

For restaurant owners, naming a dish after its creator also poses risks. Chefs tend to move between jobs, and when one leaves, dishes bearing their name could become an awkward legacy, potentially even requiring a restaurant to overhaul its menu. At the same time, chefs have traditionally enjoyed relatively low social status. Within restaurants, they often have little say in day-to-day operations and limited bargaining power to protect their own interests, making it difficult to secure adequate recognition for their contributions.

These two problems are closely related. When chefs receive little recognition for their work and feel little ownership over the dishes they create or the restaurants where they work, they may be more inclined to leave. This, in turn, gives restaurants even less incentive to credit individual chefs. It may help explain why, in the rare cases in which a dish bears its creator’s name — such as Fei Da Chu’s chili stir-fried pork, sold in cities across China — the chef behind it is also the restaurant’s owner.

Protecting and rewarding the creators of original dishes, whether through naming rights or other institutional and technological mechanisms, could help raise chefs’ social status, strengthen their bargaining power, and create a more equitable relationship between chefs and restaurant owners. Restaurants, in turn, could attract diners who appreciate the work of individual chefs and are willing to pay for originality. The result could be a positive cycle of culinary innovation, recognition, and consumption.

A dish may be replicated almost perfectly, but the experience, creativity, and reputation behind it cannot. The chef who conceived the idea, the sous chefs who tested the recipe, the team members who continually refined it, and the restaurant that provided the resources and space for experimentation all contributed to the story behind the dish. Recognizing their contributions is about more than giving credit where it is due. It is also about respecting the generations of chefs who have shaped Chinese cuisine and ensuring that their knowledge, skills, and traditions continue to be valued.

(Header image: The illustration in the center depicts Yuan Mei, a Qing Dynasty poet, scholar, and artist, in a 19th-century painting by Chinese artist Ye Yanlan. Images from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.title: China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.content:
China has approved its first domestically developed amino acid-based nutritional powder, designed to give patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) — a rare genetic disorder that affects metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine — greater freedom in what they eat. Treatment of PKU requires lifelong dietary restrictions to prevent developmental disorders and brain damage.

The new formula officially entered the Chinese market on Oct. 30 and was jointly developed by Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research, and dairy producer Bright Dairy.

PKU affects about one in every 11,000 newborns in China, with an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 registered patients nationwide.

Due to a genetic defect, people with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. The resulting buildup can damage brain cells, requiring patients to follow a low-phenylalanine diet by cutting out meat and eating low-protein grains, while relying on milk powder-like formulas to supplement the other amino acids they need.

Earlier formulas contained 30% to 60% amino acids, with the rest composed of fats, carbohydrates, and other nutrients.

“As patients grow older, they need more protein. That means consuming more of these formulas, which also means taking in more fats and carbohydrates, increasing the risk of obesity,” Cai Wei, director of the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research and leader of the research team, told domestic media.

In contrast, the new formula contains 95% amino acids, allowing patients to meet their amino acid needs without consuming as much fat or as many carbohydrates, and giving them more freedom to enjoy other normal low-protein foods.

Zhuang Yingying, a 33-year-old PKU patient, told domestic media that patients previously relied heavily on imported products, and overseas supply disruptions were common. Special low-protein foods such as rice and noodles cost five to 10 times as much as regular varieties.

The formula, designed for PKU patients aged 1 and older, could save some families more than 1,000 yuan ($140) a month, according to domestic media.

Domestic PKU formulas have existed for decades, but long faced hurdles in gaining regulatory approval in China, partly because of gaps in national standards for food-grade amino acids, according to a 2020 report by domestic media outlet China Times. High registration costs and the small patient population have also discouraged manufacturers from entering the market.

China approved its first PKU medical formula in 2018, an imported product, while the first domestically produced formula received regulatory approval in 2025.

Since 2018, some parts of China, including Shanghai and neighboring Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, have introduced public health insurance coverage for foods formulated for PKU patients. In Shanghai, annual coverage ranges from 8,000 yuan for infants under 1 to 12,000 yuan for patients over 10.

Development of the new formula began in 2024 and received regulatory approval in September 2026. The research team has also worked with companies to develop everyday foods for PKU patients, including noodles, steamed buns, cookies, and mochi.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: From the Shanghai Morning Post)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.title: Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.content:
At her desk in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai, a county in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, Chai Fenfen has hung a large print of a 100-yuan banknote.

“I came here to make money,” she says. “That’s what keeps me motivated.”

After jobs selling insurance and real estate, Chai joined the workshop in 2024. Making nails offers steady earnings and the flexibility to take her children to and from school. Workers there are paid by the piece, typically earning 3,000 to 4,000 yuan a month ($450 to $600).

But for the businesses supplying that work, the early boom has given way to fierce competition over price.

Once known for its crystal trade, Donghai used its existing e-commerce networks to build an industry around press-on nails — ready-made artificial nails that customers attach themselves. By 2024, the county had nearly 25,000 businesses in the trade, according to its press-on nail industry association.

Chai’s employer, wholesaler Li Zhifu, entered the business in 2021, and now has around 2,000 workers across his production sites and more than 20 storefronts in the county.

In the beginning, Li says, almost anything sold, regardless of color or design. Competition has since squeezed profits. He estimates that six or seven out of every 10 people who entered the trade have gone out of business.

Some businesses are competing on design, selling elaborate, handmade sets for hundreds of yuan. Others are expanding overseas sales through TikTok Shop.

As overseas orders grow, Li is experimenting with machines to make nails his workers currently produce by hand.

“For large overseas orders, consistency is key. Everything, from colors and designs to rhinestone placement, has to match,” he says. He expects machine-made nails to eventually dominate that market.

(Header image: Craftswomen work in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai County, Jiangsu province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.title: China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.content:
China’s latest viral reality show is about broken friendships — rather than failing romance — between celebrities.

“I Miss You” surpassed 100 million views within two days of its Oct. 22 debut, and topped the real-time TV popularity chart on Chinese review platform Douban since last Thursday. Topics related to the show have repeatedly trended on the microblogging platform Weibo since airing.

Produced by streaming platform Mango TV, the show brings together four pairs of celebrities who have reportedly fallen out for an 18-day trip through the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region.

The show is widely seen as a riff on China’s popular relationship reality shows and follows a similar format to “See You Again,” whose fifth season aired in late 2025, which takes celebrity couples in troubled marriages on an 18-day trip before they decide whether to divorce.

In “I Miss You,” guests discuss their former friendships as a group and one-on-one with their ex-friends, play games, and share their feelings with the production team. A panel of celebrities, a psychologist, and a journalist comment on their interactions.

The most discussed pair on “I Miss You” so far has been Xu Fei and Li Na, two contestants from the 2006 season of “Super Girl,” a popular televised singing competition regarded as a cornerstone of China’s fan culture.

The two were close friends during the competition 20 years ago, but their friendship later collapsed after Li came to believe that Xu had reported her to their management company for taking outside jobs in violation of her contract. Li said the company subsequently stopped arranging work for her, which she sees as having dealt a major blow to her career. Xu denied the accusation, instead blaming a third person.

As the two revisited their past on the show, their memories of their friendship moved many viewers, with one highly upvoted comment describing their relationship as “an epic saga of love and hate.”

Xu said in tears that she had loved “wasting time together,” and noted that her current preferred snacks are the “ones Li loved back then.” Li also recalled how, even when the two appeared to be bitter enemies, they would sometimes end up crying in each other’s arms after getting drunk at gatherings.

Yet the two remained at odds over the past accusation. During an interview with the production team, Li said she had hated Xu “for a long time,” at one point shouting, “What about the money I lost?”

The other three pairs of celebrities include an actor who cut ties with a longtime producer friend after feeling pressured to accept a role, an actress and a writer who fell out when the latter grew closer to a third person, and former professional esports teammates who fought over training strategies, eventually leading one to leave the team.

“‘I Miss You’ feels so much more pure than ‘See You Again,’” read a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that received almost 3,700 likes. “In a marriage, you have to argue about more than feelings. There’s property, children, parents, and so much else. With friendship, we can sit down and focus on just one thing: how we feel about each other.”

Fu, a 21-year-old viewer from the southern Guangdong province, told Sixth Tone that she found the show’s focus on friendship “refreshing” given how rarely such relationships take center stage on screen.

“We’re so used to understanding intimate relationships through the lens of romance, but rarely give serious thought to the love, possessiveness, jealousy, dependence, disappointment, and reconciliation that exist in friendships,” she said.

Another 21-year-old viewer based in Shanghai, surnamed You, added that the show’s appeal lies in friendship’s lack of definition.

“Friendship can be as intense and possessive as romance, full of love and resentment, or it can be something much more casual,” You said. “People can have very different ideas of what friendship means, and that alone can create tension.”

Contributions: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “I Miss You.” From Douban)

World.title: [Market Rider] Essential market insights on the recent GCash IPO
World.content:
Last month’s P60.9-billion GCash initial public offering (IPO) or more precisely of Mynt Inc., the parent company of GCash, was the largest in the history of the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE). It was also the biggest for Southeast Asia for 2026.

When the idea came out for the first time, many thought it was not possible. The market has been poor that it slowly but surely became the region’s bottom dweller in recent years. During this time, the PSE was said to “operate under a P30-billion domestic liquidity ceiling.” Public equity offerings exceeding this threshold routinely drained capital from other index stocks. It was suffering from a market structural anomaly where massive IPOs exhausted domestic liquidity, resulting in immediate post-listing price collapses. (READ: [Market Rider] Buy when there’s blood in the streets, even if it’s your own blood)

But the incredible happened. The IPO shattered local capital-raising records. The market withstood the stress test and presented an optimistic financial ecosystem for both present and future big ticket market debuts.

Let’s look at how it happened.

Essentially, the operational mechanics of the GCash debut offer definitive structural lessons in pricing discipline, liquidity management, and retail participation, fundamentally redrawing the blueprint for big-ticket public equity offerings. It also provided a glimpse into the local market’s actual capacity to absorb multi-billion-peso digital assets, frameworks that will directly dictate the strategy especially for future technology listings in the country.

Initially, the GCash IPO demonstrated that massive scale demands conservative pricing discipline; for in the past, large-cap listings on the PSE suffered from post-debut sell-offs due to overwhelming market supply.

In 2021, Monde Nissin maximized its valuation on day one by pricing at the absolute top of its range, leaving no “money on the table.” The resulting lack of a secondary market cushion triggered a multi-year valuation reset. Similarly, during its 2020 debut, Converge ICT resisted trimming its initial offer price despite pandemic-induced market volatility. When institutional selling intensified on Day 1, its local stabilization agent was forced to exhaust 85% of its defense fund within a fortnight just to establish a static floor.

True enough, even with the conservative anchoring, the trading price of GCash experienced a post-debut slump, hitting an intraday low of P5.95 or nearly 10% below offer on October 26. It required heavy post-IPO intervention from its stabilization agent (UBS) to steady the stock back to P6.61.

In this regard, GCash bypassed this market constraint through two distinct structural pillars. This is through the employment of a massive global cornerstone book and decentralized retail onboarding. GCash secured over 20 top-tier global cornerstone institutional investors, including BlackRock, Fidelity, HSBC, and Capital Group, who absorbed nearly 70% of the offered shares. This is now the new structural “floor” for new-economy tech stocks.

Conversely, by embedding the IPO natively into the GStocks PH platform, GCash unlocked an entirely new tier of retail investors. Over 140,000 everyday platform users collectively contributed P1.1 billion.

Unlike traditional day-traders who flip shares for short-term arbitrage, these platform-native users behaved as long-term, sticky collectors, effectively neutralizing immediate open-market selling pressure.

Out of this experience, global banking intervention and conservative initial pricing to withstand the local market’s finite depth are critical to meet the demands of a massive public equity offering.

Regulatory and tailwinds

Believe it or not, PSE’s decision to lower the minimum public float requirement to 12% for exceptionally large corporations like those valued over P200 billion or over, also helped contribute to the success of GCash’s IPO and listing. This reduction in the minimum requirement for public float has truly created a safer buffer against market exhaustion.

By also allowing modern tech infrastructure and fintech assets to trade on forward-looking growth multipliers, the PSE and the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) have as well contributed to the successful IPO of GCash.

This newly proven playbook for market absorption could serve heavily as market strategies for upcoming mega-public offerings. However, it appears also has that the market cannot do it in rapid, localized succession without causing investor fatigue.

Recognizing this local capacity constraint, the regulators, issuers and underwriters may have to work more to remedy the problem by introducing a delicate balance of disciplined localized pricing, decentralized retail distribution, and forging a strategic bridge to global institutional capital. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: ICC’s arrest warrant vs Dela Rosa still active, not dismissed by SC
World.content:
The International Criminal Court's arrest warrant against Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa remains in effect. Nor has the Philippine Supreme Court dismissed proceedings against him.

Claim: The International Criminal Court (ICC) allegedly declared its arrest warrant against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa invalid, while the Supreme Court (SC) dismissed the case and arrest warrant against him.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The claim originated from YouTube videos uploaded by the channel “NEWS UPDATE FILES,” which had over 80,000 subscribers, on November 1 and 2.

The video titles and thumbnails claim that the ICC had withdrawn its charges and that the SC officially dismissed the case against Dela Rosa.

As of writing, both videos reached 43,800, with over 2,000 likes in total. The comments section saw users commending the SC for the supposed dismissal and criticizing the Marcos administration’s alleged political motives.

The facts: There is no official statement, court order, or legal resolution from the ICC that invalidates the arrest warrant. It remains active and is publicly accessible in the ICC’s official records.

The tribunal unsealed and publicly confirmed the arrest warrant in May 2026. Based on the warrant, the Pre-Trial Chamber I found reasonable grounds to believe that Dela Rosa — in his former capacity as Philippine National Police chief — committed the crime against humanity of murder. This is in connection with the war on drugs campaign of former president Rodrigo Duterte, who is detained at the ICC.

Furthermore, the SC did not dismiss any ICC warrant and nor did it void the international proceedings. In fact, the former PNP chief’s legal camp continues to seek domestic remedies before the High Court, including an October 27 manifestation for reconsideration of the ruling that denied his plea for a temporary restraining order and a status quo ante order.



Dela Rosa also asked the SC to block his warrant in November 2025.

As of writing, Dela Rosa remains at large, with the interior department offering a P50-million reward for information leading to his arrest.



Lack of evidence: The video presents no official court orders, case numbers, or transcripts to prove its claims. Instead, it features an unidentified commentator reacting to unrelated, recycled clips of government officials, including former chief presidential legal counsel Salvador Panelo and Vice President Sara Duterte.

Debunked: Dela Rosa has been the target of false claims surrounding his ICC arrest warrant:

– Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

Lyndee Buenagua is a Metro Manila-based journalist who primarily covers Bicol and Baguio. She is also an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

World.title: [OPINION] Government must outlive administrations
World.content:
A persistent weakness of Philippine governance is the tendency of successive administrations to treat development programs as political legacies rather than continuing obligations of the state. Projects initiated by one administration are sometimes suspended or abandoned by its successor, not because they have become unviable, but because they are associated with the previous leadership.

This is wasteful and contrary to the public interest. Roads, bridges, hospitals, irrigation systems, and other development projects are not presidential gifts; they are public investments financed by taxpayers, borrowed funds, or assistance secured in the name of the Republic.

The Philippines needs laws and institutions to protect development commitments across political transitions and turn long-term strategies into results. I propose two complementary reforms: a Government Development Project Continuity Act and a Philippine Economic Development Board (PEDB), drawing on the strategic functions of Singapore’s Economic Development Board (EDB).

Major projects take years to plan and implement. Abandonment without compelling justification wastes public money, leaves unfinished structures, and deprives communities of expected benefits.

Abandonment is especially damaging when foreign financing is involved. It can trigger liabilities, forfeit ODA, loans, grants, or technical assistance, and undermine the Philippines’ credibility as a development partner. Agreements made in the Republic’s name should survive changes in political leadership.

Political succession should never become institutional repudiation.

A Government Development Project Continuity Act

Congress should establish a legally enforceable presumption of continuity for duly approved, funded, and contractually committed national and local development projects. Coverage should include domestically funded, foreign-assisted, and public-private projects.

The law should provide for:

Presumption of continuity. A change in administration or political priorities alone should not justify discontinuing a qualified project.

A change in administration or political priorities alone should not justify discontinuing a qualified project. National registry of protected development projects. A public, secure, interoperable registry should record each project’s cost, funding source, implementing agency, contractual obligations, status, and completion date. Blockchain or equivalent tamper-evident technology could authenticate and timestamp entries and amendments without erasing the project’s history, subject to lawful confidentiality restrictions.

A public, secure, interoperable registry should record each project’s cost, funding source, implementing agency, contractual obligations, status, and completion date. Blockchain or equivalent tamper-evident technology could authenticate and timestamp entries and amendments without erasing the project’s history, subject to lawful confidentiality restrictions. Transition reporting. Every incoming administration should inventory inherited projects and report their status, financial commitments, implementation issues, and completion requirements.

Every incoming administration should inventory inherited projects and report their status, financial commitments, implementation issues, and completion requirements. Justified discontinuation. Cancellation or substantial modification should require demonstrable grounds, such as corruption, serious technical defects, economic infeasibility, environmental or safety concerns, material changes in circumstances, or a demonstrably superior alternative serving the same purpose.

Cancellation or substantial modification should require demonstrable grounds, such as corruption, serious technical defects, economic infeasibility, environmental or safety concerns, material changes in circumstances, or a demonstrably superior alternative serving the same purpose. Independent review and accountability. Major cancellations should undergo technical, financial, and legal assessment. Foreign-assisted projects should involve consultation with development partners, consistent with applicable agreements. Proposed discontinuations should be publicly explained, with their financial and social consequences disclosed. Congress should exercise oversight, and officials who unlawfully circumvent safeguards should face appropriate liability.

The principle is simple: continuity is the rule; discontinuation is the exception that must be justified.

Protection must not be absolute. Future administrations and Congresses retain authority to correct defective projects, respond to changed circumstances, and exercise constitutional control over appropriations. The aim is to prevent arbitrary abandonment, not guarantee funding regardless of merit or fiscal capacity.

Philippine Economic Development Board: unity of command, specialized functions

Project continuity alone cannot drive economic transformation. The Philippines also needs an institution able to translate long-term priorities into investment, industrial development, and sustained execution.

Singapore’s Economic Development Board, established in 1961, offers an example of an institution that helped attract strategic investment, develop industries, and strengthen technological capabilities. These principles can be adapted to Philippine circumstances.

We already have relevant institutions: the Board of Investments (BOI), Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA), Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA), Clark Development Corporation (CDC), and other investment promotion and economic zone authorities. The problem is fragmented responsibilities and overlapping functions.

Rather than create another coordinating council, Congress should establish the PEDB by consolidating these agencies under one governing authority and executive leadership. It should be an integrated institution, not merely a body coordinating independently directed agencies.

BOI, PEZA, BCDA, SBMA, CDC, and other relevant agencies should become specialized operating divisions or constituent units. The necessary regulatory, administrative, technical, commercial, and operational responsibilities should be preserved. PEZA should retain specialized zone administration; BCDA should retain its property development capabilities; and freeport authorities should continue their geographically specific functions.

The institutional structure within which they operate must change. The principle is unity of command with functional specialization: one national authority, one coherent strategy, and one accountable executive leadership. Overlapping promotion, investor assistance, administration, and reporting should be rationalized without sacrificing expertise or regional capabilities.

The PEDB should attract investment, develop priority industries, administer economic zones and strategic properties through specialized divisions, connect foreign investors with Filipino enterprises, strengthen local supply chains and technology transfer, and facilitate investment. It should maintain the National Register and monitor implementation.

The PEDB needs professional management, merit-based appointments, staggered terms, and legally defined grounds for removal. Its performance should be measured by realized investment, quality jobs, exports, productivity, technology transfer, and stronger domestic industries—not merely investment pledges. It must remain subject to congressional oversight, Commission on Audit examination, transparency, and independent evaluation.

Consolidation must not create a competing national planning authority. DEPDev should remain responsible for national economic planning, the Philippine Development Plan, and public investment programming. PEDB should translate these priorities into investment and industrial development.

DEPDev plans; PEDB mobilizes investment and drives development; DBM handles budget formulation; DOF oversees fiscal policy and public financing; and Congress legislates, appropriates, and exercises oversight.

Legislative caveat: getting the transition right

These reforms require careful drafting and an orderly transition. The PEDB Act must specify which agencies are merged, which become operating divisions, and which corporate entities or subsidiaries retain separate legal identities. It must address assets, liabilities, contracts, financing, personnel, and ongoing projects; respect vested rights and binding obligations; and amend or harmonize agency charters where necessary. Transitional safeguards must prevent reorganization from disrupting the projects and investments the reforms seek to protect.

Unity of command must be accompanied by clarity of legal authority, continuity of obligations, and accountability for results.

The two reforms are complementary: the Continuity Act protects legitimate commitments from arbitrary disruption; the PEDB consolidates principal investment and development agencies under one authority to drive economic transformation.

Neither should perpetuate defective projects or misguided policies; both require transparency, fiscal discipline, evaluation, and accountability. But a change in administration should not automatically change the country’s economic direction.

National development is cumulative. Every administration should build on what its predecessor accomplished, not start from scratch each time. Measure leadership by its contribution to the country’s continuing progress, not by how effectively it erases previous accomplishments.

Presidents come and go. Administrations rise and fall. But the state endures, and its responsibility to the Filipino people must endure with it. National development must outlive political administrations. It is time to make that principle the law of the land. – Rappler.com



Raul F. Borjal is a BS Economics alumnus of Ateneo de Manila University and has undertaken post-graduate studies at the Ateneo Graduate School of Business. He held senior executive positions in various domestic and multinational corporations, culminating in his retirement as vice president and corporate secretary of a Filipino-owned group of companies.

World.title: Alex Eala edges Czech foe in thriller, nabs Hong Kong Open quarterfinal spot
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Filipina tennis superstar Alex Eala brushed off the threat of an extended match in the clutch, eking out a thrilling 6-4, 7-6(7) straight-setter against Czech rival Tereza Valentova to reach the 2026 Hong Kong Open quarterfinals on Thursday, November 5.

Down 5-3 in the second set after relentless back-and-forth action, Eala ignited the comeback fire with a love game to inch within 5-4, before completing a three-game turnaround to land at a 6-5 lead.

Valentova, however, stopped the bleeding in time to force the tiebreaker, 6-6.

Just as it looked like the 21-year-old Eala had her foe dead in the water with a 5-0 blitz in the race-to-seven finale, Valentova dug herself out with a scorching 6-1 rally of her own to set up yet another nail-biting finish for the Filipina sensation.

After four match points, Eala got the final break she needed on the serve, scoring the last two points to seal the deal and deny a valiant challenge from the world No. 85 Valentova.

“It was really, really tough. I think Tereza played incredibly, and we were able to bring the match to a really high level, and I think that was reflected on the scores,” Eala said after the match. “Really happy with that win, I think I escaped by a little bit.”

With the win, Eala also solved a yearlong puzzle featuring Valentova, as the Czech star swept the Filipina in their two previous meetings: a 6-1, 6-2 demolition in the 2025 Japan Open Round of 32 and a 7-6(6), 6-1 pullaway in the 2026 Qatar Open Round of 64.

“Of course, the previous two meetings [against her] were super difficult, so I knew it was going to be a tough battle,” Eala added. “I just tried to be better than the previous time we met.”

Eala faces another quick turnaround as world No. 81 Antonia Ruzic of Croatia awaits on the other side of the quarterfinal equation on Friday, November 6, around 7:40 pm. – Rappler.com

World.title: Dela Rosa’s arrest? NBI hopes by year-end
World.content:
FUGITIVE. Senator Ronald dela Rosa walks from his office to talk to journalists at the Senate on May 12, 2026.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag says there is a 'big chance' Dela Rosa will be apprehended

Is Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa hiding in Mindanao? Law enforcement agencies, unfortunately, have different answers.

The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) believes the senator is being protected by a “powerful armed group” in the Southern Philippines. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), meanwhile, says it cannot confirm his whereabouts.

“I cannot tell [if he’s in Mindanao] but we have a strong belief that he is still in the Philippines,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag said on Thursday, November 5. “Though that’s still a possibility.”

Dela Rosa has remained out of public view since May, following the issuance of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant against him over his alleged role in the Duterte administration’s bloody drug war.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla previously said he received information that the legislator was being protected by an armed group in Mindanao. He also warned that a forced arrest could cost “10,000” lives, explaining why he would rather negotiate the senator’s surrender.

Remulla did not identify the alleged armed group, but the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) was quick to distance itself from the speculation.

The interior chief also gave Dela Rosa a one-week deadline to surrender, and offered a P50-million bounty for his arrest. After the deadline lapsed, the Philippine National Police (PNP) launched an intensified manhunt operation for their former chief.

“The NBI may soon launch some operations to eliminate the areas that we will identify based on the intelligence reports…With the information we are getting, there is a great chance for his arrest,” Matibag said.

Asked whether the senator would be arrested by Christmas, Matibag replied: “We hope so.”

The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I issued a warrant against Dela Rosa in November last year due to his role in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war. He was Duterte’s first police chief who implemented the bloody anti-drug campaign, which human rights organizations said, took the lives of as many as 30,000 people.

The ICC named him a co-perpetrator in the case. It added that those involved “controlled a structure of power” which enabled them to “direct and control the actions” of those who carried out drug war killings.

Partido Demokratiko Pilipino Lakas ng Bayan, Dela Rosa’s political party, has appealed to the Supreme Court for a swift resolution of Dela Rosa’s case. The senator’s camp also urged the High Court to reverse its earlier ruling and stop the use of an ICC warrant of arrest against him.

With Dela Rosa still nowhere to be found, Malacañang has challenged the PNP leadership to ensure his arrest, putting pressure on the police force once led by the senator. Will they heed his call or remain loyal to their ex-PNP chief? – with reports by Jairo Bolledo/Rappler.com

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo announces international retirement
World.content:
RONALDO. In this file photo from July 2026, Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo looks dejected after the match as Portugal are eliminated from the World Cup.

'If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it,' says Ronaldo

Cristiano Ronaldo said on Thursday, November 5, he was retiring from the Portugal team, bringing the curtain down on one of the most illustrious international careers in the history of football.

The 41-year-old announced that he would ‘hand back the number 7 shirt’ after the November international break.

Ronaldo captained Portugal to their first major trophy at Euro 2016 and helped them win the 2019 and 2025 Nations Leagues.

“It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made only with the head. They are also made with the heart,” said Ronaldo.

“If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it.”

Ronaldo thanked his family, the Portuguese people, and the teammates, coaches, and staff he worked with over his 23-year career with the national team.

“Portugal will always be a part of me,” he captioned the announcement video.

Ronaldo has made 234 appearances for Portugal and scored 146 goals. He holds the all-time record for international appearances and for international goals.

His final international tournament appearance was at the 2026 World Cup, where he tried to win the one major trophy that has eluded him. Portugal exited in the last 16 with a 1-0 loss to eventual champions and Iberian rivals Spain.

Ronaldo did, however, join Argentina’s Lionel Messi as the only players to feature at six global tournaments, one of a host of international records set by the Al-Nassr forward.

Ronaldo apology

Ronaldo left the Portugal camp at the end of September ahead of their Nations League match against Denmark without permission and did not return. He later cited broken promises from manager Jorge Jesus as the reason for his departure.

Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return following Portugal’s 2-1 win.

After Ronaldo apologized and said he remained available for international selection, the Portuguese Football Federation suspended the forward for 30 days and fined him €255 ($287.16).

Portugal, who top Nations League Group A4, hosts second-placed Denmark on November 14 in Braga before visiting Wales in their final two group games, which will be Ronaldo’s final chances to add to his international statistics.

The Portuguese Football Federation released a statement after Ronaldo’s retirement announcement, expressing its profound and eternal gratitude for his services.

“More than an exceptional athlete, our captain was an inspiring leader, an example of dedication and the ultimate symbol of the soul of our National Team,” said the statement.

Ronaldo will leave the international stage as Portugal’s most successful player in terms of individual and team honors and has become a cultural reference point for the country around the world.

“I spent my life working to become the best player in the world. Today I realise that my greatest victory was having deserved the honor of representing the best country in the world,” said Ronaldo in his statement. – Rappler.com

World.title: Hurry Up With Our Investment Projects, China tells Myanmar Regime
World.content:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has renewed Beijing’s call for the Myanmar regime to “steadily advance” key projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which is designed to give Beijing direct access to Indian Ocean.

Wang made the remarks during a meeting on Tuesday with Myanmar Investment and Foreign Economic Relations Minister Aung Kyaw Hoe, who is in Beijing for the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

A clearly exasperated Wang stressed the need for the two sides to “coordinate” development and security, as many parts of Myanmar are plagued by civil war, making it hard for the China-backed projects to proceed.

In turn, Wang promised Chinese support for the rebranded regime’s efforts to achieve international recognition. “China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” he said.

The remarks come as the U.S. shows signs of re-engaging with Naypyitaw in search of business.

Wang also called for stronger efforts to combat scams and online gambling. He urged Myanmar to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to online scam operations that flourished along the Thai-Myanmar border.

He urged Naypyitaw to do more to ensure the safety of Chinese nationals, organizations and projects operating in the country.

Aung Kyaw Hoe, for his part, promised that his regime does want to accelerate the CMEC projects and step up cooperation with China and regional countries in combating online scam operations. He duly thanked his hosts for supporting Myanmar in international forums, according to a statement from the Chinese Embassy.

When Myanmar’s putschist leader Min Aung Hlaing last visited Beijing in June after declaring himself president, Chinese President Xi Jinping also urged him to speed up the CMEC projects, a key component of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

He too urged the regime to provide stronger security guarantees for Chinese personnel and investments in Myanmar, many of which are in areas now controlled by the resistance or ethnic armed organizations over which Beijing holds no sway.

The planned corridor includes several flagship projects, notably the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State and a railway linking Kyaukphyu through Mandalay and Muse with China’s Yunnan Province.

The Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project is particularly important for Beijing because it would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean while supporting economic development in Yunnan and other southwestern Chinese provinces.

But other than pay lip-service to the plans and hold out its hand for more investment, the Myanmar regime has done little to advance these projects, instead losing itself in dreams of reviving the long-mothballed Myitsone Dam Project in quite a different part of the country.

In its frustration, China has now reopened border crossings with areas controlled by ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan State to allow lucrative trade to resume, whether the regime likes it or not.

A China analyst told The Irrawaddy that Beijing “knows very well that Min Aung Hlaing’s stubbornness is holding everything up. The fighting is still going on, the peace talks haven’t delivered any results, there’s been no progress in northern Shan State, and the border crossings are still not operating normally.”

For the CMEC projects to move forward, Min Aung Hlaing “has to engage in talks with the ethnic armed groups first,” she added. “In that sense, I think China was quite deliberately sending that message.”

World.title: Kyat Slump Disrupts Thai Border Trade as Import Costs Rise
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of Myanmar’s currency has disrupted border trade with Thailand, prompting some traders and money changers along the border to suspend transactions as they struggle to cope with volatile exchange rates and mounting import costs.

The currency weakened to around 680 baht per 100,000 kyats this week, down from more than 700 baht in recent weeks. The currency also fell against the U.S. dollar, with the market exchange rate rising from just above 4,700 kyats per dollar at the end of October to more than 4,900 on Wednesday. The rate was just around 4,400 kyats in early October.

The latest slump is fueling concerns over another wave of inflation in a country heavily reliant on imports from Thailand. Myanmar imports a wide range of goods from its neighbor, including electrical appliances, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and foodstuffs, making fluctuations in the baht exchange rate significant for consumers.

Market insiders attributed the kyat’s latest decline to the regime’s plan to borrow 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to finance a budget shortfall for fiscal year 2026-27, which ends on March 31. The regime has already sold treasury bonds worth trillions of kyats, leading to speculation that it will simply print banknotes to cover the deficit.

They also pointed to Myanmar’s continued inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist, delays in export licensing and policy inconsistencies between ministries as factors undermining confidence in the market.

The swift depreciation of the kyat has left traders struggling to price goods and manage working capital.

“A gradual rise doesn’t create much difficulty. The problem is when rates surge rapidly,” a trader in Myawaddy told The Irrawaddy.

“If exchange rates rise further, we will need more capital to restock. Some traders have temporarily stopped trading and making payments, and are waiting to see where the market moves.”

The uncertainty has spread beyond traders. Some major money changers in Myawaddy and across the border in Thailand suspended transactions on Wednesday, opting to wait for the next day’s opening rates before resuming business, according to border exchange operators.

The volatility is not confined to the Thai border. Traders in Muse, on Shan State’s border with China, are facing similar difficulties as the kyat continues to weaken against the yuan, market sources said.

Traders warn that prolonged instability in foreign exchange markets could further squeeze trade. Importers say their profits are shrinking, but are reluctant to increase prices for fear that demand may decline further.

A trader in Myawaddy said transport costs remain a major contributor to rising prices, with expenses along trade routes increasing because of checkpoints and demands for unofficial payments.

“Price increases are caused more by transport costs than exchange rates,” he said. “Costs at checkpoints rise sharply whenever authorities announce crackdowns or tighter controls.”

Exporters also say the weaker kyat is raising shipping costs because freight charges, container fees and port services are paid in U.S. dollars. At the same time, they complain that mandatory foreign-exchange conversion rules prevent them from fully benefiting from higher market exchange rates.

Under existing regulations, exporters must convert 35 percent of their export earnings at the Central Bank’s official rate, creating a significant gap between official and market rates. The Central Bank’s official reference rate remains 2,100 kyats per dollar, while its market trading rate is about 3,660 kyats per dollar. The market rate was around 4,900 kyats on Thursday. Before the coup, the kyat traded at roughly 1,300-1,400 per U.S. dollar.

An exporter from Mon State explained that the depreciation of the kyat has sharply increased the capital required to buy export commodities such as corn and onions.

“Previously, we could buy a container of goods for 10 million kyats from local producers. Now it can require more than 15 million kyats,” he said.

Traders say prices of Thai imports, particularly electrical goods, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and food items, are already climbing as a result of the stronger baht and rising transportation costs.

World.title: Thai Foreign Minister to Visit Myanmar Ahead of ASEAN Summit
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thailand’s foreign minister said he will visit Myanmar on November 12, days before a regional summit where Bangkok will be pressing to normalize ties with the war-torn country.

Sihasak Phuangketkeow’s trip also comes during raised tensions along the countries’ shared border, where Bangkok said clashes between Myanmar’s military and ethnic rebels caused property damage and injured a Thai civilian in Thailand on Thursday.

His visit, announced late Tuesday, is scheduled shortly before a November 16-18 summit of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila.

Myanmar’s leaders have not been invited to high-level ASEAN meetings since former general Min Aung Hlaing led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war.

Sihasak told reporters in Beijing his government wants to “hear Myanmar’s latest position” ahead of the summit.

“De-escalation by all parties will help create a conducive atmosphere for essential dialogue and the peace process,” he said.

“If there is progress on these fronts, it will be a positive factor for ASEAN to consider at the leaders summit, as we decide how to move forward on the situation in Myanmar, including Myanmar’s participation in ASEAN meetings,” he added.

Sihasak, who last visited Myanmar in April, said he would meet his counterpart, Tin Maung Swe, on November 12, and a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing was “in the works”.

In July, Bangkok hosted a meeting between Tin Maung Swe and foreign ministers of several ASEAN member states, the first such gathering since the 2021 coup.

The following month Min Aung Hlaing met with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, with the two nations’ military chiefs holding talks two weeks after.

Min Aung Hlaing took over as civilian president in April following elections widely dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Since then he has been given a red-carpet welcome across the region, in India, China and several ASEAN nations.

Myanmar is expected to send a senior civil servant to the Manila summit.

Thailand has stepped up security on its western frontier following last week’s cross-border fire.

On Wednesday, Myanmar’s military blamed “terrorist insurgents”—the term it commonly uses to refer to ethnic-minority armed groups and pro-democracy forces—for wounding a Thai national, according to a statement in state media.

World.title: Myanmar’s NUG Warns US Against Prioritizing Its Interests Over Peace
World.content:
In response to the new U.S. Mission Strategy for war-torn Myanmar, the parallel civilian National Unity Government (NUG) and observers urged Washington to help solve the country’s political crisis first instead of prioritizing its own security and economic interests.

Speaking with The Irrawaddy, NUG Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister David Gum Awng said that if the U.S. had a genuine desire to see sustainable peace and economic development in the country, the root cause of the political crisis must be solved first.

“An approach that sidelines the core principles such as democracy, human rights and establishment of a federal union in favor of prioritizing its [own] security and economic interests is not sufficient and lacks the comprehensive scope needed to solve the Myanmar crisis,” he added.

The U.S. State Department recently published its latest strategy for Myanmar, prioritizing the fight against online scam networks that target Americans, increasing U.S. investment, and access to rare earth minerals. Additional objectives include expanding U.S. regional influence and brokering a peace agreement by 2030.

Recently, U.S. officials held talks with junta leaders in Naypyitaw and Tokyo, increasing Washington’s engagement with the internationally isolated coup regime that ousted the democratically elected civilian government led by pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.

Washington said in its latest statement that facilitating dialogue and supporting multi-stakeholder engagement would help lay the groundwork for lasting peace and national reconciliation.

However, Gum Awng argued that peace cannot be achieved simply by forcing stakeholders to sit together at a negotiating table, noting that the primary challenge is whether the regime is genuinely willing to give up its dictatorship and accept real change.

“Without the definitive end of the military dictatorship, the emergence of an inclusive political process involving all stakeholders (including ethnic groups), and the establishment of robust monitoring mechanisms to guarantee agreements, any hastily brokered peace driven by a specific timeline will only temporarily de-escalate the conflict without solving the underlying root problem.”

Regarding the U.S. goal of building regional influence, the NUG minister said Myanmar cannot be viewed solely as a proxy battleground for U.S.-China influence, adding that the sovereignty and the right to self-determination of the nation’s people remain paramount.

“If the U.S. wishes to build long-term, sustainable influence, engaging with the military council alone is insufficient. The U.S. must respect the democratic will of the Myanmar people, increase its engagement with federal democratic forces, and prove through practical actions that it is a reliable partner,” Gum Awng said.

“U.S. influence cannot be measured solely by its ability to counter China. It depends entirely on earning the trust of the Myanmar people and participating constructively in the building of a future federal democratic nation.”

Regarding U.S. efforts to gain access to rare earth minerals through its peace efforts, the NUG’s deputy foreign minister warned that the country’s resources cannot be treated merely as a component of a peace process or a political compromise, since they are directly tied to the long-term interests of the people, the rights of ethnic groups, and the resource management rights of the future federal union.

Regarding Washington’s move to boost engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma, said a strategy based on appeasing the root cause of Myanmar’s notorious transnational crime hubs is doomed to fail. U.S. citizens, along with the people of Myanmar and the region, continue to suffer due to this irresponsible approach, she said.

“It is like engaging serial killers in order to persuade them to kill fewer people instead of acting to stop their crimes,” she said.

“It is both illogical and immoral to bribe [coup president] Min Aung Hlaing’s junta with trade and aid to secure rare earths while looking away from the security, economic and humanitarian crises he is intensifying every day.”

She also warned that the U.S. was in danger of falling into Min Aung Hlaing’s trap, in which he is able to pit Moscow, Beijing and Washington against each other to secure more weapons, more cash and more legitimacy without concrete solutions.

Regarding U.S. peace efforts, Myanmar political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye said, “I don’t think it [a U.S.-brokered peace plan] will work. Myanmar’s political situation and its underlying problem cannot be resolved easily or quickly. Its peace plan is likely either a strategic miscalculation or merely a gesture to show the U.S. is interested in it.”

World.title: Is Myanmar’s Regime Preparing Another ‘Summit Surprise’?
World.content:
As regional leaders finalize their itineraries for this month’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila, a grim and familiar pattern is playing out in Myanmar. For four years, the military junta has delivered a “summit surprise”: a sharp escalation in violence, usually deadly airstrikes on civilians, timed to coincide with high-level diplomatic gatherings.

Human rights organizations and UN bodies have documented this cycle extensively. Ahead of the May 2023 ASEAN Summit in Indonesia, the military bombed the village of Pazigyi, killing more than 160 people. Human Rights Watch cited the attack as evidence of the junta’s disregard for ASEAN’s peace plan for Myanmar, known as the Five-Point Consensus. Later that year, as leaders were still managing the diplomatic fallout, the military struck a displaced persons camp in Kachin State, killing 28 civilians, including children. Amnesty International described the attack as a likely war crime. The brazenness grew ahead of the October 2024 summits in Laos, when the military launched some of its heaviest aerial campaigns since the 2021 coup. In September 2024 alone, monitors recorded 153 airstrikes, which destroyed schools and hospitals among other civilian targets. A report by the OHCHR, the UN’s human rights body, confirmed that airstrike fatalities nearly doubled that year.

Shortly before his visit to Malaysia in October this year, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime intensified its bombardment of Rakhine State, where an airstrike on a crowded local market killed at least 50 people, including children. The attack was so bloody that UN human rights chief Volker Türk said, “This latest attack raises serious concerns about respect for international humanitarian law with respect to the conduct of hostilities.”

The gap between diplomatic theater and reality on the ground has rarely been wider. Last week, Philippine Foreign Secretary and ASEAN Special Envoy Maria Theresa Lazaro made a two-day visit to Myanmar, overseeing humanitarian aid in Shan State and discussing the restoration of Myanmar’s ASEAN status with regime officials. She left without meeting detained State Counselor Aung San Suu Kyi. Manila has repeatedly pressed for access to the 81-year-old Nobel peace laureate, but Lazaro reportedly did not even request a meeting this time, fearing the junta would cancel her trip.

The regime was quick to exploit the optics, projecting an image of cooperation through state media. It also continues to use Aung San Suu Kyi as a bargaining chip. Recent limited contact, including a brief consular phone call with her son and a package from Britain’s King Charles, appear aimed at softening its pariah status abroad while denying ASEAN any meaningful access. Soon after the envoy’s departure, the junta’s fighter jets were back over civilian areas.

This approach is now alienating even Naypyitaw’s most accommodating neighbors. In August, Thailand rolled out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, the newly self-appointed president, in the hope of pragmatic dialogue. Many in Myanmar consider him a war criminal. Thailand is now facing the fallout of the regime’s violence. Its reckless operations along the frontier recently prompted the Thai military to summon Myanmar’s defense attaché to lodge a formal protest. The embarrassment has spilled into domestic politics, where the opposition has accused the Anutin government of being dangerously soft on Naypyitaw. Critics argue that accommodation not only undermines democratic values but also emboldens a junta willing to threaten Thai security and humiliate neighbors who extend a hand.

For the Philippines, this year’s ASEAN chair, the crisis has proven exhausting. Manila has tried to balance quiet diplomacy with firmer rhetoric, but the junta’s relentless violence has stalled any real progress. When the summit ends, Manila will likely be relieved to hand the “Myanmar headache” to incoming chair Singapore.

Singapore will inherit a deeply fractured regional approach to a crisis that continues to embarrass Southeast Asia. Though historically a champion of pragmatic diplomacy, it has grown more assertive as its chairmanship nears, and many hope it will take a firm stand against the regime. At an informal ASEAN foreign ministers’ meeting in Bangkok in July 2026, brokered by Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, Singapore’s Vivian Balakrishnan pressed Myanmar’s representatives directly to release political prisoners, naming Aung San Suu Kyi, and to allow safe, unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid. Singapore has also shown a growing willingness to scrutinize financial flows and aviation fuel reaching the junta. Yet the fundamental equation remains unchanged: the regime has proven immune to standard diplomatic persuasion and incremental sanctions.

When the gavel falls in Manila this month, there will no doubt be renewed expressions of “deep concern” and calls for an end to hostilities. But as the smoke clears over Rakhine State and diplomatic protests are filed in Bangkok, the truer story emerges. For the people of Myanmar, ASEAN’s diplomatic milestones are no longer opportunities for a breakthrough. They are dark omens of the violence that follows.

World.title: Thailand’s New Deals with Myanmar and Washington’s Changing Priorities
World.content:
