World.title: Euphoria turns to raw fear on Wall Street
World.content:
Euphoria met with raw fear as shares nosedived on Wall Street overnight.

Technology stocks were the hardest hit, with the NASDAQ plunging 6.3 per cent.

But the losses were widespread as the benchmark S&P 500 dived 4.3 per cent.

The heavy selling followed a day of unbridled optimism on Wall Street as investors mulled whether a Democrat-controlled Congress would inject some rationality around the AI infrastructure rollout.

A major rout on Wall Street has real implications for millions of Australians.

Most workers, via their superannuation, have approximately $4.5 trillion invested in financial markets and roughly 20 per cent of it is exposed to movements on Wall Street.

RBA interest rate updates: Follow coverage to today's tech fall, plus market reaction and analysis on our live blog.

The Trump short

The selling on all three of Wall Street's main indices was unrelenting, and it accelerated throughout the session, "with the euphoria of Wednesday's post-election rally rapidly evaporating", according to Tapas Strickland from trading platform Moomoo.

Front and centre is the once-in-a-generation build-out of AI and associated infrastructure, such as data centres.

The thinking on election day was that it would be better managed under a Democrat-controlled Congress — that it would slow down to a point that major players such as OpenAI and Anthropic would be able to pay for their investments with cash rather than debt or equity (shares).

That thinking turned on its head overnight.

AI investment boom Australian data centre operators have raised a record $35 billion so far this year. Meanwhile, the RBA governor says central banks globally are monitoring the risk of an AI investment bubble.

"What is clear is the Democrats' election victory is the motivation," Strickland said.

"Investors believe their control of Congress and key states fundamentally alters the outlook for the artificial intelligence sector due to voters' rejection of data centre developments in dozens of local ballots."

Take Texas for example. Both the governor and senator have indicated they are likely to halt or pause AI data centre development.

"And so the market is rapidly pricing in construction moratoriums, heavy regulation and an end to Silicon Valley's untrammelled infrastructure spending," Strickland said.

The robots take over

Increasingly too major investment firms are using automated trading software to trade the market.

Strickland said the algorithms went into overdrive overnight.

And unlike human beings, which may rationally see few buyers in the market and choose to sit tight, the bots kept selling, causing the market to "gap down" or fall rapidly.

"Right now, interpretation of the session's events is not clear cut as we also saw defensive areas of the market sold off sharply, sending the Dow Jones Industrial down 3.4 per cent," Strickland said.

"It seems automated funds are selling into a market with no buyers.

"While this clearing-out process could actually be constructive for the market, investors should stay cautious until the dust settles in a few days."

Firmus pulls blockbuster float Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors.

Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu is also treating the Wall Street sell-off with a degree of caution.

"The chip rout is the 'blue trade' doing the damage. Markets are treating a Democratic Congress as a brake on the AI build-out, but [US President Donald] Trump still has his veto, so this is largely a sentiment shock rather than a change in fundamentals," Wu said.

"And while self-feeding selling deserves respect, investors could start looking for entry points in the coming weeks.

"Meanwhile the defensive trades are working. Treasuries rallied again, pulling the 10-year yield to a two-month low near 4.84 per cent, and gold is staging a comeback above $US4,100."

Loading

A lot at stake

The next few trading sessions will be critical for gauging financial market sentiment.

Given Thursday's market optimism, you could put recent falls down to volatility.

Indeed, Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX index, soared an eye-watering 70 per cent overnight to 28 points.

Anything above 30 indicates a very nervous market, so it's something to watch.

Montgomery Investment Management's Roger Montgomery thinks some air has been let out of the AI tech bubble.

"The latest technology bubble is meeting the same fate as previous bubbles," he said.

"Hype that leads to overproduction and overpricing is hitting the physical reality of limited resources and the financial reality of inferior returns on the trillions spent."

The Australian share market is dominated by banking and mining stocks, so the flow-on effect to local investors seems muted at the time of writing this.

But the real pain may come if Wall Street selling continues and Australians, especially those in and approaching retirement, see their superannuation balances deteriorating rapidly.

You can see how a wealth shock in terms of shares and property for older Australians could also act as a further headwind for the Australian economy.

There's a lot on the line.

World.title: Socceroos still waiting for World Cup payment from FA
World.content:
Socceroos players who competed at this year's World Cup are yet to be paid their match fees, three months after the tournament's conclusion.

Just days after it was revealed that both male and female national team players were taking legal action against Football Australia (FA) in a dispute over their revenue-sharing agreement, members of the Socceroos World Cup squad in North America are also chasing match payments from the FA.

The payments were due within a fortnight of the players' departure from camp.

Socceroos, Matildas take FA to court The players' union is expected to argue the revenue share agreement between the governing body and national teams players is not being serviced properly.

Australia was knocked out of the tournament at the round-of-32 stage in a loss to Egypt on July 3.

FA, which recorded a $23 million loss over the last two financial years, said tax complications in the US were the cause of the delay.

The body said it was working with the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia (PFA), to "resolve the outstanding matters as quickly as possible".

"Football Australia is ready to make the match payments related to the FIFA World Cup," FA said in a statement.

"Before those payments can be processed, however, we require final specialist advice on the North American taxation obligations applicable to the payments, as well as some further player distribution information being provided through the PFA.

"Recognising the complexity of North American taxation requirements, FIFA facilitated access to specialist tax support for all participating member associations to help them understand and meet their respective obligations.

"We have been actively engaging with those specialist advisers since the World Cup to confirm the applicable tax and withholding treatment."

If a player sees game time or is an unused substitute for the national team, they earn about $6,000 in match fees.

The Socceroos played two friendlies against Mexico and Switzerland before three World Cup group games and the Egypt shootout defeat, meaning players named for all six games are heading into camp this week out of pocket to the tune of roughly $36,000.

There were no known payment issues for the four friendlies which took place in the US in the October and November windows last year.

Australia played Canada, the US, Venezuela and Colombia in North America in the back half of 2025 in the build-up towards the World Cup.

"It is clearly an unacceptable situation that three months after the conclusion of the World Cup the Socceroos match fees remain unpaid," PFA chief executive Beau Busch said.

"Any matter related to international tax was foreseeable and should have been addressed long before a ball was kicked at the tournament."

Members of the squad who faced Brazil in two friendlies in Queensland in September earlier this year are understood to have been paid in full.

The FA's delay in paying World Cup match fees has done little to quell discontent from Socceroos players heading into November's friendly window in the Middle East.

Some players have expressed concerns about travelling to the region — Australia will face Qatar in Doha and Jordan in Amman — in light of the wider conflict.

The purpose of those friendlies in the current climate has been brought into question since the Asian Football Confederation opted to delay the Asian Cup.

AAP

World.title: Police offer $250k reward to find offshore crime boss
World.content:
NSW Police have offered a $250,000 reward to help locate an offshore crime boss allegedly orchestrating the violence plaguing Sydney's streets.

Anthony Pele fled Australia in 2023 and is considered by police to be one of the key figures coordinating attacks on Sydney's Alameddine crime family from overseas.

Mr Pele, 25, is alleged to be leading the self-proclaimed Coconut Cartel, a Pacific Islander gang that takes its name from a historical slur against Pasifika people.

Detectives allege the group is behind a string of attacks on rival crime groups, many of which have been filmed and posted to social media over the past year.

Crime figure behind shooting, kidnapping, drug thefts

Police believe Mr Pele fled the country not long after allegedly shooting dead Ahmad Al-Azzam in July 2023 at Greenacre, in a case of mistaken identity.

Court documents claim Mr Pele was tasked with guarding the home of a Haouchar crime family associate when he mistook Mr Al-Azzam's car for that of a rival crime network and fired multiple shots.

Anthony Pele, in a post from a gym while on the run from police. (Supplied)

"I acted on my own … if this cocksucker is sitting opposite your mum's house … I had to do it," Pele is allegedly heard saying on a recording device after the shooting.

Since leaving Australia, his name has emerged in cases involving drug thefts and large-scale narcotic importations.

The ABC reported in February that Mr Pele, while overseas in December 2023, was behind a kidnap plot that was set to score associates $1 billion worth of cocaine before it was foiled.

Innocent bystander Ahmad Al-Azzam was shot dead. (Supplied)

In May, the ABC revealed Mr Pele's globe-trotting taunts to police and underworld adversaries on social media while on the run from authorities.

Police believe Mr Pele is currently in Vietnam.

'250,000 reasons' to turn gangster in

Speaking to reporters this morning, Police Minister Yasmin Catley described Mr Pele as a "horrific criminal".

"Antony Pele is alleged to be a horrific criminal here in NSW and part of the organised crime gangs and organised crime we are seeing in Sydney," Police Minister Yasmin Catley said.

Police Minister Yasmin Catley announces the $250,000 reward to find and extradite Anthony Pele. (ABC News)

"This reward is significant. It means that someone out there, and we know it, knows something and now we want them to tell the police or indeed they can call CrimeStoppers."

NSW Police State Crime Commander Brett Greentree said there were now "250,000 reasons to come forward".

"He is one of our highest-priority fugitives," Assistant Commissioner Greentree said.

"For more than three years detectives from state crime have worked tirelessly with our international partners to locate and apprehend him. We know the loyalties in criminal groups change.

"And to Anthony Pele my message is really simple we will not stop, time will not make a difference, this will not go away, we will bring you back and ensure you face justice in NSW."

World.title: Teenager found guilty of raping woman during home invasion
World.content:
A 17-year-old boy has been found guilty of raping a woman during a home invasion in Far North Queensland in February last year.

A judge-alone trial in Cairns last month heard the boy detained the woman's partner in a bedroom with a knife, while two other teenage boys raped her in different parts of the Manunda home.

The boy pleaded not guilty to five counts of rape, arguing he did not know his co-offenders intended to sexually assault the woman.

Prosecutors argued the accused was liable for rape because he prevented the partner from intervening.

Judge Joshua Treviño KC has today delivered his verdict, finding the boy guilty of a single count of rape, and not guilty of the other four counts.

The Children's Court of Queensland heard the three boys broke into the Manunda home and entered the couple's bedroom with weapons, demanding wallets, at about 3am on Friday, February 21, 2025.

Manunda is an inner-city suburb of Cairns. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

Crown prosecutor Nicole Friedewald argued the boy was aware his co-offenders intended to rape the woman and therefore "aided or enabled" the assault.

The prosecution relied on the evidence of the victim's partner, who said one of the other boys made an explicit comment as she left the bedroom to collect her wallet.

However, defence barrister Tim Grau told the court his client believed the other boys only intended to rob the woman.

The boy pleaded guilty to two counts of unlawful detention, two counts of armed robbery in company, breaking and entering at night in company with offensive weapons, and theft of a pair of headphones.

Defence counsel Tim Grau argued his client failed to hear and understand his co-offenders would rape the victim. (ABC News: Christopher Testa)

Earlier this year, the two co-offenders, both now aged 17, pleaded guilty to all 11 charges.

They have been remanded in custody ahead of a sentencing hearing listed for next month.

After delivering his judgment this morning, Judge Trevino said he was uncertain whether the boy could be sentenced by the end of the year.

The boy's case is next due back in court on December 14.

Before sentencing can take place, reports will need to be prepared looking at the boy's psychological wellbeing, prospects for rehabilitation, and how he has spent his 21 months in custody.

Mr Grau said a youth forensic report should also address evidence of the boy's developmental stage at the time of offending, when he was aged 16.

World.title: Aussie Rules has long history of footy gimmicks gone wrong
World.content:
Some blocked their ears while others dropped their jaws in disbelief, yet a surprising number cheered as if it didn't take them back to one of the worst moments in Fremantle Football Club's history.

During Freo's AFLW match against Sydney last weekend, the club reprised Wharfie Time, a home-ground gimmick that includes playing the opening bars of AC/DC's Hells Bells in a tight spot to spur the team on.

What is Wharfie Time? It was meant to be a celebration of Fremantle's moment in the grand final sun, but their viral Wharfie Time backfired spectacularly on Saturday.

That was despite the recent AFL Grand Final where Wharfie Time was activated with just four minutes to go and what was supposed to be a moment of celebration for Freo — up 17 points and looking strong — instead spurred the Lions into a ravenous frenzy to steal the match.

With many a Freo supporter still blinking in surprise that anyone would play it again so soon, CEO Simon Garlick has since stated that Hells Bells will be back for the 2027 AFL season.

Footy has a history of crowd gimmicks, and with Wharfie Time's future apparently set, it's only fair to take a look back at other stunts AFL and VFL clubs have pursued — for better or worse.

The Crows' power stance

The Adelaide Crows were the league's minor premiers in 2017 and were expected to fly through the grand final against Richmond.

But after a strong season that didn't need any gimmicks, they decided to introduce what became known as the power stance for the finals season.

During the national anthem, the team and coach Don Pyke stood in a rigid pose, arms down and facing the other team in an unwavering stare at the opposition that was probably supposed to be intimidating.

The Adelaide Crows maintained their pre-game power stance in September 2017. (Supplied: afl.com.au)

It was instead reminiscent, perhaps, of people freezing with horror as they realise they're about to pass an unexpected bowel movement.

And while the Crows thumped the Giants and the Cats in their first two finals, it was a different story against the Tigers.

A young team enjoying their first grand final appearance in 35 years, they were in no mood for gimmicks and ended up beating the flag favourites by 48 points, going on to win three premierships in four years.

The Crows' power stance was never seen again and it took the club nine years to win another final.

North Melbourne's elephant

In 1978, North Melbourne Football Club made the bizarre decision to field a circus elephant at Arden Street Oval before its round five match against Collingwood.

The club said it had organised what it called a "special surprise" as a promotion for a local circus that was owned by pennant member Jack Allan.

Handlers at Arden Street Oval try to slow a galloping elephant down. (Supplied: nmfc.com.au)

It started well and, in front of more than 31,000 people, the elephant was ridden by a member of the cheer squad and led around the oval.

But when Collingwood ran onto the field and drew a loud roar from the crowd, the elephant got spooked and started to gallop.

Afraid it could crush dozens of people, police started moving them from the area until the handler calmed the pachyderm and the crisis was over without injury to animal or human.

North Melbourne managed to win that game by nine points, but the idea of an elephant for crowd entertainment was retired.

Carlton's Betty Blue Hovercraft

In the 1990s, Carlton Football Club launched its own pre-game gimmick, a blue hovercraft ridden by Captain Carlton.

Captain Carlton rode a hovercraft dubbed Betty Blue onto the MCG in 2015. (Facebook: Carlton Football Club)

It came out onto the field during home games at Princes Park to rev up the crowd and was eventually retired in 1999.

But in 2015, Captain Carlton returned with a new hovercraft, dubbed Blue Betty, before the team's round one match against Richmond.

He rode the machine as it tore around the MCG leaving a rooster tail of fireworks.

Carlton ended up losing the match by 27 points.

Things took a turn for the worse later that year when Blue Betty reportedly wasn't allowed onto the Docklands stadium because of concerns for the turf, and Captain Carlton had to instead abseil from the roof.

Carlton lost that game to the Brisbane Lions, which had been winless until then.

The following day the hovercraft flipped over on the Yarra River and had to be dragged to dry land.

Angry Anderson in a Batmobile

The AFL itself decided that for the grand final's half-time entertainment in 1991, it would send singer Angry Anderson out onto the field with its own version of a Batmobile.

Angry Anderson and marathon runner Robert de Castella inside the AFL Batmobile. (YouTube: moto1986)

Sitting in the modified 1970 VG Valiant Coupe with champion marathon runner Robert de Castella, the now-late Anderson eventually belted out his hit song, Bound for Glory.

Unfortunately, it was an outing Anderson would probably rather forget.

He struggled to hear his backing track from the stands of Waverly Stadium, where the grand final was being played for the first and only time while renovations were underway at the MCG.

He also later said the straight-out exhaust of the Batmobile was so loud it was near-impossible to hear the music he was supposed to be singing along to.

History has not remembered the moment kindly, and the performance was mocked by an AFL sponsor in an advert nearly 20 years later.

A pig on the loose

Less of an official gimmick and instead a cheeky stunt, in 1993 a pig was let loose onto the goal square during the second quarter of the round 18 clash between St Kilda and Sydney at the SCG.

It had Plugga painted on one side and the number four on the other, and was rumoured to have been drafted by a Sydney Swans supporter who had earlier talked to players about getting in the head of legendary goal-kicker Tony "Plugger" Lockett, who was playing for The Saints at the time.

After running about the square to the delight of commentators while dodging attempts to catch it, the pig was eventually tackled to the ground by the Swans' Darren Holmes.

However, the stunt had little effect because Lockett wasn't even playing that day due to injury, and the Swans lost by 37 points.

But it may have impressed Plugger because he went on to play for Sydney, where he became club champion in 1995.

Crowd activations that work

Despite the disasters, some gimmicks have done wonders.

John Denver's Take Me Home, Country Roads continues to be sung by Brisbane Lions fans after every goal Charlie Cameron kicks at home, a moment that might induce cringe for the rest of us but clearly works for the Lions.

The club plays different songs for all its players after they kick a goal.

But considering the team is in the midst of a three-peat premiership dynasty, they have been kicking a lot of them, meaning those songs are probably off the playlist for everyone else.

The same could be said of Port Adelaide Football Club's use of Never Tear Us Apart by INXS.

INXS's Never Tear Us Apart is a much-loved pre-game anthem for Port Adelaide fans. (Supplied: portadelaidefc.com.au)

A reference to the club's chip on its shoulder towards the SANFL for insisting it enter the AFL in 1997 as a separate entity to its traditional Magpies team, fans sing it before every home game.

That separation ended last decade, but the song still invokes great passion among the faithful, even if, for the rest of us, Andrew Farriss's composition and Michael Hutchence's lyrics may be ruined forever.

Time will tell if AC/DC's Hells Bells will suffer the same fate, perhaps for Dockers fans most of all.

After all, the Lions' premiership coach Chris Fagan said after the grand final that they had talked about Wharfie Time the previous day and had agreed that, should it be activated, they would use it to "flip the switch ourselves, and turn it on them" instead.

Hells Bells indeed.

World.title: Women's pelvic health surgeon among SA's Australian of the Year winners
World.content:
An endo-gynaecologist specialising in pelvic floor treatments has been named the South Australia's 2027 Australian of the Year in a ceremony where the former recipient doubled down on her wish to secure a spot on a future space mission.

At a Thursday night event in Adelaide, Iranian-Australian surgeon Dr Fariba Behnia-Willison was recognised for helping develop a safer method of pelvic floor reconstruction and for her advocacy in restoring dignity for women seeking healthcare.

The doctor also founded not-for-profit Desert Flower Australia, which offers no-cost restorative surgery to female genital mutilation survivors.

Dr Behnia-Willison in the operating theatre. (Supplied: FBW Gynaecology Plus)

Dr Behnia-Willison said her upbringing informed her career aspirations.

"Wherever I went, I noticed that women's health issues [were] a taboo subject," she said.

"You may think what I have told you here is Iran's problem, but let me tell you I've lived on three different continents, and everywhere I noticed that women were denied freedom in different ways.

"Me wanting to be a voice for the women made me a surgeon."

Among this year's recipients are palliative medicine specialist Dr Roger Hunt, who was awarded SA's Senior Australian of the Year, 23-year-old space educator Edward Robinson named the state's next Young Australian of the Year, and violence prevention advocate Neil Davis, who was given the Local Hero award.

South Australia's 2027 Australian of the Year recipients are (L-R) Dr Roger Hunt, Dr Fariba Behnia-Willison, Edward Robinson and Neil Davis. (Supplied: NADC/Salty Dingo)

'Reframe' needed over space travel

Ms Bennell-Pegg, who was honoured in 2026, congratulated the recipients and said her own accolade led to "conversations that would not have been possible without being Australian of the Year".

Last month, the federal government made an undisclosed financial offer to the European Space Agency to send Ms Bennell-Pegg to space, a mission expected to cost around $100 million which the SA government would also contribute to.

Katherine Bennell-Pegg says her win last year opens conversations about Australia's space travel ambitions. (Supplied: Brad Griffin)

Ms Bennell-Pegg said space travel was an economic opportunity rather than a cost.

"We're often presented with a choice between space and cost-of-living," she said.

"It's one we need to reframe, because if we shy away, we not only miss out on opportunities but increase our vulnerabilities.

"In fact, by making our economy more resilient and more productive, space helps reduce our cost of living."

The Australian Space Agency space technology director said "no dream should be too big for the Australian psyche".

"Sometimes a bold national endeavour can help catalyse that shift, something that captures the imagination, spans sectors, brings people together and gives Australians a sense of ownership in what we're achieving," she said.

World.title: Fake robbery of autistic boy online leads to scam warning
World.content:
An anonymous post to a Facebook community group has left locals in northern WA out of pocket, after an alleged scam artist swindled social media users by suggesting his autistic son was attacked.

The October 26 post to the Broome Noticeboard page claims the author's 15-year-old autistic son was attacked and robbed by two men in Broome, 2,200 kilometres north of Perth.

A screenshot of the anonymously posted alleged scam before it was deleted. (Supplied: Facebook)

More than 100 outraged commenters asked how they could help before the post's author published his bank details in the comments, along with a name, Greg Sealey.

A number of the commenters said they had sent money to the account.

The same user posted bank details in the comments, which the ABC has chosen to remove. (Supplied)

But WA Police said they had no record of the incident despite the now-deleted message claiming to have made a report to authorities.

The post also claimed police had CCTV footage of the incident, which authorities told the ABC was not true.

Repeat offender?

It is not the first time someone by that same name has made a call for help on Facebook regarding a theft incident.

Another social media post asking for help by someone named Greg Sealey. (Facebook)

Greg Sealey posted on the Prayer Requests group on May 29, saying his car was broken into with money, bank cards and tools stolen, when it was his child's birthday the next day.

The ABC has been unable to verify whether this incident happened, as the post does not specify a location.

A Meta spokesperson said they were reviewing the content and would continue working with government and law enforcement to protect Australians from scams.

"Meta doesn’t want scams on our platforms, and we are continuing to invest in tools and technology to prevent them," they said.

Bypassing regulatory checks

Curtin University internet studies professor Tama Leaver said the ability to post anonymously had changed how people communicated online.

"The anonymous function has been abused widely and unfortunately has been very attractive to scammers, who don't even have to go through the effort of setting up a fake Facebook account," Dr Leaver said.

Tama Leaver's advice is to be wary of online requests for money. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Dr Leaver said scammers had gotten "cannier over time", figuring out ways to bypass Facebook's regulatory checks.

By posting the direct-transfer payment details in the comments as opposed to a call-out in the initial post, scammers could remain undetected, according to Dr Leaver.

"One of the literacies we need to develop if we're going to be part of online communities is being wary of these things," he said.

"I'm not saying anonymity is always linked to scamming, but there are ways for people to receive funds from communities that don't rely on direct transfer."

Dr Leaver said it was natural for people to want to help others in circumstances of tragedy, especially in their own communities.

"We see the grammar of scams evolving, and it's also true social media is still a very emotional space," he said.

'Practice the pause'

Kimberley consumer protection officer Ange Innes said she recommended that people not transfer money to someone they did not know.

"The Kimberley community is kind and generous, so I can see why people have opened their wallets," she said.

"However, this is a common tactic for scammers; they create stories that will tug at our heartstrings and don't think twice about taking advantage of our goodwill."

Ange Inns says online scammers "tug at our heartstrings". (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Ms Innes said people should report suspected scams to WA ScamNet.

"We always say, practice the pause. Take the time to think, is this legitimate?" she said.

"If you paid money to this person, we recommend you report it to the police and report the profile to the social media platform and admins of that community group," she said.

World.title: Live: Lamarre-Condon breaks down as he tells jury about shooting ex-partner
World.content:
Lamarre-Condon gave evidence about how he met Baird in October 2022 at a gay club in Sydney's inner-city.

Their relationship started of platonic and sexual, he says, but became romantic by the end of that year.

In April 2023, the accused says he went through Baird's phone and saw messages from another man.

They broke up that month, but intermittently texted and socialised, before getting back together in June 2023.

In August 2023, Lamarre-Condon testified he entered Baird's house in an attempt to go through his phone and was chased out by Baird.

He spoke about his time working with a NSW Police youth command in 2021, including allegations of homophobia and bullying.

Come November 2023, he testified he was hanging out with Baird "four to five" times a week and Baird cut him a key to his Paddington share house.

That same month, their relationship imploded over an Instagram Story Lamarre-Condon posted to bait a man he believed was also dating Baird.

He says he poured water into Baird's petrol tank in a "tit-for-tat" for scratches on his Tesla, and claims he "tried to avoid" the suburb Baird lived in.

We also heard the context for a "help me hide a body" comment Lamarre-Condon made to a friend, which he says was made while helping her recite lines while acting.

The accused discussed his mental health and suicide ideation in that period.

World.title: ‘Insult to my culture’: Italian chef sacked after refusing to put pineapple on pizza
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceUnfair dismissal ‘Insult to my culture’: Italian chef sacked after refusing to put pineapple on pizza Millie Muroi November 6, 2026 — 11:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. An Italian chef who refused to put pineapple on pizza because it was “an insult to his culture” has failed to regain his job after waiting too long to file an unfair dismissal application with the country’s fair work umpire. Davide Tamburella, who was a resident on a visa, began working as a chef at a now-closed restaurant in Queensland’s Fortitude Valley called La Costa in January 2023. Pineapple is a divisive ingredient on pizzas. iStock According to the Fair Work Commission, in April 2026 Tamburella was injured in the workplace when he struck a metal handrail, fracturing the fourth and fifth metacarpals of his right hand. The reasons given by his employer for Tamburella’s dismissal included that incident but also use of inappropriate language and escalation of the situation during service, failure to manage the situation in accordance with previously discussed expectations and processes, and a recent incident where he acknowledged refusing to follow a management direction relating to a customer request.



In May, Tamburella was called into a meeting to address performance concerns. Related Article Opinion

On Background Is this even legal? Ten’s staff scratching their heads over ‘buyout’ offer Calum Jaspan Media Writer During this meeting his employer raised the issue of Tamburella refusing to put pineapple on pizza for a function. Tamburella said he refused the request because “as an Italian … putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to [his] culture”, and that the direction from his boss did not need to be followed when it was offensive to his culture. Tamburella acknowledged it was the third time in four years that he refused this direction, and that he requested his employer check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza.



The employer also said there had been previous discussions and concerns regarding Tamburella’s “communication style, interactions with staff and conduct during service”, prior conduct concerns involving escalation of frustration in the workplace, and ongoing concerns regarding “leadership behaviour, professionalism, emotional regulation during service and compliance with workplace direction”. Tamburella was sacked on May 20 and needed to submit his unfair dismissal application within 21 days of being dismissed. However, he ended up filing his application 28 days late. Tamburella said he refused the request because ‘as an Italian … putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to [his] culture’. Immediately after his dismissal, Tamburella contacted the migration lawyer who had been advising him. He said the lawyer advised him “not to wake the sleeping dog” and to wait, focus on his recovery, and not to take action against the employer yet because doing so could cause them to withdraw the subclass 186 nomination needed to maintain his visa. By early July, Tamburella claimed, his injuries allowed him to attempt to use a computer.



Tamburella included a letter from his doctor in the application indicating ongoing symptoms from the workplace injury, and that the need for continued medical attention may have contributed to delay in seeking advice from the commission within the usual time frame. He also included a letter from a registered counsellor showing he reported feeling stress, heightened anxiety and disturbed sleep following the injury. Tamburella said he was under substantial stress about his employment, visa status and livelihood, and was having difficulty with his focus, finding it difficult to read, retain and organise information. He also said he was waiting for documents and that he wanted to make sure he had all materials included before submitting his application. “I decided to wait a little bit longer just to collect all the data that I needed because otherwise I would be presenting something that would be already late and plus not completed,” he told the commission.



However, Hunt said it was “very important” to get an application in on time, and that applicants can always ask for leave for adding material. Related Article Opinion

US midterms We’ve seen peak Trump, but the next two years will be a rocky ride Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Tamburella also said he was waiting for a possible subclass 186 visa nomination to be granted before taking action. While the commission can provide an extension depending on the reason for the delay and the merits of the application, commissioner Jennifer Hunt ruled there were no “exceptional circumstances” to warrant an extension of time for the application, therefore dismissing the case. “While I accept that Mr Tamburella was suffering some pain, brain fog and was taking strong prescribed drugs following his dismissal on 20 May 2026, he had capacity to engage with his first and then second migration lawyer, use his mobile phone, provide instructions to his fiancee and also enjoy two weekends away to relax,” she said.



“It cannot be said that Mr Tamburella was without capacity to bring his application within time. Only when he was advised that the nomination had to be withdrawn because Home Affairs was aware that he was no longer employed did Mr Tamburella consider that it would be prudent to bring an application. [He] was, in essence, hedging his bets.” While Tamburella argued that the termination was at least in part motivated by him suffering a workplace injury in April and making a claim, his employer said there had been a documented disciplinary process arising from workplace conduct concerns that predated the injury. “I do not consider the circumstances of this case to be out of the ordinary course, unusual, special or uncommon,” the commission said, noting the reasons provided for dismissal appeared to be strong. “Mr Tamburella’s frustration within the workplace and the way that he behaved on numerous occasions would lead me to conclude that his prospects of success [in this case] are not great.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Alleged double murderer, former NSW Police officer returns to witness box, asked about relationship with Jesse Baird
World.content:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s criminal trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

Beau Lamarre-Condon (top left), and former Ten presenter Jesse Baird, 26, and Qantas flight attendant Luke Davies, 29.

The former NSW police officer has also pleaded not guilty to an aggravated charge of breaking into Baird’s home six months earlier on August 17, 2023, and stealing his mobile phone and wallet.

Lamarre-Condon started giving evidence on Thursday and returns to the witness box today. He denied breaking into Baird’s home and said he used a key the TV presenter left for him in the letterbox, but admitted he put a bobby pin in the front door lock.

He said he wanted to take Baird’s phone outside while he was sleeping to check if he was in a relationship with another man, and “if he was to wake up and come outside, he would see the bobby pin [and] not be under the impression that it was me going through his phone”.

He has yet to give evidence about the day Baird and Davies died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued Glock pistol.

The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon developed an obsessive and jealous infatuation with Baird that escalated when Baird ended their casual romantic relationship in November 2023.

The defence case is that the accused went to Baird’s home disguised as an Uber Eats delivery rider to collect some of his belongings and that his gun went off twice during a struggle with Baird, wounding him fatally, and that Davies shot himself during a second struggle.

There is no dispute that he cleaned Baird’s share house and disposed of the men’s bodies.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Buyers left waiting after ‘serious defects’ uncovered in Sydney development
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life Buyers left waiting after ‘serious defects’ uncovered in Sydney development David Barwell November 6, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A multimillion-dollar Surry Hills apartment development has come under scrutiny from the state’s building watchdog after inspectors uncovered 13 serious defects at the site including structural cracking, critical fire safety failures and extensive waterproofing problems. The Building Commission NSW has issued rectification and prohibition orders covering the six-storey development under construction at 23-47 Flinders Street, known as The Rathbone, preventing future buyers from moving into the building until extensive repairs are carried out. The defects were identified during an inspection by regulators of the six-storey development. Wolter Peeters The intervention follows a visit by building inspectors on August 18, which identified significant concerns about the safety, structural integrity and long-term durability of the building being marketed to prospective buyers as a “luxury” and “boutique” development. Among the most serious findings were extensive defects in structural elements of the basement, including “excessive cracking” in reinforced concrete walls, exposed steel reinforcement and concrete spalling on structural beams.



The regulator warned the defects could accelerate corrosion, reduce the building’s lifespan and potentially “compromising its structural integrity”. Waterproofing failures were another area of concern, with inspectors identifying water penetrating through walls, windows and sections of the roof along with incomplete shower waterproofing works and membranes showing signs of peeling. The development is located on the site of a former petrol station in Surry Hills. Wolter Peeters NSW Building Commissioner James Sherrard said the combined defects had the potential to create unhealthy or dangerous living standards for future residents. “The penetration of water has led to water ingress and caused unhealthy or dangerous conditions, loss of amenity [and] undue dampness or deterioration of building elements,” he wrote in his orders.



Fire safety deficiencies added to concerns with inspectors identifying improperly installed fire hose reels and unprotected service penetrations through fire-rated walls that did not meet testing standards. In his statement of reasons, Sherrard warned the combined defects presented an unacceptable risk to future occupants, with the potential to cause progressive building deterioration and safety hazards if left unaddressed. The commission has given the developer Murfield Pty Ltd, which is owned by Avid Property Group, 240 days to complete the remediation works. Technical reports and rectification designs must also be submitted by January 31. An Avid Property Group spokeswoman said in a statement its current builder, Buildcorp, had been engaged to finish the development and rectify defects left by a previous contractor.



“The defects relate to unfinished work by a previous builder [and] Buildcorp are now engaged to rectify all existing defects and complete the project,” she said. Related Article City life This Sydney building was meant to be a ‘kids’ wonderland’. It sat abandoned for almost 20 years “We are preparing a program to satisfy all requirements and reach practical completion as soon as possible. We will continue to provide monthly updates to our current purchasers and look forward to welcoming them into their new homes.” Planning records show the $24.1 million development, located on the site of a former petrol station, was approved by the City of Sydney in 2018. The orders come amid heightened scrutiny of construction standards across NSW, with the Building Commission conducting a record 1015 inspections of development sites during the 2024-25 financial year and issuing 455 rectification orders.



NSW Building Minister Anoulack Chanthivong told a budget estimates hearing earlier this year that construction quality in the sector had improved following regulatory reforms, including expanded powers to cancel licences of tradespeople found guilty of misconduct. Related Series

Shoddy Sydney Shoddy Sydney “The quality has improved, but there’s more room for improvement,” he said. “Our compliance blitz is all about making sure that building compliance is actually done and done at high quality, but also working with the industry so that we have fewer defects.” The prohibition order on The Rathbone will remain in force until formally revoked by the Building Commission. World.title: ‘All I want to do is put the red jersey on’: Eli Katoa’s road to recovery
World.content:
Exclusive SportNRLRugby League World Cup ‘All I want to do is put the red jersey on’: Eli Katoa’s road to recovery Roy Masters November 6, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“Today is the one-year mark,” Eli Katoa reminds me of that shameful day in the history of international rugby league. Katoa was representing Tonga in a Pacific Championship match last November against New Zealand when the code failed him in its duty of care because he was twice ruled fit to take the field following head knocks, including one in the warm-up. Eli Katoa, in camp with the Tongan team. Steven Siewert After a third blow to the head, the Melbourne Storm back-rower failed a head impact assessment and was removed from the field. He then suffered a seizure while on the sideline and was rushed to an Auckland hospital, where he had emergency surgery to remove fluid from the brain. He has not played since.



Yet, the night before we speak, Katoa was back with his Tongan teammates, celebrating their 20-18 win over Samoa in an absorbing World Cup clash before a joyful CommBank Stadium crowd. Wearing a trainer’s shirt, he wrapped his arms around his fellow Tongan warriors. Katoa will be on the sideline again on Saturday night in Newcastle, when Tonga play New Zealand in the semi-final. Haumole Olakau’atu perform a Sipi Tau with teammates. Katoa will act as a trainer for his Tongan mates on Saturday night in their World Cup semi-final. Getty Images However, his presence is really an absence, because he reminds us of what we have missed in the 12 months since he was stood down from playing on medical grounds. His captain at club level, Harry Grant, speaks warmly of Katoa, the NRL’s second-rower of the year in 2024 and 2025.



“My admiration for him is immense. It has shone brighter through his uncertainty the past 12 months,” Grant said. “The frustration of not being able to share the field with him, or have answers, has been hard for me. I can only imagine how Eli and his loved ones feel. Your true character comes out in adversity and he’s a glowing refection of that.” Eli Katoa is awaiting medical clearance to get back on the field after his career-threatening episode last year. Getty Images In medieval England, Katoa would have been a nobleman. Polynesian culture says he possesses mana, or moral authority. He has ennobled and embarrassed his code at the same time. While three of Tonga’s medical staff were suspended for two years following an NRL investigation of Katoa’s triple head knocks, I question him as to why some of his teammates did not intercede, particularly when he lay limp on the ground following a collision with fullback Lehi Hopoate during a pre-game drill.



“People, particularly in the media, want me to blame someone,” he says after a short pause. “All I want to do is play.” Katoa concedes he can seek legal remedy for negligence in the future. Eli Katoa at his damaging best playing for the Storm against the Roosters in 2025. He just wants to get back on the field. NRL Images “I’m passionate to play for my club, my family, my tiny little Kingdom of Tonga and just the love of playing. At the moment, I must forget about that (legal) pathway and just come back and play.”



The 26-year-old will have scans in Melbourne after the World Cup to determine if he can return. “I’m heading in the right direction,” he said. “My last appointment was with the NFL’s top specialist when the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco team came out to play a match at the MCG. The doctor [a neurologist] said that if I was his son, he’d let me go out and play now.” “The doctor (a neurologist) said that if I was his son, he’d let me go out and play now.” Eli Katoa Katoa concedes the scans will always show scarring on the surface of the brain. “A scan at the six-month mark showed a little area of the past bleeding and at the 12-month mark I hope it will show improvement. But some mark will still be there in 20 years time and it doesn’t mean I can’t do what I want to do.”



At the Storm’s Geelong pre-season camp in late January, less than three months after that fit on the sideline in Auckland, where he was also given oxygen, he appeared ready to play. Related Article Rugby League World Cup ‘It touched the boys’ hearts’: Eli Katoa’s emotional return to Tonga squad He led his group in the club’s traditional quizzing of a past player and was the outstanding performer in the non-contact conditioning drills. I recall watching him with a confused mix of admiration, anger and aching sadness. It’s not as if Katoa needs to be saved from himself, particularly with controversy over CTE. He had a bedside view of another player to experience cerebral bleeding and subsequently retire. His best friend and Storm teammate, Tui Kamikamica, suffered a stroke and Katoa sat by his hospital bed for days.



“Eli called me at 6am to inform me of Tui’s stroke,” Storm football manager Frank Ponissi says. “When Craig [Bellamy] had his neurological problem, he was the first to comfort him. For the first time in 12 years, the annual Michael Moore Medal [awarded to the Storm’s club person of the year] didn’t go to a vote and was awarded unanimously to Eli.” Eli Katoa feels immense pride representing Tonga, like he did in 2025 at the Four Nations Championships. NRL Images Asked the difference between playing for the Storm and Tonga, Katoa says: “It’s the red jumper. I put it on and it reminds me of my country and all the people at home. It’s more about my family. Both my parents are Tongan. Dad passed away in 2011 when I was finishing primary school. Mum is still there and has been to Melbourne twice. I became engaged to my fiancée [Tuitofa Aloua] in September.” The feeling of pride to represent the Pacific kingdom transcends everything. His role as a blue shirt trainer for his country this Saturday involves relaying messages for the team – including tips designed to exploit his Storm teammate, New Zealand halfback, Jahrome Hughes.



“Everything is for the Tongan boys,” Katoa says. “Players will do anything to get the red jersey. I was just so happy with the boys when we beat Samoa. All I want to do is put the red jersey on and represent Tonga and know my family and my little country is behind me. Nothing compares.” News, results and expert analysis from the week in sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Bachar Houli had an offer for an AFL-bound Muslim star. It soon turned costly
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Bachar Houli had an offer for an AFL-bound Muslim star. It soon turned costly Marc McGowan November 6, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The challenge was set. Richmond’s triple premiership-winning hero and Muslim community leader Bachar Houli dangled a carrot in front of his protege Khaled El Souki: he would take the AFL draft hopeful to Dubai if he ran a two-kilometre trial in 6:45 or quicker. Khaled El Souki is a potential first-round prospect in this month’s AFL draft. AFL Photos It was Houli’s way of motivating one of his star pupils at the Bachar Houli Foundation, which includes an elite performance academy, ahead of his AFL draft season. The former Tiger started the foundation in 2012 aiming to engage and empower young Muslims through football and ideally turn them into role models.



“I’m really proud [to be a Muslim]. We’re not embarrassed of anything any more, so Bach has done a lot for the community,” El Souki told this masthead. Related Article AFL 2025 ‘Our faith helps us with our footy’: The mates dreaming of joining rare company in the AFL “Not me necessarily, but there were people embarrassed to be Muslims. Bach has been huge for all of us. He’s introduced Islam to the non-Muslims, and introduced praying to the whole AFL. “Even just our personal relationship; Bachar’s done so much for me. He’s always checking in, and checking up on me, making sure I’m doing the right things.” El Souki started seeing a nutritionist and running daily. He went on to run 6:44 exactly, and off he went to Dubai in December last year with Houli, ex-Saint Ahmed Saad and other foundation members.



In less than a fortnight’s time, the Western Bulldogs next-generation academy prospect will become the ninth Muslim to have been on an AFL list, following Sedat Sir, Adem Yze, Houli, Ahmed Saad, Adam Saad, Saad El-Hawli, Adam Sweid and Hussien El Achkar. Like those before him, the quietly spoken El Souki prays five times a day – the first before sunrise – and is devoted to his religion. About 50 family and friends were in the stands to watch the 18-year-old forward boot three goals on his VFL debut for the Bulldogs in August. Kicking goals is nothing new for El Souki, who led the goalkicking in the under-18 Talent League this year after Western Jets coach Christian Stagliano sent him into attack permanently before the 2025 season.



“It was great having the crowd behind me,” he said. “I had a lot of people from my local club, Newport, and the Muslim community as well. They just love showing me their support, and I’m so grateful for it.” However, El Souki’s draft situation is far different to fellow academy or father-son-eligible peers, such as Dougie Cochrane (Port Adelaide), Cody Walker (Carlton) and Ethan Matthews (GWS), who know where they will end up. Khaled El Souki (centre) with Bachar Houli (right) and Ahmed Saad (left) on their trip to Dubai. Photo: Bachar Houli Foundation The Dogs emptied the cupboard to trade for ex-Power star Zak Butters, meaning they are highly unlikely to be in a position to match a bid on El Souki – potentially as early as pick 20 – unless they can use future assets to tempt another club. Bulldogs list boss Michael Regan admitted as much at the end of the trade period, but left the door ajar without offering a guarantee.



“There’s probably a feeling as well to, ‘How are they going to get Khaled done?’,” Regan said. “With the future hand that we have; we’re able to read, react and understand what’s happening on draft night, and even in the upcoming pick-swap period, where we might be able to position ourselves to match Khaled.” Houli has been a huge source of inspiration for El Souki. Photo: Bachar Houli Foundation El Souki is largely unbothered whether he lands at the Bulldogs or another club. He just wants to join exclusive Muslim company in becoming an AFL player, wherever that is. “I try to ignore it [how the Butters deal will impact him], but it’s quite out there, so I see a bit of it,” he said.



“Making the AFL has been a dream for me since I was young, so it’s been a big year or two for me and my family. Related Article AFL 2026 Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft “I’m trying to make the community and my family proud, so hopefully, I can get drafted. Being the eighth or ninth Muslim on an AFL list [would be special], so I’m pretty excited.” El Souki missed all bar one match at this year’s AFL under-18 championships while recovering from an ankle fracture, but he demonstrated with several bone-crunching tackles that he will bring far more than just goalkicking prowess. “I like to play with aggression, so they know I’m not weak. I’m willing to put my body on the line,” he said.



“I’m prepared to do whatever it takes to be playing in the AFL. I feel like I just started getting more professional … watch out for Khaled.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Six books are vying for the Booker Prize. One stands above the rest
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Marlon James is the favourite. It’s obvious why. His novel The Disappearers, about eight men who are viciously attacked by gay-bashers in 1988 Jamaica and what happens to the survivors in the years that follow, is big, furious, vastly ambitious, aggressively literate and filthy. It is a cage-fighter of a book that has busted its shackles and come out roaring. And it is roaring poetry. James has won the Booker before: A Brief History of Seven Killings took the prize in 2015. That book was dazzling; this is better, partly because some of those razzle-dazzle elements – the sprawling cast of characters, the extravagant use of patois, the sweeping timescale – are more controlled here. James clearly still revels in yomping up the byways of Jamaican dialect, but he is more focused on being understood. What remains undiluted is the violence waiting to erupt around every Kingston corner. These men live hard lives. Jordan is beaten by his father daily until he leaves home; he finds living in his car, servicing rich older queers with nasty tastes in sex, is easier. Marlon James’ The Disappearers is the favourite for this year’s Booker Prize. NYT Mat survives the beatings only to invite his fellow oppressed to punish him further in the backroom of a gay club. Total strangers to pity in their own lives, they don’t hold back; we can hear his screams. This year’s Booker judges are led by Mary Beard: academic, television’s favourite classicist and all-round English eccentric. Also on the panel is another recognised national treasure, Jarvis Cocker. What those meetings must have been like, with these two duking it out; fellow judge Patricia Lockwood told the BBC that they all “wrestled like pigs in mud” to establish the six finalists. You can feel that pull of extremes in their choices, even if they do end up pulling in a common direction.



That direction points to a world – or six worlds, since they are startlingly distinct – where men are gone mad. In Elizabeth Strout’s relatively genteel The Things We Never Say, the fictional orbit feels familiar enough; we’re in picket-fence Massachusetts, where people sail their boats on weekends and the same couple always hosts the annual Christmas party. What lies beneath, however, is inchoate misery. Take middle-aged schoolteacher Artie Dam, who wants to kill himself. Why? He is comfortably married; he loves teaching; he has a successful son and a circle of friends sufficiently like him to rub along. And yet that voice nags: my god, how did I get here? Strout can be a maddeningly folksy and mannered writer, but her voice here is direct and penetrating. Artie may not understand what is happening to him, but he does know that something is very wrong in America. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say is a familiar, genteel novel. Getty Images Reading this is to realise how rarely fiction addresses the pressure of the public sphere on private life; the book also interrogates privacy itself. For Artie, keeping a respectable distance has left him with a terrible sense of isolation; he feels he doesn’t really know anybody. His story is a small one – just one man’s life, engraved on a grain of rice – but it goes to the heart of a generation’s disappointments. M. John Harrison sets The End of Everything in the coastal towns of Kent, made rather less recognisable than Strout’s New England by a mysterious cataclysm that has left society in tatters and the air swarming with mostly invisible alien beings. Aliens are rare beasts on the Booker list, for sure, but this is sci-fi of a rare order: linguistically acrobatic, expansively imaginative and shiveringly persuasive. Philip Tennant, like many others, lives by scavenging flotsam on the beach. Harrison relinquishes few details of what has happened, who or what these aliens are or why they are in Kent. He doesn’t even enumerate how everyday life has disintegrated, but it is clear that none of the old rules or moral absolutes mean anything now.



When Philip finds a corporeal, sentient alien on the beach – initially referred to as “the artefact” – his first thought is to sell it. This is a remarkable book, where strangeness is unexplained but simply hangs in the air, conveyed in metaphors couched in plain language but surprising enough to make you gasp. M. John Harrison sets The End of Everything is a rare beast on the Booker list. Getty Images In May We Feed the King, a first novel by poet Rebecca Perry, the world gone mad is medieval while the man gone mad is the eponymous king, made so miserable by his own authority that he refuses to eat. Only when his cousin’s wife visits unexpectedly and takes up residence in the palace, where he and the queen live in an amiable mariage blanc, does he begin to recover. Inevitably, the three of them become the targets of spies, gossip and plots, not least because they seem to be hatching a plot of their own. Perry bookends her record of royal riddles and recipes with the present-day story of a designer commissioned to recreate the rooms where the king once lived. The ancient rooms are dressed with plastic replicas of foods he may have eaten, damask cloths and plumes in inkwells: precious details, described in commensurately exquisite prose. Compelling but elaborately impersonal, it does not so much sympathise with its characters in either era as turn us all into observers, weighing history’s possibilities. Perhaps the maddest of these novels is Luke Kennard’s sardonic campus spree Black Bag, not least because it is told in a high comic tone coloured with hints of hysteria. Rebecca Perry’s May We Feed the King is a compelling novel. Getty Images



The unnamed hero is a desperately under-employed actor who gets a gig sitting in on a university class while enveloped in a black bag. Ostensibly, this experiment – which was conducted for real at Oregon University in 1967 – is about the students’ reactions to their silent classmate, but Kennard’s focus is on the actor, hiding in his bag from the world and sometimes bonding with people who, for whatever reason, prefer a silent black space to a man. What does that mean, to be a man? It’s the question he asks himself as he considers his failed career, miserable income and strange affair with a female professor who says she fancies having sex with an absence. Luke Kennard’s Black Bag is a sardonic campus spree. Sometimes he addresses us directly, like a stand-up; sometimes he relates dialogue that reads as banter. When he discovers that there is a bag-wearing masculinist cult out there, this pace steps up to become a tornado, picking up everything in its path. “I had an epiphany,” his friend Claudio tells him as Kennard slaloms to the finish line. “Men are mostly frightened and crazy and very easily misled. They just want someone to be nice to them, but they don’t know how to ask for that.” A clunkingly obvious conclusion, maybe, but the carnival ride getting there is highly entertaining. Which brings us to the book considered the only real rival to The Disappearers, Douglas Stuart’s John of John. Like Marlon James, Stuart has won the Booker before; his fictionalised account of a childhood spent with a drunken mother in Glasgow, Shuggie Bain, won in 2020. John of John is set in a remote community on the isle of Harris, where villagers speak in Gaelic, down tools on the Sabbath and expect to shoulder a hard life without complaint.



Stuart transports the reader into this life with such conviction that we can smell the peat smoke and feel the constant rain on our faces; the island is less a setting than a way of being that claims us, body and soul, as we read. After several years of study, John-Calum is back home at the croft with his gruff father John and maternal grandmother Ella; his mother moved away with another man. The shame and blame around that rupture remain almost unendurable; the consequences were anyone to know that John-Calum is gay are too hellish to contemplate. Douglas Stuart is in the running for a second Booker Prize after winning for Shuggie Bain in 2020. AP Photo/Andy Kropa What John-Calum does not know, as he finds himself increasingly drawn to an older neighbour, Doll, is that his father has unspeakable secrets of his own. It’s a meticulously constructed drama, but its resolution is uncertain; it wasn’t a surprise to learn that Stuart, unhappy with an earlier version, rewrote the second half. It still takes turns that seem very unlikely, undermining the marvellously muddy, salty realism of its beginning. Of course, it is still an absorbing read, but it’s not going to trump The Disappearers. Neither should any of the other books; good as they all are, nothing has its bravura scope or sheer vitality. Another cigar, please, for Marlon James. The Booker Prize will be announced at 8.45am on Tuesday, November 10 (AEST).

World.title: Socceroos squad announcement delayed as players ‘overwhelmingly’ oppose Jordan trip
World.content:
Breaking SportSoccerAustralian soccer Socceroos squad announcement delayed as players ‘overwhelmingly’ oppose Jordan trip Vince Rugari November 6, 2026 — 11:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The planned release of Tony Popovic’s Socceroos squad for this month’s friendlies has been delayed amid mounting pressure on Football Australia to relocate their match against Jordan, with players strongly opposed to travelling to the country over security fears. Professional Footballers Australia has called for the November 17 match in Amman to be moved to another venue or date, after Indonesia withdrew from its own scheduled friendly in the Jordanian capital, citing concerns for player safety. Loading The developments come amid heightened regional tensions and renewed violence within Jordan, where a security officer was stabbed to death in a suspected terrorist attack in Amman on Thursday, less than two weeks after nine people were killed when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in the country’s south. Football Australia was on Friday due to unveil Popovic’s squad for two games against Qatar and Jordan. They were originally booked as warm-up fixtures ahead of the AFC Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia, which was set to take place in January but has been postponed until December 2027.



The squad announcement will occur over the weekend, an FA spokesperson confirmed to this masthead - but the chances of the window unfolding as scheduled appear to be increasingly unlikely. View post on X While the Jordan Football Association said in a statement that their match against the Socceroos is “still scheduled to take place, without any changes”, the PFA says Australia’s players are reluctant to travel to the country, which borders Israel, Palestine and Saudi Arabia. Those players are comfortable playing in Qatar next Saturday (1.45am AEDT) - one of only two Middle Eastern nations, along with the United Arab Emirates, in which the Australian government’s travel advice is at level two, which means to exercise a high degree of caution. Jordan, by contrast, is at level three, with Australians advised to reconsider their need to travel there.



Football Australia’s executive director of football, Heather Garriock, told this masthead on Wednesday that players who did not want to participate in the matches could remove themselves from selection without consequence. Socceroos players pose before the World Cup match against Egypt. Alex Slitz But according to sources familiar with the situation, not authorised to comment, it remains unclear if players would be able to be selected if they were willing to play in Qatar only, or if all players in the squad due to be revealed over the weekend would need to be open to playing in both. “The PFA has worked with Football Australia over recent weeks in relation to security concerns regarding the upcoming assembly and engaged its own independent security experts,” said PFA chief executive Beau Busch in a statement to this masthead. “With the full support of the PFA, the players have overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated.



Related Article Asian Cup Socceroos set Christmas deadline for Popovic decision as rival coaches circle “We are committed to working with FA to reach a sensible solution.” Qatar and Jordan were finalists from the last Asian Cup, and were viewed as ideal opponents for the Socceroos in their preparation for the next edition of the tournament. The postponement has not only thrown those plans into disarray, but raised questions over the future of Popovic, who signed a short-term contract extension earlier this year which officially ends in March. To remain in the job for the 2027 Asian Cup’s new dates - which take place over the Christmas and New Year’s period to avoid Ramadan, which begins on January 28, 2028 - Popovic and Football Australia will need to agree terms on a new contract, whether it be another 12-month term or encompassing the full World Cup cycle through to 2030.



Garriock has set a Christmas deadline to sort out Popovic’s future, warning that other coaches were “knocking on the door” - including, sources say, Kevin Muscat, who shapes as their primary target if Popovic decides to step away from the Socceroos. Muscat’s contract with Chinese Super League club Shanghai Port expires at the end of the year, and the former Melbourne Victory and Yokohama F. Marinos title-winning coach has long held ambitions of steering the national team, who he represented on 46 occasions.

World.content:

A teacher at a Catholic college on Sydney’s upper north shore has been sacked after “deeply distressing” allegations of producing and possessing child abuse material. Richard Kenneth Harman’s employment at St Leo’s Catholic College Wahroonga was terminated on Thursday, Catholic Schools Broken Bay said in a statement. St Leo’s Catholic College says Harman is no longer employed at the Wahroonga school. Edwina Pickles Harman, 61, appeared in court on Thursday afternoon charged with five counts of intentionally recording intimate image without consent, producing child abuse material and possessing child abuse material. He was arrested on Tuesday after reports of child abuse material on electronic devices at a Hornsby home brought detectives to the address about noon.



One USB drive was allegedly found containing covertly filmed footage of females in public and in a school environment, police said in a statement. Harman was taken to hospital for assessment while police continued searching the home, seizing devices for further examination. Detectives allegedly found several recordings captured on the grounds of the Wahroonga school where he worked. ‘Staff, parents and students have been briefed and offered support.’ Catholic Schools Broken Bay Catholic Schools Broken Bay said after they learned of the arrest “for alleged serious, criminal, non-contact offences which allegedly occurred in 2024” his employment was terminated in line with its protocols. “This is deeply distressing news, and our main priority remains the safety and wellbeing of our students.



“Staff, parents and students have been briefed and offered support,” the statement said. After Harman was discharged from hospital on Thursday afternoon he was charged with five counts of intentionally recording intimate image without consent, producing child abuse material and possessing child abuse material. Harman did not apply for bail and it was formally refused at Hornsby Local Court, where he is due to appear again on November 18. St Leo’s describes itself as the only co-educational Catholic secondary school on Sydney’s upper north shore, located on six hectares in “the leafy suburb of Wahroonga”.



The school made headlines in March after advising families it was conducting a trial of increased supervision over toilets, including using CCTV to monitor students going in and out, and alerting parents when their children went to the toilet during class time. The move followed incidents of vandalism and “poor decision-making” in the freshly renovated toilets, the school advised parents in a newsletter. Alerts to parents about their children using the toilet during class time were not intended to “police normal behaviour” but to encourage students to use the toilet during recess and lunch breaks or between classes. Harman’s alleged offending predated that trial, the school said. Harman began teaching at the school in 2024 according to a profile on LinkedIn. It lists previous experience at the American School of The Hague in the Netherlands, and a decade-long stint at Barker College.



The profile also lists close to two years working at Trinity Grammar School. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.
