World.title: Shares in cancer diagnostics company Pacific Edge rise after Medicare coverage of tests
World.content:
Shares in Dunedin-based cancer diagnostics company Pacific Edge have risen by 8 percent after it announced Friday morning that its cancer-marker urine tests had been granted Medicare coverage in the United States.

Its Triage and Triage Plus tests are reimbursed at between US$1057 and US$1328, and the company estimates there are about 1.14 million eligible testing opportunities a year.

That represents an addressable testing opportunity worth well over US$1 billion annually, although Pacific Edge would capture only a proportion of that market.

Pacific Edge's Cxbladder tests use a non-invasive urine sample to help doctors assess a patient's risk of bladder cancer and make better-informed decisions about whether a cystoscopy is needed.

Pacific Edge chief executive Peter Meintjes said the decision was a "significant milestone" for the company, patients and urologists.

"It provides clear guidance on the eligible haematuria patients for which Triage and Triage Plus should be reimbursed," he said.

Meintjes said the decision also gave Pacific Edge an important competitive advantage.

"The LCD confirms Pacific Edge as the market leader, with only Triage and Triage Plus tests covered under the policy."

The new coverage policy takes effect on 20 December, with competing tests and generic billing codes not covered.

That gives the company a potentially important advantage as it tries to increase the number of US urologists using its tests.

More than 5,000 US urologists have already ordered more than 130,000 Cxbladder tests, but the company says established Medicare coverage removes a reimbursement obstacle that had made some doctors reluctant to order them.

Medicare covers more than 71 million people in the US, although the company believes the decision could also help it secure greater coverage from commercial insurers, which collectively cover about 223 million people.

Pacific Edge says it is making selective investments in its US commercial team and digital technology as it prepares to take advantage of the expanded market opportunity.

World.title: Orana Wildlife Park needs another $2 million to plug funding gap
World.content:
Christchurch's Orana Wildlife Park warns it still needs at least $2 million by mid-2027 or the board could face "very hard decisions" about the zoo's future.

The park's leaders said they were grateful to Christchurch City Council for a recent $1.2m emergency grant but it was not enough to resolve the park's serious funding shortfall.

In September the park warned that its cash reserves were set to run out by March 2027.

Orana Wildlife Trust co-chair Ken Hughey said it was devastating for the park to be in financial trouble in its 50th year.

Orana Wildlife Trust Board co-chairperson Emeritus Professor Ken Hughey and Orana chief executive Rachel Haydon. RNZ / Adam Burns

"There is a perception that because council has approved this grant, we are now okay. We are not," he said.

Hughey said the board and staff had met Waimakariri and Selwyn district councils, as well as potential donors, businesses and MPs to seek support.

Significant donations or business partnerships could make a difference in closing the park's funding gap, he said.

RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"We still need just over $2m to meet the immediate funding gap while our recovery plan takes effect. Without that support, the board will have to make some very hard decisions about Orana's future," Hughey said.

The park said it had developed a financial sustainability and recovery plan aimed at increasing visitor income and securing more ongoing financial support.

Chief executive Rachel Haydon said work was continuing on the park's conservation programmes.

RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"Our kākāriki karaka breeding season is off to a promising start. We have five breeding pairs and all five females have either laid eggs or are showing interest in nesting, usually a sign that eggs are on the way," she said.

Haydon said the park's new meerkat, lemur, mini moo and giraffe encounters had been popular.

World.title: WA quick Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris hopes to be even faster after surgery
World.content:
It has been just over a year since Lance Morris had the surgery he hopes will save his cricket career.

For three years before going under the knife, the Western Australian fast bowler had struggled to string together games as he tried to manage a fracture in his spine.

"I was going under an MRI machine every six weeks and just checking up and it would occasionally get a bit worse after a bigger day," Morris said.

" Just having that in the back of your head, knowing that is there all the time and looming over you, that was really frustrating. "

Lance Morris regularly hit 150kph before surgery. He's confident he'll be back there again. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Morris was first called into Australia's Test squad in late 2022 after a stunning start to the Sheffield Shield season, and it appeared just a matter of time until he pulled on the baggy green.

Since then, he has played just three one-day internationals, six Shield matches and 22 Big Bash games, as injury repeatedly left him sidelined.

Ahead of the 2025-26 domestic season, Morris decided enough was enough and elected to undergo pars stabilisation surgery, which involved bolts and wire being put into his lower back.

Bancroft reaches acceptance over Test recall chances after 'dejection' Cameron Bancroft says he no longer gets worked up over being ignored at the selection table despite scoring mountains of Shield runs.

"I was playing a game, missing a game and really trying to pick and choose which games to take on without overdoing the load," Morris said.

"I was pulling up with back soreness as I was trying to get ready for a series and I didn't want to carry that into the season.

"We had tried to go, I guess, the natural way about healing the back and giving it a good three-months stints to recover, doing absolutely nothing and then starting again, but we just weren't really having any luck.

" It got to the point where it was a bit of a line in the sand moment where it's like, 'Alright, let's really address this and get some certainty around my back.' "

No speed limit

State teammate Cameron Green, Indian quick Jasprit Bumrah and England spearhead Jofra Archer are among others who have travelled to New Zealand to see specialist Rowan Schouten for the surgery in recent years.

Their returns to cricket have left Morris optimistic he will be as quick as he was before injuries started taking their toll.

Jofra Archer is one of several high-profile players to undergo pars stabilisation surgery and make a successful return to international cricket. (AAP Image/Joel Carrett)

"That [a loss of pace] was a huge question for me leading into the surgery because I knew that was the asset that made me potentially selectable for red-ball cricket," he said.

"I had to look around at other guys that have had the surgery, the likes of Jofra, Jasprit Bumrah, the guys that have returned to Test cricket at the same speed if not better.

"I've got one eye on the speed gun at all times to see where things are at, but I'm pretty happy with where it's at."

Australia has an enormous Test summer on the horizon, with a visit by New Zealand, a tour of India and the 150th Anniversary Test in March, before the Ashes in England in the winter.

Lance Morris looked on the cusp of a Test debut after touring with Australian side in 2023. ((AAP Image/Darren England))

If last summer is anything to go by, there will be opportunities for the country's fast bowlers across the 18 Tests through to the end of the Ashes.

Josh Hazlewood missed last summer's Ashes with hamstring and ankle issues, while Pat Cummins only played once in that series, leaving Mitchell Starc as the only first-choice bowler available.

Morris, who lost his Cricket Australia (CA) contract because of his surgery, has an eye on a Test return.

"There's a heap of Test cricket there and red-ball cricket has always been a pretty big priority for me," he said.

"Basically, targeting Shield games where we see fit and prioritising them is how I got around the Test squad in the first place and how I think I'll put my name back up for a potential selection.

"There was also some pretty pretty positive conversations [with CA] that I'm still a player of interest, and it's just a matter of getting back and bowling fast in front of the group."

World.title: Aussie Hijikata backs up Djokovic triumph with another big win in Paris
World.content:
Rinky Hijikata has backed up his statement win over Novak Djokovic with another impressive victory in Paris, downing Alex de Minaur's conqueror, Tomas Martin Etcheverry, to reach his first ATP Masters quarterfinal.

The 25-year-old Australian came from behind to beat the Argentine world number 31 2-6, 6-3, 7-5.

Besides making the last eight, where he will face local favourite Luca Van Assche, he has climbed into the world's top 60 for the first time in his career.

Rinky Hijikata defeats Novak Djokovic at Paris Masters Rinky Hijikata has pulled off a stunning upset over 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, eliminating him from the Paris Masters and ending his hopes of qualifying for the end-of-year ATP Finals.

Beginning the event in qualifying, ranked at number 83, Hijikata has beaten five higher-ranked players so far and will climb to number 48 if he does it again.

Many a tennis underdog has pulled off a shock win but, drained by the feat and the attention, they rarely back it up.

It seemed as if this would be the case with Hijikata in the French capital on Thursday, local time, when he lost the first set in 26 minutes. The Sydneysider lost the first eight points, and while he then held to love to get into the tie, he was broken again in his third service game.

Hijikata survived a break point in the 12-minute opening game of the second set, then broke in the fourth game. He maintained that advantage to win the set in 43 minutes and force a decider.

That went with serve until 5-5. Hijikata had to save three break points at 1-2, but his other four service matches had all been serenely held to love. However, he had not forced a break point of his own.

Now, at the key moment, he did, and he took it. That left Hijikata serving for the match. He opened with an ace.

Etcheverry levelled to 15-all, but Hijikata won the next three points to take the game, set and match, ending with an emphatic forehand smash across court.

Hijikata celebrated joyously, prompting television pundit Ryan Harrison, the American former top-40 player, to comment: "He is a guy who is typically mild-mannered; he's as fired up as I've ever seen him before."

Next up is 47-ranked Van Assche, who beat Lorenzo Musetti 7-5 3-6 6-4 in a seesaw epic that had the crowd gripped after watching two French defeats.

Hijikata has never played Van Assche and will also have to deal with a home support that helped Van Assche come back from two break points down at 3-4 in the third. He won 12 of the next 13 points to seal the match.

That came after Ben Shelton and Tommy Paul overcame home hopes to set up an all-American quarterfinal. Twelfth-seed Paul saw off Quentin Halys 7-6 (7-3) 6-4, but Shelton was pushed hard by Arthur Rinderknech. The third seed eventually won 3-6, 6-4, 7-6 (7-5).

Earlier, Carlos Alcaraz received a walkover into the quarterfinals after ‌Matteo Berrettini withdrew from their third-round clash with an arm ‌injury.

The match had been ‌scheduled to headline the evening session, but the Italian world number 43 pulled out after experiencing pain in his arm.

Second ‌seed Alcaraz advanced directly to ‌the last eight, where he will face Taylor Fritz, who inflicted another American defeat on the hosts when he beat Arthur Fils 6-3, 6-4.

In the other quarterfinal, Portuguese lucky loser Nuno Borges, who beat Ignacio Buse 6-0, 6-2, will play Casper Ruud or Jan-Lennard Struff.

AAP

World.title: LIV Golf to wind down after five years of rebel league
World.content:
LIV Golf, the breakaway rebel golf league spearheaded by Australian Greg Norman, will collapse after five years, with a bankruptcy court hearing it plans to wind down operations rather than launch a new version due to a lack of support.

LIV Golf, which launched in June 2022 by offering nine-figure signing bonuses to lure top names away from the PGA Tour, lost Saudi Arabian funding in April after spending more than $US5 billion ($7 billion).

LIV held four events in Australia, all in Adelaide, and was scheduled to host its fifth tournament in March at Kooyonga Golf Club.

LIV Golf has died on a flawed premise and a broken promise While Adelaide showed just how good LIV Golf could be, the flawed premise of the breakaway tournament always spelled trouble.

"The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan," lawyer Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said during a hearing in New Jersey. "Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximising wind-down in their business."

LIV filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 8 and thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $US300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable "LIV 2.0". But players like Jon Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton, and Louis Oosthuizen were not interested.

"BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf," BC Partners said in a statement.

"While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders."

Instead of planning for a new version for 2027, LIV is entering a liquidation phase.

Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV — said to be worth some $100 million — to get out of his contract. He is back on the European Tour, hoping there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban in place for players dating back to their last LIV appearance.

LIV Golf paid $US15.6 million to retain seven of its executives, including $US6.375 million to chief executive Scott O'Neil, in the months between the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia and LIV filing for bankruptcy. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided given that LIV is not going forward.

LIV suffered two big setbacks, both before and after filing for bankruptcy.

The Asian Tour, which received financial support from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew its alliance with the PGA Tour and the European Tour.

Then, European Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings last month said anyone signing up for LIV 2.0 need not apply for membership on the tour, which put European players at risk of having no part in the Ryder Cup.

But the biggest setback was in April, two weeks after the Masters and two months after the start of the Iran war. PIF changed its investment strategy and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season.

LIV was originally run by Greg Norman, who tried unsuccessfully to start a world tour in 1994 only to have it quashed by Arnold Palmer and the PGA Tour. Norman had Saudi money at his disposal and promoted LIV as "Golf, but louder" with blaring music, 54-hole shotgun starts and $US25 million in prize funds — individual and team — at each event.

But it had no broadcast deal the first year, meaning it had to cover production costs. It got the CW Network in 2023, and eventually got Fox Sports to sign on in 2025.

The year began with Brooks Koepka getting out of his LIV deal with one year remaining, and the PGA Tour created a path — with financial penalties — to return. Patrick Reed chose not to extend his deal and is now poised to return to the PGA Tour next year through his performance in Europe.

Rahm had said on Tuesday he would be willing to pay the same price as Koepka, though it was unlikely that same deal would be offered.

LIV 2.0 was pushing player equity and prize money that was more than half the $US20 million purses for individuals when it began in 2022. LIV's final event was in August in Indianapolis, won by Michael La Sasso. He failed to get through the second stage of European Tour Q-School last week.

AP

World.title: Superstar Cristiano Ronaldo retires from international football
World.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from international soccer following a fallout with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

Ronaldo, 41, has scored the most goals (146) and made the most appearances (234 matches) in Portugal's men's international soccer history.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come to hand back the No. 7 shirt of the national team that belongs to us all. I never felt it was exclusively mine," Ronaldo said in a video posted on Instagram.

Loading Instagram content

"But for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and taking it with me to stadiums all over the world. Today the time has come to hand it over to the future.

"It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made solely with the head; they are also made with the heart."

Ronaldo's announcement comes one day before Jesus names the roster for the Nations League matches against Denmark and Wales.

It also comes on the heels of the superstar forward serving a 30-day suspension for walking out on the national team.

In his explanation, Ronaldo admitted his decision to leave camp was not the best way to handle the situation. But he added that Jesus "broke his word" more than once.

Jesus told Portugal's Channel 11 that he asked Ronaldo to stay on with the team.

"We already had the chance to talk about this before the first squad announcement. I asked him to stay on with me," the coach said. "He will always be in the hearts of the Portuguese people, and in the national team.

"He will always be a point of reference for our national team, for our people, and for our history."

World.title: Wallaroos wunderkind eager to tackle 'world's leading' club comp in England
World.content:
Do not let Caitlyn Halse's nickname deceive you.

The Wallaroos fullback, who turned 20 in September, might be known as "The Kid" but she is wise beyond her years.

This was clear when Halse recently explained to ABC Sport how she was approaching an upcoming stint with Leicester Tigers in England's Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR) competition.

"I've still got a lot to learn around my game, in attack and defence," said Halse, who has played 18 Tests.

"I'm willing and eager to learn.

"I just want to go over there and soak up all the information I can and bring it back to Australia and use that to my advantage for the Wallaroos."

Caitlyn Halse (right) has played 18 Tests for the Wallaroos. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Halse has already achieved a great deal in her promising rugby career.

She became the youngest player in Wallaroos/Wallabies history to make a Test debut, managing the feat as a 17-year-old in 2024.

Her first Rugby World Cup appearance came the following year but as Halse points out, she is not the finished product.

She believes her game can reach another level in PWR, which is described by its organisers, with justification, as the "world's leading domestic women's rugby competition".

Nine clubs contest PWR across an 18-round season before two weeks of finals decide the champion.

Australia's domestic equivalent, Super Rugby Women's, has five teams (Waratahs, Reds, Brumbies, Force and Fijian Drua) playing four round-robin matches each ahead of a two-week finals series.

PWR attracts players from Australasia, Europe and North America, and features the entire world champion England squad, who are full-time.

England's governing body, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), recognises PWR's importance.

RFU announced in June it was committing 24 million pounds ($46.1 million) to PWR across 10 years, which is a further illustration of the wise investment it has made in women's rugby since first offering full-time contracts to players in 2019.

Wallaroos back-rower Tabua Tuinakauvadra will also play for Leicester. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

Rugby Australia (RA) is mindful of PWR's status as the world's best domestic competition, which is why it encourages Wallaroos players to seek opportunities with the English clubs.

Halse will be joined by Wallaroos teammates Tabua Tuinakauvadra and Ash Fernandez at Leicester, while uncapped Australian Grace Freeman is also on the Tigers' books.

Another Wallaroo, prop Bridie O'Gorman, will play for PWR's Gloucester Hartpury.

"Gaining experience in a competition like the PWR will be invaluable for the players' development as we build a Wallaroos program with the goal of competing on the final weekend at the Rugby World Cup in 2029," RA director of high performance Peter Horne said in June.

'A different type of rugby'

One of the Wallaroos' most consistent players in 2026, Kaitlan Leaney, knows firsthand the benefit of playing in PWR.

She spent time with the famous Harlequins club earlier in her career.

"I learned so much," Leaney told ABC Sport last month.

"I definitely think I wouldn't be the player I am or the person I am today without that experience.

"I went over there at the age of 22 and played three years over there.

Kaitlan Leaney had a stint playing for Harlequins in PWR. (Getty Images: Henry Browne)

"The way my game grew in terms of playing consistent games and so many games … you've got internationals all across the park in all the clubs.

"I think the standard and level you're playing at each week is really special."

Halse similarly wants to make the most of her PWR opportunity when the 2026/27 season kicks off in a fortnight's time.

"I'm just super excited to experience a different type of rugby," Halse said.

"They've got girls from Canada, USA and all over Europe.

"I'm just keen to go over there and learn something new and experience something different."

World.title: Nearly $2m to scrap Hobart stadium thermal power plant
World.content:
The Tasmanian government has paid about $2 million not to build a thermal power plant at Macquarie Point, the site of the planned Hobart stadium.

The government is in final negotiations with BESIX Watpac to build the 23,000-seat stadium at the 9.3-hectare site on Hobart's waterfront.

Waste and energy company Veolia had signed an agreement with the Macquarie Point Development Corporation (MPDC) to develop a District Energy Infrastructure Scheme (DEIS), including a thermal energy plant.

However, it will not go ahead, as the government looks for other options to power the site.

The government is considering connecting the stadium to the existing electricity network, but the cost of the connection is yet to be finalised. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The minister in charge of the precinct, Eric Abetz, has now written to Tasmanian Greens Deputy Leader Vica Bayley to reveal the cost of exiting that agreement.

"The final invoice received was $1,788,236.50 plus GST and was paid on June 24, 2026," Mr Abetz wrote.

Minister Abetz said connecting to the current network was "lower risk and cost" than continuing with the thermal energy plant concept.

He said the cost was not included in the stadium project budget of $1.13 billion.

Eric Abetz revealed the government paid almost $2 million to exit the agreement with Veolia. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"The DEIS predated any discussion on the development of a stadium on site and is not required for, or part of, that project," he wrote.

The cost is on top of $667,407 paid to a Melbourne-based firm, Renewable Intelligence, for earlier project work.

Mr Bayley said it was another example of "the slow-moving train wreck that is the Macquarie Point stadium".

"The fact that the government's so willing to just throw away millions of dollars of money, not to proceed with projects that they thought were important once upon a time — it just shows an absolute wilful disregard for our money, the taxpayers' money," Mr Bayley said.

Vica Bayley has criticised the government's spending on abandoned Macquarie Point projects. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Power connection yet to be costed

In his letter, Mr Abetz said Veolia's work would "inform the final power supply and mechanical design solution".

"To deliver power to the stadium, an electrical supply connection will be made from the North Hobart substation, using capacity in the existing network which I understand is more cost effective than proceeding with the DEIS thermal power plant," Mr Abetz wrote.

He said the cost of connecting the stadium was still being finalised, and was not included in the current cost estimates.

Hobart stadium power options uncosted, not finalised Major upgrades to Hobart's power grid to supply the Macquarie Point stadium are yet to be finalised or costed, with the final estimate for the precinct's energy demand increasing by almost 50 per cent in a year.

Mr Abetz told a budget estimates committee earlier this year the stadium would require 9.7 megavolt-amperes (MVA) of power.

However, documents obtained by the ABC show TasNetworks has told MPDC the precinct would require 15.7 MVA — more than the existing capacity within the Hobart network.

At the time, the network operator put forward three potential locations for a new substation, either at Macquarie Point or the nearby suburb of Glebe.

Millions paid to cast aside plans

Property developer Milieu was paid $1.257 million to abandon its plans for the Escarpment housing project, slated for Macquarie Point.

The Hobart Brewing Company was also paid $1.84 million to terminate its 10-year lease of The Goods Shed.

The proposed Macquarie Point stadium is expected to cost $1.13 billion, with the final price still uncertain. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Meanwhile, the ABC revealed last week that an unsuccessful bidder for the stadium construction tender would be reimbursed $2 million for its costs.

Failed stadium bidder to get millions reimbursed A failed bidder in the tender to build Hobart's stadium is set to have $2 million of its costs reimbursed by the Tasmanian government.

The figure was revised up from the original cap of $250,000.

While the stadium was priced most recently at $1.13 billion, it is widely expected to cost more due to worldwide inflation caused by the Middle East war.

When announcing BESIX Watpac as the preferred construction bidder last month, Premier Jeremy Rockliff refused to repeat his commitment to cap the state's contribution at $875 million.

He has committed to releasing the cost before a final contract is signed.

World.title: Raiders 'couldn't have offered any more' to want-away Hudson Young
World.content:
Ricky Stuart says the Canberra Raiders "bent over backwards" to keep Hudson Young at the club, as the star back-rower touched down in Port Moresby ahead of a potential move the the PNG Chiefs.

Canberra stunningly pulled their $4.4 million, four-year offer to the Blues star on Monday.

Young travelled to Papua New Guinea this week, with the 2028 expansion club having already offered the six-time Kangaroo international $900,000 per year.

That tax-free package would have meant he would take home far more in his pay packet than the Raiders' offer, but the NRL established Young's market value at $1.1 million, which has since been revised to $1 million.

ARLC chairman Peter V'landys told Nine Newspapers that players can seek to challenge their "official" market value and make their own submissions to the salary cap auditor.

"Let's say a player wanted to be with his family or there are other specific reasons," V'landys said.

"We just don't want the salary cap rorted. However, we know that at times there are exceptional circumstances, so we take those exceptional circumstances into account.

"We won't have a situation where people manipulate the salary cap.

"The unfortunate thing is with the tax-free status of PNG, we have to be extra cautious with the market value of the players there."

Hudson Young has played nine State of Origin matches for the Blues. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Raiders' $1.1 million per season offer was understood to be the biggest in the club's history, with Stuart saying the club could go no higher.

"We couldn't have offered Hudson any more," Stuart told 666 ABC Radio Canberra.

"I mean, we bent over backwards to try and keep Hudson and it would have been unfair on the club if we had went any further.

"We were at a stage where it was probably too much, yet we look after our players and we do everything we possibly can for them.

"But it gets to a stage where you've got to make a decision [and] my position and [Raiders CEO] Don Furner's position is we have to look after the club."

The 28-year-old made his NRL debut with the Raiders in 2019 and has played 155 NRL games for the Green Machine.

Stuart acknowledged that Young was well within his rights to seek out new opportunities, and that all the clubs agreed with the expansion to PNG and the challenges that would hold for the rest of the competition.

However, the veteran coach was under no illusions why Young was looking for pastures new.

Ricky Stuart says money was the driving factor moving forward. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

"Money," Stuart said.

"Absolutely it is [all about money].

"That doesn't bother me one bit. If Hudson wants to make that decision and take those tax-free dollars, you've got to understand he's got to live in Papua New Guinea."

It was put to Stuart that Young, who is currently recovering from an Achilles rupture that he suffered against South Sydney in July, may well look for a release from his contract for the 2027 season, with the Chiefs not coming in until 2028.

Stuart said any decision on that would be up to the player's management, but bemoaned the "messy" process that allowed players to sign a year in advance for a new club.

"Unfortunately … with our rules and the regulations, the guidelines we have with our ability for players to go off and sign at another club 12 months in advance, it makes it very messy," he said.

"I don't agree with that interpretation or the guidelines we've got in the competition. I think it makes it very messy and I feel very, very sorry for the fans, because you got some of your favourite players, players you want to watch, players you want to keep with your club in 12 months' time playing elsewhere.

"I think it's very unfair on the fans, but it is what it is."

Hudson Young has played for the Raiders since 2019. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

Stuart, despite acknowledging that players moving on was just business, said he did take it "personally" when players move on.

"I do take it personally, and I take it very personally about coaching this team, this club," Stuart said.

"I do find it difficult at times, but you got to lose the emotion and see the business side of it.

"I'm not disgruntled with the fact that Hudson's looking elsewhere, that's his choice and decision.

"But what my club's done is give him probably the highest offer that's ever been offered to a player at this club in its time. It was a very, very generous offer, probably too big of an offer. But we did it [and] now he's knocked it back.

"We've got to move forward. We've got to move on."

ABC/AAP

World.title: NAS weighs in more than 33kg heavier than Paul Gallen
World.content:
Nelson Asofa-Solomona has landed another low blow on Paul Gallen, claiming that even his premiership-winning former Cronulla teammates want the Sharks legend laid out on Friday night.

A day after the Big Nasty riled his rival by dragging Gallen's wife into the verbal sledging, Asofa-Solomona got even nastier as he lobbed explosive accusations about the Sharks' only grand final-winning captain.

"There's been so many people jumping in my DMs," Asofa-Solomona said on Thursday.

"People that have played with him, people that have played against him, people who have worked with them in the past. They were telling me all these stories about him and saying 'Yeah, bro, please do a job on him.'

"That was my plan all along anyway."

Nelson Asofa-Solomona says his plan is to knock Paul Gallen out. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

The Cronulla-Melbourne rivalry is one of the fiercest in the NRL, with the two sides featuring in a series of spiteful encounters either side the Sharks' stirring 2016 grand final triumph over the Storm.

Having already copped a drugs spray from Asofa-Solomona (3-0, 3KOs) in light of the Cronulla peptides saga, Gallen (16-2-1, 8KOs) will be livid after the ex-Storm star's latest verbal jabs.

Asofa-Solomona would not be drawn on specifics but said Gallen's former State of Origin teammates and "work colleagues" were among those who he claimed had reached out to him in the hope of doing over the 2014 series-winning Blues skipper.

"I can't say too much, but probably just stuff to do with money and bits and pieces," Asofa-Solomona said.

"But, look, he's grown up in a different era. He's a bit of a different cat, but the new era is here."

Asofa-Solomona's inflammatory allegations came after the two heavyweights featured in a spicy weigh-in at Sydney's TikTok Entertainment Centre.

The ex-New Zealand Test enforcer promised Gallen he would proudly take the mantle of NRL-boxing crossover king on Friday night.

"And if it's not a knockout, I don't want it," the 200cm, 137.56-kilogram behemoth said.

"That's the only result I'm here to get. I'm here for a highlight-reel finish."

Nelson Asofa-Solomona is much heavier than Paul Gallen. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

But the retiring Gallen, 45, is having none of it, despite weighing in at 104.18kg.

"I'm really proud I'm fighting a bloke now, 30-odd kilos heavier than me, 15 years younger than me and I'm still willing to compete — and I'll win this fight, at my age," he said.

"That's what I'm proud of, and this is a no-lose situation for me. I'm going to get paid a ton of money and go home happy and healthy and live the rest of my life with my family.

"That's my goal in life and that's what I'm here to do."

Tech.title: Salon is shutting down after 31 years
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Salon launched 31 years ago as one of the first online-only news magazine outlets, and it announced today in an unsigned post that it’s ceasing publication.

The company said that the “business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years,” and it decided that its publishing model is “no longer sustainable.” It didn’t go into detail about why, but many websites are grappling with “Google Zero” and the impact of AI tools. When reached for comment, Salon general manager Amanda Wolfe pointed The Verge to today’s announcement post.

“Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them,” Salon said in its post. “Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.”

On Bluesky, Salon chief content officer Erin Keane says that the editorial archive will “stay live for now.”

Current Salon owner Find.co acquired Salon in 2023 and describes itself as a “Performance Marketing Ecosystem transforming crypto marketing with performance and precision.”

Tech.title: The midterms proved once and for all that X is not real life
Tech.content:
A week before the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance hosted a town hall in Texas with Fox News host Jesse Watters. It was a friendly event with a friendly audience in what should have been a friendly state, and maybe that’s why Vance couldn’t help himself. When a college student earnestly asked how the right expected young people like her to settle down and have kids, given the ever-growing cost of living, Vance replied with a quip about Jon Husted’s ass.

The student, Kate White, introduced herself as the vice president of the Texas Christian University chapter of Turning Point USA, the conservative group started by Donald Trump ally Charlie Kirk. She was offering Vance an opportunity to explain how MAGA could work for young people, and he turned it into a joke. Vance did eventually answer the question, saying Republicans don’t pay enough attention to the issue of affordability and blaming rising housing costs on institutional investors and the “20 million illegal aliens” supposedly living in the United States. But the order of operations revealed the fatal flaw of Republicans’ 2026 strategy: Everything is a gag to them, and they’re way too online.

For the past decade, Republicans have adhered to Steve Bannon’s maxim that politics is downstream from culture. This fixation with liberals’ alleged capture of elite institutions has animated the right’s war against Big Tech and in particular social media platforms — which the right claims actively silenced conservative voices — and its crusade against diversity, equity, and inclusion. With his purchase of X, Elon Musk finally succeeded in building a conservative platform where right-wing voices not only had real influence but also a direct line to those in power. More recently, some people have claimed that Musk’s X is the only social media that really represents the people, unlike platforms like Bluesky, which have more left-leaning user bases.

Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise. They ignored their base’s valid concerns about affordability and served them nonsensical memes instead. And they failed spectacularly in the realm where it actually mattered: politics. X, we can now declare once and for all, is not real life. Republicans not only lost historically red states like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina, but barely managed to win Florida. The Senate race in Mississippi, of all places, is still too close to call.

Vance, especially, is a creature of X, where his following list includes such illustrious accounts as Raw Egg Nationalist, Bronze Age Pervert, Howling Mutant, and Captive Dreamer. But White House aides, department employees, and Hill staffers are stewing in the same ecosystem. Writer John Ganz has termed this phenomenon “groyperfication,” after followers of influencer Nick Fuentes, who call themselves groypers. This is a useful shorthand, though Fuentes’ fans are mostly too NEET-pilled to land jobs on the Hill. American Moment, a boot camp for young conservative up-and-comers, reportedly screens out groypers. There’s a real need for such protective measures. Kingsley Wilson, the hard-right press secretary for the Department of War (or per its legal name, Defense), has posted antisemitic conspiracy theories about Leo Frank, a Jewish man who was lynched in Georgia 1915 for allegedly raping a teenage girl. (Historians largely believe Frank was innocent.) The Department of Homeland Security regularly posts fascist fancams and wink-wink references to white supremacist memes.

Republicans saw their 2024 victory as a mandate. Having clawed the White House and Congress back from Democrats, they assumed the public was on board with MAGA’s cultural project when in fact people were largely mad about the price of eggs. And with two years of dominance under their belt, they decided to go even harder on culture, not realizing — or maybe just not caring — that people are still mad about gas prices and groceries.

Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise.

In the run-up to the midterms, the Department of Education was posting about “Malfoid” — a gender-swapped version of Draco Malfoy from Harry Potter that far-right influencers claimed would save Western literature from the scourge of wokeness. The Department of Homeland Security was bragging about record lows in legal immigration, which outside white nationalist circles is typically not considered a negative thing. Pseudonymous shitposters like Howling Mutant were posting memes comparing themselves to noted child murderer Anakin Skywalker, the new avatar for the online right. Musk, a Republican megadonor, got in on the fun, as did Katie Miller, wife of ultranationalist White House adviser Stephen Miller, who dressed up as Anakin’s wife Padmé Amidala for Halloween. (Katie Miller’s last government role was advising Elon Musk’s failed Department of Government Efficiency; now she devotes her time to throwing lavish parties and hosting a podcast no one listens to.)

Most of the American public isn’t on X, but the conversations conservatives have there do bleed out into the mainstream — often with disastrous results. Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas railroad commissioner, lost his election by a huge margin after posting anti-Indian memes on X. (Asian American voters, including Indian Americans, moved to the left in Texas elections down the ballot.) Musk did his part to drive turnout, spending nearly half a billion dollars on Republican candidates and PACs. But even Musk’s money failed to make up for voters’ dissatisfaction with Republicans’ performance, perhaps because the ads he funded focused largely on culture war issues that were out of step with voters’ concerns about the cost of living.

And Miller, it turns out, didn’t even vote, telling CBS Newsshe feared doing so would put her safety at risk, since Virginia law makes voters’ home addresses public. (The Millers, like other members of the Trump administration, live on a military installation with tight security; it’s unlikely intruders would be able to get to their home.) Republican myopia may have contributed to their poor performance across the board, including with groups that were touted as their new base. One poll found that a majority of young men of all races — including young white men — voted for Democrats in the midterms.

In a long postmortem on X — reportedly posted without input or permission from White House officials — Vance said he asked “the smartest data guy” he knows for insight on the electorate ahead of the midterms. Vance claims several pollsters told him that voters’ main concerns were the war against Iran, the cost of living, and America’s relationship to Israel. So why didn’t Republicans listen?

The answer lies in the algorithmic nature of social media, X especially. If you interact with even one post about a relatively niche topic — say, genderbent Harry Potter fanfiction — the algorithm will feed you post after post after post about the same thing. Just like Trump spent the early years of his first term obsessing over Fox News, the single mainstream network that would reflect his biases back to him, MAGA is now all in on X. And if you’re the kind of person who spends a lot of time scrolling, you may even delude yourself into thinking the issue clogging up your feed is something people just can’t stop talking about.

Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space.

In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process.

“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”
